By KAREN PAXTON 

DEDHAM, Mass. — Bradlees, 
which hasn’t reported a profit all year, 
is holding fast to its vear-long efforts to 
use selected, everyday low pricing and 
increased promotions sales to snare a 
larger market share. 

Harold Frank, chairman, empha- 
sized that the chain’s latest competi- 


tive strategies have been adapted for 


the long haul. To that end, the Brad- 
lees operation is being overhauled to 
more efficiently handle its promotions, 
improve technology, stre, *then cus- 
tomer service and eventually push 
back into the black. 

Besides previously announced plans 
to install POS systems chainwide by 
mid-1987, Frank, along with George 
Granoff, executive vp of merchandis- 
ing, and Richard Silverman, senior vp 
of operations, outlined other pro- 
grams: 

@ Renovated backroom plan to assign 
a different system for handling differ- 
ent types of merchandise—basic, pro- 
motional or fashion. 

® Red help phones being installed at 
20) in-store sites for customers who 
need assistance. 

@ An exclusive men’s wear 


line— 


Harold Frank, left, George Granoff and Richard Silverman, discuss Bradlees’ low- 
price strategy, which is strong in the brand-driven H&BA department. 


Ardsley by Cluett—introduced for fall 
that provides the wider margins of a 
private label, plus a brand name.

French-Based Carrefour 
Tests U. S. Hypermarket 


SECAUCUS, N.J. — The hypermarkets are coming, 
the hypermar kets are coming. 

Carrefour, the French-based $6.3 billion international 
retailer that is the leading hypermarket operator in the 
world, plans to spend about $50 million to test single units 
in the metro New York and Philadelphia markets next 
year as a prelude to a full scale thrust into the United 
States. 

The stores will follow the hypermarket format that com- 
bines a supermarket and a discount store into a unit that 
can reach 150,000 sq. ft. or even larger. 

In Metropolitan New York, Carrefour plans a proto- 
type hypermarket as part of a 725,000-sq.-ft. shopping 
center in Brookhaven, L. I., about a mile from the 1.4 mil- 
lion-sq.-ft. Smith Haven Mall and a 100 ,000-sq.-ft. Price 
Club membership warehouse.

Liberty Bell Shopping Center planned for the site of the

Porno Crackdown 
To Spare Retailers 


WASHINGTON — Justice 
Department prosecutors will 
not be targeting discount 
stores and other retail outlets 
that sell magazines such as 
Playboy and Penthouse in a 
new federal crackdown on 
pornography, according to 
U.S. Attorney General Ed- 
win Meese III. 

In a press conference late 
last month, Meese unveiled a 
long-awaited plan to combat 
pornography and told report- 
ers that the Justice Depart- 
ment will be focusing on dis- 
tributors of material that 
contains, among other things, 
child pornography and rape 
scenes and that are “violent 
and degrading to women.” 
Specifically, federal agents 
will follow guidelines set down 
by the Supreme Court in its 
ruling on pornography, Meese 
said. 

Meese’s plan endorses more 
than 90% of the 93 recommen- 
dations that were contained in 
a 1,960-page report on por- 


INDIANAPOLIS — Dan- 
ners personnel can breathe a 
sigh of relief following the 
signing of a standby agree- 
ment with the company’s 10- 
bank lender group. 

The discounter had failed to 
meet the sales and profit lev- 
els of the revolving credit 
agreement and exceeded pre- 
scribed borrowing guidelines 
as of Aug. 30. Danners had vi- 
olated its loan agreement be- 
fore, but the lender group had 
waived the violations. 

The standby agreement, 
which expires Jan. 15, 1987, 
provides the chain with cash 
flow to repay banks and pay 
vendor and supplier bills dur- 
ing the Christmas season. 

Mark S. Danner, company 
president, announced that the 


nography prepared by an 11- 
member panel and released 
this past summer. 

Meese said his plan is not 
aimed at retail outlets that sell 
materials that are “offensive 
to some but nonetheless have 
been recognized by the courts 
as within the bounds of pro- 
tected speech.” But he did en- 
courage “hundreds of thou- 
sands of concerned citizens” to 
make their anti-obscenity 
views known to retailers 
across the country. Meese 
said that consumer boycotts 
have been a traditional form of 
expression for moral causes. 

Critics of Meese’s new plan, 
including the American Civil 
Liberties Union, said that al- 
though retail outlets that sell 
magazines such as Playboy 
and Penthouse will not be re- 
pressed by federal agents, 
publicity about the the plan is 
enough to frighten publishers 
and retailers out of the busi- 
ness of selling sexually orient- 
ed materials.

With Credit 


Agreement 


standby agreement will let 
Danners operate, “without 
the fear that the default under 
the revolving credit agree- 
ment will cause the calling of 
the loan,” as long as the chain 
can abide by the agreement. 

Danners began working 
with a financial consulting 
firm, Bear, Stearns & Co. 
Inc., last month to help it dur- 
ing this highly unstable peri- 
od. The firm is reviewing op- 
tions for financial 
restructuring.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, November 10, 1986 


NEW YORK—The take- 
over battle between Lucky 
Stores and New York inves- 
tor Asher Edelman is over. 

Edelman dropped his $37 
a share bid following 
Lucky’s most recent move to 
increase the amount of stock 
it was willing to buy back to 
40% from 22%. 

“We are pleased that 
Edelman dropped his pro- 
posal, which was previously 
rejected by Lucky Stores’ 
board, ” said John M. Lillie, 
chairman of Lucky Stores 
Inc. 

Lillie said that the board 
will evaluate plans for either 
selling its specialty units or 
spinning them off to share- 
holders. There is also a pos- 
sibility that if the units are 
sold, the company may raise 
its repurchase offer. 


Edelman Withdraws Bid to Acquire Lucky 
As Board Stands by Stock Buyback Plans 


Lucky’s most recent offer 
called for a layout of $818 
million against the $450 mil- 
lion originally proposed. 

That proposition was re- 
ported by sources who at- 
tended a meeting between 
Edelman and Lucky Stores. 
Edelman, whose last bid 
was $37 a share, equal to 
$1.88 billion, had said he was 
unimpressed 

“Nothing at the meeting 
convinced me,” he said, 
“that what they intend for 
shareholders is as good or 
better than the $37 1 of- 
fered. They’re offering con- 
siderably less than the $37 I 
am, which I believe is a ma- 
jor breach of their fiduciary 
duties to shareholders.” 

Edelman reportedly 
countered by suggesting 
that Lucky Stores initiate a 


leveraged buyout, with or 
without him as an equity 
participant. Sources quoted 
Edelman as saying he would 
be satisfied if Lucky liqui- 
dates or restructures to 
maximize shareholder value 
by minimizing taxes the 
company would owe on the 
proceeds from divestiture. 

The takeover specialist is 
reported to own more than 
3% of outstanding Lucky 
shares and would profit from 
an increase in its stock price. 

After rejecting Edel- 
man’s initial offer of $35 a 
share, Lucky said last 
month it will close 80 Gemco 
stores, and it sold 54 loca- 
tions to Target for $374 mil- 
lion. Edelman called the sale 
a bad move because it will 
not be a tax-free transac- 
tion.

chains The Federated Group 
and New York-based The Wiz 
are offering the Blue Chip 
chainwide. 

Wal-Mart and Toys “R” Us 
were mentioned as retailers 
that are planning to test mar- 
ket the personal computer.

ing, indicate data collected

(RAB).

ond largest percentage 
change, following government 
spending, with a 61% gain.

$514,000 during the first six 
months of 1985 but spent more

Off-Price Chains Dominate TV Apparel Ads 


NEW YORK — Off price 
chains dominate the list of the 
top 15 clothing store television 
advertisers for the first six 
months of the year, reports 
the Television Bureau of Ad- 
vertising. 

Spending on local television 
ads rose 9% for all clothing 


stores during the first half of 


1986 to $41.5 million, an in- 
crease from almost $35 million 
for the year-earlier half. 
Increases for the 12 off- 
price chains on the chart gen- 
erally outpaced that overall 
jump in spending. K mart’s 
Designer Depot chain went 
from an all-but-invisible $200 
to more than $500,000 in local 


television ads in the first half 


of this year. Marshalls, which 
leads the group with $41.5 mil- 
lion in local spots, increased its 
spending by 19%. 

Kuppenheimer Clothiers, 
which was this year reposi- 
tioned and renamed from 
Kuppenheimer Factory Out- 
lets, doubled its spending on 
television advertising be- 
tween January and June to 
more than $2 million. 

S&K Famous Brands, 
which like Kuppenheimer 
sells only men’s clothing, in- 
creased its television ad out- 
lays by 113%. 

While those chains adver- 
tised in multiple markets, 
some of the top spenders spent 
all their money in one or two 
regions. C&R Clothiers, No. 
2, advertised in Los Angeles

Stuarts Takes Fashion Show on Road, 
Opening First Store in Connecticut 


HOPKINTON, Mass. — 
Continuing its expansion 
plans, Stuarts Department 
Stores has opened a 52,000- 
sq.-ft. store in New Britain, 
Conn. 

This is the first Connecticut 
store for the New England 
discounter, which operates 20 
other units. It chose this city 
because its low-to middle-in- 
come population meshes well 
with the company’s target 
customer. 

To promote the discounter’s 
soft lines departments, which 
comprise more than 50% of the 
overall merchandise mix, Stu- 
arts kicked-off the store open- 
ing with a fashion show featur- 
ing merchandise on sale. 

“The fashion show is a suc- 
cessful new concept in pro- 
moting discount clothing,”’ 


said Anthony Cincotta, vp of 
merchandising. “You expect 
to see professionally-executed 
fashion shows at ‘upscale’ 
stores like G. Fox or Bloom- 
ingdale’s, but not at a discount 
department store. 

“We first tried the fashion 
show concept in September at 
the grand opening of our 
Worcester (Mass.) store, and 
it contributed to making 
Worcester the most successful 
opening in Stuarts history.” 

Besides the fashion show, 
free balloons, refreshments, 
merchandise gift certificates, 
and tickets to a Sesame Street 
stage show at the Hartford 
Civie Center highlighted the 
New Britain opening. 

In 1987, the company plans 
to open 10 more stores in New 
England. 


Business Leaders Paint Gloomy Economic Picture 


NEW YORK — Business 
leaders are losing their confi- 
dence in the U.S. economy, 
noted a recent survey re- 
leased by The Conference 
Board. 

Less than a third of the 
1,000 executives in 24 major 
industries anticipate an im- 
provement in the U.S. econo- 
my during the next six 
months. 

“Business leaders are: ap- 


parently less sanguine than 
they were earlier this year 
about the economic impact of 
new federal tax policies, this 
country’s trade balance and 
even the still relatively low 
rates of inflation,” said Steven 
Malin, an economist with The 
Conference Board. 

The report notes that 
strong competitive pressures 
will limit price hikes during 
the rest of 1986 and 1987. :

Vew Colors, Gadgets Will Sweeten Housewares Sales in 1987 


By HAROLD RUBIN 
President, 

HalMar Distributors 
In 1987, houseware sales 
ill be whipped up with new 
lors and products, sweeten-

iste for discounters during 
le past couple of years. 
New bath colors and gadget

manufacturers are replacing

hangers, as well as in kitchen

racks and soap dishes.

and hot pink will turn around a 
department that had relied on 
almond, brown and white.

partment stores.

recarded packaging. The new

(Continued on page 33) 


By Lloyd Barnblatt 
Vice President 
Bacar Ine. 

While 1987 won't be a re- 
cord setting year, I think we'll 
see 5% growth, especially 
with new product introduc- 
tions in the increasingly com- 

etitive cookware and 
akeware categories. 

Consumers, unsure of how 
the tax laws will deplete or 
boost their discretionary dol- 
lars, are going to be thinking 
twice before picking up a new 
housewares item, especially 
higher ticket merchandise 

In bakeware, Baker’s Se- 
cret by Ekco continues to be 
the dominant line we carry, 
but it’s possible Corning’s 
Clear Advantage, non-stick 
glass cookware could hurt Ek- 
co’s sales, even though Cor- 
ning costs about 25% more. 

The new Great Cooks line 
by Mirro/Foley, featuring a 
non-stick surface both inside 
and out is competing against 
the Wear-Ever Preferred line 
which has a SilverStone inte- 
rior and a heavier guage met- 
al. 

While the Wear-Ever line is 
more expensive, it has been on 
the market longer and is prob- 
ably more recognizable to con- 
sumers. It’s too early to say 
where this vendor struggle is 
going to end up. 

The T-Fal line remains 
steady, but I belive Silver- 
Stone is making some inroads 
into the company’s volume. 

In bath and closet, tubular 
hangers are still up to speed. 
We have added some new pas- 
tel colors such as lavender, 
rose and grey to supplement 
the earth tones. 

The Corning Visions line is 
generating phenomenal sales, 
in fact, maybe too good. 

At this point, the company 
is only shipping 70% of the or- 
ders aan with the factory 
by the beginning of October. 

Corning just didn’t antici- 
pate the kind of demand the 
Visions line is drawing. 

The Pastel Bouquet motif is 
selling well. The fact that it’s a 
new design is in itself a reason 
for the success of the pattern. 
The way the colors fit in with 
home decor is also a big factor. 

The manufacturer’s French 
White line is still having prob- 
lems, and I’m really not sure 
what’s happening here. As of 
Jan. 1, 1987, the company is 
cutting prices by 10%.

in clearware, such as Pyrex,

Anchor Hocking’s Freeze, 
Heat & Serve line represents 
our best resource as a micro- 
wave product line, but the 
Rubbermaid Microwave 
Turntable and Nordic’s Micro- 
wave Compact Turntable are 
the leaders as far as individual 
items are concerned.

category is still going through 
a weeding-out process. We'll 
just have to wait and see 
which lines consumers choose 
as dominant.

carrying a full line of kitchen 
tools from Bonny with coordi- 
nated, easily identified pack- 
aging. We’ll see what else the 
housewares show offers in this 
category.

tle off, because we now include 
oil lamps and lamp oil in the 
category.

business is. still strong, al- 
though this report doesn't re- 
flect their sales, because it’s 
such a low-priced category.

with glassware sets, working 
on new merchandising con- 
cepts to encourage volume 
and dollars.

impulse sales category for us, 
especially stackable, small 
rectangular and round bas- 
kets.

tor in plastics. The standard 
chocolate, almond and white 
are being supplemented with 
yastel colors that help to 
bricditen shelves and sales. 

tubbermaid’s new Rough- 
neck Totes are really taking

stackables.

Highland Superstores to Enter Three New Markets Next Year 


TAYLOR, Mich. — High- 
land Superstores has turned 
up the volume on its expansion 
and will enter three new mar- 
kets next year, Milwaukee, 
Minneapolis-St. Paul and the 
Greater Boston area. 

The 11 to 13 Highland Su- 
perstores projected for the 


three markets are among the 
16 to 20 units to be opened 
next year. The remaining 
stores will go into two current 
markets, one in Detroit and 
six to eight i in Chicago. 

This year, Highland en- 
tered two markets, Houston 
and Shreveport, La., and 


opened 13 stores to reach a to- 
tal of 53. 

To support this growth, the 
$520.5 million consumer elec- 
tronics/major appliance retail- 
er in the spring ’87 will move 
its headquarters from a com- 
plex of office buildings and a 
warehouse here totaling about 


Report: Home Video Products Sales Gain 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — 
Home video products, 
spurred by camcorders, con- 
tinued to post impressive 
sales gains through Septem- 
ber, reported the Electronic 
Industries Association (EIA). 

Among the highlights of the 
EIA report were: 
e Videocassette recorders 
(VCRs) registered a 20 per- 


cent sales gain in September 
compared to same period last 
year; 

@ Camcorders again were a 
growth item as sales jumped 
97 percent in September over 
last year. During the first nine 
months of 1986, camcorders 
posted a 254% increase over 
the same period last year; 

@ Color TVs posted a 6.5% 


sales gain in September. The 
EIA predicted that the flag- 
ship product is headed for its 
best year ever with sales for 
1986 totaling 17.9 million 
units; 

@ Black and white TVs expe- 
rienced a 20% increase in Sep- 
tember. The EIA attributes 
the sales increase to palm-size 
and other portable models.

creased 8.9% to $4.9 million 
from $4.5 million.

small gain in earnings to high 


advertising and promotional

the Chicago market and en-

the first quarter.

in that area.” The poor outlook

weak sales in the company’s

and opened one in Shreveport. 
It doesn’t plan any new stores

up the Southwest Division.

growth in its Southwest Divi-

Designer Depot Failure Shows 
Off-Price Shakeout Continues 


By KAREN PAXTON 

TROY, Mich. 
— K mart’s plans 
to close its 79-unit 
Designer Depot 
off-price apparel chain signals 
that the s Hiekeout among off- 
price apparel chains contin- 
ues. 


Industry sources said they 
had expected the announce- 
ment and also predicted that a 
few chains that lack the deep 
pockets of a large parent com- 
pany to eventually fall by the 
wayside. 

K mart’s recently an- 
nounced streamlining also in- 


cluded the sale of its profitable 
food operations, Furr’s Cafe- 
terias and Bishop Buffets, to 
Calvalcade Holdings for 
$237.5 million. K mart said it 
will use the proceeds to re- 
deem some high-cost, long- 
term debt. 
(Continued on page 4) 


K mart's four-year-old Beskner Depot off-price apparel division will be phased out by the end of 
next January. The 79-unit chain is the latest in a long list of failed off-price ventures.

pected. The color coding was

Net Cost Club Joins Warehouse Fray 


MONTGOMERYVILLE 
Pa. — Net Cost Club (NCC) 
has become the newest com- 
pany to enter the burgeoning 
membership warehouse field 
by opening here a store with 
89,000 sq. ft. of selling space. 

It’s the first of four units 
planned for the Greater Phila- 
delphia-Wilmington, Del., 
market, now the fifth largest 
in the nation. NCC’s entry 
into the area could turn what 
had been an untapped market 
into a battleground for mem- 


bership warehouse chains. 
NC C has developed mer- 
chandising, operating and 
marketing features different 
from other membership ware- 
houses. These include captur- 
ing UPC codes to reduce oper- 
ating costs, stocking an 
extensive selection of truck 
tires, holding tri-annual auc- 
tions of goods that sell poorly 
and providing a number of free 
community services.

vately held company, in the

Ames Adopts Poison Pill 
Anti-Takeover Defense 


ROCKY HILL, Conn. — 
Ames Department Stores is 
offering shareholders the 
right to purchase preferred 
stock as a defense against “co- 
ercive or unfair takeover tac- 
tics.” 

Ames will offer investors 
the right to buy one share of 
newly issued preferred stock 
at $100 a share for each one 
hundred shares held as of Oct. 
31. The rights, which expire 
Oct. 31, 1996, will be usable 
only if a person or group ac- 
quires ownership of 20% or 
more of the common shares or 
announces a tender or ex- 
change offer aimed at acquir- 
ing 30% of Ames common. 

isted on the New York 
Stock Exchange, Ames has 
traded between $19 and $34 
over the past year and was 


selling at $24 at press time. 
Herbert Gilman, chairman 
and ceo of Ames, said “the 
lan is intended to protect the 
interests of shareholders in 
the event the company is con- 
fronted with coercive or unfair 
takover tactics.” Gilman told 
shareholders that similar 
plans have been adopted by 
more than 300 companies. 

Ames operates 315 discount 
department stores and 1438 va- 
riety stores in 20 east coast 
and midwest states. 

By year’s end, Ames will 
have opened 17 new stores and 
expects to add 25 to 30 more in 
1987. 

The company reported sales 
of $1.1 billion for the 35-week 
period ended September 27, a 
gain of 36% from sales of $840 
million for the 1985 period.

Discounters Take Smaller Markups 


As Markdowns Rise, NMRI Reports 


NEW YORK — The na- 
tion’s discounters took smaller 
markups and bigger mark- 
downs, while their turnover 
rates slumped overall during 
the last fiscal year, according 
to a study by the National 
Mass Retailing Institute. 

The turnover rate was off in 
all but one of the 26 categories 
included in the group's annual 
Mass Retailers Merchandis- 
ing Report, conducted for the 
NMRI by Cornell University. 

The survey covered 27 self- 
service discount chains, oper- 


ating 3,162 stores with aggre- 
gate sales of $27.1 billion. 

The apparel categories, 
which had shown strong turn- 
over rates in the past fiscal 
year, showed slower turns in 
all areas. Girls’ wear was off 
by 0.66 to 4.42 turns; boys’ 
wear down by 0.47 to 3.76 
turns, and infants’ wear 
slowed by one full turn to 4.24, 
against 5.32 the previous fis- 
cal year. 

In women’s clothing catego- 
ries from dresses through 
sportswear, leisure and 


beachwear, turns slowed per- 
ceptibly, with only the linge- 
rie, robes and sleepwear cate- 
gory (off 0.07) coming close to 
the pace of the preceding fiscal 
year. 

Fabrics, notions and yarns 
turns fell almost by half, drop- 
ping to 2.41 turns from 4.7 the 
preceding year. Other signifi- 
cant declines were reported in 
candy, where two full turns 
were lost and in sporting 
goods, and lawn and garden, 
where turns slumped by one.

FTC Orders Max Factor to Halt Discrimination in Its Pricing 


WASHINGTON — Ignor- 
ing pleas by iederal Trade 
Commission chief Daniel Oli- 
ver—a vocal critic of the fed- 
eral Robinson-Patman anti- 

rice discrimination law—the 
‘TC ordered Max Factor to 
stop offering. discriminatory 
romotional allowances to 
arge chain purchasers. 

In an unusual dissenting 
statement, Oliver accused his 
fellow commissioners of “ig- 
noring (their) obligation to act 
in the public interest” by in- 
sisting on an order that is cer- 
tain to have “anti-competitive 
consequences.” 

“This Commission’s record 
in enforcing the Robinson- 
Patman Act” has “worked 
staggering injury on consum- 
ers, to say nothing of small 
business such as Max Factor,” 
Oliver charged. 

By a vote of three to two, 
the commission late last 
month issued a consent order 
that forces Max Factor to 
make promotional allowances 
available on a proportionally 
equal basis to all retail chains 
that sell its cosmetics and 
beauty aids, as well as provide 
alternatives to retailers for 
whom its basic. promotional 
plans are unusable. ! 

Additionally, the Connecti- 


cut-based cosmetic compan 
has been ordered to inform all 
retail customers about its pro- 
motional programs. 

The Max Factor case began 
in 1979, when the FTC region- 
al office in Los Anyeles start- 
ed a Robinson-Patman Act in- 
vestigation of Max Factor’s 
promotional allowances based 
upon what the company 
claimed were “stolen internal 
company documents.” 

After three years of investi- 
gation, the Los Angeles office 
and the FTC Bureau of Com- 
petition recommended closing 
the case. But in 1984, the com- 
mission rejected the recom- 
mendation and issued a formal 
complaint that the firm “dis- 
criminated against” particular 
retailers by not making pro- 
motional sierations available 


_ on proportionally equal terms 


to all. of its retail customers, 
and “failed to offer alternative 
terms and conditions” to those 
customers unable to use basic 
promotional allowances. 

A consent agreement was 
publicly announced by the 
commission, subject to a 60- 
day comment period. During 
the comment period, Max 
Factor criticized the consent 
order -it signed, and argued 
that it should not be put into 


effect. Max Factor claimed 
that the underlying facts were 
ancient and pointed out that 
the company had gone 
through several changes in 
ownership and management 
since then. 

Additionally, Max Factor 
said it is “today only a small 
and struggling factor in the in- 
tensely competitive U.S. cos- 
metics industry,” and that the 
commission’s order would 


cripple its ability to compete. 

The commission’s final deci- 
sion in this case is an indication 
of where the commissioners 
stand on Robinson-Patman 
enforcement in view of the 
new chairman’s repeated call 
for repeal of R-P anti-price 
discriminatory laws. 

In his dissenting statement, 
Oliver questioned the commis- 
sion’s ruling in this case on the 
grounds that “the staff has un- 


covered no evidence that any 
allegedly disfavored buyer 
lost sales or was placed at a 
<r disadvantage as a 
result of any conduct engaged 
in by Max Factor. 

“By insisting on an order 
that is certain to have anti- . 
competitive conse- 
quences. . . , the commission 
majority turns and retreats 
away from rational antitrust 
enforcement,” Oliver said.

rent fiscal year, which ends 
Aug. 31, 1987, pushing its

All those additional stores 
will follow a new, soft lines- 
oriented format the chain 
started testing earlier this 
year.

attractive dis * of soft lines 
merchandise has produced en- 
couraging initial sales resuits, 
without changing the mer- 
chandise mix,” said Lewis E. 
Levine, president of the

ery week, store count had 
reached 1,140 earlier this 


month. “Our present plan is to 
open all new stores with this 
new format and, if the sales re- 
sults continue to be positive, 
we will consider converting all 
existing stores to the new for- 
mat beginning in January 
1987.” 

Same store sales in Family 
Dollar stores were. running 
virtually flat during the first 
two months (September and 
October) of fiscal 1987. This 
continues the pattern set dur- 
ing fiscal 1986.

ings. Net income increased 9% 
to $30.5 million. The year-end 
results also benefited from 


disegntinuing the company’s 
pension plan. The company re- 
ported a gain in income before

commencement of the next e .- 
pansion phase of the distribu-

crease its area 775,000 sq. ft. 
by the end of the current fiscal 
year. Expansions were fi- 
nanced with internal funds; 
the company owes no long- 
term or short-term debt.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, November 24, 1986 


Toy Chains Rely on Space Age Items to Power Holiday Sales 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Toy chains hope that the 
traditional holiday sales surge 
will offset what generally has 
been a soft year so far for the 
industry. 

Toys “R” Us, the sales lead- 
er, is one of the few chains to 
report strong figures going 
into the holiday season. 

Many others, entering the 
Christmas season with flat or 
weak results to date, are pin- 
ning their expectations for a 
strong finish on the popularity 
of this year’s space age win- 
ners, the Lazer Tag, Photon 
and Pfazer Force, along with 
old reliables, such as Barbie 
Doll in new dress. 


TRU Sales Increase 


Toys “R” Us, based in Ro- 
selle Park, N. J., showed sales 
for the third quarter of fiscal 
1987 at $471.4 million, up 
25.3% over the $376.1 million 
for the third quarter of the 
previous year. 

Over a nine month period, 
TRU reported $1.266 billion, 
20.3% more than the $1.0952 
billion in net sales in the com- 
parable nine months of last 
year. Same store sales were 
up 8.5% in the third quarter 
and rose 4.5% for the first nine 
months. 

Few other toy chain execu- 
tives could be as optimistic as 
TRU chairman and chief exec- 
utive officer Charles Lazarus. 
‘We are continuing to in- 
crease our market share from 
new store openings and from 
good comparable store in- 
creases,” Lazarus said. 

While final figures weren’t 
in at press time, Lionel Lei- 
sure vice president and sales 
director Joel Weiner said that 
“third quarter sales have gone 
just about as anticipated and 
we expect to experience small 
increases over last year.” 

Like TRU, which added 139 
stores in 1986, Philadelphia- 
based Lionel was on the march 
last year, opening 11 stores as 
well as modernizing and ex- 
panding several others. 

At Toy King in Orlando,

holding pattern, “waiting to 
see what the economy does 
and trying to get more volume 
out of existing operations,” 
Fetty said. 

At upscale Hobby Center in

surgence in video game sys- 
tems. The category could be 
coming back, now that we 
have a new generation of kids. 
The new Atari 2600 came out 
this year in a more compact 
size and is selling well. 

The Teddy Ruxpin talking 
doll is strong at Lionel and 
other chains, with several 
heavily promoting the toy. 

Child World, based in 
Avon, Mass., recently ran 
sharp price promotions offer- 
ing Teddy Ruxpin at $49.99, a 
$10 savings over the chain’s 
regular price. 

But Lazer Tag is the big 
one. Russ Gerald, ad manager 
for Karl’s Toys in Los Ange- 
les, said, “It sells out before 
our ad runs, and it’s such a hot 
item, we should be able to hold 
our price at $59.99.”

Hard to Beat Supermarkets 


Food will account for about 
30%-32% of the mix “because 
its more difficult to get net 
prices on food lower than su- 

ermarkets. These retailers 
tt in large quantities, so 
clubs work on a short markup 
on this merchandise.” 

The Montgomeryville NCC 
carries a larger nonfood mix 
that the industry’s average, 
he added, because of the bet- 
ter markup on such merchan- 
dise. The membership ware- 
house’s gross margin will fall 
in line with the industry’s 
range of 8% to 12%, but Hoff- 
man said it was too early to 
know the exact figure. 

Using the tire expertise of 
its founders, NCC has “put a 
heavy emphasis on tires, in- 
cluding service bays to do our 
own mounting. We also offer 


truck tires in all sizes, while 
most other clubs only carry 
small camper sizes,” he said. 

NCC also handles white 
goods from five vendors, Gen- 
eral Electric, Whirlpool, Em- 
erson, White Westinghouse 
and Kelvinator, with about 
75% obtained directly from 
the manufacturer, he said. 

In operations, NCC has re- 
duced its checkout labor cost 
by eliminating the caller-pack- 
er member of the two-person 
checkout team used by all oth- 
er membership warehouses. 
This person calls out the mer- 
chandise identification num- 
ber on goods while packing. 

At its checkouts, NCC uses 
wand scanners to pick up the 
manufacturer UPC codes on 
premarked goods, rather than 
company-assigned digits. This 
system allows one clerk to ring 
up purchases as well as pack. 

CC also prints UPC tick- 
ets for goods that aren’t pre- 
marked by the vendor, such as 
— 

he company’s purchase or- 
ders for palletized, trailer- 
load shipments include a spe- 
cial UPC number assigned by 
manufactures to facilitate re- 
ceiving at the store. NCC will 
issue a UPC code for use on 

urchase orders when ven- 
ors don’t, Hoffman said.

tv. services include a travel

ment from an in-store mini 
film lab, free refreshments 
from a milk shake bar and a 
popcorn machine, monthly 
visits by an optometrist to 
tighten eyeglass frames and 
free blood pressure tests.

year, to clear out stock that

CARMICHAEL, Calif. — 
Shoppers in this Sacramento 
suburb now can research and 
buy merchandise from mail or- 
der catalogs in their local li- 
brary while they check refer- 
ences in Standard & Poor’s or 
the Encyclopedia Britannica. 

Warren Harris thought of 
the new wrinkle in merchan- 
dising in 1981 when he asked a 
Sacramento librarian where 
the catalogs were and was told 
they weren’t to be had. 

By September 1985, he cre- 
ated what he calls, “The Ki- 
osk: Mail Order Catalog Cen- 
ter,” and persuaded the Fair 
Oaks-Orangeville library to 


Sacramento Library Provides Mail Order Catalog Shopping 


install his kiosk. 

Harris’ concept is simple. 
He leases a freestanding unit 
to the library for about $5,000 
a year and charges catalog 
houses $18 a year to be includ- 
ed. He refunds the library $1 
for each order placed at the Ki- 
osk. He had been taking a per- 
centage on orders but gave 
that up because it required 
more bookkeeping than it was 
worth. Harris also offers li- 
braries the opportunity to 
purchase a kiosk for $9,000. 

At this point, there’s only 
one installation, but Harris 
expects to place a catalog cen- 
ter in a library in Schaum- 


WASHINGTON — Dis- 
count retailers will be faced 
with bigger contributions to 
employee benefits programs 
because of a flurry of 1986 
state legislation, just one of a 
number of changes, good and 
bad, for retailers. 

A Discount Store News re- 
view of bills enacted by state 
lawmakers this year shows 
that four states passed laws 
requiring employers to allow 
former employees and their 
dependents to remain tempo- 
rarily in group health care pro- 
grams. The state laws are sim- 
ilar to a provision of the 1985 
Federal Consolidated Omni- 
bus Reconciliation Act (CO- 
BRA) mandating continued 
health benefits for some for- 
mer employees and their fam- 
ilies. Although ex-employees 
will be paying the premiums, 
industry sources complain 
that administrative costs will 
be burdensome. 

Under Tennessee law, em- 
ployers must allow depen- 
dents due to be terminated

American soldiers and their 
families there, demanding 
U. S. merchandise,” he said.

Cabbage Patch Kids Ruling 
May Threaten Gray Market 


WASHINGTON — The In- 
ternational Trade Commis- 
sion took another swipe at the 
so-called “gray market,” issu- 
ing a controversial “exclusion 
order” restricting unautho- 
rized “parallel imports” of Co- 
leco’s once-hot selling Cab- 
bage Patch Kids dolls. 

That ruling marks the Com- 
mission’s first decision on the 
legality of gray market mer- 
chandise since President Rea- 
gan overturned a similar ITC 
exclusion order seeking to ban 
parallel imports of Duracell al- 


kaline batteries last year. 

In issuing its new Cabbage 
Patch ruling, the agency up- 
held charges by Coleco and the 
dolls’ trademark holder, Orig- 
inal Appalachian Artworks, 
that unauthorized parallel im- 
ports of these toys constitute 
an unfair practice in violation 
of the U.S. Tariff Act. 

The complaint that led to 
the order surfaced a year ago 
as Coleco and OAA sought to 
curb an influx of gray market 
Cabbage Patch Kids when

Discounters Hire Check Approval 
Services to Cut Bad Check Losses 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Despite predictions to the 
contrary by the banking in- 
dustry, national statistics in- 
dicate Americans are writing 
more personal checks than 
ever. 

As consumer preference for 
paying by check increases, the 
obvious problem for retailers, 
including discount stores, is 
how to guarantee that a check 
won’t bounce. Another factor 
is the speed with which a 
check can be approved at the 
check-out. For many dis- 
counters the solution has been 
to subscribe to a check approv- 
al service. 

K mart uses the country’s 
second-largest check approval 
service, Tampa, Fla.-based 
Telecredit, in about 25% of its 
2,071 units. P. C. Way, 
K mart’s director of loss pre- 
vention, said the chain is re- 
searching the possibility of ex- 
panding the service te more 
stores. Decisions will be made 
. on a regional basis, he said. 

The major considerations 
are check-out speed, losses 
from bad checks, cost of the 
service and the abiiity to ac- 


cept a larger number of 
checks, Way said. K mart 


stores lacking the service do | 


accept checks—but only from 
their local market area. “The 
check approval service allows 
a store to accept a check from 
anywhere in the country,” 
Way said. 

Telecredit’s services cost 
K mart, based in Troy, Mich., 
less than credit cards—but 
cost is still a factor, Way con- 
tinued. Roughly one-third of 
K mart’s sales are a. for 
with checks, he added. 

Vince Staranski, controller 
at Stereo Discounters, a 28- 
unit Baltimore-based elec- 
tronics specialty chain, also 
uses a check approval service. 
“T’m not going to turn a sale 
away because the customer 
wants to give me a check,” he 
said. “But if we had to cover 
every bad check ourselves, 


. the losses would be too great.” 


Checks accounted for about 
40% of Stereo Discounters’ 
$60 ‘million in sales last year, 
Staranski said. The company 
subscribes to JBS Asso- 
ciates, a Ringwood, N. J.- 
based check approval firm. 


The cost of these services 
varies with the subscriber’s 
check volume, average 
amount of purchase and loss 
record, check approval ‘ser- 
vice executives said. 

For Stereo Discounters, the 
cost of JBS services is 1.6% of 
the sales, slightly higher than 
its cost on bank-issued credit 
cards but much lower than the 
cost on. American Express 
charges, Staranski said. 
“Some of our competitors 
won’t accept checks at all,” 
said Bob Sussman, chief finan- 
cial officer for the 22-unit 
Brick Church Appliances 
chain based in Orange, N. J. 
“We consider our ability to ac- 
cept checks with ease a defi- 
nite competitive advantage.” 

Brick Church subscribes to 
Denver-based Telecheck, the 
nation’s largest check approv- 
al service with more than 50% 
of market share. Telecheck 
services cost Brick Church 
slightly less than bank-issued 
credit cards. “We have a low 
rate based on our loss record. 


We take. bad checks very per- 


sonally,” Sussman said.

This article, which was researched 
and written by Arthur Young, a Big 
Eight accounting firm based in New 
York, analyzes and compares finan- 
cial data from K mart, Wal-Mart 
and Zayre. 


NEW YORK — With more than an 
80% penetration of the general mer- 
chandise market and nearly 4,000 
general merchandise and specialty 
retail stores, K-mart appears to have 
reached a turning point in its discount 
store career. Fully-matured and suc- 
cessful in the discount and general 
merchandise market, where is 
K mart going and how successful will 
it or can it expect to be? 

To answer these questions, this 
analysis will compare K mart with 
two of its competitors, Wal-Mart and 
Zayre, as well as examine K mart’s 
financial results for its fiscal year 
ended January 1986, against fiscal 
1985. 


K mart has invested $40 
million in a data and video 
satellite communications 
network connecting 2,100 
stores. The chain realizes it 
must tighten up and 
modernize operations with 
high-tech systems and better 
inventory control. 


Wal-Mart and Zayre were chosen 
as comparisons because they and 
K mart have a high penetration in the 
discount store market segment, 
while each retailer’s position in the 
corporate life cycle is slightly differ- 
ent. While K mart can be considered 
mature, Wal-Mart continues its ex- 
pansion role, and Zayre remains the 
relative newcomer in terms of signifi- 
cant sales growth and profits. 

Where is K mart going? Current 
history may help in answering this

THE K MART STORY 


With Reservations, Analysts Look Favorably on Stock 


NEW YORK — While Wall Street 
wizards may be less than wildly infat- 
uated with K mart, generally they 
see hopeful signs ahead. Securities 
analysts who follow the company 
most often rate K mart either a “neu- 
tral” or “buy” stock. 

Stock analysts hold two different 
views about the chain. Some cite the 
company as a metaphor for the dis- 
count industry at large, while others 
point to particular aspects of K mart, 
such as its push toward specialty re- 
tailing, that set it apart from the 
pack. 

Since the Troy, Mich.-based behe- 
moth dominates the discounting in- 
dustry by sheer numbers of stores, 
analysts who like discounting are 
likely to recommend K mart. Those 
who see the industry in trouble are 
quick to pull the plug on K mart. 

“We’re positive on K mart when 
we’re positive on the general mer- 
chandise category,” said Daniel Bar- 
ry, vice president of retailing at Kid- 
der Peabody & Co. Inc. He currently 
rates the stock “neutral.” 

“The [near-term] key to K mart re- 
volves around whether the consumer 
is all bought out,” added Jack Tracht- 
man, senior security analyst at Grun- 
tal & Co. Because Trachtman be- 
lieves the consumer “is not giving up 
on retailing even though he’s spent a 


lot of money lately on cars,” he rates. 


the stock a “buy,” particularly for in- 
vestors looking for long-term appre- 
ciation. 

As for discounting as a category, 
Joseph Ronning, analyst at Brown 
Bros. Harriman & Co. added: “For 
years we’ve clearly been seeing a seg- 
mentation between the low-end, me- 
dium, and upscale discounters. That 
this is happening at all indicates the 
field has considerable strength.”

$33,406,200 budget. 


Steady Pace 


In comparison, Sears, the 
top spender among retailers, 
held a steady pace, increasing 
its television advertising bud- 

et by 21% to $87,540,100 
rom 1981 to 1982, adding 33% 
more in 1983 and an addition- 
al 20% in 1984. 

While it’s still too early to 
draw conclusions about 1986, 
by September Sears had spent 
$31,451,300; by the third 
quarter of 1985 Sears had 
spent $87,309,300 television 
ad dollars. 

From 1981 to 1982, J. C. 
Penney cut spending by 1%, 
but numbers since have 
climbed as the retailer shifted 
its emphasis to network, in- 
stead of spot television. 

In 1983, the Penney’s bud- 
get was expanded by 25%, 
with most of those dollars de- 
voted to network, not local ad- 
vertising. 

The , spent in 1984 
were essentially unchanged, 
$44,364,300 in 1983 versus 
$44,440,500 the next year. 
Spot advertising was cut to 
$10,411,000 from $12,506,600, 
while network expenditures 
were increased to $34,029,500 
from $31,857,700.

Chairmen of Major Chains Average 
$420,100 in Base Pay, Survey Finds 


(Continued from page 7) 
There were, however, a few exceptions. 

Average salaries for senior administra- 
tive executives in companies with annual 
sales of $150 million to $400 million were 
$188,200, as of August 1986, while in compa- 
nies with sales of $400 million to $750 million 
they were $148,800. Salaries for the same 

ost in the smallest sales category averaged 

100,000, and in chains with annual sales of 
more than $750 million, the base was 
$191,000. 

Senior financial executives in chains with 
annual sales below $150 million also earned 
more than those in chains with annual sales 
volumes of between $250 million and $400 
million. Salaries for the former averaged 
$94,200, and for the latter, $85,700. These 

executives averaged $123,500 annually in 
companies with sales of $400 million to $750 
million and $132,400 in the largest-volume 
companies. 

In merchandising, salaries followed the 
same progression of higher pay in higher 
volume chains—in this case, with one excep- 


tion—but the range from lowest pay to top 
was far less. 

The one exception was division/category 
merchandise managers in the $400 million to 
$750 million sales category, whose salaries 


averaged $77,200, compared to $74,200 in' 


the top-volume chains. In the smallest vol- 
ume chains, these managers averaged 
$50,800 and $51,700 in chains with sales of 
$150 million to $400 million. 

Salaries for general/senior merchandise 
managers ranged from $52,000 in the small- 
est companies to $116,500 in the largest 
sales category. Multiple buyers in chains 
with sales under $150 million made an aver- 
age of $31,800 annually, compared with 
$48,900 for hard lines buyers in chains with 
sales over $750 million. 

The NMRI based its report on a survey of 
74 firms operating 13,923 discount stores 
throughout the United States. Salaries 
were rounded off to the nearest $100. In 
some cases, firms indicated that decreases 
in salaries were the result of hiring new per- 
sonnel to replace long-term employees.

21-unit men’s wear discounter 
based in Secaucus, N. J., con- 
sidered handling its own 
checks but instead opted fora 
check approval service for a 
number of reasons, said Bob 
Lieberman, N B O’s assistant 
corporate controller. 

“The service is both cost ef- 
fective and serves as a buffer 
between us and the customer. 
We’d rather have the service 
take the blame for rejecting 
them and for whatever collec- 
tion methods are used,” Lie- 
berman said. 

Speed of approval, along 
with guarantees against loss, 
was cited by most retailers as 
a major consideration in their 
decision to subscribe to a ser- 
vice. Check validation usually 
takes only a few seconds. 

30th Telecheck and J BS 
offer three systems for linking 
up with their computers: 
touch-tone telephones; bank- 
card terminals, which can also 
be hooked into check services, 
and electronic cash registers. 

Telecheck requires either a 
driver’s license or one of five 
major credit cards to approve 
a check. 

J BS has a similar policy 
and also has arranged with 
some of its clients to accept re- 
gional credit ecards. Both 
check approval firms said 
their average turndown rate 
is low, 1% to 2%. 

The use of checks, mean- 
while, is growing by about 5% 
a year in the United States, 
despite efforts by the banking 
industry to curtail the growth. 

Americans wrote more than 
40 billion checks last year, and 
Telecheck, alone, approved 
more than 60 million of them. 
While 51% of the population 
have credit cards, 86% have 
checking accounts. 

“Discounters are beginning 
to consider check approval 
services because of the in- 
creased customer demand for 
retailers to accept checks,” 
said Thomas A. Hellegers, 
Telecheck’s district manager 
for New York and northern 
New Jersey.

Best Repositions Core Biz 
In Bid to Cure Stagnation 


RICHMOND — Best Products plans to make some 
“fundamental changes” in its core catalog business this 
year as the latest step in an intensive, ongoing effort to re- 
vive the stagnant company. 

The three-tiered plan will see the $2.2 billion company: 
@ Cutting back its merchandising to just jewelry and core 
hard lines categories to become a discount specialty retail- 
er that matches customers’ perception of the chain; 

@ Realigning its advertising to place greater emphasis on 
media that can be targeted to specific audiences like news- 
papers, TV and seasonal mini-catalogs to offset the re- 
duced impact of the annual catalog and monthly flyers; 
@ Enhancing customer services by providing more 
trained salesclerks on the selling floor, along with more 
rapidly delivering clipboard ordered goods to shoppers 
to speed up the checkout process. 

Best now describes itself as a discount retailer, rather 
than a catalog showroom, and the development and execu- 
tion of the strategic plan is the key final step in Best’s ex- 

ensive and extensive restructuring to live up to that mar- 
eting stance. 

The repositioning during the past three years has al- 
ready seen Best remodel and upgrade about 50 showrooms 
to sharpen its focus on jewelry and other high margin cate- 
gories, relocate scattered offices and regional operations 
into a recently expanded headquarters, sell the ailing 
Ashby’s apparel specialty store chain (see separate 
story) and close 17 unprofitable Best stores.

Best Divests Ashby’s 


NEW YORK — Fifth Avenue Cards, a multi-divisional 
specialty retailing company, has reached an agreement 
with Best Products Co., of Richmond, Va., to buy its ailing 
32-unit women’s discount apparel chain, Ashby’s Ltd. 

Best announced earlier this year that it planned to di- 
vest Ashby’s as part of a plan to regain the parent compa- 
ny’s profitability. Ashby’s had sales of about $33 million in 
1985, with a pre-tax loss of $3.5 million. 

Last February, Fifth Avenue purchased the Kellwood 
Co.’s 100-unit discount apparel chain, Ashley’s Outlet 
Stores, based in St. Louis, Mo. The combined acquisitions 
“will make Fifth Avenue a major discount suhadlse in the 
Southeast with total revenues aproaching $100 million,” 
chairman and president Hal J. Upbin said. Ashley’s sales 
for 1985 were about $40 million. 

No changes in the Ashby’s management are planned, 
Upbin said. Fifth Avenue refused to comment at press- 
time on the possibility of combining the two chains.

WASHINGTON, 
The international “gray mar- 
ket,” an increasingly impor- 
tant alternative supply source 
for the nation’s discount 
chains and other off-price re- 
tailers, could be shut down al- 
together within months as a 
result of a multi-front assault 
on “parallel importers” in 
Washington. 

The most immediate threat 
to the continued availability of 
genuine, but “unauthorized” 
merchandise, imported on the 
so-called gray market is a rul- 
ing by a Federal appeals court 
in Washington that invalidat- 
ed long-standing Customs 
Service rules permitting par- 
allel importation. 

In that case, which now 
faces a go-for-broke show- 
down at the U.S. Supreme 
Court, attorneys for K mart 
and other major sellers of gray 
market goods are locked in a 
battle to preserve the indus- 
try’s off-shore supply lines. 

On the opposite side oi the 
issue is Coalition to Preserve 
the Integrity of American 
Trademarks (COPIAT), an 
organization of multinational 
manufacturers seeking to 
avid price competition on 
their own products from inde- 
pendent parallel importers. 

At the center of the dispute: 
a controversial Customs Ser- 
vice regulation that for years

With the market for low-end video

will scour the coming consumer elec- 
tronics show for a hot new product 
that will be as strong a performer as 
the VCR.

and Venture, are heading for the 
show on an upbeat note following a 
healthy Christmas season for con- 
sumer electronics. For the most part, 
the consumer electronics department 
registered double digit sales gains— 
outpacing most other areas in the 
store. Privately, buyers said that the 
sales gains may have come, however, 
at “ty expense of gross margins since 
prices had to be slashed to keep up 
with encroaching competition from 
electronic superstores and wholesale 
clubs. Nevertheless, retailers en- 
tered 1987 with clean inventories. 

Although few buyers and senior 
chain officials expect any surprises at 
the show, which kicks off Jan. 8 in Las 
Vegas, most plan to examine particu- 
lar categories. Upgraded video cas- 
sette recorders and televisions, com- 
pact disc players, dual cassette tape 
players and anything with color or 
new styling head the list. Several 
buyers expect big things from a few 
categories staging comebacks, such 
as personal computers and video 


games. And a few hope to catch a 
glimpse of the new digital audio tape 
players—even if that high-tech 
equipment might take a few years to 
reach discount stores. 

“We'll be looking at stepped-up 
VCRs for the consumer who bought 
at the low-end and is ready to give 
that one over to the kids and buy a 
more sophisticated one for himself,” 
said Jamesway’s buyer John Zurlo, 
based in Secaucus, N.J. “We're not 
afraid to go higher with price points.” 


Potential for High End Sales 


Jamesway recently featured a 
four-head, 14-day, four-event JVC 
VCR for $359.99, a price too high for 
some discounters. Yet, Zurlo sees po- 
tential for the discount store custom- 
er who is more familiar with VCRs. 

Zurlo remains unsure, however, 
whether the next step is stereo. “We 
still haven’t decided on that one, but 
we are testing one stereo TV in 15 
stores. People may be more likely to 
want stereo quality in the TV.” 

Video Marketing calculates that 36 
million households own a VCR, and 
by 1990, penetration will reach 
67.3%, or 63.3 million homes. To keep 
growth strong, retailers will have to 
court customers who are ready to buy 
a second unit. Some retailers said this 
signals a boom in video cassette play- 
ers (VCPs).

Blank Videotape Competition Boils; Brand Mix Drops 


By JOSEPHINE FIAMINGO 
Nationwide DSN Report 

The competition in the $1 billion 
blank videotape market is getting 
hotter. The key question is which 
manufacturers’ promotional ap- 
proach will retailers support, espe- 
cially since the number of brands car- 
ried by most discounters has dropped 
to about four. 

Said Joe Schirtzinger, videotape 
buyer for Worthington, Ohio-based 
Gold Circle, “When we started stock- 
ing videotape we wanted to maximize 


the business with a large selection of 


brands, but it is not realistic to go for- 
ward with as many brands. 
“From our research we found there 


is a real correlation between the au- 
dio tape and videotape customer who 
wants to buy both products of the 
same brand,” noted Schirtzinger. 
“This is why we are dropping brands 
that do not offer an audio tape pro- 
gram along with their videotape of- 
ferings.” 

Gold Circle now carries standard 
videotape brands—3M, TDK, JVC, 
Memorex, Polaroid and Kodak—and 
high-grade in TDK and 3M—in all 
stores. The chain said it will be drop- 
ping Polaroid and Kodak. 

Most sales for blank videotape are 
still in the standard grade, the basic 
commodity item used as a traffic 
builder and highly promoted as such 


by retailers. Sales i the high-grade 
videotape were stronger in the begin- 
ning of 1986, said Schirtzinger, but 
are flattening out now due to rebates 
depressing prices of standard video- 
tapes, along with a decrease in the 
units of upgraded hardware, with 
more low-end VCRs being sold and 
more entering the marketplace. 
The low-priced, non-licensed 
goods have had a large impact on the 
videotape business. “You now see the 
no-name videotapes popping up all 
over the place, with 30 to 40 different 
manufacturers offering them at $1.99 
and $2.99. This hurts the 
branded goods,” he said. 
“We started in the fourth quarter 


sale of 


selling Intermagnetics ATO stan- 
dard T-120 VHS videotape promot- 
ing it at $2.99 with a $1 rebate be- 
cause we needed the price point,” he 
said. “We can’t stand by and not react 
to what is happening in the market- 
place. | expect there will be more re- 
bates from brand names.” 
Schirtzinger said that rebates 
show more value to the consumer 
than a multi-pack with a free tape of- 
fer. Sony offers one where you buy 
five standard size tapes at $4.99 and 
get one high grade free. It carries a 


possible retail to the consumer of 


$3.99 for all six tapes. 
“You still have to mail it in with

RTA FURNITURE 


Style, 
Quality 


Build Sales 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discount chains are cashing in on strong sales of ready-to- 
assemble furniture as consumers appear to be more receptive 
to the improved quality and style of RTA goods. 

Although entertainment centers, utility carts and home, 
office and storage furniture have been reported as the indus- 
try’s big sellers, many retailers and manufacturers believe 
consumers now are ready for RTA furniture in other rooms 
in the house, specifically the bedroom. This RTA fur niture, 
should look more like “conventional” furniture with style fea- 
tures like rounded lines, moldings, wood grains and decora- 
tive handles, they said. 

Discount stores account for the largest share of all RTA 
furniture sales, reported Furniture Today, a weekly trade 
journal, estimating that discounters garnered 33% of the to- 
tal $500 million worth of domestic and imported RTA furni- 
ture shipped in the U.S. in 1986. 

To meet the growing demand and capitalize on the profit- 
ability of the category, some retailers are allotting more floor 
space to RTA furniture. 

In October, Clover, the 21-store Pennsylvania-based chain, 
expanded its RTA area, providing more space with a gondola 
run and carpeted 30-in. high platform for display with stock 
stored underneath

From KD to RTA 


Ready-to-assemble furni- 
ture has come a long way from 
its former knock-down (KD) 
fringe category of just 10 
years ago. Reflected even in 
the name itself, a dramatic 
change has taken place in the 
category, particularly in the 
last several years. 

KD, which carried a nega- 
tive connotation, was per- 
ceived by shoppers as cheap, 
boxy storage units. In con- 
trast, RTA reflects consumer 
trends toward better quality 
and a good value in furniture 
that can be easily assembled at 
home. Much of RTA furniture 
has been upgraded to the point 
of competing with some “real” 
preassembled furniture. And 
this is only beginning. 

“T think just changing the 
name from KD to RTA helps 
the industry,” said Clausing. 

Several manufacturers 
cited the European market as 
an example of what is to come 
here. One vendor put it simply 
when he said, “European 
RTA looks like ‘furniture.’ 
They've had hidden fasteners 
for 10 years.” 

In the U.S., RTA furniture 
makes up somewhere be- 
tween 4% and 6% of the furni- 
ture business. In Europe, 
however, RTA comprises a 
steady 30% to 36% of the furni- 
ture marketplace. And manu- 
facturers here hope to catch 
up by making RTA products 
that look good and are reason- 
ably priced. 

Frank Aquila, of Affordable 
Furniture, Dowagiac, Mich.., 
said, “The business has dou- 
bled in the past five years” and 
predicted, “It will double 
again in the next five years.” 
His company has prepared for 
this growth by expanding fa- 
cilities, investing almost $20 
million in two years. 

Foremost Furniture, a divi- 
sion of Sauder Woodworking, 
Archbold, Ohio, has tripled its 
warehouse space in the past 
few years to accommodate the 
growing demand, in addition 
to upgrading its overall opera- 
tions. “We’re meeting the cus- 
tomer’s needs with a value 
product that’s easy to assem- 
ble with good instructions and 
a warranty,” said president 
Maynard Sauder. 

Paul A. Gusdorf, chairman 
of the board at Gusdorf Corp.,

K mart to Add Bank Services in 150 More Stores 


TROY, Mich. — In a major expan- 
sion of its financial services operation, 
K mart plans to add leased banking 
centers in 150 stores this year, giving 
the discounter more than 450 units 
that offer banking service.

WASHINGTON — The fate of the President’s record 
trillion-dollar budget proposal for fiscal year 1988 now 
rests in the hands of the 100th Congress, and it will be up 
to Congress to decide whether discounters and other re- 
tailers will be subject to new government user fees and ad- 
ditional Social Security payroll tax contributions. 

Although the Administration’s request for $1.024 tril- 
lion contains no new taxes for fiscal ‘88, it does he ose 
several “revenue changes” estimated to increase Fe 
receipts by $6.1 billion in 1988. 

Included in these revenue changes is a proposal to re- 
quire discounters with in-house food-service operations 
and other employers to pay the employer portion of the So- 
cial Security Payroll Tax on the total amount of employees 
tip income. Under current law, employers are not re- 
quired to pay a portion of Social Security tax for employ- 
ees’ tip income as it is considered a benefit. This proposal 
would raise an estimated $200 million during fiscal ’88. 

Another revenue raiser contained in the Administra- 
tion’s budget are user fees for certain government ser- 
vices ranging from U.S. Customs inspections to Federal 
meat and poultry inspections.

NEW YORK — Wal-Mart executive vice president of 
merchandising and sales, Al Johnson, will be the opening 
speaker at the National Mass Retailing Institute’s 
(NMRI) 15th Annual Advertising Conference. Johnson,

ence is slated for March 11 through 13 at the Sheraton Ho-

Bar Coding Seminars Scheduled 


PITTSBURGH — The Automatic Identification Manu- 
facturers Inc. (AIM) will help present technically ad- 
vanced programs on bar coding as part of the American 
Management Association’s educational seminars. The bar 
coding seminars will be held in New York, April 23 to 24; 
Chicago, May 18 to 19, and Atlanta, June 8 to 9. To attend 
a seminar, contact AIM, 1326 Freeport Road, Pittsburgh, 
PA 15238. Phone: (412) 963-8588. 


American Wholesale Opens Unit 


RICHARDSON, Tex. — American Wholesale Club will 
open a 105,000-sq.-ft. membership warehouse near the 
own East Mall in the Mesquite suburb of Dallas/Fort 
Worth this spring as its second store. The company pro- 
jects that the first year’s sales for the new club will reach 
$40 million, the same rate at which volume at its Plano, 
Tex., unit is running.

MINNEAPOLIS — Cable Value Network (CVN), the

mas holiday period. CVN president Peter Barton said the 
holiday sales “met and exceeded the expectations,” of the 
seven-month-old teleshopper whose programming 
reaches over 10 million onneliatan CVN, which is jointly 
owned by closeouter C.O.M.B. and a consortium of 23 ca- 
ble TV systems, expects to hit $600 million in sales this 


year. 


Last of Mr. HOW Units Sold 


NASHVILLE — Service Merchandise, the catalog 
showroom chain based here, has disposed of the remainder 
of its home center stores by selling two Mr. HOW Ware- 
houses in Cinncinnati and two in Nashville to Central 
Hardware, a hardware and building material chain based 
in Bridgeton, Mo., for an undisclosed sum. 

Service, which just one year ago operated 27 Mr. HOW 
Warehouses, previcusly sold five of the home center out- 
lets in Chicago to Handy Andy Home Improvement Cen- 
ters, a Gurnee, Ill., chain, and 12 other Mr. HOWs in sev- 
eral markets to Builders Square, K mart’s warehouse 
home center subsidiary. Raymond Zimmerman, Service’s 
chairman and president, said that former Mr. HOW units 
in Chattanooga, Tenn., Oklahoma City, Okla., two in 
—— la., and two in Cinncinnati all have been 
closed. 


Acquisition of Zale Completed 


TORONTO — Peoples Jewelers Ltd. and Swarovski In- 
ternational Holdings A.G. announced they have complet- 
ed their acquisition of Zale Corp. through a limited part- 
nership indirectly owned by them. P.S. Associates, the 
partnership, completed its cash tender offer for all out- 
standing shares of Zale’s common stock at a price of $50 
per share. The companies reported that about 10.4 million 
shares had been tendered by the Dec. 24 deadline. 

Irving Gerstein, president of Peoples, was elected pres- 
ident and ceo of Zale. All the other Zale directors, except 
Gerstein and two other Peoples representatives on the 
board, resigned. A new board will be organized consisting 
of an equal number of Peoples and Swarovski appointees.

Shoppers Pick Top Promo Items 


Discount Store News first annual Traffic Builders study 
was conducted by the Chicago-based research and marketing 
firm Leo J. Shapiro and Associates. It entailed polling 2,082 
shoppers in seven markets, who were to shop in nearly 4,178 
stores during a 10-day period last October. 

This special report examines: 

@ Top traffic building product categories and brands and the 
extent to which different types of retailers depend on promo- 
tional items to draw traffic; 

@ The efficiency of promotions of different retailers and dif- 
ferent product categories at attracting new customers; 

® How successful different product categories are at gener- 
ating a purchase and encouraging additional spending; 

@ Shoppers’ responsiveness to promotions. 

In addition, DSN breaks out data on traffic building in the 
three sections—Apparel, Home Products and Hard Lines. 

This report was written by John Caulfield, a retail industry 
reporter who is currently senior «ditor/merchandising for 
DSN’s sister publication, Nationai dome Center News.

Nationwide DSN Report 

Discounters are relying far more heavily 
on promotions to draw customers into their 
stores than do mass merchants, depart- 
ment stores or specialty outlets. 

And it appears as if shoppers are more 
aware of promotions when they are run by 
discount stores than when other types of 
dealers put their merchandise on sale, 
finds an exclusive study that Discount 
Store News commissioned.. 

While discount stores can lure in custom- 
ers with lower-ticket items such as house- 
hold goods, automotive supplies, candy 
and toys, they are less able than their retail 
counterparts, however, to attract consum- 
ers’ attention when it comes to promoting 


Household cleaners and paper products, 
personal care items and edibles like food 
and candy were the biggest traffic building 
categories for discount department stores, 
according to DSN’s new survey of traffic 
building products and promotions. Other 
leading product categories for drawing 
shoppers into discount stores were toys, 
home storage, home care and women’s 
shoes and sleepwear. 


Discounters Utilize Promos More 
Kor Draw Than Other Retailers 


other merchandise, particularly women’s 
and children’s clothing. 

In addition, there is a wide disparity 
among retailers in general and various dis- 
counters in particular as to the level of 
awareness consumers have about their re- 
spective promotions. This is an important 
distinction, because apparently a strong 
correlation exists between knowledge 
about promotions and shopping frequency 
among consumers. 

Consequently, discounters have the op- 
portunity to capitalize on their promotional 
acumen to use a wider selection of higher- 
end items to increase the average sales per 
shopper propelled by advertised specials.

These and other findings emerged 
from the first annual study on traffic 
building products and promotions 
commissioned by DSN from the Chi- 
cago research firm, Leo J. Shapiro & 
Associates. Nearly 2,100 consumers 
were interviewed over a 10-day peri- 
od last October regarding their 
awareness of different stores’ promo- 
tions. 

The purpose of the survey, as de- 
fined by George Rosenbaum, vice 
president, Leo J. Shapiro & Asso- 
ciates, was to “get consumers to enu- 
merate the stores they visited and 
find out if they knew of a special be- 
fore coming.” The polling also exam- 
ined how much consumers spent, how 
many visits they made to a store ina 
given period and whether they 
bought what they came for. 

Its conclusions focus on how pro- 
ductive these promotional items 
were at generating dollars for differ- 
ent types of retailers. 


Housewares, Consumables Noted

that sescnansonMb te and household

Consumer responses 
demonstrate that 
consumables and household 
products were the biggest 
traffic builder categories for 
discounters. 


Nearly 13% of all the mentions of 
promoted products by consumers 
who were going into a discount store 
fell into categories of consumables 
such as candies or beverages like 
beer. 

In addition, about 10% said they 
knew that household products were 
being promoted by the discount unit, 
followed by hair care products (7.5%) 
and home care products such as light 
bulbs and leaf bags (4%). 

Looked at another way, of the 51 
top product categories consumers 
knew were on sale at all retail outlets, 
the highest percentage of mentions 
for 37 of those categories were by dis- 
count shoppers. For example, there 
were a total of 43 mentions by shop- 
pers who knew toys and games were 
on sale in the store they were about to 
enter; 38 of those mentions were from 
consumers going into a discount unit. 


But Clothes Bought Elsewhere 


This is not to say, though, that dis- 
counters’ promotions dominated ev- 
ery product group in which consum- 
ers were aware of a promotion. 

Of the 229 shopper awareness men-

buck, J. C. Penney and Montgomery 
Ward, the highest number, 30, were 
for sheets, comforters and bed- 
spreads, compared to a 2% mention 
level of these products at discount 
stores.

mentioned promoted category was 
women’s blouses and shirts (which 
ranked 37th among the 51 items men- 
tioned as being on sale at a discount 
store), while at other retail outlets, 
such as catalog showrooms and spe- 
cialty outlets, women’s sweaters 
arose as the item that shoppers were 
the most aware of being promoted.

The mean sales ticket generated by 
consumers coming into a discount 
store to buy a product on sale is lower 
than the mean ticket for mass mer- 
chants, department stores, catalog 
showrooms or specialty units. 

When taking into account the retail 
price of the products that discounters 
and other retailers promote, it ap- 
pears—based on mean ticket fig- 
ures—that consumers who know of 
sales are more likely to buy other 
products in a discount store than they 
are when shopping at other types of 
retail outlets. 


The more expensive the 
promoted item, the more 
likely it is to draw shoppers 
interested only in promoted 
goods and disinclined to 
buy anything else. 


Data discovered during DSN’s 
Traffic Builders study shows that 
consumers are shopping discount 
stores more regularly for lower- 
priced promoted items. But whereas 
other dealers may be getting the big- 
ger single purchase, their promotion- 
al items apparently fail to prompt 
add-on sales to the degree that dis- 
count stores’ promotions do. 


Promos Heavily Bought 


About 70% of those consumers who 
know a product was being sold on 
promotion actually bought the ‘tem, 
and the mean ticket of their total pur- 
chase was $35. 

The study divides the 51 most-fre- 
quently mentioned products consum- 


jewelry (58.3%, $332); 


ers knew were being promoted in or- 
der of their relative cost, and 
examines how often these products 
were purchased (see table 9). 

For example, household cleaners, 
which customers most frequently 
mentioned as a promoted product, 
were purchased by these shoppers 
73% of the time, but generated a 
mean ticket of only $13. But relative- 
ly inexpensive motor oil was bought 
by 75% of the customers who knew it 
was on sale, and generated a mean 
ticket of $37, which shows how well 
this category is able to produce add- 
on purchases. 


Price Affects Add-on Sales 


Among mid- and higher-priced 
product categories, a trend develops 
wherein customers buy only the item 
that they saw on promotion. Eighty 
percent of customers aware of pro- 
motions on toddlers’ wear actually 
bought the product but spent only 
$19: nine out of 10 purchased small 
kitchen appliances they knew were 
promoted, but paid a mean ticket of 
only $47; more than 75% bought 
stuffed animals whose promotions 
they knew of, but the mean ticket of 
those customers was $33. 

This trend becomes most evident 
when examining more stylish items 
like furniture (bought by &5.7% of 
those knowing it was on sale but gen- 
erating a mean ticket of $285); fine 
and micro- 
wave ovens (71.4%, $173). The 
study’s findings demonstrate that 
the more expensive the item being 
promoted, the more likely it is to 
(raw shoppers interested only in the 
rome goods and disinclined to 
buy anything else.

within the perspective of each store’s 
merchandising and marketing

mass merchandiser said they had 
been in these stores less than twice 
over the past month; nearly seven out 
of 10 consumers who knew of a de- 
partment store’s promotions were in- 
frequent shoppers; and nine out of 10 
shoppers who said they were aware 
of a sale at a catalog showroom had 
been there less than twice ina month. 

Wards (61.3%), Sears (58.9%) and 
Penney (58.1%) offer promotions 
that appear to be successful at at- 
tracting first-time and infrequent 
shoppers (see table 7, page 22). 

The study broke down shopping 
frequency by product category and 
found that domestics, cosmetics, ap- 
parel, furniture and jewelry are pro- 
motions that attract new or infre- 
quent traffic, while small ticket 
merchandise may be better at gener- 
ating more trips from existing cus- 
tomers (see table 8). 

Sut the study found rare excep- 
tions to this rule. For instance, three 
in five customers aware of a store’s 
promotion on low-priced home-care 
‘eget such as tool boxes and light 


yulbs, were infrequent shoppers of 


that store. By and large, however, 
the higher-end items seem to lure the 
customer making a special visit. 

On the surface, this finding would 
appear to present competitive prob- 
lems for discounters, whose lead pro- 
motional items, such as aise abt 
goods, hair care products and candy, 
are low-priced goods and are drawing 


mostly frequent shoppers to their 
stores. And when discounters pro- 
mote higher-priced goods like wom- 
en’s shoes, only around 9% of those 
consumers aware of the promotion 
were infrequent shoppers. 


Discounters are sacrificing 
promotions on big ticket 
goods in favor of promoting 
items that draw their 
regular shoppers—who 
usually buy more than what 
they came for. 


As other sections of the study 
show, however, it is likely that a cus- 
tomer coming into a discount store to 
purchase a cheaper product on sale 
will add to that purchase with other 
items, whereas if, say, a woman 
makes a special trip to a department 
store to buy ashirt onad, it’s less like- 
ly that she'll buy anything else. 

Consequently, it appears that dis- 
counters, in their marketing strate- 
gy, are sacrificing promotions on big 
ticket goods that bring in the infre- 
quent shopper in favor of promoting 
those items that draw their regular 
shoppers—who usually buy more 
than what they came for.

Low Sale Priority on Clothes 


That apparel, as a category, ranks 
lower in promotional importance for 
discounters than other items is clear 
(see table 13). For example, the num- 
ber of consumers who knew a dis- 
count store had women’s shoes on 
sale ranked ninth among all product 
category mentions for discounters, 
whereas women’s shoes was the 
fourth highest mentioned promotion- 
al category for department stores, 
and the second highest for “other” re- 
tailers (including specialty outlets). 

Similar examples abound. Con- 
sumer awareness of promotions for 
men’s coats ranked 28th for all stores, 
55th for discounters, but seventh for 
mass merchants; recognition of pro- 
motions on women’s skirts was 34th 
overall, 65th for discount stores, but 
In a tie for fifth for department 
stores; women’s blouses fall into 37th 
place for discounters, but first place 
for department stores. 


However, when total mentions in a 
given category are grafted onto data 
about where consumers knew Ben 


tions were occurring, asomewhat dif- 
ferent picture emerges (see table 14, 
page 38).Take women’s skirts: more 
than 75% of the consumers who knew 
of a skirt sale noted that the promo- 
tions were being run by a mass mer- 
chant. But ina product line that’s not 
too niaheereot significant for dis- 
counters, nearly 25% of the consum- 
ers said they knew of a skirt promo- 
tion at a discount store. 

Whether this is a misperception on 
the consumer’s part is hard to tell, 
but more than half of the shoppers 
aware of a women’s skirt promotion 
at all stores wound up buying the 
product there. 

Similarly, infant’s clothing ranked 
14th overall, 23rd for discounters, 
but fifth and second, respectively, for 


mass merchants and department 
stores for consumer promotional 
mentions. Nevertheless, discounters 
got nearly two out of every five men- 
tions in the product category in which 
about eight out of every 10 consum- 
ers who is aware of a promotion 
winds up buying the advertised prod- 
uct. 

Where discounters and other deal- 
ers part company, though, is in the 
kinds of consumers apparel promo- 
tions bring into their stores. 


New Shopper Preferences 


Most of the 16 apparel categories in 
the study were identified as being on 
sale more often by consumers who 
were not frequent shoppers of the 
store they were visiting. But in every 
case where consumers knew of a pro- 
motion at a discount store, these 
same shoppers said they had been to 


that discount outlet at least twice in 
the past month. 

One prime example of this would 
be women’s jogging suits, a product 
used regularly for promotions by all 
retail stores. More than 75% of the 
shoppers who knew of a discounter 
promoting this product said they 
were frequent customers of that 
store; only two in five who knew of a 
jogging suit sale at either a mass mer- 
chant or department store were reg- 
ular shoppers of these stores. Wom- 
en's sweaters, infant’s clothing and 
lingerie are other categories which 
follow the same pattern.

tiously in deciding which apparel! 
items to promote because it does not 
appear these items are all that

NEW YORK — Kurt Salmon <4 
sociates projects a 3% growth i 
sales of soft lines, including inane 
and domestics, for retailers in 1987. 

The company’s report asserts that 
retail prices will remain almost static 
with tighter inventory controls and 
improved execution boosting produc- 
tivity. 

On a unit basis, KSA sees only a 
2.5% increase in apparel for the year. 
Consumers aren’t expected to go on 
any spending sprees. Other factors 
such as lower inventory levels at 
manufacturers and retailers, as well 
as defined fashion directions, should 
a business strong, the report 
saic 

In men’s wear, unit sales are ex- 
pected to increase 2% this year with 


loosely fitting sportscoats, casual 
shirts, active sportswear and sweat- 
ers as the growth areas. 

The projection of 3% more unit 
movement in women’s wear also de- 
pends on a continued strength in ac- 
tivewear and sweaters plus a swing 
to more feminine suits and skirts. 

In both girls’ and boys’ wear cate- 
gories, activewear is again expected 
to chalk up the largest gains. Overall, 

a 2% unit increase was predicted in 
ihe wear and a 1% gain in girls’ 
wear. 

Accessories should pick up 3% in 
unit consumption this year, KSA 
stated in the report, with snakes 
skin, crocodile, big cat prints and tor- 
toise shell buckles as the hot fashion 
features. 


Athletic footwear, up by 15% 
through the first half of 1986, is ex- 
pected to rise again by another 20% in 
1987. 

A group of 68 a yparel makers who 
were polled by K SA expect to shi yan 
average 5% more units in 1987. They 
also predicted an average 4% rise in 
wholesale prices, a 3% drop in inven- 
tory levelsand an 11% rise in profits.

Purchases 


Nationwide DSN Report 
Discounters are strong promoters 
of household items such as cleaners 
and laundry and paper products. But 
these stores don’t seem to actively 
promote other “home” related goods 
such as linens or window coverings to 
the same extent as do mass mer- 
chants. 

In addition, it appears as if these 
household items are being shopped 
primarily by regular discount store 
customers—and are generating add- 
on sales— while other home-related 
products, when promoted, may bring 
new shoppers into mass merchants’ 
units but are not stimulating addi- 
tional purchases. 

In other words, the higher the tick- 
et on these home products, the more 
likely it is that they are attracting 
new customers who are shopping 
only for that product. 


Cleaners Lead List 


DSN’s Traffic Builders study found 
that household cleaners were the No. 
1 product mentioned as being on sale 
by consumers of all stores and dis- 
count store shoppers. Paper prod- 
ucts, the sixth-mentioned item over- 


all, ranked third by those aware of 


sales at discount units (see tabie 15). 
Even cookware, which doesn’t ap- 
pear to be promoted that frequently 


by any retailer, had nearly nine out of 


10 consumers who knew of a sale say 
it Was going on in a discount store. 

Sheets and comforters, on the oth- 
er hand, were known to be on promo- 
tion by more consumers of mass mer- 
chants’ stores than any other 
category mentioned, with window 
coverings and bath towels taking up 
the third and fourth places among 
those items mass merchant shoppers 
said they knew were on sale before 
entering the store. 

Perhaps the most surprising find- 
Ing shows television sets—which 
ranked 65th in mentions by discount 
shoppers and 47th overall—was the 
17th most frequently mentioned item 
being promoted by mass merchants 

But the home products group is not 
one that either department stores or 
other retailers such as specialty and 
catalog showroom units promote on a
