EDISON, N.J. — Crazy Eddie 
has formed a new office of the presi- 
dent consisting of Mitchell Antar, ex- 
ecutive vice president, marketing; 
Sam E. Antar, executive vp and chief 
financial officer, and Dr. Isaac 
Kairey, executive vp, operations. 
Eddie Antar, who has relinquished 
the title of president, will continue as 
chairman of the board and chief exec- 
utive officer. Crazy Eddie has also 
added to its Board of Directors: Solo- 
mon E. Antar, Esq., senior vp, secre- 
tary and general counsel; David V. 
Panoff, senior vp, consumer service 
operations and telemarketing; Ed- 
mond Levy, vp, real estate and de- 
velopment; Steve Pasquariello, vp, 
store operations, along with Sam E. 
Antar and Dr. Kairey. 


In another development, the board 
has adopted a stock repurchase pro- 
gram to reduce the number of out- 
standing common shares. Under the 
program, the company will, from 
time to time, make open market pur- 
chases of up to 3 million shares of its 
common stock. 


NEW YORK — Will rebates be a 
thing of the past? Two major house- 
wares manufacturers have an- 
nounced plans either to eliminate or 
reduce rebates. Black & Decker 
U.S. Household Products Group will 
eliminate consumer rebates on all 
househoid products on March 31. 
1987 and on all personal care products 
on June 30, 1987. 


Moreover, Sunbeam announced it 
will reduce the amount of rebates by 
60% in 1987. 


Dennis Heiner, president of 


B & D’s U.S. Household Products 
Group, said that rebates no longer 
make sense in this industry because 
they cut into inherently low profit 
margins for the retailer and the man- 
ufacturer.

Discounters are actively promoting brand 
names in the home products category, while 
branded ite:as are hardly mentioned by 
mass merchants, department stores and 
other retailers in their promotions of these 
goods, according to DSN’s Traffic Builders 
survey. 

The DSN Traffic Builders study ask :d 
consumers to name the branded items Uney 
knew were on sale before they entere a par- 
ticular store. The top 48 brands mentioned 
accounted for 45% of the total brands named 
by consumers. 

In this home products grouping (which for 
this article’s purpose includes household 
cleaners), Comet was the most frequently 
mentioned brand known in advance to be on 
sale by all shoppers in general and custom- 


ers of discount stores in particular. 

Top brands in this grouping to receive 
high brand recognition included Lux (the 
dishwashing detergent that ranked seventh 
in overall mentions); Vanish (which ranked 
12th overall and 9th among discount store 
shoppers); and Real Lemon (the furniture 
polish brand that also placed 9th among 
mentions by discount shoppers).

overall, 9th among discount store shoppers), 
Penthouse Paper Goods, Tide, Sani-flush

counters), Mr. Coffee (28th and 24th), Scot

and 28th among discount store shoppers).

hard lines were not mentioned as 
items shoppers knew were being pro- 
moted by nondiscount operations.

2 | MARKETWATCH 


LANHAM, Md. — While the num- 
ber of auto parts stores in the U.S. 
rose more slowly over the last three 
years than during the previous three- 
year period, the growth rate among 
discount stores handling automotive 
products climbed to 10%, the highest 
of 14 categories of retail outlets sur- 
veyed by the Automotive Parts & 
Accessories Association’s research 
arm. According to preliminary data 
released by the Foundation for After- 
market Industry Research (FAIR), 
automotive products were added by 
700 discount stores between 1983 and 
1986. Auto parts outlets recorded a 
7.6% growth rate to nearly 41,000 
stores in 1986. The rate of growth for 
auto parts stores from 1980 to 1983 
was 33%. The preliminary data 
seems to indicate that more mass 
marketers are adding automotive 


parts to their inventory. The number 
of grocery outlets selling automotive 
products rose by 6,300, or 7.4%, in 
three years. In addition, automotives 
were added by 600 drug stores and 
800 hardware stores since 1983. Spe- 
cialty repair shops—those specializ- 
ing in tune-ups, oil changes and the 
like—gained 900 new outlets, while 
new car dealerships dropped 900. 
The study also counted 16,100 fewer 
service stations in 1986 than in 1983, 
for ari 11% decline.

knowledgeable customers

Automotives, Toys Brands 
Lead Hard Lines Promos 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Automotives, toys, some stationery items and small ap- 
pliances are some of the branded “hard lines” that dis- 
counters are promoting to increase customer traffic. 

But in selected products in this grouping, discounters 
are being challenged by mass merchants and other retail- 
ers that are promoting as heavily and are getting consum- 
ers’ attention. 

DSN’s Traffic Builders study—in which the top 48 
brands named by consumers as promotional products ac- 
counted for 45% of all brands mentioned—found that Pres- 
tone antifreeze, Fisher Price toys and Bic pens ranked 
2nd, 3rd, and 4th, respectively, among the brands known 
by shoppers to be on sale at all stores and at discount units. 

Oddly enough, though, while AC Delco auto products 
ranked 6th overall and 5th in mentions by discount shop- 
pers, Quaker State motor oil—presumably sold in the 
same area of a store—ranked only 24th as a promotional 
brand on sale in discount stores. Quaker State was the 7th 
most mentioned brand overall, and ranked 2nd in men- 
tions by shoppers of mass merchants. 

Discounters were doing most of the promoting on the 
products falling into the “hard lines” group, although 
there were some noteworthy exceptions. For example, 
Bic pens were the most-mentioned brand being promoted 
by “other” dealers that included specialty stores, catalog 
showrooms and drug combo units. Quaker State oil ranked 
9th as a product on sale at these stores. 

General Electric light bulbs—ranking 12th overall and 
14th among discount shoppers—tied for 9th at “other” re- 
tail units. Kodak film, which ranked 2&th overall and at 
discount units, received the 13th highest number of men- 
tions by shoppers of mass merchants. 

And the Arvir brand of smalj electric appliances was the 
3rd highest-mentioned brand known to be on sale by mass 
merchants, even though the brand placed 34th overall as a 


product name recognized to be on promotion.

To Suppliers in Price Fixing Cases

Although that ruling upheld 
the “per se” (automatic) ille- 
gality of “Fair Trade-style” 
RPM activities, it also made it 
virtually impossible for vic- 
tims of these practices to 
prove the existence of RPM 
conspiracies in court. 

Rodino’s bill (H.R. 585) 
would reverse the Monsanto 
standard by shifting the bur- 
den of proof in RPM cases to 
the manufacturer.

ing retailer in response to 
complaints from full-price 
dealers was not sufficient to 
establish the existence of an il-

Founder’s Absence Raises Concerns 


NEW YORK — Crazy Ed- 
die’s commercials screaming 
of “insane” prices have always 
attracted a lot of attention. 

But the goings-on at the re- 
tailer’s Edison, N.J., head- 
quarters are creating far more 
fuss these days, even though 
management is trying to keep 
things extremely quiet. 

The big mystery is— 
where’s Eddie Antar? 

The founder and guiding ge- 
nius of the company has not 
surfaced for nearly two 


DSN 25th ANNIVERSARY 


months. The report earlier 
this month (DSN, Jan. 19, 
page 43) that he had resigned 
as chief executive with his du- 
ties being assumed by a troi- 
ka—his brother, cousin and 
one non-family member—sim- 
ply raised more questions 
about the future of the firm. 

What is known is that Eddie 
Antar will remain as chairman 
and a director. 

What is also known is that 
Crazy Eddie’s business did 
not live up to expectations in 


the Christmas period. While 
sales for the four weeks ended 
Dec. 28 were $62 million dol- 
lars, up 50.3%, comparable 
store sales were down 9%. 

It is generally believed that 
the 39-year-old founder is 
ill.“I was told that he was ill 
and had not been at the office 
since early December, proba- 
bly even before then,” said an- 
alyst Edwin L. Underwood of 
Seott & Stringfellow in Rich- 
mond, Va.

stock analysts to begin to beat the drums for the 
developing discount industry. Emphasis was 
less on earnings and dividends, and more on 
new store commitments and broader, one-stop 
shopping offerings, as emerging chains began 
to put their flags up in key markets.

By MARY ELLEN KELLY 

CHICAGO The National 
Housewares Manufacturers Associa- 
tion (NHMA) has taken the first 
steps toward what could be a reversal 
of last year’s decision to switch to a 
single-show schedule. The associa- 
tion is currently exploring the possi- 
bility of returning to a two shows-a- 
year format. 

If approved by association mem- 
bers, the biannual schedule could 
threaten the existence of privately 
sponsored shows created in response 
to the original single show decision. 

The William T. Glasgow Inc.-s oe 
sored Summer Housewares Sho 
scheduled to make its debut July 20 to 
22. in Chicago, has been cancelled. 
This gives the NHMA the option of 
using those dates to establish a sec- 
ond show as of 1988. 

The decision to reinstate a biannual 
show calendar will be contingent 
upon the results of an NHMA mem- 
bers poll regarding their schedule 
preference, said Sue Palmore, direc- 
tor of communications. 

Results of the poll, which will be 
eonducted by mail this month, should 
be completed by the time the indus- 
try convenes at the NHMA show in 
April, Palmore said. 

The NHMA has sought since last 
November to nail down dates in Chi- 
cago to prevent The Interface 
Group’s HouseWorld Expo, which is 
sponsoring a competing show in Las 

egas, from getting a foothold in 
what has historically been the 
NHMA city. 


Brian Casey, show director for the 
the NHMA, had sent a letter to Mc- 
Cormick Place in November 1986 re- 
questing first right of refusal in the 

event Glasgow failed to go through 
with plans, an NHMA source said. 


July Show Dates Held for NHMA 


William Glasgow Sr., show manag- 
er, said his organization has reached 
an agreement with the NHMA ensur- 
ing that the July show dates will be 
available for the association in 1988 
should the NHMA decide to reinstate 
a second show. Citing manufacturer 
participation that was below expec- 
tation, Glasgow also said that exhibi- 
tor fees will be refunded to those ven- 
dors who had committed themselves 
to the show. 

If a second NHMA show were re- 
established, big name vendors and 
retailers might not attend the other 
shows, said housewares retailers and 
manufacturers, who claim that com- 
peting trade shows will fragment the 
industry. 

Eight months ago, the NHMA had 
switched to a single-show schedule 
based on a unanimous vote of its 
board members. 

Since that time, several manufac- 
turers including Richard Stern, pres- 
ident of Associated Mills, have tried 
to persuade the NHMA to continue to 
offer its members a second show al- 
ternative. 

Stern, who commissioned a Chica- 
go-based research firm to conduct a 
telephone survey regarding the

Executives Debate Domestics’ Place in Off-Price Apparel 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Do the domestics departments 
that many off-price apparel chains ei- 
ther lease or operate themselves 
really fit into stores that specialize in 
clothing bargains? 

Some off-price chains and leased 
department operators say the heavy 
traffic that the off-price apparel 
stores generate creates many oppor- 
tunities to hook the female customer. 
But others claim domestics belong in 
apparel stores about as much as auto- 
mobiles belong in grocery stores. 

“Any type of store that attracts 


heavy traffic is a good climate for do- 
mestics,” said Donaid Abrams, presi- 
dent of Three D Departments, an 
East Hartford, Conn.-based compa- 


ny that operated leased domestics de-" 


partments in K mart’s Designer De- 
pot off-price apparel stores. 

K mart announced last November 
it would close the 79-unit chain, and 
Three D has filed a breach of contract 
suit in Federal Court against K mart, 
seeking damages “substantially in 
excess of $1 million” for revenue 
losses it says it will incur as a result of 
the closing. 


“Leased domestics departments 
have been good business for us and 
we would expand in that direction if 
more opportunities were available,” 
said Abrams, referring to recent off- 
price apparel chain fatalities. 

Three D also once operated leased 
domestics departments in the Los 
Angeles-based Zodys Discount De- 
partment Stores chain before that 
company folded last year. Three D 
had annual sales of $2.5 million in one 
5,000-sq.-ft. Zodys department, 
Abrams said. 

Three D now operates only six 


leased departments, all in the Cincin- 
nati-based Van Leunen’s discount. 
store chain. In addition, it operates 
27 freestanding off-price bed and 
bath stores in California, New Hamp- 
shire, New York, Connecticut and 
Massachusetts under its own name. 
The company also shares space in 
three California units with Nord- 
strom Rack, an off-price apparel divi- 
sion of Nordstrom department 
stores, in which each operates under 
its own logo. Three D had sales of $44 
million in 1986, Abrams said. 
(Continued on page 27)

Toys ‘R’ Us Trims Expenses, Passes Along Tax-Cut Savings 


ROCHELLE PARK, N.J. 
— Toys “R” Us (TRU), the na- 
tion’s largest toy store chain, 
is moving aggressively in 1987 
to open about 60 new stores, 
including its first attempts to 


crack into two new markets. 
At the same time, the 271- 
store giant is reducing operat- 
ing expenses to offset in- 
creases and cutting prices by 
passing along its expected 


savings from the new tax law. 

Like many other retailers, 
TRU will benefit from the re- 
cently passed tax law, but— 
unlike most others—TRU an- 
nounced it will pass along tax

The chain’s effective tax

strategy this year is to cut op-

spokeswoman said that TRU 
will install laser scanners dur-

effort to increase efficiency at 
store level. This technology is 
expected to speed customers 
through the register and Gou- 
ble the sales volume capabili- 
ties available at the stores. 
Yet TRU anticipates making

will test a new cosmetics bou- 
tique near its apparel and jew- 
elry departments in an effort 
to create a snyergy between 
these fashion-oriented cateyo- 
ries. 

The chain expects to test 
the new merchandising strat- 
egy in 50 stores during the 
first half of this year. 

“The idea is to develop the 
fashion potential of the health 


& beauty aids department by 
bringing apparel, jewelry, 
cosmetics, fragrances and nail 
care into one area of the 
store,” said Leo Camara, a 
former H & B A buyer who is 
developing the concept. Ca- 
mara’s new buying responsi- 
bilities include only cosmetics, 
fragrances and nail polishes.

atory and acne formulas, for-

linear feet on a black lacquer

TRIVIA QUIZ: 1965 


The mood in 1965 continued as heavily ex- 
pansionist. Some department store personnel 
began to come over to the discounters. Penn- 
sylvania discounter druggists k.o.'d pharmacy 
board opposition and discounter pharmacies. 
Lessees continued to shrink as chain central 
merchandising control grew more dominant.

events of 1965 with the questions that follow. As

on an expansion kick, ex- 
plored downtown locations in

c) Woolco.

Retailers Target Purchase Order Systems for Improvement 


NEW YORK — Mass mer- 
chandisers and discount store 
operators queried in a survey 
late last year reported that 
purchase order management 
is their hottest application 
area for future systems devel- 
opment. 

More than half of executives 
representing 32 discount, gen- 
eral merchandise, drug and 
variety store chains anticipat- 
ed that they would develop or 
improve a purchase order 
management system within 
the next two years, concluded 
a study entitled, “Retail MIS: 
Expenses and Trends,” con- 
ducted by Arthur Young, the 
accounting and consulting 
firm based here. 

While 63% of these respon- 
dents said they plan to develop 
or improve their purchase or- 
der management system, 19% 
more said that they have re-

Gear Apparel to Young 


Family Man, Poll Says 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The typical discount store 
shopper may be a woman, but 
men on 60% to 70% of their 
own basic clothing items, ac- 
cording to a recent consumer 
poll. 

Who are the men who buy 
those basics at discount 
stores? How often do they 
buy? When? What do they 
look for? 

A recent consumer poll con- 
ducted for DSN by Leo J. Sha- 
piro and Associates, the Chi- 
cago-based research firm, 
examines how men approach 
their basic clothing buys for 
the colder seasons using last 
year’s fall/winter shopping as 
a barometer. 

The survey asked men 
about several basic items: 
jeans, socks, dress shirts, ca- 
sual shirts, sweats, dress 
shirts, neck ties, outdoor jack- 
ets and underwear. 

The findings suggest that, 
in general, discounters should 
merchandise their sections to- 
ward a powers male who has 
a family. In addition, dis- 
counters should get out of the 
winter-oriented garments by 
the end of January. 


Men who purchase 
apparel at discount 
Stores are younger, 
from larger 
households and 
more likely to have 
children than the 
total population. 


Men buy the majority of 
their basic clothing for them- 
selves, according to the sur- 
vey. Those polled said pur- 
chases made by others, 
presumably the women in 
their lives, accounted for any- 
where from 30% to 40% of to- 
tal purchases in each catego- 
ry. 
Men reported buying their 
own underwear, neckties and 
outdoor jackets more often 
than the other apparel items. 

For the fall and winter sea- 
sons, about a third of the men 
polled made their first pur- 
chase in September. When 
asked when they make their fi- 
nal purchase of fall/winter 
ciothes, 30% said December or 
January. However, as expect- 
ed with such basic items, 26% 
said they would buy slacks, 
jeans, neckties, dress shirts 
and other staples any time of 
the vear. : 

Just over half, 52% of men 
surveyed, reported that at 
least one of the nine items was 
purchased at a discount store. 
Close to a quarter (22%) of the 
respondents spent over $100 
on clothing at discount stores 
in the past year. 

Men making purchases 
from a discount store are 

annges and from larger 
a olds than the total pop- 
ulation. They are also more 
likely to have children. 


That age factor influences 
color preferences as well as 
styles and places to shop. For 
example, twice as many men 
in the 30 to 44 year age range 
are thinking of buying some- 
thing red this year, compared 
to men 45 and over. In the un- 
der 30 age group, three times 
as many said they were think- 
ing of buying a red-colored ar- 
ticle of clothing. 

Likewise, tan/beige was 
mentioned twice as often by 
men 45 and over, than by 
those under 45. Gray and 
brown were also more popular 
with older men.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, February 16, 1987 


Population’s 


WASHINGTON — The demo- 
graphic trend for the rest of the cen- 
tury suggests a promising scenario 
for the ready-to-wear marketplace, 
according to a study by U.S. Com- 
merce Department economists. 

Expected shifts in the makeup of 
the U.S. population during the next 
dozen years created by an aging U.S. 
consumer, “bode well for the apparel 
market and for companies who take 
advantage of the opportunities,” re- 
searchers said. 

According to the Office of Textiles 
and Apparel, “the fastest growth in 
the population will be among those 
from 30 to 54 years old, who typically 
have rising incomes and high rates of 
consumption, and therefore are a key 
element in the growth of demand for 
—. 

.S. ready-to-wear manufactur- 
ers got some help from the “substan- 
tial acceleration” in 1986 personal 
consumption expenditures on cloth- 
ing—about 6% after adjustment for 
inflation. However, economists re- 
ported that apparel imports (valued 
at $17.8 million) were a key factor in 
the 1986 growth. 

Last year’s consumer spending for 
clothing triggered only “a relatively

“slowdown” in domestic apparel ship-

parel manufacturers rose 3% in from 
1985 to 1986, to $59.1 million, after 


dropping 0.2% from 1984 to 1985. 
“Faced with the challenge of rapid- 


ly growing imports, the U.S. apparel 
industry has developed a number of 
strategies to maintain its position in 
the domestic market and to take ad- 
vantage of emerging marketing op- 
portunities,” Commerce Department 
economists said. 

Among the competitive responses 


in the works for American ready-to- 
wear manufacturers are increasing 
use of high tech equipment and better 
production sites, they reported. The 
industry is emphasizing quick re- 
sponse systems including faster feed- 
back of marketing information be- 
tween retailer and manufacturer.

As a group, those who shopped for 
men’s wear at discount stores are as 
affluent and as educated as those who 
did not. On average, men spent $236 
for fall and winter clothes last year 
and of that figure, 41%, or $96 was

the fall/winter season; 54% said they 
got new socks and 50% said they got

an item that men often add to their

49% of those polled did. Sweats got

21% buying new sweats for the fall/

times a year; half of those surveyed 
shopped more often than five times, 
and half shopped less often. 

All told, 36% of those polled had 
purchased clothing at J. C. Penney in 
the past year; 31% had bought some-

Prerecorded Videotape Sales Explode as Prices Tumble 


Nationwide DSN Report 
The sell-through market of prere- 
corded videotapes to discounters is 
booming due to lower price points of 
both the software and hardware and 
the ease of operating the department 
through use of rack jobbers. 
Discounters, who initially thought 
the rental market would be the more 
romising one, now say the sale mar- 
et has become their true profit mak- 
er. K mart, Jamesway, Heck’s, Gold 
Circle and Ames are among the 
chains that are more aggressively ad- 
vertising prerecorded videocassettes 
and enlarging their departments. 
They cite three reasons for their 
optimism: 


e@ Prices of even the most popular ti- 
tles have dropped by as much as 60%, 
and further price slashing is predict- 
ed. The decline in the price of the soft- 
ware follows the already well-docu- 
mented boom in the sale of more 
affordable videocassette players. 
® Studios that release the tapes are 
becoming more sensitive to discount- 
ers’ needs, especially in terms of lead 
time required for retailers to estab- 
lish their advertising plans. 
@ And, the studios are devoting 
more attention, and money, to pro- 
motions geared for discounters. 

In 1987, 110 million prerecorded 
videocassettes, worth $2.8 billion, 
will be sold to retailers, the Electron- 


ic Industries Association forecasts, 
with prices per unit averaging $25. In 
sa” the average price per tape was 

A, 

Despite this increased awareness 
of the sale market, most discounters 
feel that studios are just beginning to 
understand how to sell through their 
outlets. 


Falling Price Points 


When studios became interested in 
capturing discount store business, 
they dropped price points from be- 
tween $60 and $80 to between $24.99 
and $29.99 for their top hits. Howev- 
er, they failed to take into account the 
necessary lead time discounters need 


due to long-term advertising plan- 
ning. For instance, it was announced 
in January that the videotape of the 

opular film Top Gun ‘oa be re- 
eased on March 11. By the time they 
received the announcement, most 
discounters had already set their ad 
plans for March. 

But, studios appear to be waking 
up to discounters needs by providing 
more advance notice on release 
dates. Promotions for Christmas 
1987 will be unveiled at the June Con- 
sumer Electronics show. 

Studios are also beginning to de- 
vote more promotions to discounters. 
For example, HBO/Cannon plans ad-

departments usually weekly 
or biweekly. 

The jobbers use computers 
to track retail sales by catego- 


ry and item, monitoring the 
store’s movers and replenish-

categories in the chains, and 
based on results, decide 
whether to expand selection.

to 25 ft., and has plans to re-

in early 1987, said Rutkowski,

has also expanded selection 
from 200 titles to 400 titles.

bookshelf-type end fixture 
with plexiglas shelves. The 
frontline movies, selling for 
$18.95 and up, are located in 
two showcases in the electron- 
ics center.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, February 16, 1987 


CONSUMER ELECTRONICS pias _HOME PRODUCTS 


VCR Sales Grow Faster than Color TV: S, Commerce Reports 


WASHINGTON — Color 
TVs may soon lose center 
stage in retail consumer elec- 
tronics departments—dis- 
placed by the skyrocketing 
growth of VCRs. 

“VCR growth has outpaced 
that of color TVs over the past 
10 years,” U.S. Department 
of Commerce economists re- 
ported in a recent study. Ship- 
ments of video recorders to re- 
tailers—a total of 40,000 units 
in 1975—rose to 14.2 million 
by 1986. 

“Current estimates of the 
number of households that 
own a VCR vary from 33% to 
40%, and most industry ex- 
perts believe that about two- 
thirds of U.S. households will 
have at least one VCR by 
1990,” Commerce Depart- 
ment researchers said. 


Color TVs 
continued to be the 
consumer’s 
electronic favorite. 


Despite rapidly multiplying 
VCR shipments, however, 
color TVs continued to be the 
consumer’s electronic favor- 
ite. According to the study, 
about 94% of U.S. homes have 
at least one color set. Nearly 
one-half of U.S. TV owners 
have two or more units. 

Unfortunately for the U.S. 
consumer electronics indus- 
try, too many of those TVs 
(and all of the VCRs) were 
manufactured overseas. 

“Imported color TVs and 
VCRs were an estimated 63% 
of apparent consumption in 
1986, up from 59% in 1985,” 
economists reported. Imports 
of color TVs rose 39.2% in the 
first half of 1986. In contrast, 
they estimated that U.S. pro- 
duction of color TVs in 1986 
declined 1.3% from 1985. 

On another consumer elec- 
tronic front, researchers re- 
ported that shipments of com- 
pact disc players were “not up 
to industry expectations.” 

“Despite a dramatic drop in 
the retail price from $1,000 to 
about $200 in the last two 
years, sluggish sales, coupled 
with inventory buildups, led 
to a glut of CD players in late 
1986,” researchers said. Only 
one U.S. plant manufactures 
CD players, they reported. 

Total domestic consumer 
electronic shipments are ex- 

cted to decline 2.7% to $6.6 

illion when final 1986 figures 
are analyzed. Imports will rise 
an estimated 2.1%. 

Projections for the industry 
for 1987 are guarded. Accord- 
ing to Commerce Department 
economists, a 1987 “slow- 
down” by the industry leaders 
(color TVs and VCRs) will re- 
sult as prices “stabilize” and 
consumers cut back on spend- 
ing for consumer electronics. 
Limited growth in other con- 
sumer electronic sectors can 
be expected by 1990. 

“Domestic shipments of 
consumer electronic products 
are expected to decrease at a 
compound annual rate of 1. 6% 
during the next five years,’ 
they predicted.

Price Cuts Spur 
Videotape Sales

mainly been lower prices. 

“We don’t buy current mov- 
ies sold to rentals at $90 to 
$100,” Rutkowski said. “We 
only sell a combination of new 
and old titles for under $30.” 
“We would like gross margins 
of 28% to 30% with prerecord- 
ed videotape,” said Rut- 
kowski. “It is a volatile type of 
business, though, with titles 
frequently changing, prices 
falling dramatically, and in- 
creasing competition. But I 
feel prices will settle and be- 
come much like a record or 
book department.” 

The bulk of sales for K mart 
are in the popular movies from 
major studios, accounting for 
45% of the business. With the 
frontline movies and exercise 
tapes which retail for over 
$18.95, the chain can make as 
much as a 50% increase in dol- 
lar sales this year, Rutkowski 
said. Children’s titles are 
presently a growth area for 
K mart, generating 20% of 
sales. Exercise tapes gener- 
ate about 4% of sales while 
music, how-to and miscella- 
neous each account for about 
2% of sales. 

“The how-to category is 
small now but it will develop 
later,” Rutkowski said. 

Heck’s, after gaining $1.2 
million in sales in 1986 in pre- 
recorded videotape, is ex- 
panding its display from 4 ft. 
to 12 ft. this year. “The time is 
right for the sell-through mar- 
ket with retail under $30 for 
most videotapes,” said How- 
ard Holshouser, electronics 
buyer for the Nitro, W. Va.- 
based chain. Some 40% to 50% 
of Heck’s sales come from vin- 
tage video, the classic movies 
that sell for $7.99. Heck’s is 
also planning to test videotape 
rentals in its stores this year. 

Gold Circle is also expand- 
ing its department to 12 run- 
ning feet of all categories, 
ranging in price from $29 to 
$4.99. Rocky Hill, Conn.- 
based Ames has also expand- 
ed its prerecorded video de- 
partment with a 4 ft.- 
freestanding rack in all stores. 
It makes most sales with chil- 
dren’s titles and old movies.

Skilled Home Craftsmen Drive Powered Hand Tool Market 


WASHINGTON — A new 
consumer breed, the “sophis- 
ticated. do-it-yourselfer,” has 
changed the U.S. power-driv- 
en hand tool market, a U.S. 
Commerce Department study 
concludes. 

The introduction of new 
cordless hand tools was para- 
mount in the sector’s growth, 
the study found. For example, 
cordless screwdrivers, priced 
at about $20 at discount stores 
and other outlets, “attracted 
consumers who do not ordi- 
narily use power tools,” Com- 
merce researchers reported. 

“In recent years, power tool 
manufacturers have ae 
trated on introducin 
ucts aimed at more skill "but 
nonprofessional, consumers,’ 
the study said. 

The growing popularity of 
more professional tools, such 
as upscale power drills, mitre 
boxes and table saws, in the 
DIY market is good news for 
retailers and manufacturers of 
small, power-driven tools.

Consider Fashion, Function When Buying Security Hardware 


49 


bolts and double dead bolts to 
doors and windows. 

Sales of double dead bolts 
are especially strong, because 
consumers realize that all it 
takes for burglars to break 
into homes is to smash a single 
window, which essential] 
makes the single dead bolt 4 
most worthless. 

Double dead bolts must be 

unlocked from the outside 
with a key, as well as from the 
inside. 
Retailers should promote lock 
sets to encourage these sup- 
plementary lock purchases, as 
well as to continue to target 
women shoppers. 


Packaging Gets Better 


Catering to females, both 
domestic and import manufac- 
turers continue to improve 
pecan, and installation di- 
rections. Such improved pack- 
aging makes it easier to shop 
for them—especially women. 

Several years ago, latches 
and that type of security hard- 
ware were sold from bins. The 
carding that’s common now 
has helped women customers 
identify what item they need. 

Bronze and brass finishes in 
oval, round and other decora- 
tive shapes are selling more 
strongly than in the past, part- 
ly because of the influence of 
women hardware shoppers. 

Buyers need to look at fash- 
ion and function equally when 
selecting lines to include in 
their assortments. 


Are you carrying the rechargeable 
lanterns that outsell the competition 2:1? 


Are you selling the brightest 
rechargeable flashlights on the market? 


Will you be offering consumers the primary 
cell flashlights that can last up to 10 years? 


Are you getting free dealer tagged . 
TV advertising?

Nherer step Clubs Push Growth 


By Ralph Raffio 
Special to DSN 
Nationwide Report 

Increased competition 
and lingering difficulties at 
turning a profit won’t deter 
membership warehouse 
clubs from continuing the 
rapid-fire growth they’ve 
achieved during the past 
four years, most retail ana- 
lysts and warehouse club 
executives said. 

Most observers said cash 
and carry warehouses have 
only scratched the surface 
of the market’s full poten- 
tial. Through steady devel- 
opment of new units and 
rising consumer familiarity 
with the buying concept, 
membership warehouses 
are expected to emerge one 
day as an even greater 
force than they are now. 
Their higher visibility, said 
experts, will lead to even 
greater sales and profits 
and likely will alter forever 

the way many people shop.

Heck’s Files Chapter 11 Bankruptcy 


By Peter Hisey 
NITRO, W. Va. — Heck’s, 
whose battle to rebound from 
mounting losses ended when 
its group of lending banks 
ulled the plug March 1, filed 
protection from creditors 
under Chapter 11 March 5. 
The action comes in the 
wake of a series of disputes be- 
tween the company and New 
York financier Robert Tous- 
sie, who recently canceled a 
planned $145 million acquisi- 
tion of Heck’s and sued the 
chain for $1 million. Heck’s 


had previously announced 
plans to close 29 of its 158 
stores (see DSN, March 2, 
pose 1), then offered them to 

ussie after he criticized the 
decision. 

A $50 million credit agree- 
ment with several banks ex- 
pired on Feb. 28 and a combi- 
nation of repayment demands 
and a cut-off of merchandise 
by at least some suppliers pre- 
ceded the Chapter 11 filing. 

Reached for comment after 
the chain's filing, Toussie said 
Heck’s had not presented him 


with an official offer to pur- 
chase the closed units, al- 
though Heck’s representa- 
tives did tell him such 
information would be forth- 
coming. In early March, the 
company was advertising go- 
ing-out-of-business sales at all 
29 stores, according to a 
Heck’s spokesman.

charged that the bankruptcy 
filing is the result of “unable 
and incompetent” direction

seeming contradiction is an

a membership warehouse 
cm per can use a credit card 
obtain a check to pay a club. 
The FundsNet Cash Call

without requiring us to in- 
crease our prices to cover the

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, March 16, 1987 


Direct Marketers Foresee Viability 
Of Selling Machines Within 3 Years 


CHICAGO — Interactive 
video systems, the so-called 


ELECTRONIC 


RETAILING 


Court Decision Could 


Apparel Heads Categories Likely 


Federal appeals court 
decision two years ago 
may have done in tele- 
| shopper Shopping Line, and that 
| ruling could also generate static 
| for other video retailers targeted 
for broadcast TV stations. 

The court’s decision allows cable 
TV systems to freely select what- 
ever broadcast TV stations they 
wish to carry—and to drop those 
commercial channels they don’t. 

One New York City station may 
have been caught up in this situa- 
tion and, for self-protection, 
— Shopping Line, thereby triggering its demise. 

e court’s decision upset the Federal Communication 
Commission’s 20-year-old “must-carry” rule that requires 
cable TV systems to air all the local broadcast TV stations 
in their market viewed by a large number of households. It 
has resulted in cable operators selectively dropping public 
service and weak commercial stations, usually V f sta- 
tions that broadcast on the channel 14 to channel 83 band. 

Shopping Line went off the air in January, about two 
months after it was launched as an around-the-cleck tele- 
shopping service for broadcast, rather than cable, TV sta- 
tions. Its key outlet was WN YC/channel 31, a public ser- 
vice station owned by New York City, which had 
pioneered a unique lease-time arrangement to present the 
teleshopping 5 rok am in nonprime time, 11 p.m. to 1:30 
a.m., to get add 
tional fare. 

Shopping Line president Reese W. Schonfeld called 
WNYC “far and away our best, best station. In the month 
of November we did $400,000 worth of business with 
them, paying them 10% or $40,000; in the month of Decem- 
ber we did $1,200,000 worth of business in just those two- 
and-a-half hours a day. With them, we had a business, 
without them we didn’t.” 

Despite Shopping Line’s results, WNYC hesitated on 
renewing the 13-week contract, Schonfeld said at a New 
York chapter meeting of Television Academy. The reason 
why: some cable systems dropped WNYC because of the 
shopping show. 

“This was ovr real problem with WNYC. It was 
dropped by two cable systems. Both have deals with other 
shopping networks, and they weren’t being compensated 
by WNYC for carrying Shopping Line.” 

He noted that even Galees Shopping Line went on the 
air, Suburban Cable, one of the largest in New Jersey, had 
dropped WNYC and replaced it with a home shopping 
show in which it owned an interest. 

“The natual question is, did the cable systems drop 
WNYC because it was carrying gees Line? The cable 
systems deny it but I don’t think YC executives be- 
lieve it for a minute,” Schonfeld said. 

WNYC director Mary Nichols a . “We got a glim- 
mering that the cable systems didn't like what we were do- 
ing [carrying Shopping Line].” But she added there were 
two other reasons the station didn’t renew the agree- 
ment: the show’s “poor” programming and “revenues 
weren't as high as promised.” 

Schonfeld told the Television Academy that the lesson 
to be learned from the Shopping Line saga is clear. “I’m 
sure you are all aware of the must-carry law. A cable _ 
tem can drop a marginal TV station for any reason. If a 
marginal TV station starts carrying a lot of teleshopping, 
it will probably cause the station to be dropped.”

SWING-A-WAY MANUFACTURING CO. e ST. LOUIS, MISSOURI 63116 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, March 16, 1987 


$c 


The membership warehouse club industry has exploded in recent years, with the top 10 chains racking up some $7. 5 billion in sales last year from 208 units. 


Competition, Losses Won’t Deter Warehouse Club Growth 


(Continued from page 1) 

Since 1982, the number of warehouses has 
jumped from approximately eight West Coast 
Price Clubs to more than 230 warehouse clubs all 
over the country, owned by more than a dozen dif- 
ferent companies. Total sales among warehouse 
clubs are estimated at about $8 billion, but they are 
expected to balloon to $20 billion by 1990, with sim- 
ilar gains in new units. 

Some executives said the market can move even 
faster than that, however. 

“Frankly, I think $20 billion is a conservative es- 
timate,” said Walter Teninga, president of Skokie, 
Ill.-based Warehouse Club, one of the companies 
that has had to pull back on new store development 
this year due to losses. “We’re still a very long way 
from realizing the full potential of this channel of 
distribution.’ 


Though still in its infancy, the warehouse club 
concept already has evolved since its inception. 

“There isn’t anything about PACE that’s exactly 
the same as three years ago,” said Henry Haim- 
sohn, chairman of Denver-based PACE Member- 
ship Warehouse. Like many of its competitors, 
PACE has narrowed sku’s to 3,000 to 3,500 from 
4,000 to 5,000 sku’s. Groceries and sundries contin- 
ue to generate more than half of PACE’s total 
sales, while hard lines is the next largest category. 

With the industry still working on profit margins 
of around 10%, streamlining assortments for high- 
er inventory turns persists. Past moves to broaden 
assortments and increase sku’s have widely meant 
lower inventory turns and decreased profits for 
warehouse clubs that have made such adjust- 
ments, most industry watchers said. PACE and 
others have pared assortments across the board. 


“Those who don’t make these kinds of changes 
will be left [further] behind,” Haimsohn asserted. 

How many warehouse clubs the American econ- 
omy ultimately will support is a question frequent- 
ly raised but rarely answered, at least with any 
great degree of certainty. For a market as young as 
this one, there has been a lot of talk regarding a 
shakeout. 

“People are already hitting head-to-head in ma- 
jor markets, and that will continue,” predicted 
Alan Pennington of Pennington Associates, a retail 
consultant. “Eventually there wil! have to be a ma- 
jor shakeout.” 


Plenty of Industvy Expansion Foreseen 


Most industry analysts, however, still see plenty 
of growth left for the industry. 

“It’s almost impossible to predict how many 
warehouses the country can absorb. The market is 
much too young still,” said Fred Windsor, a retail 
analyst with Alex. Brown & Sons, Baltimore. “The 
only thing we know for sure is that expansion will 
definitely be swift.” Windsor expects to see soon 
600 to 700 units. 

The leading warehouse club chains are: The 
Price Company, San Diego; Sam’s Wholesale Club, 
the Wal-Mart division based in Bentonville, Ark.: 
and Seattle-based Costco Inc. Price and Costco 
both are operating profitably, and Sam’s—though 

'al-Mart declines to report its earnings separate- 
ly—is widely thought to be profitable as well. 

Analysts and competitors applaud all three com- 
panies for their insistence on making wholesale 
customers their top priority, rather than expand- 
ing assortments to attract more retail customers. 

Charging that many other warehouse chains 
have developed “open oor policies” in order to in- 
crease retail sales, Costco chairman Jeffrey H. 
Brotman said he sees little benefit in doing so.

ern markets as a challenge to

whether competition is really 
the major problem. 

“West Coast markets and 

laces like Texas are relative- 
y new, wide open markets,” 
Teninga said. “Chicago, Mil- 
waukee and Detroit aren't. 
Traditional sources of tne fd 
are more firmly entrenched in 
that region. As a result, | 
think it’s going to take longer 
for warehouse clubs to get in- 
dividual business owners 
away from their traditional 
source of supply than it took 
on the West Coast. We’re talk- 
ing about severely altering a 
traditional supply source, one 
that’s been around a whole lot 
longer than any one of us.”

When we heard the results of a recent independent retailer 
survey, it was music to our ears. 

Researchers talked to VARs and PC retailers over a five-month 
period. And during that time, more of them named Fuji as their 
best-selling diskette than any other brand. 

The reason? Fuji disks, like cur other high-quality magnetic 
products, offer consumers exceptional performance. And they

Commerce Projects 5.9% Slump in 1987 Toy Shipments 


WASHINGTON — The 
Teddy Ruxpin-inspired ava- 
lanche of dolls, plush toys and 
action figures on the 1986 toy 
market will continue to glut 
retailers’ inventories through 
1987, the U.S. Commerce De- 
partment predicts. 

Inarecent study ofthe U.S. 
marketplace, government 
economists cautioned that the 
rise in personal disposable in- 


come expected this year 
(2.4%) will not offset the 1986 
toy glut, which left many busi- 
nesses with unsold stock still 
in warehouses. 

“The inability of the indus- 
try to establish new product 
trends resulted in increased 
inventories being carried over 
into 1987,” economists said. 
As a result, they projected 
that shipments of dolls will 


drop about 1.8% this year. 
Toys and games will be hit 
even harder, with shipments 
predicted to slump more than 
6.5%. Overall, toy shipments 
are expected to drop 5.9%. 

Significantly, U.S. toy in- 
dustry performance in 1986 al- 
ready was “lackluster.”

Large-size and petite women put 
their wardrobes together different- 
ly, found a Discount Store News-com- 
missioned shopper survey. 

For example, large-size women 
see nightgowns as much more impor- 
tant to their wardrobes than other 
women. Those women also place 
much less importance on skirts. 

Petite women, on the other hand, 

ut more emphasis on blouses and a 
ittle less on dresses than do either 
regular or large-size women. 

A recent consumer poll conducted 
for DSN by Leo J. Shapiro & Asso- 
ciates in Chicago gauged the apparel 
shopping habits and attitudes of 
women, focusing on the special quali- 
ties of both large-size and petite 
women. 

Nationally, the telephone survey 
conducted earlier this year found that 
more than half of all women are either 
large-size (size 16 and up) or petite (5- 
ft., 4-in. and shorter). Of the 63% of 
those polled who qualify as special- 
size women, 27% wore large sizes and 
36% fit the petite requirements. 

—— women have a harder 
time finding tops that fit them than 
petite or regular size women. Petite 
women share a concern with —. 
slacks and dresses with the r 


woman. But fit on all items of apparel 
seems to be a problem for large-size 


women more often than for petites. 

It also appears that discount stores 
have a greater share of the large-size 
business than of petites, which is not 
surprising, since many chains still do 
not have petite departments. 

In fact, fewer petites are used to 
their own sections in any store. Al- 
most 75% of the large-size women 
said they shop in special departments 
of stores with regular sizes, com- 
pared to only about half of the pe- 
tites. 

Only about a third, 32% of the pe- 
tite women had ever shopped in a 
special-size store. But 59% of the 
large-size women had. 

nly 38% of large-size women said 
they mainly shop at special-size 
stores. That was true of just 13% of 
the petite ladies. 

ere is a contradiction in the way 

special-size women approach costs of 
clothing. The survey revealed that 
55% of all women who have shopped 
in a special-size department or spe- 
cialty store think that special-size 
clothing costs more. (60% of lar 
size women, 49% of petites and 52% 
of regular women think so.) 

However, in most specific cases, 
petite and large-size women actually 
planned to - less than their regular 
size peers for clothing.

NEW YORK — Ross Stores plans 
to have full-fledged ladies’ special- 
size departments up and running in 
80% of its stores by Aug. 1, according 
to Bernard Tulman, a New York- 
based buyer for the California off- 
price chain. 

Space that had previously been de- 
voted to home textiles will be rede- 
signed as a boutique catering to pe- 
tites and large-size women. Special 
signing and strictly fashion-type fix- 
tures such as four-ways and rounders 
are planned. That way, Tulman said, 
the chain can make a dramatic state- 
ment to the large or small woman. 


Moderate Price Points 


The sections will average from 
2,500 to 3,000 sq. ft. The “full-scale” 
departments will include tops, bot- 
toms, dresses, outerwear, coordi- 
nates, hosiery and lingerie. “We 
want to give them a mirror of the 
missy assortment,” said Tulman. 
Merchandise should be mainfloor or 
second floor department store 
brands with moderate price points. 

Ross’s major competitors, such as 
Marshalls, already carry petite and 
large-size merchandise, but not in a 
separate shop that spans the apparel 
categories, he said. “We’re catering 
to a special-size customer who hasn't 
found what she wants in Marshalls. 

“We see special sizes—-petites and 

e sizes—as a growth area,” said 
an, a former missy buyer who 
now buys both size ranges. 

“T’ve just been out in the market 
and what I see in sizes are very 
exciting,” Tulman added. 

Petites hold untapped potential for 
the 121l-unit chain because of the 
number of stores concentrated on the 
West Coast and in the Sunbelt, 
where Oriental and Mexican women 
are a big portion of the customer 
base, he added. In Florida, where the 


pert Wye a: ae 


Domestics at Ross 


chain also operates, Cuban women 
are often petites. Women who meet 
the criteria (5-ft., 4-in. and shorter) 
may have already been buying junior 
sizes, but will be better served in pe- 
tites, Tulman said. 

The litmus test for the new bou- 
tique was performed in six Ross 
stores in Seattle starting last Au- 

st. Sections of those stores were 
eased to Virginia Specialty Stores, 
which also operates freestanding up- 
scale and off-price apparel stores for 
special-size women.

special-size customer who 
hasn’t found what she 
wants in Marshalls.’ 


—Bernard Tulman,

private labels. 


The test convinced Ross of the via- 
bility of the two categories. In the fu- 
ture, Ross will operate the depart- 
ments itself. 

More conviction and expertise in

C.0.M.B. to Acquire CVN 


MINNEAPOLIS — Closeouter C.0.M.B. plans to com- 
plete its transformation into a video retailer by acquiring 
the 50% interest in teleshopper CVN that it doesn’t own 
and adopting the CVN name. C:0-M-B. -will buy the other 
half from a consortium of 23 cable TV operators, paying 
them eight million warrants, convertible into stock of the 
new CVN at $18.125 a share. The cable operators, who 
would obtain a 44% stake in new CVN if all the warrants 
are exercised over the next five years, must agree to an 
undisclosed long-term commitment to carry the service. 


Ross’s Losses Top $41 Million for 1986 


NEWARK, Calif.— Ross Stores reported heavy year- 
end losses stemming from closing 25 underperforming 
stores. A resulting $39.4 million non-recurring pre-tax 
charge increased losses to $41.4 million on sales of $534 
million, for the year ended Jan. 31. Without the store clos- 
ing charge, the company said it would have reported a $6 
million pre-tax loss. In fiscal 1985, the off-price chain had 
registered earnings of $7.1 million on sales of $376 million. 


Hafts Raise Stakes in Supermarkets Bid 


WASHINGTON — Dart Group, the holding company 
controlled by former Dart Drug owners Herbert and Rob- 
ert Haft, has upped the ante in its bid to take over Super- 
markets General (SGC), parent of Pathmark supermar- 
kets, Purity Supreme and Rickel Home Centers. The new 
offer is $45 per share, $42 in cash and $3 in preferred stock, 
up from $41.75 previously. With 38.5 million shares of 
SGC stock affected, the price totals $1.73 billion. 


Heck’s Reports $17.8M Loss for 1986 


NITRO, W. Va. — Heck’s, which filed for protection 
under:-Chapter 11 bankruptcy March 5, lost about $17.8 
million on net sales of $566.3 million in 1986, show the un- 
audited operating results the company released. Fourth 
quarter losses totaled $7.8 million net on $181.2 million in 
net sales. Heck’s reported that it had been able to “gener- 
ate positive levels of cash” since the Chapter 11 filing.

NEW YORK — Troy, Mich.-based K mart Corp. and 
Secaucus, N.J.-based Jamesway declared stock splits and 
raised dividends last month. K mart increased its quarter- 
ly dividend rate by 18% and declared a 3-for-2 stock split. 

he dividend has increased to 43.5¢ a share from 37¢ ona 
-split basis, payable June 8 to holders of record May 21. 
The Jividend on post-split shares will be 29¢ a share. 

Jamesway increased its quarterly cash dividend rate by 
33% and declared a 2-for-1 stock split. The dividend in- 
creased to 4¢ a share from 3¢ on the pre-split stock, pay- 
able May 23, the same date of stock distribution to holders 
of record on April 20. Outstanding shares will increase to 
13.9 million from 6:9 million.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, April 13, 1987 


Proposed Law Establishes Subsidies 


For Companies that Employ Seniors 


WASHINGTON — Dis- 
counters who employ older 
workers would be eligible to 
receive hefty Federal tax sub- 
sidies under new legislation. 

Rep. Silvio O. Conte (R- 
Mass.) has introduced a bill to 
provide a Targeted Jobs Tax 
Credit (TJTC) for employers 
hiring senior citizens. 

Conte told his coHeagues 
that “with the average age of 
Americans rising, it is impera- 
tive that we in Congress cre- 
ate means by which this older 
class of individuals can be 
gainfully employed while still 
enjoying their Golden Years.” 

His bill would allow employ- 
ers to take TJTC for each new- 
ly-hired worker at least 55 
years of age earning not more 
than $20,000 in gross income 
per year and not receiving 
wages subsidized under the 


Older American Community 
Service Employment Act. 

Under the current TJTC 
program, discounters can re- 
ceive $2,400 subsidies (up to 
40% of the first year salaries 
paid to each qualified individ- 
ual) for each newly-hired 
worker from targeted groups, 
such as the handicapped, Viet- 
nam vets, co-operative educa- 
tien students, SSI recipients 
and poor youths. 

In addition, a bill similar to 
Conte’s has been drafted by 
Rep. Pat Williams ( D-Mont.) 
that would extend TJTC not 
only to older workers but also 
to those who lose their jobs 
from foreign competition. 

Even though TJTC pro- 
vides substantial financial in- 
centives, many employers 
over the past several years 
have shied away from active 


participation in the program. 

The main reason 1s the un- 
eertainty over Congressional 
reauthorization of the pro- 
gram. For example, TJTC 
was declared technically dead 
for most of 1986 before Con- 
gress retroactively reautho- 
rized the program as part of 
last year’s tax reform bill. 
Furthermore, the tax reform 
provision will make targeted 
job credit available to employ- 
ers only through 1988. 

To overcome such reluc- 
tance, Sen. John Heinz (R- 
Pa.),a long-time TJTC advo- 
cate, has started a campaign 
on Capitol Hill to encourage 
employers to participate. 

Heinz has unveiled a that 
would make TJTC permanent 
at its current level. “It is time 
to give this proven program 
genuine permanence.” 


Kennedy Wage Bill Gains Support 


WASHINGTON — The 
drive for legislation to in- 
crease the national minimum 
wage gained fresh momentum 
on Capitol Hill when the Con- 
gressional Democratic leader- 
ship in both chambers joined 
the chorus calling for steep 
hikes in the current $3.35 
hourly pay floor. 

The new legislation, spon- 
sored by Senate Labor and 
Human Resources Committee 
chairman Edward M. Kenne- 
dy ( D-Mass.) ,would raise the 
minimum wage rate by $1.30 
per hour in three steps begin- 


DSN 25th ANNIVERSARY 


ning January 1 of next year. 

Like other proposals al- 
ready pending in Congress, 
the new Kennedy bill, S837, 
ultimately would index the 
minimum to the average hour- 
ly earnings of all private sec- 
tor workers, a move that vir- 
tually would assure automatic 
annual pay adjustments. 

Kennedy’s counterpart in 
the lower chamber, House 
Education and Labor Com- 
mittee chairman Augustus 
Hawkins (D-Calif.), has an- 
nounced plans to sponsor com- 
panion legislation. 


With Democratic leaders in 
both houses actively pressing 
to raise the Federal minimum 
wage, prospects for enact- 
ment of a bill this year have 
brightened considerably. 

Many industry lobbyists 
privately concede that pas- 
sage of some type of wage hike 
appears inevitable. 

The best hope for avoiding a 
steep minimum wage hike this 
year may be the threat of a 
presidential veto.

initially took no position on the

CATALOG : 
SHOW ROOMS 


Jewelry Will Sparkle 
In Industry’s Future 


atalog showrooms are pas- 
sé; long live catalog show- 
rooms. 
| This doesn’t mean the industry 
is dead. It’s still a lively $5 billion- 
lus business, a hard lines retail- 
ing powerhouse moving items that 
% #@ range from footballed small appli- 
| Wm ances to fine diamonds that sell for 
=4 $10,000 and more. 

But the traditional catalog 

a £6 showroom approach of relying just 
ARTHUR on an.annual book to market an 

MARKOWITZ overpowering assortment of hard 
eS —— showrooms is past 
tense for a major portion of the industry. 

Instead, catalogers have ae themselves as a 
new type of retailer: a diversified jewelry and hard goods 
specialty store that exploits a market niche between full- 
line merchandisers like discounters and conventional de- 
partment stores and one-category fe gered retailers like 
consumer electronics, sporting goods or toy stores. 

The industry’s new look has seen catalogers recast their 
hard goods merchandising more narrowly to focus on jew- 
elry and giftware as the core, high profit center, with four 
ancillary categories, houseware and home goods, consum- 
er electronics and photo, leisure (toys and — goods) 
and juvenile, positioned as traffic driving areas that gen- 
erate fast-turning, gross margin dollars. 

The annual catalog is now supplemented with targeted 
advertising using direct mail flyers, radio and TV. 

The industry’s repositioning reflects the ongoing evo- 
lution that has marked all segments of retailing. Catalog- 
ers have had to seek a new marketing niche because their 
merchandising stance of the 1960’s and 70’s did not prove 
viable for the 80’s. The annual catalog’s low, everyday 
price was undercut by sharper promotions from other re- 
tailers, while the showroom’s order and pickup system 
failed to provide the fast checkout or personal service cus- 
tomers demand. 

Catalogs now can be broadly segregated into one of two 
distinct types, one that harkens back to the industry’s pio- 
neer days and the other that points the way to the future. 

The first group merchandises jewelry and giftware and 
the four other categories in large showrooms that typically 
run 40,000 sq. ft. and more in size. These chains tend to 
mass display most categories except for jewelry and, in 
some cases, consumer electronics and photo. 

These nes showrooms are fossils from the industry’s 
early days when catalogers tried to merchandise a vast as- 
sortment that included hardware, auto accessories and 
even health and beauty aids. Catalogers still operating 
these mass display, self-service giants have been forced to 
merchandise the broadest hard lines mix, including the ex- 
tensive use of not-in-catalog goods, to fill space. 

The other group follows a tighter merchandising ap- 
proach in salesclerk service-oriented showrooms that 
rarely are larger than 35,000 sq. ft. They focus more heavi- 
ly on jewelry and giftware, often appearing to be jewelry 
stores that have wandered into the housewares, home, 
consumer electronics and photo categories, and usually 
avoid the leisure and juvenile areas. 

The industry’s future lies with these jewelry-driven 
showrooms. Recognizing this, a number of catalogers that 
in the past operated large showrooms now are opting in 
their expansion ——s for scaled-down stores that re- 
flect the sharply edited, hard lines merchandising ap- 
proach of the jewelry directed chains.

HOME PRODUCTS 


LAKE GENEVA, Wis. — 
The Cookware Manufactur- 
ers Association has reported 
that industrywide sales of 
metal cookware, bakeware 
and miscellaneous kitchen- 
ware items declined 4.8% in 
1986. Imports of cookware 
showed an increase of approx- 
imately 10%, while exports 
decreased about 30%. 

The association reported 
that U.S. manufacturers sold 
$570 million of non-electric 
metal cookware, bakeware 
and miscellaneous kitchen 
items at factory eons, iy 1986, 
compared to manufacturer 
sales of $599 million in 1985. 

The association reported 
that top-of--stove sales ac- 
counted for 74.7% of industry 
sales in 1986, compared to 
76.4% in 1985. Metal 
bakeware rose to 21.4%, 
against 20.2% in 1985. Miscel- 
laneous kitchenware sales hit 
3.9% in 1986, up from 3.4%. 


Aluminum cookware, both 
stamped and cast, represent- 
ed a market share of 57% of all 
metal cookware in 1986, com- 

ared to 56.4% in 1985. Stain- 
ess steel cookware accounted 
for 39% in 1986, compared to 
39.2% in 1985. Cast iron and 
other types such as porcelain 
and copper, totaled 4% in 
1986, down from 4.3% in 1985.

TOWSON, Md. — The 
Black & Decker Corporation 
has proposed the sale on the 
European market of seven- 
year bonds in the principal 
amount of 100 million deut- 
sche marks (approximately 
$56 million). The sale will be 
made through a syndicate to 
be formed by a bank. 

Net proceeds from the bond 
sales will be used to pay short- 
term debt that was incurred 
Tries og to retire certain 

igh-interest, long-term debt 
in 1986. 

The bonds will not be regis- 
tered under the Securities Act 
of 1933 and will not be offered 
or sold in the United States or 
to United States nationals.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, April 13, 1987 


Retailers Now Call Shots in Market 


By Jeffrey C. Kasch 
President, 
M.W. Kasch Company 


I t will be a challenge this 
year to maximize the 
tential in toy volume due 
to the current uncertaint 
over which products will 
emerge to drive the business 
in the fourth quarter, as well 
as a flood of choices available 
to distributors and retailers. 

A major change occurring 
this year in the industry is that 
it is becoming much more 
buyer/merchant-driven, rath- 
er than manufacturer-driven, 
thanks to the varied choices of 
product availabie at earlier 
dates, allowing retailers much 
more flexibility. 

Toy manufacturers have 
been heavily involved in ship- 
ping products to distributors 
and retailers since January. 
There has been more toy busi- 
ness in the first eight weeks of 


this year than ever before. 

However, it seems that the 
hot product for Christmas 
1987 will surface later than in 
the past. There is no consen- 
sus at the moment over which 
product and/or category will 
drive the business. 

At the current time, the hot 
sellers for us are: G.I. Joe, 
low-end Transformers retail- 
ing for under $10, Silver- 
hawks, Ghostbusters, Barbie 
Rockers, Pogo Bal, Sweet Se- 
crets Jewelry and board 

es in general. On the other

Plush Will Grow

on highly recognizable toys.

will also be renewed interest 
in Disney plush toys. 

Board games came to life in

steady rebuilding of interest 
in preschool, and“I expect a 
20% increase in that category 


this year.

owever, with increased 
competition and lower mar- 
gins, the exercise market as a 
whole has leveled off. 

Growth in 1987 will be in the 
outdoor sports market, partic- 
ularly in fishing and camping 
gear. With extraordinarily 
mild late winter and early 
spring weather around most 
of the United States, sales in 
these two categories, as well 
as in most other outdoor activ- 
ities, have taken off. Camping 
equipment has shown the 
most impressive gains in re- 
cent years, and shows no sign 
of slowing down. Young peo- 
ple are flocking to outdoor ac- 
tivities in record numbers, 
and that shift has resulted in 
strong sales of cabin tents and 
sleeping bags. 


Mini Team Games Trend 


There has also been a strong 
trend toward ‘‘mini’”’ team 
games like Tee ball and mini 
basketball, and aluminum 
baseball and softball bats are 
doing extremely well. 

The mild winter has also 
benefited fishing equipment, 
which will be a leader in strong 
spring sales. Among the prod- 
ucts I expect to perform weil 
are three promotionally 
priced reels:

In general, racquet sports 
have become very slightly 
profitable staples, and I don’t 
see them going radically up or 
down in the near future. Rac- 
quetball, in particular, is very 
nearly a dead issue as the con- 
struction of new courts contin- 
ues to slow down. 


Tough Foreign Competition 


The meteroic upswing in re- 
cent years of exercise equip- 
ment was so remarkable that 
it had to cool off eventually, 
and it did in 1986. There is sim- 
ply too much product on the 
market. A combination of 
price pressure, a flood of du- 
plicate equipment and tough- 
er foreign competition, which 
has reduced prices precipi- 
tously in the past two or three 
years, effectively leveled 
profitability at retail. For ex- 
ample, the equivalent of an ex- 
ercycle selling for $300 two 
years ago soy, 2 had, via Tai- 
wan, for $49 in many discount 
stores. The sales were still 
there, but the impressive 
growth of the early 80’s is 
over. 

On the other hand, the 
growing preference among 
young people for activities 
that keep them outside is good 
news for retailers; most out- 
door sports equipment is no- 
where near peaking and re- 
mains very profitable.

most mass merchandisers. 
Another major growth area 
in 1987 will be the incontinent 
category. Incontinence pres- 
ently affects 10 million Ameri- 
cans. With the over-50 popula- 
tion growing twice as fast as 
the total population and with 
exorbitant cost of hospital 
care and nursing homes, the 
category is expected to grow 
from $92 million in 1986 sales 
to over half a billion dollars by 
1990. Kimberly-Clark’s De- 
nd will come up against 
rocter and Gamble’s Attend 
and Personal Products’ Sure- 
ty this year. 
The H&BA industry 
— has traditionally been 
riven by new product intro- 
ductions. In 1987, this basic 
tenet of our business is in jeop- 
ardy. Most vendors have 
found that it is more expedient 
and economical to attain mar- 
ket share by purchasing 
brands or entire companies as 
opposed to launching new 


products. 
Revlon bought Barnes- 
Hind and Max Factor; Lever 


Brothers has taken over 
Chesebrough-Pond’s, and 
Procter & Gamble bought 
Vicks and its Olay, Nyquil, 
Sassoon and Pantene brands. 
As the trend continues, more 
dollars will-be spent en Wall 


Street instead of on Madison 
Avenue. 

Sales increases will be hard- 
er to come by in the future as a 
result.

PACE Jumps into LA 
Warehouse Club Fray 


By Pamela Krein 

LOS ANGELES — PACE 
Membership Warehouse has 
entered the competitive mar- 
ket here with the intent of 
making customer satisfaction 
its primary goal and the differ- 
entiating factor from the nu- 
merous club operations here. 

The opening of two units in 
the greater Los Angeles area 
(El Monte and Woodland 
Hills) this month introduced 
PACE to the breeding ground 
of the membership warehouse 
business, placing the company 
head-to-head with such com- 
petitors as the Price Club, 
Costco and Price Savers. 

PACE plans to open five ad- 
ditional stores in the region 
this year, said Henry Haim- 
sohn, PACE founder, presi- 


dent and chief executive offi- 
cer. Focusing expansion on 
this area and the other PACE- 
established markets through- 
out the country is one key ele- 
ment of Haimsohn’s plan to 
make his 27-unit warehouse 
chain profitable after four 
years in operation. 

Despite the tough competi- 
tion PACE faces on the West 
Coast, Haimsohn said he is 
sure his company can carve 
out its niche. “We are noted 
for having a broader assort- 
ment of merchandise and a 
very high level of merchan- 
dise. We’re more interested in 
our customers,” he said. 

For Haimsohn and PACE, 
this interest translates into 
providing a broad and deep

Seedman Scraps Deal to Sell 
TSS Chain to Price Company 


SAN DIEGO, Calif. — 
Fickle George Seedman, the 
90-year-old chairman of 
Brooklyn, N.Y.-based TSS- 
Seedman’s discount chain, has 
spurned yet another suitor. In 
a surprise move, The Price 
Company here has announced 
that its agreement with Seed- 
man to acquire his 81% inter- 
est in the 69-year-old discount 
chain has been terminated by 
mutual agreement. 

The sale of TSS-Seedman’s, 
a privately held company, 
would have brought share- 
holders at least $50 million. 


“Mr. Seedman expressed 
his desire to terminate, and 
The Price Company agreed 
provided it was reimbursed 
for out-of-pocket expenses,” 
The Price Company an- 
nounced in a prepared state- 
ment. Executives at The Price 
Company would not comment 
further. 

“The reason we are termi- 
nating the negotiations is that 
it was their intention, which 
was not expressed to us at the 
time that we made the con- 
tract, to change the character 
of the stores,” said Seedman, 


who is still active in manage- 
ment at the chain. 

“They would not be offering 
any customer service, and our 
entire reputation has been 
built on customer service. 
That’s the difference between 
us and 100 other stores on 
Long Island that have gone 
out of business since 1972. We 
would not go along with 
changing the store character.” 

Seedman has turned down 
other prospective buyers in 
the past, including Associated 
Dry Goods, at the time the

K mart to Add Bank Branches in Florida 


TROY, Mich. —- K mart announced: plans to open 21 
First Nationwide Bank branches in K mart stores in St. 
Petersburg, Bradenton, Sarasota and Orlando, Fila., 
bringing to 57 the number of branch locations of the bank 
in the ine State. The ment is part of a long 
term, multi-state plan by K mart and First Nationwide to 
add a minimum of 150 convenience banks to K mart stores 
across the nation this year. The completion of this goal 
would give the discounter 450 units that offer banking. 


Warehouse Club Shuts Two Units 


SKOKIE, Ill. — The Warehouse Club earlier this 
month shut its year-old membership warehouses in the 
Chicago suburbs of Arlington Heights and Lombard, IIl., 
leaving the chain with three units in the Windy City area. 
The closing, which reduced the chain’s count to 12 clubs, 
will result in a one-time $5 million charge in the third quar- 
ter ended June 30. The move to reduce the undisclosed 
losses from the two stores was part of Warehouse Club’s 
efforts to become a profitable company that has also seen 
the chain call off an yer a during the fiscal year end- 

SN, March 2, page 3). In its past 

ended Sept. 30, 1986, Warehouse Club sales of 

$157.3-million were up 77% from $89 million, but its net 
loss. of $1.7 million was more than double the $516,000 
corded in the fiscal year ended Sept 30, 1985. | 


Seedman to Be Honored at UJA Dinner 


NEW YORK — George J. Seedman, chairman and ceo 
of TSS-Seedman’s, the East Coast discount chain that just 
called off its proposed sale to The Price Company, will be 
honored at the annual dinner of the United Jewish Appeal- 
Federation Hardware, Housewares, Paint and Seasonal 
Division, on May 21 at the Hotel Plaza here. The 90-year- 
old Seedman has enjoyed one of the longest and most illus- 
trious careers in the discount industry. TSS-Seedman’s 
operates 12 full line department stores, four small dis- 
count stores, 15 Finders Keepers off-price apparel outlets 
and several wholesale and manufacturing divisions. 


Ford to Head K mart’s Eastern Region 


TROY, Mich. — K mart Corp. has promoted James E. 
Ford to vice president of K mart’s Eastern Region located 
in East Brunswick, N.J., effective June 1. Ford replaces 
Arthur E. Riley who retires May 31. Ford has been with 
the $23.8 billion company for 24 years and most recently 
served as regional niger se K mart’s Eastern Region has 
jurisdiction over the activity in the 440 K mart, Kresge 
and Jupiter stores located within the region, including op- 
erations, merchandising and personnel. Currently, there 
are 83 employees at this office.

Luria has started investing 
in first quality merchandise to 
fuel the program, although 
the specific mix of merchan- 
dise has not been determined.

teleshopping, Luria also an- 
nounced three executive level

have issued a strong warning 
to their fellow colleagues that

driven out of the marketplace 
unless legislation is quickly 
enacted to safeguard long- 
standing Congressional policy 
barring resale price mainte- 
nance activities.

N.J., and committee member 
Henry J. Hyde, R-IIl., jointly

Hochberg, president of Sport-

FTC Sides with Retailers 


Over Price Discrimination 


WASHINGTON — Top Federal Trade Commission 
antitrusters may soon be defending discount chains and 
other mass merchandisers charged with soliciting dis- 


criminatory price cuts from suppliers in violation of the. 


Robinson-Patman Act. 

The F TC’s plan—which is reminiscent of the Justice De- 
partment’s aborted “Private Action Program” to under- 
mine the federal ban on resale price maintenance conspira- 
cies—involves intervening in private Robinson-Patman 
lawsuits in an effort to pressure the courts toward a more 
restrictive interpretation of the federal anti-price dis- 
crimination law. 

Robinson-Patman, which was enacted during the De- 
pression to Penang small merchants from emerging retail 
chains, prohibits suppliers from offering discriminatory

Buyers Primed to Exploit New Trends in Intimate Apparel 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The winds of change that have 
blown through the intimate —_— 
market have picked up enough mo- 
mentum to prompt shifts at the dis- 
count store level, according to a re- 
cent DSN-sponsored poll of buyers 
from chains. 

A confidential poll of intimate ap- 
parel buyers at 32 discount chains, 
representing 6,650 discount, off- 
price and dollar stores across the 
country, was conducted last month 
by Jerard Less Inc., a New York- 
based retail apparel consultant, ex- 
\ elusively for Discount Store News. 

. The responses paint a portrait of 
departments with unrealized volume 
potential and buyers planning higher 


quality goods, increased fashion ap- 
peal and in a few cases, improved pre- 
sentations. 

More than a few buyers believe 
more space and new fixtures would 
pay off in the intimate apparel de- 
partment but have yet to convince 
management. “It’s a profitable area,” 
one respondent said. “Yet, it hasn’t 
been given enough support by man- 
agement.” 

The impetus for change is seen ev- 
erywhere; from the success of The Li- 
mited’s intimate apparel specialty 
operation, Victoria's Secret, to a re- 
kindling in the fashion industry of lac- 
ey feminine looks, romance and a 
trend to more natural fabrications 
like cotton. 


According to the DSN-sponsored 
survey, buyers are primed to exploit 
the possibilities presented by all 
three trends. But changes in fabrica- 
tions have, so far, made the most far- 
reaching impact. As one respondent 
said, “ ... through the Victorian 
look, which will pass, natural fibers 
will stay.” 

In fact, one merchandiser called 
the industry’s shift to natural fibers 
“the first major change in 40 years.” 


Cotton Gains Importance 


Of those polled, 93% see cotton as 
gaining in importance in the intimate 
apparel category. More specifically, 
responses indicated that nght now 
about 44% of the robes, 42% of the 


sleepwear and 41% of ladies’ panties 
sold in their stores are made of all cot- 
ton or high-cotton blends. 

In general, the 15 smaller opera- 
tions of 50 units or less were more 
likely to react to trends in fashion and 
tastes than the 17 larger chains 
polled. 

For example, the return to ro- 
mance and femininity in clothing was 
considered very important or impor- 
tant by just over half (53%) of the en- 
tire group polled. But among the 
smaller chains only, 67% said the 
trend was either important or very 
important compared to 41% of the 
merchandisers at larger chains. 

At larger chains, nearly half—

Discount Cosmetics to Spur 2.6% Gain in ’87 Shipments 


WASHINGTON — Growing sales 
through discount outlets and “at the 
mass merchandising level” will gen- 
erate increased shipments by U.S. 
cosmetic manufacturers in 1987, ac- 
cording to a newly-released analysis. 
by the U.S. Commerce Department. 

“Price will continue to have a 
strong influence on sales,” econo- 
mists said, adding that “sales of pres- 
tige fragrances and cosmetics 
through discount outlets” will show 
particular gains in 1987 for specific 
retail sectors. The value of U.S. cos- 
metic industry shipments—almost 
$13 billion in 1986—is expected to in- 
crease by 2.6% this year. Long range 

wth in shipments should continue 
at about 2.8% oi year through 1991, 
they predicted. 

According to Commerce Depart- 
ment researchers, men’s products, 
particularly “effective, practical and 
rational skin care products,” should 
experience major sales growth in 
1987. Sun lotions (led by sun screens 
which are expected to command 50% 
of the sun care market by 1990) are 
also expected to be a fertile area for 
U.S. manufacturers. Other sectors 
destined for growth include solid de- 
odorants, skin care preparations for 
the over-35 age group and ethnic 
products, they predicted. 

According to the report, purchas-

they said.

one-stop, year-round mailing centers 
that allow customers to purchase ev- 
erything they need to mail poser.

All products meet U.S. Postal Ser-

The water resistant photo mailers

and are suitable for mailing anything

ie box features an FDA-approved lin- 
ing to preserve freshness.

Competition to Slice Discount Chains’ Greeting Card Sales 


WASHINGTON — Greeting card 
revenues for U.S. discounters and 
other “traditional department store 
channels” will drop during the next 
five years, significantly affected by 
specialty stores and supermarkets. 

In a recent analysis by the U.S. 
Commerce Department, economists 
predicted that stores specializing in 
greeting card sales “will show some 
gain” over other retailers. 

In addition, supermarkets will be- 
come a leading card retailer, and 
more retail outlets of all kinds will en- 
ter the market. 

“Stores providing a diverse mix of 
traditional and new cards will capital- 
ize best on the demands of the card- 
consuming public,” they said. 

According to researchers, greet- 
ing cards are a market worth fighting 
for. Despite a leveling off from “the 
exceptional growth of the early 1980s 
(6% from 1979-1984),” greeting card 
shipments continued to rise—about 
2% in 1986, they reported. Value of 
shipments last year totalled more 
than $2.7 billion. Economists also ex- 
pect industry shipments to increase 
about 2.5% this year, and project 
similar annual gains (2% to 3%) 
through 1991. 

Government researchers reported 
that competition in the industry was 
stepped up by the snowballing
