Philadelphia Bradlees to Test 
Custom Window Treatments 


WARWICK, R.I. — Twenty-two 
Philadelphia-area Bradlees stores 
will be the testing ground for an ex- 
periment in mass marketing custom 
window shades and blinds. Kenney 
Manufacturing, a Rhode Island pro- 
ducer of a full range of window treat- 
ments, will supply a new 4-linear-ft., 
seven-product endcap display for the 
effort, which it hopes will eventually 
roll out to discounters nationwide. 

The first Bradlees newspaper ads 
for the new program will run this 
month, and Kenney expects results 
to be in by early May. 

“Popular wisdom is that mass mar- 
keters can’t sell specialized prod- 
ucts,” said Kenney vice president 
Perry Mazza. “Wallpaper, for in- 
stance, was a flop, and the jury is still 
out on whether we can do it. But 
we’re taking a stab at it.” 

Mazza added that customers are of- 
ten overwhelmed by choice and the 
fear of hanging wallpaper. He said 
these symptoms are peculiar to the 
wallcoverings market and that con- 
sumers are much more comfortable 
with window treatments. 

Historically, though, anything 
more exciting than precut vanilla 
shades has failed miserably in a dis- 
count environment. Mazza feels that 
Kenney may be successful where oth- 
ers have failed because the company 
has solved two problems that have 
plagued other attempts; taking de- 
posits and notifying customers when 
their orders arrive. 

“We’ve taken advantage of exist- 
ing systems which have been proven 
to work,” Mazza said. “Deposits will 
be handled by Bradlees’ layaway de- 
partment and their raincheck system 
will be responsible for notifying the 
customer.” 

Mazza is well aware of the track 
record of other attempts to market 
service products in a non-service en- 
vironment. “Bradlees pushed us for 


Answers: 7. b, 2. c, 3. D, 4. b, 5. c. 


six months, but we wanted all bases 
covered,” Mazza explained. 

The company said that its simpli- 
fied ordering procedure will be the 
key to success where others have 
failed. ‘‘We did our homework,”’ 
Mazza continued. “We went onto the 
street and gave people the actual or- 
der forms and said, ‘Read this, do you 
understand it?’ and kept making 
changes until the answer was yes. 

“We had the luxury of looking at a 
lot of other programs and learning 
from others’ mistakes,” Mazza said, 
“and the main thing we learned was 
not to confuse the customer. We lim- 
ited choices and made the program a 
simple step-by-step process so a 
choice can be made right away.” 


‘We limited choices and 
made the program a simple 
step-by-step process so a 
choice can be made right 
away.’ 


—Perry Mazza, 
vice president, Kenney 


Kenney is tempted by the great po- 
tential for sales in the discount mar- 
ket. While a discounter may never 
make inroads into the specialty mar- 
ket, where service and wide choice 
are necessities, the company does 
think that millions of Sears and Pen- 
ney customers can be lured away by 
the promise of paying 20% to 30% 
less. “To keep the choice manage- 
able, we’re only offering 30 sku’s in 
verticals and aluminums, but a lot of 
analysis went into choosing colors 
that move,” Mazza said. 

And, he thinks discounters will 
find the program attractive. “Brad- 
lees only has to handle the product 
operationally,” he said, “which gives 
them a luxury they’ve never had be- 
fore—no inventory.” |

Wal-Mart Expands Discount Drug Stores 
BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Wal-Mart’s three-year-old 


dot discount drug store concept has been successful ~ 


enough in Des Moines and Kansas City to prompt acceler- 
ated expansion this year. Last month, the company 
fgg two dot stores in Kansas City, Kan., and Lincoln, 
eb., bringing the total count to seven. By the end of the 
year, there could be as many as 14. In early summer, dot 
openings are slated for Hazelwood, Mo., outside of St. 
Louis, and Witchita, Kan. By the end of the summer, two 
more are planned for Kansas City, Mo., on Bannister 
Ridge and Noland Road. Two or three more are expected 
this year, said Stacy Duncan, corporate spokesperson. 
Locations for these units have not yet been determined. 


Supermarkets General Eludes Dart Group 


NEW YORK — Dart Group’s attempt to purchase re- 
tailing giant Supermarkets General, parent of Pathmark 
supermarkets, Rickel Home Centers and Purity Supreme 
stores, sf tap ended late last month when a group led 
by several key employees bid $1.8 billion for the company. 
The buyout offer was made by Merrill Lynch Capital Part- 
ners, along with caercerncts General senior manage- 
ment, and exceeded Dart’s last offer by roughly $100 mil- 
lion. Dart, which still owns about 5% of Satanisleets 
General stock, is eo examining its options, which 
include entering a still higher bid an mounting a proxy 
battle. Supermarkets chairman Leonard Lieberman was 
not included in the group making the offer. His place, if the 
management buyout goes through, will be taken by Path- 
mark president Kenneth Peskin. 


Ross Installs 5 Cosmetics Boutiques 


NEWARK, Calif. — Ross Stores has included a new 
cosmetics and fragrance boutique in five new stores. 
Looking to “provide a one-stop shopping experience for 
our customers,” the off-price retailer said it had been test- 
ing the department in a San Francisco Bay Area location, 
and decided to go ahead and include the section within the 
five stores it opened in April. The new store locations to 

et the cosmetics and fragrance Seger toent are in Los 
1 Nay Oregon, Maryland and the Bay Area. Saying it is 
“the first major off-price retailer to of er this,” Ross said 
the sections will average about 15,000 sq. ft. and handle 
brand names, such as Almay, L’Oréal, Clarion and Revlon, 
at “less then department store prices.” Expansion beyond 
these new stores will be based on a “wait-and-see” basis, 
the company said. : 


Ames Profits Slide While Sales Climb 


ROCKY HILL, Conn. — Ames Department Stores re- 

rted last month that year-end net earnings fell 33% to 
$27, 1 million from $40.4 million, for the period ended Jan. 
31. Sales increased 24.8% to $1.9 billion, while comparable 
store sales rose 6.4%. The chain, which opened 17 stores 
last year, confirmed a —— inventory shrinkage at 
its distribution center in aucus, N.J. Ralph Shulansky, 
senior vice president, finance, and chief financial officer, 
said that while there was a suspicion of theft or fraud, it 
was too early to pinpoint the exact extent or area of losses. 
He refused to eo or deny a published report that 
pegged the shortage at more than $° million, but said that 
more details should be available shortly. At year-end, 
Ames operated 321 discount department stores and 142 
variety stores in 20 states and the District of Columbia.

Store Brands Succeed When Retailers Guarantee Quality 


Nationwide DSN Report 

. The success of store brand sales is 
directly tied to the commitment re- 
tailers make to their private label 
programs and begins at the point-of- 
Spiga says a new study by the 

ew York City-based Private Label 
Manufacturers Association (PLMA). 

When retailers provide consumers 
with quality products that are fully 
guaranteed, at a good price, consum- 
ers say they buy a greater number of 
retailers’ store brands. 

Consumers also say that their faith 
in a store brand is enhanced when 
they see that retailers emphasize 

uality—as opposed to price—in 
their store brand advertising. They 
are quick to cite such advertising. 

“A lot of times you'll see them say 
that the store brands are ‘guaranteed 
quality’ in the circulars they mail 
out,” said one consumer. “They 
should do it more, because I know it 
made me feel better about buying 
them [store brands].” 


Once convinced of the 
quality of store brands, 
customers stay with a 
particular retailer and the 
store brands sold there. 


When retailers do not include qual- 
ity and guarantees in their store 
brand advertising and focus more on 
price, consumers express less trust 
and acceptance of those store brand 
products. 

The PLMA study, based on focus 
group research conducted over a two- 
year period in four U.S. cities, re- 
flects a broad cross section of con- 
sumer attitudes toward and 
experiences with major mass mer- 
chandisers, deep discounters, ware- 
house stores, membership clubs, su- 
permarkets and drug chains. 


Focus Group Answers ‘Why’ 


The focus group format was chosen 
because the PLMA felt that such 
groups can answer the “why” that 
statistical research cannot answer. 
To provide as broad a cross section of 
attitudes and experiences as possi- 
ble, focus group panels were conduct- 
ed in a medium sized east coast mar- 
ket, a medium sized midwest market, 
a major metropolitan market, and a 
rapidly growing sunbelt market. Fo- 
cus group participants were at least 
21 years of age and the primary shop- 

r for a household of two or more. 

ousehold income ranged from 
$15,000 to $25,000 annually. 

The study shows that the more so- 
histicated the shopper is, the more 
ely such a shopper is to try store 
brands. Store brand shoppers typi- 
cally use labels as a basis for compari- 


son and purchase. “If it has the same 
stuff on the label, to me it’s ridiculous 
to pay more for the national brand,” 
said one member of the focus group. 

Regardless of what they purchase, 
consumers in all four focus group cit- 
ies generally agree that both store 
brands and national brands are made 
by the same manufacturers. 

“The national brands make them 
[store brands] and just put them out 
under the store’s name,” said one 


shopper. 


Perceptions Vary by Market 


Perceptions of manufacturers and 
store brand quality vary by market, 
however; in the medium sized east 
coast market and in the major metro- 
politan market, where full-scale pri- 
vate label programs are in place, con- 
sumers notice that store brands and 
national brands often list identical in- 
ema and grades on their labels. 

onsequently, focus group members 
expressed the belief that store 
brands and national brands are one 
and the same product, of equal quali- 
ty, from the same manufacturers. 

By contrast, members of the focus 
group in the medium sized midwest 
market, where private label pro- 
grams are not as strong, voiced the 
belief that store brand products were 
usually overruns or leftovers of na- 
tional brands. “I think someone buys 
their surplus from the manufactur- 
ers. And that’s why the quality var- 
ies,” opined a midwesterner. 

While the key inducement to try- 
ing store brands is price, customers 
do not buy again unless they are sat- 
isfied with quality, said the study. 
Once convinced of store brand quali- 
ty, customers stay with a particular 
retailer and the store brands sold 
there. They say they would switch 
only if the alternative were cheaper. 
A product’s end-use can be a key fac- 
tor in influencing a customer’s deci-

Atlanta Market Embodies Challenge of Specialty Chains 


(Continued from page 97) 
eee promotions, doe bor Floyd 
aynes, vp and regional manager for 
Gold Circle’s Region 2 stores, which 
are still called Richway in Atianta. 

Considered understored just three 
years ago, Atlanta has emerged as 
the gateway to the Southeast for 
many specialty retailers. Specialty 
store operators looking to establish a 
foothold in the Southeast increasing- 
ly anchor in Atlanta. 

Amcena, which operates some 

1,300 s ecialty stores, including 
Millers Guleaak and The Lodge in ev- 
ery other region of the nation, want- 
ed to launch its newest concept—Up- 
ton’s family apparel stores—in the 
Southeast, said Irving Sacks, senior 
vice president of finance and adminis- 
tration. The company chose Atlanta 
over Miami and Charlotte as its 
launching pad with three stores here 
in the fall of 1985 and another four 
units in 1986. 

Dayton-Hudson launched its Bran- 
dens operation here a few years ago 
and later expanded that housewares/ 
home textiles format into Miami and 
Jacksonville. Two other Dayton- 
Hudson operations tackled the 
Southeast last year by opening stores 
in Atlanta. 

West Coast-based Mervyn’s family 
apparel stores made the Southeast 
part of its territory last year with five 
Atlanta outlets and will add another 
this year. Hard lines specialist Lech- 
mere leapfrogged from its North- 
eastern markets into Atlanta with 
four stores last fall. 

This year Pep Boys, which oper- 
ates in the Southwest and along the 


East Coast from Northern New Jer- 
sey to Richmond, Va., announced its 
plans to enter the growing retail pop- 
ulation in Atlanta. Between Septem- 
ber and December, six of the 20,000- 
sq.-ft. automotives shops will open 
here with at least one more slated for 
1988. The entry into Atlanta was de- 
scribed as “the beginning of our 
Southeast market development” by 
Joe Sarelle, director of construction. 

So far, the specialty stores seem to 
bang away hardest at each other. 
Late last year, Stereo Village here 
filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy pro- 
tection and has closed its five stores 
in Atlanta. A company spokesperson 
said the bankruptcy was a result of 
internal management problems. 

Others in the market point out that 
Circuit City’s arrival with four stores 
in 1985 heightened the competition 
among consumer electronics retail- 
ers. Earlier this year, off-price ap- 
parel retailer Ross stores announced 
it would shut down its four stores 
here, citing a saturated retail envi- 
ronment as the reason. 

“If it is overstored, I doubt most 
people have felt it yet,” said Peter 
Cleaveland, regional manager, retail 
services thy, at Kurt Salmon Asso- 
ciates. h the number of specialty 
stores in the area growing, he be- 
lieves there will be some fal outs, but 
adds that any saturation of the mar- 
ket by retailers is temporary. The 
population growth will feed the new 
retail operations, he said. 

Several retailers, however, do con- 
sider the market overstored. “Some- 
times it is difficult to capture the mar- 
ket share you feel you deserve 


because the market is so divided up,” 
said Elise Jaffe, director of real es- 
tate for the Conn.-based ladies’ off- 
price chain, Dress Barn. Ironically, 
the way to improve market share is to 
open more stores so that more shop- 
pers can get to the outlets, she said. 

Dress Barn opened four stores last 
year to bring its Atlanta total to nine. 
Now, business is on the upswing, said 
Jaffe. The market can probably su 
port one additional unit, she aaded. 

While real estate costs have 
jumped phenomenally since the early 
1980s, several chains have been ex- 
panding within the market. As usual, 
the larger chains can get a better deal 
than smaller operators, but one strip 
center developer here has seen the 
average rent go up from $13.50 per 
Square foot to almost $19 per square 
foot in the past three years. 

T.J. Maxx, an off-pricer that has 
been in the market for five years, 
added two of its family apparel stores 
last fall, bringing its total to six, re- 
ported Bernard Cammarata, ehair- 
man. He thinks the market can take 
another two T.J. Maxx locations _ 
is looking for sites for 1988 openin 

Drug Emporium, the y* eep- “ 
count operation, opened two more 
stores in the past 12 months, pushing 
its presence in Atlanta to 11. 

pton’s, which is now facing off 
with Mervyn’ s in this market, added 
four stores last year. Upton’ Ss now 
has seven stores and Mervyn’s has 
five. Upton’s is planning two or three 
more stores here. 

At least two of the city’s four dis- 
counters are back on the expansion 
trail as well. For Wal-Mart, with 14 


stores around the outskirts of Atlan- 
ta, the planned expansion moves the 
chain into the city. Its four store 
openings scheduled for 1988 include 
two in Marietta: one on Robinson Rd. 
and another on U.S. 41. A third is in 
Stone Mountain and a fourth is in 
Norcross on Jimmy Carter Blvd. 

K mart, which now has 31 stores in 
the 18-county market area, will push 
its total to 36 during the next year 
and a half, according to Roy Johnson, 
Southern regional manager. 

Johnson is one retailer who does 
not consider Atlanta overstored. He 
does, however, see the competition 
toughening as Wal-Mart makes the 
aggressive move toward downtown 
and Pep Boys steps in to challenge 
the chain’s automotives business. 
(Besides its usual auto departments, 
K mart operates some service cen- 
ters in Atlanta.) 

Johnson and Haynes at Richway 
both agree that discounters cannot do 
much to improve their forte—a 
strong price/promotional stance. 
They emphasized that chains have to 
live up to their promises of improved 
customer service. 

“The thing that’s going to distin- 
guish any retailer is customer ser- 
vice,” said Johnson. “We’ve got some 
of the best locations inside and out- 
side of the perimeter. I also feel 
we've got a super ad program with 
circulars twice a week.”

Richway Bolsters Customer Service in Atlanta Home Base 


ATLANTA — Richway, 
which merged with Ohio- 
based Gold Circle last year, is 
strengthening its customer 
service stance in its old home- 
town of Atlanta, thanks to 
several new chainwide pro- 
grams. 

Scanning, which was al- 
ready in use in some Gold 
Circle stores before the merg- 
er, will be set up in Atlanta by 
this fall, according to Floyd 
Haynes, vice president and 
Southern regional manager 
for the chain. That should cut 
checkout times, once the sys- 
tem is running smoothly. 

Lay-aways will be intro- 
duced to Richway shoppers in 
the market by this summer as 
Gold Circle expands that cus- 
tomer service throughout the 


chain, Haynes added. 

The merged chain’s new 
management, which includes 
former Richway executives as 
well as Gold Circle executives, 
has also recently restructured 
the lineup of store level work- 
ers to focus more on customer 
service. Out of eight exempt 
employees in the store, two, 
or 25%, are assigned to cus- 
tomer service, said Haynes. 
In the past, only one of 14 ex- 
empt workers was responsi- 
ble for customer service. 

That emphasis on customer 
service is carried through in 
training and hiring, Haynes 
added. The store managers 
look more for extroverted 
people when hiring. Plus, the 
customer service employees 
must attend and pass manage- 


A year ago, just after the merger, Richway 
implemented the ‘End of the Line’ program 
used at Gold Circle. That policy states that 
there can never be more than three people on a 
line unless all the registers are open. The chain 
also added a portable service desk. 


ment and customer service 
training seminars. There they 
are taught how to handle eri- 
ses at the service desk and 
how to deal with customers of 
various personalities.

ed the “End of the Line” pro- 
gram that was being used at 


Gold Circle. That policy states 
that there can never be more 
than three people on a line un- 
less all the registers are open. 
At that time, the chain also 
—— a portable service

Next year, Richway stores 
here are scheduled to get the 
first round of retrofits to fit 
the new chainwide prototype, 
Haynes added. 

With that design, already 
up in Ohio and the Carolinas 
(where Richway has been re- 
named Gold Circle), depart- 
ments are color-coded and the 
toy department is moved clos- 
er to kids’ wear to create a 
children’s world. 

The only question is wheth- 
er Richway, which has the 
largest proportion of shoppers 
to stores among discounters in 
the Atlanta market, will be re- 
named Gold Circie here when 
that new look is unveiled.

“Customer service is the 
way to battle the specialty 
stores,” said Haynes. He ad- 
mitted that discounters don’t 
compete with all specialty 
stores, but added that, in At- 
lanta, “the pie has been sliced 
pretty thin.” 

Richway, which was head- 
quartered in Atlanta until it 
became part of Gold Circle last 
year, positions itself as the 
upscaler among discounters 
here. The merged company 
has further sharpened that 
niche by targeting specific cat- 
egories such as apparel, home 
textiles, toys and home enter- 
tainment where the chain is 
more dominant in terms of as- 
sortment, Haynes explained. 

“We can’t really take on the 
home improvement specialists 
or automotive chains except in 
the high velocity items,” he 
added. 

Some programs borrowed 
from Gold Circle or instituted 
since the merger promise to 
help the customer service 
stance (see separate story). 

Richway’s new rain eek 
reducing program is unique to 
Atlanta, said Haynes. The 
policy says that if the store 
runs out of a sale item it will 
take the same percentage off 
the price of a similar item-—a 
program that is paying off, he 
said. Some 60% to 70% of peo- 
ple who would ordinarily get 
rain checks are opting for the 
substitution; they do not want 
to leave empty-handed after 
making the trip, he said. 

Another new service tactic, 
a “teleservice program” used 
in Atlanta and other Gold Cir- 
cle Region 2 stores, has gotten 
a great response from con- 
sumers. Shoppers who dial 25 
on one of the in-store service 
phones ring cordiess phones 
carried by one or two sales- 
floor associates. 

“TI truly believe that there’s 
not going to be a lot of differ- 
ence in assortments and pro- 
motions,” said Haynes, ex- 
plaining the nature of the 
competition Gold Circle faces. 
“The reason why shoppers go 
to one retailer over another is 
going to be customer service.”

(Continued from page 1) 
relatively ignored, as retailers con- 
centrated primarily on such “hot” 
markets as Southern California, 
Florida and other Sunbelt areas. 

But with many of those markets— 
Los Angeles in particular—begin- 
ning to reach a retail saturation 

oint, discount retailers are now 
ooking closer at the Pacific North- 
west. And although discounters are 
by no means ready to give up on the 
lucrative California market yet, ar- 
eas like Beaverton, Ore.,:and Belle- 
vue, Wash., are beginning to draw in- 
creased attention from expanding 
discount, off-price and promotional 
chains like Target, ClothesTime, T.J. 
Maxx and Mervyn’s. 

However, retailers venturing into 
this market will not find complacent 
competition. Regional retailers such 
as Fred Meyer, G.I. Joe, Bi-Mart, 
Costco and Pay Less NW dominate 
this healthy area. And a number of 
other chains, including K mart, Mar- 
shalls and Price Savers, have preced- 
ed the newcomers into the market. 

The most riveting and extensive 
expansion plan to hit the area was re- 
vealed in March when Target an- 
nounced its plans to place 35 stores in 
Washington and Oregon by 1992 (see 
DSN, March 30, page 2). 

According to the Sherwood Group, 
developers for Target, a planned 
blanketing of the area is now almost 
necessary for the retailer’s success in 
the market, because of the existing 
competition and economies of scale 
associated with advertising costs. 

“We’re seeing retailers coming in 
now and doing major penetration,” 
noted Sherwood Group president and 
chairman, Sherwood Korssjoen. 

“I definitely think there is a niche 
that they [Target] can fill,” said 
Ralph Siegel, an analyst in the Seat- 
tle office of Touche Ross, the account- 
ing and management consulting firm. 

In penetrating the market, Minne- 
apolis-based Target strategically 
looked for areas in the Portland and 
Seattle markets where it could “get 
the dominant share by being in the 
right locations,” explained Dan Peb- 
bles, director of retail marketing for 
the Sherwood Group. _ 

Part of Target’s planning strategy 
rested with careful evaluation of the 
various regions in the Pacific North- 
west, according to Pebbles. If an area 
was strong, in terms of good sales po-

Although the reason for the rela-

Korssjoen pointed out that the “avail-

is significantly greater ” than in oth- 
er parts of the country. 

Also working to increase the areas’ 
popularity has been the recent real 
estate scouting by out-of-state devel- 
opers. Korssjoen said these firms 
have checked out much of the area 
and then passed on their findings to 
their nationwide retail clients. 

Target’s move into the Pacific 
Northwest will not only increase the 
Dayton-Hudson subsidiary’s current 
store count of 252, but is also expect- 
ed to bring in other retailers on its 
coattails, since all of the Target 
stores will be built in new locations— 
primarily strip centers. According to 
Pebbles, other chains, including Mar- 
shalls, T.J. Maxx and ClothesTime, 
are interested in following Target 
into many of the locations.

on the opening of a distribution cen-

Hayward, Calif.-based Mervyn’s, 
another division of the Dayton-Hud-

not currently the company’s focus for

majority will be located in the state of 
Michigan. 

Wakefield, Mass.-based Marshalls 
entered the Portland/Seattle area in 
1984. The 266-store off-pricer is “ac- 
tively looking to in-fill stores in both 
Portland and Seattle,” according to 
Pebbles, whose company is also a de- 
veloper for Marshalls. 

These relatively new-to-the-area 
retailers will meet stiff competition 
from Fred Meyer, the 94-store Port- 
land-based discount chain with wide- 
spread consumer appeal throughout 
the Northwest. Fred Meyer, which 
went public last year, currently has 
40 stores in Oregon and 24 stores in 
Washington. This year, the company

Seattle Market Holds Great Potential for Retail Expansion 


SEATTLE — Surrounding 
the eastern side of Washing- 
ton’s massive Puget Sound 
waterway is the bulk of the 
state’s population and growth, 
with Seattle at its hub. 

Located .in King County, 
Seattle combines with other 
area cities,like Renton, Belle- 
vue, Kent and Auburn, to 
comprise some 31% of the 
state’s population, or 1.37 bil- 
lion people. 

Like ortland, this area has 
also worked in recent years to 
diversify its economic reliance 
on just a few industries. Al- 
though Boeing and the timber 
industry still occupy a major- 
ity of the workforce, Pacific 
Rim trade, financial business- 
es and many service indus- 
tries are creating varied forms 
of employment. 

With its large harbors and 
ports, the Puget Sound area is 

especially seeking to develop 
its trade with the Orient. Re- 
cent restrictions by the Unit- 
ed States have caused some 
worry among the import/ex- 

ort businesses in the area, 

ut area analysts expect little 
short-term problems from this 
action.

ulation, according to the Census Bu- 
reau and Strategy Research, a me- 
dia-sponsored research organization, 
bringing the total number of Latin 
people to 853,200. Preliminary esti- 
mates for January 1987 update that 
number to 936,200. 

The Cuban minority—which is 
quickly becoming a Miami majority— 
has several virtures that make these 
customers a prime target for retail- 
ers. 

Among Hispanics, Cubans were 
described as having the highest in- 
come and education level and the low- 
est unemployment rate, according to 
a 1985 minority study conducted by 
Management Horizons, the research 
arm of Price Waterhouse. 

To attract these Hispanic shop- 
pers, retailers are adding merchan- 
dise that appeals to Cuban custom- 
ers. 

Lucas, K mart’s district manager 
in Dade County, said the chain has 
had to rework its assortments in rec- 
ords, stationery, housewares and 
clothing to meet Cuban needs. 


Retailers are adding 
merchandise to attract 
Hispanic shoppers, and 
Cubans in particular. 


“Latins use different kinds of cook- 
ing utensils,” said Lucas. “One exam- 
ple is the rice pot. If nothing else 
were available, they could make due 
with a typical pot, but chances are 
they would go somewhere else to find 
the specific item. 

“Latins also like to drink strong 
coffee in demitasse cups. We didn’t 
carry them in the past,” Lucas said. 
Miami K mart stores have gradually 
increased the Latin cookware section 
of their housewares department to its 
current 25 linear feet. 

Leonard Luria, president of cata- 
log showroom operator L. Luria & 
Sons, said his company has made sim- 
ilar changes in housewares merchan- 
dise. His showrooms have eliminated 
Lenox, Hummel and other lines that 
do not fit into a typical Latin house- 
hold. 

“You don’t need many different 
items to sell to the Latin market,” 
said Luria. “If they like chicken and 
rice, don’t give them steak. Ethnics 
like to buy from people they feel com- 
fortable with—and we are an ethnic 
store. Store help in Spanish areas are 
primarily Spanish themselves,” said 
Luria. 

But keeping well-stocked in Latin 
music is a little more difficult than 
having the right cookware, especially 
as the proportion of Central and 
South Americans in the Miami His- 
panic community rises. 

“Each country has its own kind of 
music and to keep up to date in each 
means carrying an extensive assort- 
ment of Latin records and tapes,” Lu- 
cas of K mart said. 

In the stationery department, the 
greeting cards assortment had to in- 
clude a selection of Spanish verse. 

“At first the card company we 
work with tried to take an American 
card and translate it word for word 
and that just doesn’t work at all. We 
ended up insulting our customers. 
Some things do not translate. Now 
we have a manufacturer that deals 
just in Latin greeting cards,” Lucas 
said.

TV Spending Propels Ad Budgets to New Highs 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Led by Circuit City, the Virginia- 
based consumer electronics chain, 
and Wal-Mart, the giant Arkansas- 
based discount department store re- 
tailer, the 25 leading discount store 
television advertisers increased their 
TV ad expenditur es by 22% last year. 

At the same time, half the discount 
stores interviewed in a recent survey 
said they expect to increase their to- 
tal advertising budgets—by a mean 
of 5.2%—in 1987. They said their TV 
advertising expenditures this year 
on would rise to 8.3% of total consum- 
er ad spending, from 7.7% in 1986. 

Clearly, discount stores are bet- 
ting that a heavier investment in ad- 
vertising will help them maintain and 
increase their share of the retai! mar- 
ket. And, more than ever, they are 
staking a larger portion of the ad bud- 
gets on television to reach the con- 
sumer of today (and tomorrow) with 
their message. i 

Total TV expenditures by the top 
25 discounter TV advertisers rose to 

238.2 million last year, from $195.4 
million in 1985. Circuit City posted a 
160% increase in TV spending to 
$16.3 million, lifting the nation’s larg- 
est CE chain to fourth place on the 
top TV advertiser list. 

Wal-Mart made dramatic gains in 
TV advertising last year, investing 
$30.2 million in the electronic medi- 
um. TV expenditures by the fast- 
growing discount department store 
chain were up 88% over 1985. The 
chain closed a huge spending gap on 
No. 1, K mart, which maintained its 
premiere ranking with a 19% gain in 
TV expenditures to $39.9 million. 


Increase in Network Spending 


Reflecting the use of more institu- 
tional and image commercials, the 
bulk of K mart’s increase was in net- 
work TV spending, which went up 
62.3% to $26.3 million. Spot market 
spending by the nation’s Leagan dis- 
count chain fell off by close to 21%. 

Toys “R” Us was the only other top 
discounter to register any network 
TV spending, according to the Tele- 
vision Bureau of Advertising (TvB), 
which compiles its TV spending fig- 
ures from Broadcast Advertisers Re- 
ports data. However, with declines in 
both national network and spot TV 
expenditures, the Rochelle, N.J.- 
based toy chain registered the larg- 
est percentage decrease in T'V expen- 
ditures among the top 25 spenders. 
Toys “R” Us cut back on its TV 
spending by nearly $3.7 million last 
year, dropping four notches from 
fourth to eighth on the list. 

After Circuit City and Wal-Mart, 
the other leading percentage gainers 
were Best Products, up 55%; Brad- 
lees, up 53%; Caldor, up 37%: Lech- 
mere, up 33%; Crazy Eddie, up 29%; 
Meijer, u 28%: T.J. Maxx, up 24%; 
and The Federated Group, up 20%. 

As a group, the five top-spending 
discount department store chains, 
K mart, Wal-Mart, Target, Hills and 
Zayre, spent 42% more on TV com- 
mercials last year than they did in 
1985. The top five CE Rehtan 
chains in TV ad spending, hland 
Superstores, Circuit City. Silo, The 
Federated Group and Newmark & 
Lewis, increased their TV spending 
by 34.9% last year.

Three chains dropped out of the top 
25 list this year. Target’s acquisition 
of Gemeco erased the West Coast 
chain from the top spenders. Service 
Merchandise, which spent $8.3 mil- 
lion on TV ads in 1985, cut back by 
75% to just $2.1 million last year, ac- 
cording to the TvB figures. K mart’s 
discount drug store subsidiary re- 
duced its TV spending from $2.1 mil- 
lion in 1985 to $1.7 million last year. 

Worthington, Ohio-based Gold 
Circle did not make the top 25 list in 
either of the past two years. Yet, the 
discount chain showed its increased 
commitment to TV advertising witha 
109% gain in TV ad spending to 
$839,600 in 1986. 

While TV ad spending is growing 
at most of the major discount chains, 
discounters’ expenditures on news- 
paper and magazine ads has been de- 
clining slightly. According to a recent 
survey by the Chicago research firm 
Leo J. Shapiro & Associates for 
DSN’s sister publication, Chain 
Store Age/Executive, discount chains 
spend the highest proportion of their 
consumer advertising dollars on 
newspaper and magazine ads, but 
less ao a majority of their total ad 
budgets is spent in this area. From 
1985 to 1987 (projected), average dis- 
counters’ newspaper and magazine 
expenditures have slipped from 49% 
of their total budget in 1985 to an ex- 


pected 47.3% of budget this year. 

Direct mail, which garners the sec- 
ond largest portion of discounters’ ad 
budgets, has been rising: 28.6% of to- 
tal consumer ad spending in 1985; 
29.2% in 1986; and an anticipated 
30.1% in 1987. 

In ’85 and ’86, average expendi- 
tures by discounters were slightly 
higher for radio advertising than for 
television. In 1987, discounters ex- 
pect to devote 8.3% of their ad dollars 
to TV commercials vs. 7.5% for radio. 

Compared to discount stores, ap- 

arel specialty stores spend a larger, 

ut still declining, percentage of their 
ad budgets in newspapers and maga- 
zines. These stores, according to the 
survey, reported spending 63.6% of 
total ad bucks on newspapers and 
magazines in 1985; 61.4% in ’86; and 
expect to devote 59.4% of their ad 
budgets to this area in ’87. 

Direct mail has increased from 
12.4% of total ad spending in 1985, to 
13.6% in 1986 and an anticipated 
14.5% this year. Both radio (9.1%) 
and point-of-purchase materials (9%) 
will rank ahead of TV ad spending 
(5.6%) this year at apparel specialty 
chains. But, TV spending has been on 
the rise at these stores, climbing 
from just 3.1% of total ad expendi- 
tures in 1985. 

The Shapiro survey also showed 
that discounters ranked second to de- 


partment stores in the percentage of 
total dollar sales volume spent on 
consumer advertising. The 30 dis- 
count stores in the survey projected 
they would devote a mean of 2.9% of 
sales to their total advertising in 
1987. The 30 apparel stores said their 
advertising as get would constitute 
about 2.6% of total sales this year. 

The study compared advertising 
budgets and expenditures among dis- 
count stores, apparel specialty 
stores, department stores, drug 
stores, supermarkets and home cen- 
ters. 

Six out of 10 discount stores in the 
survey said their advertising expen- 
ditures rose in 1986 compared to 
1985. They pegged that increase at an 
average of 6.6%. When asked about 
planned increases in 1987, five out of 
10 discount stores said they would in- 
crease ad expenditures this year—by 
an average gain of 5.2%. 

A ges specialty stores pretty 
much followed the discount stores’ 
trend in the number of chains increas- 
ing their ad es ets in 1986 and plan- 
ning to in 1987. But, their average in- 
creases far out) aced all other 
categories of retailers in the study. 
Apparel specialty retailers pumped, 
on average, 16.3% more deen into 
their ad budgets in 1986, and expect- 
ed to increase total ad spending an 
average of 12.1% this year.

Retailers are placing greater em- 
phasis on apprehensions, found an in- 
formal survey of loss prevention di- 
rectors prompted by the release of 
An Ounce of Prevention, the annual 
study of loss prevention in the retail 
industry. 

This year’s version of the study, 
which was released by the National 
Mass Retailing Institute (NMRI) and 
Arthur Young, reports that the na- 
tional average of overall shrinkage 
for 113 companies (representing 
30,000 locations) remained at 1.8% of 
sales for the last two consecutive re- 
porting periods. 

Responding companies attributed 
approximately 42% of the inventory 
shrinkage to employee theft, 31% to 
customer shoplifting, 23% to paper- 
work errors and 4% to vendor theft. 

Because retailers have no way of 
accurately measuring the compo- 
nents that cause shrinkage, appre- 
hensions can be used as a barometer 
to test these retailers’ perceptions of 
the causes of shrinkage. At the same 
time, retailers can identify a few of 
the latest trends in loss prevention. 

Nine mzjor companies (represent- 
ing 749 individual store locations) 
were contacted and a consistent an- 
swer was heard from the majority of 
these companies: Each of the loss

sions rose 5.5% from last year. 

The increases in shoplifting appre- 
hension percentages ranged from a 
high of 60% for one company to a low 
of 1% for another. The company re- 
porting the greatest increase had not 
increased its staff. “We have one of 
the strongest anti-shoplifter initia- 
tives that can be applied,” said the 
company’s director. ‘““Employee 
training has improved greatly. We 
target problem stores and give em- 
ployees certificates of appreciation 
when they help by reporting suspect- 
ed shoplifters.” 

Another company said that a re- 
duction in its floor staff has negative- 
ly affected the preventive aspects of 
its program. Others credited their 
employee awards programs with en- 
couraging apprehensions. The com- 


pany reporting the smallest increase - 


in apprehensions said the value of 
goods recovered in each case has in- 
creased dramatically. 

Other trends reported by these re- 
tailers reflect a greater sophistica- 
tion in attacking and dealing with 
their problems: 
® High-tech security appears to be a 
shrinkage control tool that is here to 
Stay. 

@ Point-of-sale investigative reports 
are providing better information con- 
cerning dishonest cashiers and fraud- 
ulent refunders. 

e EAS is considered an effective 
anti-shoplifting device. 

@ Some stores now operate comput- 
erized shrinkage and auditing soft- 
ware programs. 

e The popularity of closed-circuit 
television cameras for assisting in in- 
ternal theft investigations now ranks 
high on many investigators’ “wish 
list” of security tools. 

Retailers continue to place great 
store in their employee training pro- 
grams. Self-teaching audio-video 
training programs are widely used 
throughout the industry. Partici- 
pants in the NMRI/Arthur Young 
study rated — training pro- 
grams to be the most effective 
shrinkage control device available.

Year-Round Sales to Drive Tomorrow’s Toy 


By Josephine Fiamingo 
Nationwide DSN Report 

Discount toy buyers can look for- 
ward to even tougher decisions in the 
coming years as a deluge of new prod- 
ucts taxes their ability to operate 
profitable departments. 

More product choices, 
available year-round by 
manufacturers, are cre- 
ating confusion for retailers in decid- 
ing on the right mix to maintain 
leaner inventories. 

Further, earlier advertising cam- 
paigns accompanying the dizzying ar- 
ray of high-tech toys are adding these 
costs to the price retailers have to 
pay for the product. 

While retailers and distributors re- 
port stronger toy business in the first 
eight weeks of this year than ever be- 


News 
Analysis 


(DSN photo) 


fore, they are quick to point out that 
capitalizing on this increase in year- 
round toy business is dependent upon 
whether retailers can continue to de- 
termine the right product mix. 

After all, a toy’s life generally only 
lasts anywhere from eight months to 
two years, and that is only if it sells 
when first introduced. A mistake can 
sit on a shelf for a long time. 

- Out of the 150,000 individual toy 
products produced each year, accord- 
ing to the Toy Manufacturers of 
America (TMA), 5,000 to 6,000 of 
those involve new technologies and 
styles. Only a relatively small per- 
centage become success stories. A 
product that sells in the first half of 
the year might not sell in the second 
half—and what sells in the second 
half might not sell next year. 


By Donald Longo 
Nationwide DSN Report 

In the beginning, there were hard- 
ware stores. These mostly indepen- 
dent operations featured convenient 
neighborhood locations where con- 
sumers could get person- 
alized service from some- 
one who knew the differ- 
ence between a T-square 
and a T-hinge. 

Then, as discount department 
stores began phasing out their hard- 
ware department lessees to operate 
the areas themselves, the home cen- 
ter came along. These home improve- 
ment stores generally offered less 
service than the neighborhood hard- 
ware outlet, but certainly much more 
than the typical discounter. At home 
centers, shoppers could find a wide 
assortment of top quality name brand 
products—-but at prices usually high- 
er than discounters would offer. 

The home improvement ware- 
houses burst on the retail scene in the 
late ’70s and early ’80s. These 80,000- 
sq.-ft. to 100,000-sq.-ft. retail ware- 
houses aggressively advertised their 
unmatched selection at price points 
as low as any discounter. 

In the face of this competition, it is 
not surprising that the traditional

Employers Can Take Measures to Control Health Care Costs 


By F. Kevin Ty!us 


QB 


Touche Ross & Ca. 


oes it sound inconceivable that 

your company’s cost for health 

care benefits could equal its af- 
ter-tax profits? That may appear im- 
possible to believe, but it was one find- 
ing in a study recently conducted by 
the Harvard Business School. The 
study of the Fortune 500 industrial 
companies and the 250 largest nonin- 
dustrial companies showed the cost of 
health care benefits equaled nearly 
25% of after-tax profits from 1981 to 
1983. The researchers predicted that, 
at the present rate of increase, these 
costs could equal profits by 1992. 

A look at the numbers and trends re- 
veals that such a prediction is far from 
outlandish. Contributions = by em- 
vloyers for employee health insurance 
surpassed $100 billion in 1985 (see ac- 
companying exhibit 1). That figure 
represents a 106% increase over the 
1980 expenditure of $49 billion, four 
times the 1970 level of $12 billion. 

The per-employee gauge shows a 
7.7% increase 1n 1986 over 1985 medi- 
cal cost expenditures, found a survey 
by an insurance broker (see accompa- 
nying exhibit 2). This represents a na- 
tional average cost of $1,857 to the em- 
ployer for each employee. Employers 
with more than half their workforce 
under collective bargaining paid about 
28% more, or $2,555 per employee, 
than did employers with less than half 
their employees under collective bar- 
gaining: $1,764 per employee. 

The cost for health care today con- 
sumes approximately 10% of this 
country’s total output. Even with the 
enrollment gains in 1986 by cost con- 
scious Health Maintenance Organiza- 
tions (HMO’s) and Preferred Provider 
Organizations (PPO’s,) health care 
costs failed to decline to 9% of the 
Gross National Product as was pre- 
dicted by some industry analysts. By 
the year 2000, the cost of medical care 
may reach a predicted 12% of the GNP. 
Moreover, the rate of health care infla- 
tion was about 6% in 1986, or about 
double that of inflation, as measured 
by the consumer price index. 


Relief May Be on the Way 


While the costs for health care bene- 
fits have escalated, the business of pro- 
viding these services has been chang-

For instance, hospitals, physicians, 
and alternative providers such as 
HMO’s, PPO’s, walk-in care facilities, 
and entrepreneurial enterprises are 
battling industry environment issues 
to gain market advantages. Relief may 
result from: increased competition in 
the industry; excess capacity for hospi- 
tal-based care; price sensitivity; 4 - 
mand for high quality, convenient, and 
attractive service modes and the ef- 
forts of government and employers to 
reduce the cost of providing or arrang- 
ing for health benefits. 

The excess capacity in the hospital 
setting and the increasing saturation 
of providers in alternative settings 
translate to a greater say for the pur- 
chaser—government and employers in 
particular—in the selection of provid- 
ers and the prices to be paid for health 
care services. 

The industry has seen numerous ini- 
tiatives to control health care costs.

The most visible of these, perhaps, is 
the federal government’s efforts to 
control expenditures of the Medicare 
program. The government hopes to 
lower costs, in part, by paying fixed 
rates for each hospital admission, fore- 
going per diem cost-based reimburse- 
ment and eliminating most automatic 
cost pass-through payments. 
Employers are taking these kinds of 
steps to control costs: 
@ Employees incur copayments and 
deductibles: Most employers are in- 
cluding a deductible in their benefits 
programs, with a $200 deductible be- 
ing common. Many employers recently 
have begun copayments and, though 
they may not like passing the cost on to 
employees, they feel it is necessary, 
because the cost for health care has 
become unacceptable to bear alone. 
Benefits programs are invoking re- 
straint wherever possible. 
@ Second opinion programs: Most 
employers are encouraging second 
opinions on prescribed surgeries, with

many providing incentives for a second 
opinion. It is common to find a policy 
imposing a penalty if a second opinion 
is not obtained. 

@ Managed care arrangements: Sec- 
ond surgical opinions are a start in 
managing care arrangements. Beyond 
that, employers are taking a more ac- 
tive role in monitoring the entire 
health care contract, often hiring utili- 
zation review companies to police the 
type, duration and cost of care given to 
employees. But managing employees’ 
health care includes more criteria, like 
requiring certain procedures be per- 
formed in outpatient or same-day 
treatment facilities. Employers are 
collecting data on their employees’ use 
of services and comparing it to antici- 
pated norms or required output. They 
are also using the ine to shed light on 
usage and cost predictability. 

@ HMO contracts: Employers are 
still skeptical about whether HMO’s, 
organizations that arrange for and 
sometimes provide care directly, re- 
duce costs. Generally, employers con- 
tend the HMO premium cost is too sim- 
ilar to their indemnity rates, referred 
to as “shadow pricing,” to see any sig- 
nificant reduction in premium cost. 
Critics also charge that HMO’s are not 
investing in the promotion and mainte- 
nance of good health. 

But HMO’s have enrolled nearly 
10% of the United States population, 
and the percentage runs even higher in 
some regions. And many HMO’s are 
responding to employer demands. En- 
rollment increased to more than 23 mil- 
lion last year, a 25% jump from June 
1985 to June 1986, shows an Inter- 
Study update. The number of HMO’s 
increased more than 50% to 595 during 
that year. A 1985 poll by Louis Harris 
& Associates and the Kaiser Family 
Foundation found that, of employers 
with at least 10% of their workforce in 
HMO’s, enrollment has increased any- 
where from 26% to 45% since 1982. 
Also the study found little evidence 
that members are dropping out. 

@ PPO arrangements. A coalition re- 
port said local and regional PPO devel- 
opment will continue its appeal to em- 
p oyers. Various business coalitions in 
ealth care issues support this posi- 
tion. Many employers said provider- 
purchaser contracts give employers 
more flexibility and involvement in 
health care issues than do traditional 
indemnity or HMO arrangements. 
Generally, employees are allowed to 
select a nonparticipating provider, but 
at a reduced benefit. Some say that no 
two PPO’s are alike and that any cre- 
ative arrangement offering to reduce 
employers’ cost yet boost providers’ 
business is worthy of serious trial. 
Likewise, more employer-provider di- 
rect contracts are emerging and being 
tested as a cost-control measure.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, May 11, 1987 


Employers Can Control 
Health Benefits Costs 


(Continued from page 232) 

These arrangements are be- 
ing tried by unionized and non- 
unionized employers, self-in- 
sured or not, and by for-profit 
and not-for-profit health care 
providers. They are not limit- 
ed to progressive markets 
such as Southern California. 
In fact, one northeastern 
Pennsylvania community hos- 
pital recently entered into its 
fifth direct employer contract, 
with each of the five slightly 
different from the others. Em- 
ployers intend to achieve cost 
savings and data management 
reports in exchange for vol- 
ume commitments. 
@ Flexible benefits: Many 
employers are allowing em- 
ployees to decide which bene- 
fits they want from an array. 
For example, an employee 
might opt for a major medical 
plan over a dental plan. These 
pick-and-choose benefit plans 
enjoyed their greatest growth 
in 1986, concludes a report by 
a leading benefits consulting 
firm. Flexible benefits plans 
may help reduce overall costs 
and may provide more of what 
each employee needs for the 
same cost. 
@ Self-insurance: The move- 
ment toward self-insurance is 
helping employers save the 
payments to insurance compa- 
nies that fund the insurance 
companies’ reserved require- 
ments. In many locations of 
the country, at least two- 
thirds of employers have 
switched to self-insured sta- 
tus. This kind of arrangement 
does not necessarily reduce 
benefits costs, but it allows 
the employer to earn interest 
on funds that otherwise would 
have contributed to the insur- 
er’s reserves. 


A Warning Is in Order 


Implicit in all of these initia- 
tives is the desire to maintain 
a high quality of health care 


for employees. Health care 
providers are asked to pro- 
duce convenient access to 
quality services at a reason- 
able cost. Yet our health care 
system has become capital-in- 
tensive. For example, just a 
few years ago, the state-of- 
the-art CT scanner cost nearly 
$1 million. That piece of equip- 
ment is now considered less ef- 
fective for certain imaging 
studies than the newer mag- 

netic resonance imaging ma- 
chines, which can cost almost 
twice as much as CT scanners. 
Yet, when considering pro- 
gram alternatives to reduce 
cost, employers must main- 
tain the quality of care. 


The Jury Still Remains Out 


It will take at least three 
years—and as long as five 
years—to know whether em- 
ployer initiatives have re- 
duced the real rate of increase 
in health benefits costs, the 
cost to the employer and em- 
ployee. The vehicles by which 
health care benefits are pro- 
vided definitely are changing 
rapidly and presumably will 
continue to do so. As the third 
chart shows, even if health 
care industry analyst Sanford 
Bernstein & Co. and Inter- 
Study are only half right, the 
health insurance business will 
be transformed into a very dif- 
ferent business by the early 
1990s. (see exhibit 3 on page 
232). Alterations to benefits 
plans and employer demands 
will be part of the transforma- 
tion. 


About the Author 


F. Kevin Tylus is manager 
in the New Jersey offices of 
Touche Ross. Besides assist- 
ing hospitals, health care pro- 
viders and purchasers with 
business decisions and plan- 
ning, Touche Ross provides 
extensive benefits consulting 
services.

and soaps and cleaners extensively, 
plus those chains that carry alcohol- 
ic beverages are doing a much more 
aggressive job merchandising that

Drug store retailers like Al Neh- 
man of Dart, Don Gross at Geno- 
vese, Gary Lefferts at Austin Drug, 
all speak of promotional groceries as 
“traffic builders,” designed to “pro- 
vide an added incentive for people to 
shop our stores.” 

Most of the drug chains don’t give 
permanent sections to their promo- 
tional groceries, instead they usual- 
ly merchandise them on endcaps or 
in the high traffic promotional aisles 
sometimes referred to as Bargain 
Alley’s and they often display their 
best buys in cut cases. 

“We price so competitively on the 
grocery consumables,” says a Peo- 
ple’s manager, “that we don’t usual- 
ly have a problem with residuals. 
They come in the store and within a 
few weeks, they’ve blown out and 
we've brought something else in.” 

“We advertise grocery items ev- 
ery week,” says Al Nehman, sr. vp 
of merchandising for Dart Drug in 
Landover, Md. “We pioneered pro- 
motional groceries in the drug 
trade. 

“And because we don’t just dab- 
ble in this type of advertising, we’ve 
been able to maintain a nice steady 
market share growth pattern in 
what I think is one of the most com- 
petitive markets in the nation.” 


Snacks: growth area 


By far, the biggest growth area 
for the grocery products in nonfood 
stores’ today, however, is snacks. 
Both the drug and discount store re- 
tailers call their snack food depart- 
ment one of the most “undeveloped” 
high potential profit and_ traffic 
building departments in their 
stores. 

“Snacks are what we’re pushing 
the strongest,” says a Walgreen’s 
source. “We advertise some four or 
five candy items every week in our 
circulars and we do almost as much 
with nuts and cheese balls and items 
like that.” “Most shoppers don’t 
think of drug chains or discount 
chains when they want snacks and 
candy,” says one drug chain food 
buyer, “but Walgreen’s has such an 
extensive snack and candy depart- 
ment and they promote it so much 
that their shoppers think of that 
area as a key department in the 
store.” 

Sources at Wal-Mart, K mart, 


Zayre’s and Venture make similar 
observations. 

The discount chains also make 
their snack food departments high- 
ly visible to their shoppers, almost 
always locating them in the front of 
their stores, and snacks are fea- 
tured in just about everyone’s ads. 

“Everybody will tell you that in- 
cremental sales are becoming hard- 
er and harder to get,” says a source 
at Wal-Mart. 

“Our strategy is to go after the 
traffic and low everyday prices on 
our consumables, plus to make the 
higher turning snacks like candies 
and soft drinks very visible in our 
stores.” 

Both the drug and the discount 


store retailers also point out the dif- 
ficulties they are having today in 
maintaining strong year-to-year 
growth in sales in existing stores. 

“People can only buy so much 
toothpaste or so many radios or 
televisions,” says a Venture manag- 
er. “But if they see groceries or 
snacks at a good price, they'll buy on 
impulse and they often buy multi- 
ples which gives us a better average 
sale. 

“If you ask me why so many of us 
are getting into groceries, that’s the 
answer. They create the traffic. 
They create impulse sales, and they 
help us generate the year-to-year 
sales growth we need in order to be 
successful.”

How drug chains treat c-foods 


Drug chains court “convenience minded” shoppers by expanding convenience 


food departments 


etail drug chains, trying to en- 

hance their appeal to the “con- 
venience minded shopper” are ex- 
panding their assortments of 
convenience style groceries. 

Many chains including Wal- 
green’s, Eckerd, Perry’s and Peo- 
ple’s now have limited assortments 
of select convenience foods in all 
their stores and a large number are 
experimenting with expanded con- 
venience food departments featur- 
ing canned and packaged groceries 
as well as refrigerated and frozen 
foods. 

Retailers like Dave Peterson, vp 
of merchandising for Perry Drug in 
Michigan, say that convenience 
foods are a “growth area” for drug 
store merchants as well as an “op- 
portunity to satisfy the convenience 
minded shoppers.” 

Today approximately 10% of all 
chain drug stores have at least a lim- 
ited assortment of convenience 
foods, not counting their sections 
for candies, chips, nuts, soft drinks 
and other traditional snacks. 

Most also have “convenience” de- 
partments for shoppers looking to 
purchase pet foods, household 
chemicals and paper goods as well as 
wine, beer and alcohol wherever li- 
quor licensing is feasible. 


Walgreen's 


Walgreen’s, which first started 
experimenting with c-foods back in 
1979 with just a handful of stores, 
now has about 440 stores with full c- 
food departments, and manage- 
ment says they plan to add about 60 
more in 1987. 

In addition, almost all Walgreen 
stores carry at least some assort- 
ment of convenience foods, particu- 
larly milk, ice cream, cold. soft 
drinks, and whenever possible cold 
beer and wine. All stores also have a 
full candy and snack section plus 
sections for pet foods, household 
chemicals, paper goods and laundry 
supplies. 

Currently about 900 Walgreen’s 
also have liquor departments, and 
Walgreen’s top management says 
that it will continue to expand its li- 
quor sections “wherever we can.” 

Walgreen’s makes it a priority to 
keep prices in its c-food depart-

An estimated 25% of all chain drug stores have limited assortments of convenience foods in- 
cluding soft drinks, milk, bread, ice cream and snacks.

The mix in a chain drug convenience food department varies by neighborhood, but the dry 
packaged grocery assortment almost always includes juices, cereals, ketchups and relishes. 


Convenience foods in discount stores 


In the discount store field, most chains have stopped trying to carry 
foods every day to concentrate instead on just using foods as a traffic 
builder. 

“We're not like drug stores,” said a Target source. “We can’t sell 
convenience. All we can offer our shopper is price.” 

However, Wal-Mart, which has a number of stores in small towns 
and country markets, and Venture Discount stores in the midwest, 
are both exceptions. 

Wal-Mart faces less competition from food stores, and its small 
town stores can offer their customers the convenience of one-stop 
shopping. 

Consequently Wal-Mart has an everyday food section that features 
about 100 sku’s in some 80 ft. of shelf space. Except for the Thanksgiv- 
ing/Christmas season, Wal-Mart maintains about three gondolas of 
food/grocery items every day. 

The usual setup is for the candy, nut and chip section to lead into the 
packaged grocery section. The nonsnack assortment includes pickles, 
chili, juices, teas, ete. 

Paper goods and household cleaners are it: other sections of the 
store as they are in Walgreen’s, and pet foods are usually in two loca- 
tions, along the perimeter or the walls in large 25 and 50 lb. bags dis- 
played on pallets and ina gondola that is usually toward the rear of the 
store. 

Like Walgreen’s, Wal-Mart does not usually promote its everyday 
sections in ads or circulars. Most of the sales come from ‘lisplays and 
from in-store impulse sales. 

Venture has a similar merchandising program. They carry more of 
the mainstream categories like cereals, pancake mixes, jellies and 
beverages. 

Venture does advertise its foods, working basically on promotions 
of products carried in its everyday department. 


on the overall size of its c-food sec- 
tions. The chain currently has con- 
venience foods in about 150 stores, 
but only 30 to 40 stores have full de- 
partments with extensive packaged 
and refrigerated groceries. 

Five years ago, it wasn’t uncom- 
mon for the refrigerated section in 
SupeRx’s mini-combo stores to have 
about 24 doors. Now the average 
section is closer to 12 doors. 

SupeRx sources say the c-food 
concept is practical for a drug store, 
but that it can be “overdone. The 
key is to provide convenience, but 


not to over-develop the food part of 


the business,” said one source. 
“You can’t forget that you’re a 
drug store first.” 


Perry 


At Perry Drug headquartered in 
Pontiac, Mich., there are more than 
two-dozen stores with full conve- 
nience food sections plus limited as- 
sortments of convenience foods in- 
cluding milk and other cold 
beverage are now in over 93% of the 
chain’s stores. 

The full convenience food depart- 
ments are in all Perry’s 24 hour 
stores, and in select stores where 
there is no direct competition from 
traditional supermarket or conve- 
nience food stores. 

The typical Perry convenience 
food department takes up about 30 
linear feet and includes milk, juices, 
breads, cookies and other baked 
goods snacks. 

Stores with the full convenience 
assortment have the 30 linear feet 
plus another 64 ft. of packaged and 
canned groceries. 

Perry does not advertise its c- 
food sections and does not use any 
outside signage to attract new shop- 
pers. “The c-food departments,” 
says Peterson, “are for the conve- 
nience of the neighborhood shop- 
pers and they’re very visible to any- 
one walking into the store.” 

Perry, which is currently doing a 
direct product profit analysis on all 
its drug store merchandising cate- 
gories, Says that the ¢-food depart- 
ment is “standing up very well” as a 
profit center, even though it is sup- 
plied entirely by jobbers and food 
wholesalers. 

“All 24 hour stores will definitely 
have full ¢-food departments as we 
open them,” says Peterson, “and so 
will any other stores where we feel a 
need exists.” 

Milk is currently the only conve- 
nience food Perry is now promoting.

Many drug chains like to merchandise beverages, snacks or other consumables on the endcaps anchoring their c-food sections. 


Drug stores: strategies for convenience foods 


Chain drug store retailers have two primary merchandising strate- 
gies for convenience foods. 

They either see the category as an opportunity to service a large 
base of regular everyday users as Mickey Kole does at Perry Drug or 
they see it as a chance to cater to a shopper “who hasn’t got a food 
store nearby and who'll use us until something better comes along.” 

Walgreen’s president Fred Canning’s says his strategy is to make 
Walgreen’s a “convenient, midweek fill in store”. 

“We’re very competitive on basics like milk and coffee,” says Can- 
ning, “and we’ll continue to add food centers to new and existing 
stores wherever appropriate.” 

Many drug chain executives say, however, that it’s virtually impos- 
sible for corporate management to know exactly how many c-food de- 
partments they will open in any given year. 

“There is no such thing as a big charge that wins the battle once and 
for all,” one source says. Instead, he compares the rolling out of con- 
venience food departments to trench warfare. There are a lot of “little 
battles to be fought and won,” he says. 


Operations controls expansion 


“Even Walgreen’s,” he says, “which has done the best job of all of us 
in developing ¢c-foods knows about the little battles. You.can identify 
the right location and go in and be very successful for a year or two. 

“Then the local food store will get smart and clean up its act and put 
in scanners or extra help and suddenly people will go back to shopping 
there because they’ve made it more convenient again.” 

Or, as another source puts it, “the sleepy 7-Eleven you’ve been 
competing against will suddenly get tough and they’ll lower their 
prices or start tying into the Southland promotions, and then you 
have a fight on your hands.” ; 

On average, drug store retailers who have c-food departments say 
that it’s crucial to put them in the right stores and to stock them witha 
product mix that features the items that people buy most often. The 
corporate concensus also is that this is a business that has to be driven 
operationally. | 

“Convenience foods is not a department that can be controlled to- 
tally from the central offices,” says Perry’s Dave Peterson. “The field 
people know the individual markets best and they can spot a need, and 
react the fastest if that need disappears or if the market changes.” 


Food Merchandising for Non Food Retailers, Spring, 1987 


“Milk is definitely a planned pur- 
chase and a good traffic builder,” 
says Peterson. “so we use it as a 
leader. We feel the rest of our sales, 
however, are motivated by impulse 
shopping and the need to make fill- 
in purchase.” 


People’s 


At People’s Drug headquartered 
in Alexandria, Va., there are now 
about 60 stores with c-food depart- 
ments compared to about 20 in 1982. 

Here too, managers say the suc- 
cess is totally dependent on the mix, 
the neighborhood demographics 
and the external competitive mar- 
ket in each location. 

Most People’s managers say their 
departments have been very suc- 
cessful, turning about 10 times a 
year and doing a lot to create “new 
business for us.” 

A few, however, say that People’s 
can’t always be sure of success. “The 
situation can be fine for a while, 
then something will happen to 
change all that,” said one manager. 
“We still don’t know all the answers. 

“But if food stores can be drug 
stores too,” he added, “then why 
ean’t drug stores also be conve- 
nience food stores. Everybody to- 
day is taking a piece of someone 
else’s market. Packaged groceries, 
laundry cleaners, pet foods, cold 
beers, these are all things we can of- 
fer our customers as a convenience. 

“As I see it, if I can make their 
shopping trip more convenient, 
then my stores are ahead of the com- 
petition.”

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, May 25, 1987 


Minneapolis, Minn.-based Best Buy is one of the fastest growing CE chains in 
the U.S.; sales grew 112 percent to $239 million for its last fiscal year. 


(Continued from page 1) 
chains operated 653 stores last year 
and are =o to be running near- 
ly 1,000 outlets by the end of 1988. 

Store wth figures from these 
leading chains show that one of 
the biggest challenges facing these 
top chains is the intensifying compe- 
tition, especially in major metropoli- 
tan areas. 

This year, according to San Fran- 
cisco-based Montgomery Securities, 
two or more chains will operate in 77 
percent of the 35 largest metropoli- 
tan markets in the US. Twenty-six 
een of these markets will a 

attleground for three or more CE 
chains. 

Developments at the industry’s 
leading chains illustrate the incredi- 
ble growth and special problems of 
CE specialty retailers. 


Circuit City 


While a number of other rapidly- 
expanding chains experienced de- 
clines in same store ales growth, in- 
dustry leader Circuit City achieved 
comparable store sales growth of 18 
percent for the fiscal year ended Feb. 
28. Larry Wilson, assistant treasur- 
er, projects comparable store sales 
growth of 6 percent to 8 percent dur- 
ing 1987. In fiscal 1988, total square 
footage is projected to increase by be- 
tween 40 percent and 45 percent.-Ex- 
pansion plans call for the opening of 
some 20 new superstores in each of 
the next two years, with more impor- 
tance being placed on the 25,000 to 
35,000-square-foot superstores. 

The chain will enter new markets 
in San Francisco, Memphis and Balti- 
more this year, bringing the chain’s 
~ total to 48 markets. 

Circuit City has been extremely 
successful in the greater Los Angeles 
market since its entrance there in 
November 1985 with seven stores. 
Circuit City, which now has 20 stores 
in L.A., claimed to have captured 
$300 million to $350 million of the $2 
billion greater Los Angeles CE mar- 
ket, accounting for 30 percent of total 
Circuit City sales at the end of its last 
completed fiscal year. The chain gar- 
ners roughly 15 percent of the CE 


specialty market in L.A., compared 
to 10 percent for rival Federated 
Group, according to Montgomery Se- 
curities estimates. 

Washington D.C. is the chain’s sec- 
ond strongest market, accounting for 
15 percent of total sales. The West 
Coast analyst estimates Circuit 
City’s CE market share in Washing- 
ton at 30 percent compared to 10 per- 
cent for competitor Luskin’s. 

Circuit City’s strategy involves 
generating high levels of sales per 
square foot, leading to lower operat- 
ing cost ratios and the ability to oper- 
ate with low gross margins. 


Highland Superstores 


Highland Superstores, the second 
largest CE chain in the U.S., experi- 
enced a 25.9 percent increase in sales 
to $656 million, even though 35 of its 
current 53 stores are located in such 
depressed areas as Texas (18) and 
Michigan (17). 

“Our timing is unfortunate,” said 
Ira Mondry, executive vice presi- 
dent. “However, we know how to op- 
erate successfully in depressed mar- 
kets such as Detroit and know how to 
come out a winner when the economy 
improves.” ; 

ighland entered the Minneapo- 
lis/St. Paul market on May 8 with 
three stores in Minnetonka, Brook- 
yn Center and Inner Grove Heights. 
St. Paul is a strong market with 2.2 
million people comprised of many 
professional, young married couples 
with a good deal of disposable in- 
come, primary customers for con- 
sumer electronics. 

According to Mondry, Best Buy, 
which is the dominant CE retailer in 
Minneapolis, will be a tough competi- 
tor but, “we feel that the area is large 
enough to support another quality re- 
tailer.” The area is also close to divi- 
sional headquarters and Highland’s 
distribution center in Chicago. 

In addition to St. Paul/Minneapo- 
lis, Highland plans three stores in 
Milwaukee in early summer, which 
will compete with Best Buy and 
American TV, a smaller chain in the 
market. This fall, Highland will open

Silo 

Dixons Group, the leading 
retailer of consumer electron- 
ics in the United Kingdom, re-

Silo generates approxi-

12,000-square-foot stores. 


The Federated Group 


Despite softness in its Dal- 
las and Houston markets, The 
Federated Group’s sales grew 
18.3 percent from $363.6 mil- 
lion to $430 million. The West 
Coast-based chain said it plans 
to concentrate on improv ing 
internal operations in its 65- 
store base. Cautious expan- 
sion is a possibility in 1988. 

“We went from 20 to 65 
stores in the last three years 
and it is time to digest the ac- 


celerated expansion program 
we have had over the last 
three years,” said chairman 
Wilfred Schwartz. 


Crazy Eddie 


Edison, N.J.-based Crazy 
Eddie remained the leader in 
the greater New York market 
capturing an estimated 7 per- 
cent of the consumer electron- 
ics business and compiling one 
of the highest sales per square 
foot figures in the industry. 
Crazy Eddie stores generate 
$2,900 per square foot. 

However, despite a 34.4 
percent increase in sales over 
the last fiscal year, profits 
suddenly became more elusive 
for Crazy Eddie. At the end of 
the fiscal year ended March 1, 
earnings dropped 19.7 percent 
to $10.6 million from $13.2 mil- 
lion a year ago. 

Estimated annualized sales 
are more promising at Crazy 
E:ddie’s newer stores in Cher- 
ry Hill, N.J. (at least $20 mil- 
lion), and Philadelphia ($16 to 
$17 million) compared to pro- 
jected average annual vol- 
umes of $13.7 million per store 
chainwide, according to ana- 
lysts following the chain. 


Best Buy 
Fast-growing Best Buy, 
based in Minneapolis, Minn., 
plans to expand from 23 stores 


at the end of 1986 to an esti- 
mated 40 by the end of 1987. 
Its 1986 sales skyrocketed 112 
yercent to $239 million from 
$113 million. 

In June, the chain will in- 
vade St. Louis with three 
stores and will unveil a new 
500,000-square-foot central 
warehouse in Minneapolis for 
its brown goods. It will also 
open its first stores in Kansas 
City and some other rural 
markets this year. 

Best Buy, which currently 
dominates the Minneapolis 
market, was prepared for 
Highland’s entry this month. 
“Highland moving in will not 
cost us any market share,” 
said Lee Schoenfeld, market- 
ing vice president. “There is 
plenty of business here with 
the retail climate getting even 
healthier for CE.”

Newmark & Lewis is the lead-

main emphasis in expansion 
will be in Connecticut and the 
upper Westchester County 
area of New York. Sales grew 
50.7 percent to $214 million 
from $142 million last year.

Specialty Parts 


By Richard C. Halverson 
Nationwide DSN Report 

If discount automotives buyers get 
discouraged by dismal sales projec- 
tions for things motorists “need,” 
such as spark plugs, they might cheer 
4 by looking at sales projections for 

ermarket parts for pickups, vans, 
and four-wheel drive vehicles. 

The pickup truck has become the 
“hot rod of the ’80s,” and owners are 
spending thousands of dollars to 
make it look better or run hotter. 

The Specialty Equipment Manu- 
facturers Association (SEMA), 
Whittier, Calif., provides a look at 
the specialty automotive market in 
its 1986 study, conducted by Lang 
—- Resources, Midland Park, 

In a survey of 1,200 buyers of spe- 
cialty equipment, Lang found that 
the average consumer spent $1,880 in 
1985 with discount stores and auto 
chains snaring a sizable share of those 
discretionary automotive dollars. 

And market analysts say the dis- 
count segment could do even better if 
it were to follow the example of The 
Pep Boys—Manny, Moe & Jack (see 
story, page 1) by installing the 
parts it sells and paying attention to 
the predicted rise in the number of 
older drivers who tend to prefer 
DIFM (do-it-for-me) over DIY (do-it- 
yourself). 

The study contains information 
with numerous implications for dis- 
counters: 

@® Spending Declines with Age. 
Customers aged 21 to 24 spent an av- 
erage of $2,400, compared to $1,560 
for those aged 35 to 39. 

@ Strong Brand Loyalty. Of the to- 
tal number of buyers, 75 percent had 
a specific brand in mind before they 
stepped inside a store. Only 5 percent 
bought another brand if a store was 
out of the one they wanted. A third of 
customers allowed a store to order 
the brand they requested, while two- 
thirds went to another store. 

@ Psychographic Factors. The 
most important factor behind a pur- 
chase is how it will make a vehicle 
perform. A high second factor is how 
it makes buyers “feel” about their ve- 
hicles. Another major factor is how 
customers think the purchase will

@ Discount Store Market Share. 
Discounters hauled in the lion’s 
ssare—29 percent—of dollars that 
“light buyers” spent on specialty 
products. Light buyers were defined 
as those spending less than $500 per 
year on specialty automotive acces- 
sories (see charts). Discounters tied 


for the largest chunk—22 percent— 
of dollars that “medium buyers” 
spent. And they placed fourth at 17 
percent for the share of dollars that 
“heavy buyers” spent. Medium buy- 
ers spend $500 to $1,000, while heavy 
buyers are those spending more than 
$1,000 per year on specialty automo- 
tive accessories. 

Moreover, manufacturers sur- 
veyed expect that discount stores 
and auto chains will “substantially in- 
crease their retail share” in coming 
years at the expense of other retail- 
ers, such as full-line automotive parts 
dealers and performance/speed 
shops. 
® Sales Trends. From 1981 to 1985, 
specialty equipment sales grew at an 
average annual rate of 11.6 percent, 
more than twice the rate of the total 
automotive aftermarket. From 1986 
to 1990, manufacturers expect the 
specialty market to grow by an aver- 
age of 11.2 percent a year, more than 
2% times the growth rate of the total 
market, which is expected to slow 
even more.

“Traditionally, consumer 
spending on specialty equip- 
ment products declines as age 
increases.; Programs will be 
needed to market specialty 
equipment products to middle 
and older age categories, 
which will have the highest 
growth rates,” the Lang study 
cautioned. 

@ More Installation Service. 
“The population profile shift 
from younger to older con- 
sumers will reduce do-it-your- 
self activity. Retailers will 
have to increase installation 
services to appeal to the rapid 
growth of buyers in their 30s, 
40s and 50s. Greater installa- 
tion services will help expand 
the size of the specialty equip- 
ment market.” 

@ Population Shift. Moun- 
tain states will experience the 
sharpest growth in coming 
years. Growth in the West and 
South will be positive for the 
specialty market, the SEMA 
study concluded, because con- 
sumers there tend to buy more 
specialty products, such as 
pickup truck accessories. 

The specialty market is ex- 
tremely profitable, said Jim 
Lang, head of the research 
firm, because margins are 
good, and tickets and turn- 
over are high. 

Opinions of market analysts 
differ as to why the specialty 
market is growing, while the 
general aftermarket lan- 
guishes. 

“People are keeping their 
cars longer,” said Walter Lah- 
mann Jr., president of Ameri- 
can Specialty Equipment 
ee Long Island, N.Y., and 
a SEMA board member. “I 
think that helps our market. 
When you keep a car for five to 
10 years, you tend to upgrade 
the appearance and perfor- 
mance.”

Hopkinton, Mass.-based

Economists reported one 

positive aspect of the trade 

icture for the U.S. footwear 
industry—the declining value 
of the dollar. 

“The gap between the U.S. 
factory price and the price of 
imports, which had widened 
from 1982 to 1985 as the U.S. 
dollar strengthened, finally 
began to narrow,” they re- 
ported. Even so, in the first 
six months of 1986, the aver- 
age U.S. factory price for non- 
rubber shoes was $13.77, 
while the import price was less 
than half the U.S. cost— 
$5.99. 

However, economists said 
the price disparity is expected 
to be below 100 percent when 
reviews of 1986 figures are 
completed. 


Rate of Decline to Slow 


Of equal significance were 
government predictions that 
the declining value of U.S. 
currency will slow the nine- 
year slide in the value of do- 
mestic shipments. While U.S. 
footwear shipments are ex- 
pected to decline for the 10th 
straight year, the rate of de- 
cline should slow to 5.3 per- 
cent in 1987. Moreover, econo- 
mists predicted an average 
annual rate of decline of only 3 
percent for the next five 
years. 

Another 1986 trend which 
could be good news for the 
U.S. footwear industry was 
the increased use of leather by 
domestic manufacturers. 

“Profit margins are higher 
for leather footwear,” re- 
searchers said. Leather’s 
share in 1986 was estimated at 
57 percent, up from 55 percent 
the previous year. 

Rubber and plastic foot- 
wear, like the non-rubber sec- 
tor, continued a “long-term 
decline” in 1986, researchers 
reported. Shipments of “pro- 
tective” footwear (e.g., ga- 
loshes) increased 13 percent, 
but rubber-soled, “fabric-up- 

er” shoe shipments (athletic 
ootwear and espadrilles) 
dropped 20 percent. In addi- 
tion, economists predicted 
that U.S. shipments of “fab- 
ric-uppers” will continue to 
decline in 1987 “as imports re- 
place domestic production.”
