RETAIL MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT SERIES 


DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, June 8, 1987 


Survey Reveals Computerization Improves Bottom Line Profits 


By Randy Allen and Daniel McCarthy 


a 


Touche Ross & Co, 


OS and MIS are key elements in 
the success of major retailers 
today, and they will play an 
even greater role in that success in the 
future. The results of the 1986 Nation- 


P 


al Retail Merchants Association/ 


Touche Ross survey of POS indicate 
that retailers are investing heavily in 
this technology and receiving a num- 
ber of types of benefits from the in- 
creasing widespread use of POS sys- 
tems. Respondents in the current 
survey are getting much more from 
their systems than did the retailers in 
the 1977 and 1981 surveys. It appears, 
however, that the full potential benefit 
of this investment is still to be reaped. 


Survey Respondents 


Responses to the survey came from 
retail companies throughout the 
world, representing more than $233 
million in sales, generated in over 
68,000 stores. 

Regarding POS installation, 45 per- 
cent of all respondents have converted 
fully to POS, a 10 percent inerease 
over the 35 percent of the 1981 survey. 
The percentage with no POS has fallen 
dramatically, from 43 percent in 1981 
to 5 percent today. 


Point-of-Sale Environment 


In the 1981 study, most retailers did 
not believe POS could be cost-justified 
because of the difficulty in assigning 
dollar values to such factors as im- 
proved information and better mer- 
chandise planning and control. Today, 
however, respondents feel that POS is 
cost-justified and does pay for itself. 
Experience has shown that the infor- 
mation generated through POS is 
readily translated into dollars at the 
bottom line. 

With more than 243,000 terminals 
installed by the respondents to this 
survey, there is and will be an even 
greater used-equipment market grow- 
ing for POS terminals. The majority, 
87 percent of the companies, bought 
new equipment but the remainder 
bought used equipment. The manufac- 
turers are the purchase source in just 
over half of the companies, 55 percent. 

NCR and IBM generally rank No. 1 
or No. 2 in POS among the respon- 
dents regardless of type or size. 

Portable data-capture units are 
used extensively in the industry to re- 
cord sales and inventory and to place 
orders. 


Implementation and Use 


In general, respondents in the cur- 
rent survey have realized more of the 
expected benefits than did the 1977 or 
1981 participants, especially in the 
area of merchandising main. More 
than 72 percent of the respondents 
who expected POS to lead to improved 
gross margins achieved their goal, 
whereas less than 20 percent in the 
1977 survey realized that benefit. 

Most of the responding companies 
who have POS are communicating 
their data to a host computer. A num- 
ber of the respondents use a combina- 
tion of methods for completing this 
communication, depending on the type 
of store and the age of the equipment. 
Of those firms not currently communi- 
cating to a host, 13 percent plan to im- 
plement some type of communications 
ability in the future. 

The responding companies have a 
broad range of options for handling 
credit and accounts receivable. Bank- 
card and credit authorization is the 


most extensively used application. 
Among those who do sot currently 
perform this authorization, 13 percent 
plan to implement it within the next 
three years. Interestingly, very few 
firms have any concrete plans to imple- 
ment debit card processing, an applica- 
tion driven by market pressures rath- 
er than by retailers. 

Firms that are fully installed make 
much greater use of ie POS capabili- 
ties. Particularly among discount 
chains, sku data is almost universally 
captured, while hard goods chains 
have had significant progress in the 
use of price lookup. Evidence of the in- 
terest in this subject is seen in an addi- 
tional 23 percent of the respondents 
having plans to implement price look- 
up in the future. 

Retailers have come to expect a 
wide array of benefits from their POS 
systems. The benefits most frequently 
sought are faster, more accurate infor- 
mation and additonal sales informa- 
tion. In the area of disappointments, a 
number of retailers did not realize in- 
creased sales or reduced bad debts. 

As compared to 1981, it is in the key 
areas of increased sales, reduced bad 
debt, and ability to handle peak season 
that the realization of benefits has in- 
creased. More companies have come to 
expect merchandising benefits. 

he number of full-time equivalents 
assigned to the initial POS implemen- 
tation nas increased substantially 
since 1981. While the greatest empha- 
sis is from the areas of E DP, store op- 
erations and training, a number of 
firms are also assigning staff from mer- 
chandising and finance. 


On-going Operations 


In general, the useful life of the re- 
spondents’ equipment is considered to 
range from five years to 11 years. 
Since the installed base has a mean age 
of about four years, many firms are be- 
ginning to think about replacing their 
equipment. 

Approximately 50 percent of the 
firms, regardless of segment, plan to 
begin replacing their equipment with-

Back-Office Environment 


Who has an in-house computer? Al- 
most everybody, regardless of seg- 
ment, region and even size. Though 
IBM is the number one primary back 
room minicomputer, other makes are 
found in significant numbers. Interest- 
ing breaks from the pattern show 44 
hai of discount chains using the 

EC computer and 22 percent of the 
soft goods specialty companies using 
Burroughs. Twenty-two percent of 
varity chains use Honeywell. The vari- 
ances are explained in part by the in- 
ternational composition of the sample. 

In choosing microcomputers, re- 
tailers overwhelmingly chose IBM. 
Texas Instruments, however, is the 
choice of 57 percent of the soft goods 
specialty chains who responded to the 
question. 

As a group, the respondents spend 
— ot over 1 percent of their sales on 
MIS. The actual range can be quite 
broad, however, with firms reporting 
as little as 0.1 percent or as much as 
over 2 percent. As firms grow in size, 
they do gain some economies of scale. 
However, the rate of decrease falls off 
as the percentage reaches 1 percent. 

As would be expected, personnel ac- 
counts for the largest MIS expendi- 
ture, ranging from 36 percent amon 
variety chains to 56 percent among so 
goods specialty companies. There is 
also a wide range of budget figures in 
the area of POS equipment, mainframe 
equipment, operating software, voice 
communications and maintenance. 

The amount budgeted for personnel, 
as a percent of sales, declines with the 
increase in total sales. Among the 
smallest companies, 55 percent of the 
MIS budget is dedicated to personnel, 
whereas the largest companies dedi-

Systems and Processing 


In terms of applications in 
the selling cycle, sales audit

The print-only ticket is still

while UPC has made tremen-

ing fairly rapidly. 

Today more department 
store companies (59 percent) 
are keying into POS than were 
doing so in 1981 (43 percent). 
In contrast, the 48 percent of 
discounters keying data at 
POS today is a decline from 
the 62 percent in 1981. 

Among specialty stores, 
both hard goods and soft 
goods, this year’s percentages 
(50 percent and 44 percent, re- 
spectively) keying at POS are 
much higher than in 1981 (28 
percent). 

As for wanding and scan- 
ning at POS, even the small 
percentage of stores repre- 
sents an increase over the 
numbers given in 1981. There- 


fore, progress is being made in 
these technologies. 

In spite of the small number 
of firms currently scanning, 
almost 40 percent plan to in- 
troduce this procedure in the 
future. Such plans are com- 
mon in all segments. 

What types of machine- 
readable tickets are retailers 
planning to introduce? The 
dominant preference appears 
to be EAN/UPC, which is pre- 
ferred by almost half the re- 
spondents. The bar code is in 
the plans of a number of dis- 
counters (21 percent), depart- 
ment stores (33 percent) and 
specialty store companies (29 
percent and 48 percent). 
Twenty-one percent of dis- 
count companies also show 
significant interest in OCR-A. 

Among those firms not 
planning to use UPC ticketing 
in the future, those firms with 
sales under $50 million domi- 
nate; 68 percent of retailers in 
that category have no plans 
for EAN/UPC. At the other 
end of the scale, 86 percent of 
those with sales over $350 mil- 
lion eventually plan to use 
UPC in the future. 

For the most part, as the 
size of the firm increases, so 
does the frequency of elec- 
tronic communication with 
suppliers. For instance, 
among firms with sales under 
$50 million, 73 percent state 
that they have no plans at 
present to institute electronic 
communication, while a ma- 
jority of firms with sales over 
$150 million plan to do so with- 
in the next year. The primary 
data being transmitted elec- 
tronically to suppliers is for in- 
voices and purchase orders. 

The complete results of this 
survey have been pubiished in 
book form in “Point-Of-Sale: 
Current Trends and Beyond,” 
written by Randy Allen and 
Danie] McCarthy. It is avail- 
able from NRMA.

New Costco Card Policy 
Shuns Casual Shoppers 


By Peter Hisey 

PALM HARBOR, Fla. — 
Costco, the Seattle-based 
wholesale club chain, opened 
its 40th store here with an in- 
dustry innovation—general 
public memberships which 
cost more to buy than their 
business memberships. 

Group members, who used 
to have an option between a 
free membership, which al- 
lowed them to buy at 5 percent 
above the wholesale cost, and 
an expensive “gold card’’ 
which allowed them to buy at 
the same cost as_ business 
members, will no longer have 
a choice of memberships. 
They will now pay $30 for a 
yearly membership, versus 
$25 for business members, 
and existing free member- 


ships will not be renewed 
when they expire. 

In return, consumers will 
be able to buy at the same 
prices as business members. 
The public normally pays a 5 
percent surcharge for mer- 
chandise at wholesale clubs. 

“We’ve been phasing out 
the old group memberships 
since last fall,” said Costco 
president Jim Sinegal, “and all 
new openings offer only the 
($30 group] gold card.” The 
gold card allows group mem- 
bers to buy at the same price 
as wholesale customers. 

Industrywide, group mem- 
bers have traditionally re- 
ceived cards for free or for a 
relatively minor investment of 
$10 or $15 for a lifetime mem-

Zayre Will Accept Joint Discover Card 


FRAMINGHAM, Mass. — Zayre has signed an agree- 
ment to accept the Discover Card, a revolving-credit card 
owned by Sears/Dean Witter. Zayre will accept the card at 


all of its subsidiaries except BJs Wholesale Clubs, which - 


doesn’t accept any credit cards. Zayre chairman Malcolm 
Sherman noted that the Discover Card has “demonstrated 
consumer acceptance.” According to Discover, its card 
“provides consumers with a revolving line of credit, a sav- 
ings account paying money market interest rates, and a 
Cashback Bonus each time the card is used.” 


Jamesway Sets Sights on $700M Sales 


SECAUCUS, N.J.— Jamesway Corp. is targeting 
sales for the current fiscal year ending Jan. 30, 1988, at a 
record $700 million, Herbert Fisher, chairman, said at the 
retailer’s recent annual meeting. Last fiscal year’s sales 
were a record $612 million. Fisher also said the company 
would open a total of 15 stores this year, the largest num- 
ber of openings ever for the company. In 1988, Jamesway 
is scheduled to add another 15 units. The company also 
said that shareholders approved an amendment to the re- 
stated certificate of incorporation, increasing the compa- 
ny’s authorized number of common shares to 30 million 
from 20 million. 


Sears Buys Specialty Eye Care Centers 


CHICAGO — Sears has made the first move in its re- 
cently annuunced strategy of acquiring new specialty re- 
tailers. The company announced plans to acquire San An- 
tonio-based Eye Care Centers of America, which operates 
a 41-store chain of “optical superstores” under the names 
Eye Pro Express, 20/20 Eyecare and Eye Masters, mainly 
in the Southwest. Under the agreement, which must be 
ratified by Eye Care Center stockholders, current ceo 
Jack Gunion will continue in his post and report to Sears 
specialty merchandising president Alfred Goldstein. 


Tower Cancels Its Fall Housewares Show 


ATLANTIC CITY, N.J. — Tower Conference Man- 


naa Sey has canceled its Fall Housewares Show sched- 
uled for Sept. 27 to 30 here. The absence of Tower Confer- 
ence which, like The Interface Group, had pursued. the 
housewares show opportunity that was created after the 
National Housewares Manufacturers Association’s initial 
decision to switch to a single show format—establishes 
HouseWorld Expo and the NHMA show as the sole con- 
tendors for the trade show audience.

Will Feature Magazine-Type Format 


By Arthur Markowitz 

WHITE PLAINS, N.Y. — 
Trintex has begun to lift the 
curtain on its long-awaited 
computer videotex service 
that has been touted as usher- 
ing in a new era in direct mar- 
keting and home shopping. 

Trintex’s technology uses a 
computer and telephone to 
provide consumers with inter- 
active videotex in a magazine- 
type format that bundles at- 
home shopping and services 
like banking and travel reser- 
vations with news updates, fi- 
nancial reports, health and fit- 
ness features and entertain- 
ment like games, puzzles, 
cartoons and movie reviews. 

Trintex can function only on 
IBM, IBM-compatibles, Ap- 
ple. and other high-powered 
computers with 512K capabili- 
ty that are tied into a 1200 
baud modem. Trade observ- 
ers question the current size of 
this specific market and the 
number of consumers willing 
to purchase this equipment. 

Harry E. Smith, Trintex 
vice president, product and 
commercial development, 
who presented “peeks” at the 
service in three separate pre- 
sentations, asserted, “Trintex 
will establish the home once 
and for all as the shopping cen- 
ter without peer. For many 
categories of merchandise, we 
think it will become the shop- 
ping medium of choice.” 

He added: “Trintex lets you 
buy what you want when you 
want to buy it; it’s very per- 
sonal, focused and totally user 
controlled.” 

Trintex is a four-year-old 
joint venture of IBM and 
Sears involving 500 people 
that has already cost the part- 
ners an estimated $450 mil- 
lion. IBM views the service as 
helping to transform home

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, June 22, 1987 


lh 


CHICAGO — Despite nearly flat sales indica- 
tive of a maturing industry, many housewares 
manufacturers reported they expect to raise prices 
this year, according to the National Housewares 
Manufacturers Association’s annual study of the 
housewares industry. 

On average, prices are expected to rise by 6.5 
percent in 1987, with the largest percentage of sup- 
pliers, 20 percent, anticipating increases at the 5 
ghee level, according to the study conducted by 

. Angell & Associates for the NHMA. Price in- 
creases averaged 6.1 percent in 1986, when about a 
third of manufacturers reported higher prices. 


More than half of those surveyed expect price in- 
creases in 1987. 


Declining Dollar is a Factor 


Forty-four percent of respondents to the survey 
cited the declining dollar as a factor in the rising 
heey of their goods. The cost of materials, over- 

ead, labor, inflation and, to a lesser extent, higher 
freight costs were also mentioned as contributing 
factors to the decision to raise prices. 

Overall, housewares industry sales were up 1.9 
percent to $23.6 billion last year, a figure below 
1984’s volume level. In real dollars—subtracting 
the impact of a 1.1 percent inflation rate—sales 
grew by only 0.8 percent. About $20.5 billion of the 
total industry sales were through retail outlets last 
year, according to the survey by the Chicago- 
based research firm. 

The higher manufacturers’ prices may be offset 
somewhat by suppliers’ growing tendency to sell 
directly to retailers. Nearly nine out of 10 vendors 
in the survey said they sold directly to retailers 
rather than-through distributors. In contrast, 20 
years ago, more than half of the total housewares 
business was handled by wholesalers. 

Discounters and mass merchandisers, among 
the retailers fueling this direct-sell trend, continue 
to command the major share of the housewares 
marketplace. The mass merchandisers’ share rose 
3 percentage points last year to 35 percent of indus- 
try business—broadening the gap between that re- 
tail channel and all others. 

Retail housewares sales by mass merchandisers 
grew to $7.2 billion last year, up from $6.1 billion in 
1985. 

In specific product categories, mass merchan- 
disers were dominant. These outlets generated 41 
percent of furniture dollars, 62 percent of plastic- 
ware and 47 percent of outdoor products, accord- 
ing to the survey. 

Catalog showrooms returned to their historic 
third place ranking under department stores due 
to a drop of 5 percentage points in market share 
and an cena pes percentage point gain by 
department stores. Department stores garnered 
11 percent of all retail housewares business, while 
catalogers captured 7 percent of that total. In dol-

lars, department stores generated $2.3 billion from 
housewares categories, up from $1.9 billion the 
previous year. Catalog showrooms’ volume fell 
from $2.3 billion in 1985 to $1.4 billion last year. 

Housewares/hardware stores rang up 5 percent 
of the business, while drug stores and variety 
stores each registered 4 percent market share fig- 
ures. Home centers were next with a 3 percent 
share of the market. 

Membership warehouse clubs were listed for the 


first time among retail outlets tracked by the 
housewares association. These units garnered 2 
percent of retail housewares business for a total of 
about $410 million. 

While overall sales have not skyrocketed for 
manufacturers, the percentage of the business 
handled by larger companies continues to rise. 
Manufacturers doing over $5 million worth of busi- 
ness increased their share of the total to nearly 40 
percent, from about 12 percent in 1966. In con- 
trast, companies under $1 million have seen their 
share of the market decline from about 45 percent 
in 1966 to less than 25 percent last year. 

In colors, white, blue, pastel and mauve were 
the top sellers in 1986 in both the decorative acces- 
sories and bath accessories categories. White and 
blue were tops in kitchen accessories and serving/ 
buffet accessories while white dominated the color 
preferences in kitchen appliances, closet and out- 
door accessories. 

Looking at the future color trends that will drive 
sales in this industry, manufacturers see white los- 
ing popularity in most areas. While white contin- 
ued td be the leading color in every category by a 
large margin in 1986, it is not expected to sell as 
well next year, according to manufacturers. For 
example, white’s popularity is expected to decline 
from 26 percent of sales to 20 percent next year in 
decorative accessories and from 64 percent to 54 
percent’ in closet accessories.

Sluggish Sales in Texas Contribute 
To FedGroup’s Income Loss for ’86 


CITY OF COMMERCE, 
Calif.— Poor sales in oil-de- 
pendent Texas contributed to 
a $5.23 million net income loss 
for The Federated Group in 
fiscal 1986. 

Unlike some other retail- 
ers, the West Coast-based 
consumer electronics chain 
said it is not pulling out of Tex- 
as, where it runs some 20 CE 
superstores. Wilfred 
Schwartz, chairman of the 
board for the company, told 
DSN, “We have made the de- 
cision to continue our opera- 
tions in Texas.” 

The company’s extensive 
expansion plan—which took it 
from 15 stores four years ago 
to its current 65—“has cost us 


rofitability,” according to 

chwartz. However, he said 
the company is not retreating 
in its effort to make a substan- 
tial stand in the CE market. 

Schwartz said Federated 
has “managed to tailor our op- 
erations” in Texas, through 
staff reductions and the clos- 
ing of some smaller stores. 

ederated Group said it has 
enlisted the financial help of 
Goldman, Sachs & Co., while 
also restructuring its $48 mil- 
lion credit line. 

The company’s loss for the 
year ended March 1 followed a 
net earnings gain of $10.7 mil- 
lion on sales of $364 million the 
previous year. The compan 
did post 1986 sales of $430 mil- 


lion, and benefited from an 
$864,000 after tax gain result- 
ing from a change in inventory 
costing methods. 

Results for the recent 
fourth quarter showed a net 
income loss of $6.04 million on 
sales of $136 million, com- 

ared to a net income gain of 

2.42 million on sales of $123 
million for the same period 
during 19806. 

Looking ahead, Schwartz 
said, “Overall, we expect to 
achieve a moderate level of 
profitability in the current 
year, which together with 
positive cash flow from opera- 
tions, will establish a sound 
base for further growth in the 
future.”

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, June 22, 1987 


LAWN & GARDEN SUPPLEMENT _ 


By Richard C. Halverson 
Nationwide DSN Report 


Discounters Rake In a Share of L & G Biz 


Sales of lawn & garden products, 
including outdoor power equipment, 
lawn furniture and outdoor grills, will 
grow 10 percent to 15 percent in 1987 
from the 1986 total of $29.9 billion, 
predicted Chuck Greenridge, presi- 
dent of Greenridge & Associates, Ev- 
ergreen, Colo., an L & G industry 
consultant. 

Moreover, the discounter share of 
the market is creeping up from its 
traditional one-third of total L & G, 
Greenridge said, and should peak at 
40 percent over the next 10 years. 

In other positive news for retailers 
of L & G products, trends in consum- 
er purchasing, such as the popularity 
of ready-to-use formulations and 
larger sizes in green goods, are re- 
sulting 1 in better margins. And, the 
nation’s population is experiencing a 
surge in the number of consumers in 
the 30-year-old to 49-year-old brack- 
et, the big-spender segment of L & G 
consumers that accounts for 44 per- 
cent of sales. 


Discounters Impact In L & G 


Indicating the growing importance 
of discounters in L & G, the K mart 
label in garden chemicals is now the 
second largest seller in the country, 
trailing only Ortho, Greenridge said. 

According to Greenridge, some 
major L & G consumer trends that 
will impact discounters include: 

a caccaes are opting for smaller 
sized gardens, but increasingly they 
want larger sizes of nursery stock 
and expect to see a broader selection 
of varieties; 

e They are dragging their feet on 
pre-season purchases and _ instead 
wait until the weather breaks and 
plant or apply products the same day 
they buy; 

@ Although the gardening season is 
starting later, it is extending later, 
sometimes until after Labor Day or 
even Oct. 1; 

@ Gardeners are willing to pay more 
for ready-to-use formulations, such 
as liquid fertilizers, over dry fertiliz- 
ers, and for convenience packaging, 
such as liquid lawn fertilizer that is 
available in a spray applicator that 
screws onto a hose nozzle. 

The implications for discounters 
are obvious, Greenridge said: They 
should pay attention to smaller and 


Power mowers at Michigan decounter Quality Shores: L & G sales will rise to more than $33 billion in 1987.(DSN photo) 


more convenient packaging, consider 
carrying a broader assortment of 
green goods, including larger sizes, 
and keep L & G departments open 
until at least after Labor Day, in- 
stead of breaking them down in July 
(as some discounters do). 

Sales of green goods at retail will 
total $8 billion in 1987, Greenridge es- 
timated, which compares to the $7.5 
billion in 1986. 

Margins on green goods are the 
highest of any segment of L & G, and 
retailers can squeeze 5 percent to 20 
percent higher margins if they capi- 
talize on the trend of gardeners to 
size up to, for example, a 10-foot tall 
tree from a 3-foot tall tree, Green- 
ridge said. 

Turns are, of course, essential in 
perishable green goods. However, 
proper promotion, display and as- 
sortment can ensure that stock 
moves promptly, Greenridge said. 


The success of green goods deter- 
mines the success of the rest of the 
L & G department, he emphasized. 

The results from early, pre-season 
sales have fallen dramatically, 
Greenridge said. The days when one 
supplier like Scott could drive the 
market with promotions and adver- 
tising are gone, he said. “Customers 
now wait until the weather breaks 
and the bugs start biting before they 
buy. Then they go home and plant the 
same day.” 

In addition, “Ready to use formula- 
tions, although not the cheapest, are 
here to stay,” Greenridge said. Re- 
tailers enjoy better margins on what 
essentially are “watered down” prod- 
ucts, he stressed. 

Lawn furniture represents an im- 
portant growth category, Green- 
ridge said, predicting a 12 percent to 
16 percent gain over the 1986 total of 
$2.2 billion. 


Bruce Butterfield, research direc- 
tor of the National Gardening Associ- 
ation, Burlington, Vt., said retailers 
also stand to benefit from a popula- 
tion bulge in the key 30-year-old to 
49-year-old bracket. 

The first baby boomers turn 40 
next year, and those in that age 
bracket are in their prime home ac- 
quisition years, Butterfield said, and 
account for almost half of all L & G 
sales. Those age 50 and older account 
for 33 percent of sales, he added, 
while those 18 to 29 account for the 
balance of 23 percent of sales. 

“Customers in that age bracket are 
better educated and more affluent,” 
Butterfield said. “They expect value 
for the price,” he emphasized. 

“Lawn and garden can be a very 
profitable, seasonal department,” he 
said, “but quality has to be there.” He 
added that the green goods can be ev-

TROY, Mich. — K mart is seeing 
stars on its silver anniversary. The na- 
tion’s No. 1 discounter has continued 
its 25th Anniversary celebration with 
the release of a “Stars of the Decades” 
baseball card set which features prom- 
inent baseball players from the last 25 
years. Divided equally into stars of the 
’60s, ’70s and ’80s, the 33-card set fea- 
tures such luminaries as Hank Aaron, 
Mickey Mantle, Dwight Gooden, 
Wade Boggs, Willie Mays, Reggie 
Jackson and Dale Murphy. According 
to K mart, about 900,000 of the sets, 
which sell for $1.97 each in all K mart 
stores, were printed. The company ex- 
pects to sell out the card sets by the 
end of the summer. A company spokes- 
man said that the company has no 


plans to reissue the set, or to print a 
second series, “at this time.” Steve 
Ellingboe, editor of Sports Collector’s 
Digest, a well-known weekly hobby 
publication, commented that while the 
set was selling for “$4 or $5” within the 
hobby, there was little or no specula- 
tion on the sets. Apparently 
collectors hoarded a previous K mart 
set that was “burned when a second 
rinting was issued. Sets were going 
Sige ittle as 10 cents,” coe 


‘said. "The set is printed by To Topps: the 


leading producer of sports c in the 

country. The set is but one of “at least a 
dozen” special sets released by various 
retailers throughout the country. Oth- 
er retailers selling the sets include 
F.W. Woolworth and McCrory’s.

tal units, called Nothin’ Fancy stores. 
Full-line stores range from 14,000 
square feet to 30,000 square feet, 
with an average of 24,000 square 
feet, while the Nothin’ Fancy units 
are about 10,000 square feet. 

The chain opened one full-line store 
this spring in Walker, Mich., a sub- 
urb of Grand Rapids, and a down- 
sized unit in Bluffton, Ind. It expects 
to open another of each type by the 
end of the year but hasn’t yet settled 
on locations. A 235,000-square-foot 
distribution center in F Pacing Ohio 
supplies the three-state operation. 

Hilt describes the Nothin’ Fancy 
test units as hard lines convenience 
stores, geared toward the male do-it- 
yourselfer. They carry no apparel, 
consumables, sporting goods or toys. 

All growth will be financed 
through internal profits and con- 
trolled debt, Hilt said. His chain’s 
debt-equity ratio is “good and im- 
proving,” Hilt said. “We have no 
plans at all to go public.” 

In addition, Quality is installing a 
new $2 million IBM point-of-sale sys- 
tem that will permit stores to look up 
promotion prices, eliminating the 
need to re-price promotional goods, 
approve credit online and communi- 
cate with headquarters on such mat- 
ters as the status of shipments. 
Hooked to the chain’s mainframe 
IBM computers, the interactive POS 
system is expected to go online this 
September, starting with Quality’s 


flagship store in Muskegon which is 
near the company headquarters. 

To support its new thrust, last year 
Quality Stores began a $1 million, 30- 
second spot television campaign in 
seven major markets, including 
Grand Rapids, Dayton and South 
Bend, Ind. In addition to the cam- 
paign, the company airs a series of 60- 
second radio spots and puts out two 
to four circulars a month, totaling 1.6 
million inserts a year. 

The chain conducts 8,000 exit in- 
terviews every six months to stay in 
tune with its customers. The tag line 
on both broadcast and print advertis- 
ing and in-store signs is, “You Work 
Too Hard to Pay too Much.” 

Along with price and quality, ser- 
vice is an important part of the value 
Quality Stores offers, he said. “Our 
employees really do care,” said Hilt, 
whose retired father and uncle found- 
ed the company and remain on its 
board of directors. 


Helpful Store Managers 


Visits to three Quality Stores show 
that even store managers drop ev- 
erything to help customers find what 
they’re looking for and explain how to 
use it. 

Product knowledge is an important 
factor in merit raises, said Ken Vug- 
teveen, a senior salesperson at the 
store in Hudsonville, where the chain 
got its start in a 4,000-square-foot 
converted service station 

Hilt noted that the stores take spe- 
cial orders for agricultural! products 
(such as plow shares and rake teeth), 
as well as automotive products (such 
as exhaust pipes and mufflers) and 
major overhauling of power lawn 
mowers. 

To improve relations between ven- 
dors and sales staff, Quality Stores 
this month is putting on a product and 
information show that will bring 
1,000 of its salespeople in touch with 
170 vendors over two days. The 
chain’s own audio visual studio pro- 
duces more than 50 videotapes a year 
for training 1,400 employees. 

Customer surveys show that male 
customers outnumber females two- 
to-one, Hilt said, compared to per- 
haps a one-to-one ratio at K mart. 
“The male customer expects differ- 
ent service.” 

David Bliss, Quality president, 
said the “real strength of the organi- 
zation revolves around its service ori- 
entation.” The chain’s C.A.R.E. pro-

Pickup Accessories Market 


One new trend is that a huge 
market is developing for pick- 
up truck accessories and, to a 
limited extent, performance 
market accessories. 


Some of the more popular | 


truck accessories include: run- 
ning boards, sliding rear win- 
dows, lighting accessories, 
truck bed liners and truck bed 
tool boxes. 


Limited Speed Accessories 


In a limited way, discount- 
ers can handle speed perfor- 
mance accessories, even 
though they may lack sales- 
people who are experienced in 
the field. 

Discounters can successful- 
ly sell the lighter stuff, such as 
under-the-hood dress-up kits, 
even if they can’t handle the 
heavier speed performance 
products. 

An under-the-hood dress- 
up kit typically would sell at 
discount for $39.99 and consist 
of such chromium items as a 
valve cover, air cleaner cover, 
oil cap and dip stick. _ 

Although the dyed-in-the- 
wool performance speed freak 
leans toward brand names, 
brand names for the lighter 
equipment appear to make no 
difference to the consumer.

Discounter Apparel Sales to Total $24.9B 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Apparel will continue to be the 
leading volume category for full-line 
discount department stores this 
year. Taken together, ladies’, men’s 
and children’s wear will generate 
$24.9 billion in sales by year-end, ac- 
cording to DSN research. 

On average, full-line discounters 
will devote some 17,800 square feet of 
selling space to these apparel catego- 


ries, which will grr roughly 20 
percent of total full-line discount 
store sales. 

In home products, housewares 
products, including personal care, 
small electrics, non-electrics and 
RTA furniture, will be the leading 
volume category. Full-line discount- 
ers are expected to total $11.4 billion 
in housewares this year, while devot- 
ing an average of about 7,450 square 


feet of selling space per store to the 
category. Consumer electronics is 
expected to chip in another $6.3 bil- 
lion at full-line discount stores. 
Hardware, including paint, will 
enerate the largest sales figure, 
.7 billion, in full-liners’ hard lines 
area. Automotives will add another 
$5.5 billion, while health & beaut 
aids will contribute $5.9 billion to full- 
line discount stores’ sales this year.

A shakeout among consumer elec- 
tronics chains, which began in 1986 
with the closing of Pacific Stereo, is 
expected to continue in 1987 due to 
flattening sales and rapid expansion 
of many retailers into each other’s 
markets. 

Six leading consumer electronics 
chains have moved up over the last 
year to be included in the nation’s top 
15 CE chains. Ranked seventh in the 
country is an Edison, N.J.-based 
two-store chain, Tops Appliances, 
which grew 41 percent from $185 mil- 
lion to $260 million in 1986. 

The fastest growing chain last 
year, Minneapolis-based Best Buy, 
took over the eighth position, with a 
112 percent increase from $113 mil- 
lion to $239 million in 1986. American 
TV, a six-store chain based in Madi- 
son, Wis., grew 6 percent last year to 
become the 12th on CE chain in 
the country with sales of $160 million. 

The other three newcomers to the 
DSN list of the top CE specialists, 
The Wiz, Trader Horn and Brick 
Church, all compete in the greater 
New York market, one that is so com- 
petitive that even Circuit City, the 
nation’s leader, exited it in 1986. New 
York-based The Wiz, the 11th largest

Top Off-Pricers Achieve Sales Gains in Difficult Market 


Nationwide DSN Report 
After a harsh shakeout period that 
many believe is not yet over, several 
of the stronger apparel off-price 
chains are refining their merehandis- 
ing strategies in order to continue to 
rosper in this hotly contested mar- 
et. 
To achieve improved growth going 
forward, the top three chains have 
undergone key management changes 
or company restructuring over the 
— 12 months, reflecting just how 
inely tuned a chain has to be to com- 
pete effectively. 


Yet despite the recent tough 
times, sales for these off-price appar- 
el specialists continue to grow, cut- 
ting into the discount soft goods pie 
dominated by the K marts, Wal- 
Marts and Zayres. 

Marshalls, the off-price division of 
Melvilie Corp., and T.J. Maxx, Zayre 
Corp.’s off-price chain, remained 
Nos. 1 and 2, respectively, dominat- 
ing the remainder of the field. How- 
ever, a closer look at these two bil- 
lion-dollar-plus chains show two 
distinctly different paths traveled 
last year. 


Marshalls’ sales were up last year 
but its earnings were down, and by 
the end of the year it became appar- 
ent that changes in strategy, as well 
as in management, were required. 

Over the years, Marshalls had be- 
come a dumping ground for all kinds 
of brands, with store management as 
concerned with price points and 
keeping the rapidly expanding chain 
supplied with enough product as with 
anything else. In the process, Mar- 
shalls’ traditional targeting of the de- 
partment store shopper became less 
of a priority, which led to a stagnation

Organizations want help

Introducing the PDI 
Employment Inventory (ED 
from Personnel Decisions, Inc. -

need 


Testing for honesty has become the target of 
increasing nationwide criticism over the past several 
years. Legal challenges to the reliability, validity, and 
intrusiveness of both the polygraph an honesty 
testing have created the need for a new instrument 
properly validated to meet governmental and 
professional psychological standards. 


Personnel Decisions, Inc. developed this completely 
new instrument to meet the need. 


The EI, a proven, affordable 
predictor of motivated and 
dependable employees 


Validity data from over 150,000 applicants and 
employees has shown that EI scores correlate with 
job performance resulting from. motivation, 
dependability, and responsibility. The EI can save 
money through decreased inventory shrinkage, fewer 
worker compensation claims, lower turnover, and 
reduced absenteeism. 


PDI maintains a continuing program of test 
validation research to assure an even broader and 
more accurate application of the Employment 
Inventory to an organization’s needs. 


Personnel Decisions, Inc. - 
Setting the standards in 
Staffing decisions 


The PDI Employment Inventory has been developed 
based on over 20 years of research experience in 
test development and validation at Personnel 
Decisions, Inc. 

PDI is nationally recognized as an expert in 
identifying and selecting conscientious, reliable 
employees. A half-million individuals have been 
screened using PDI’s techniques to select the right

officers and fire fighters, security personnel, prison 
guards, nuclear facility operators, ‘and others. PDI 
testing methods have withstood each legal challenge.

K MART | “ANNUAL REPORT 


TROY, Mich. — A changing of the 
guard is under way at K mart Co 
but the move won’t slow down t e 
$23.8 billion discounter’s drive to be- 
come the nation’s dominant retailing 
conglomerate. 

e change in top management 
comes as the country’s leading dis- 
counter celebrates its 25th anniver- 
sary. And retiring chairman and chief 
executive officer Bernard M. Fauber 
forecast that sales this year for the 
entire company will pass $26 billion. 

Fauber, who has been K mart’s top 
executive since 1980, will retire later 
this year. In May, Samuel G. Left- 
wich retired as vice chairman, while 
five months earlier Norman G. ‘Milley 
retired as president, K mart Stores, 
the retailing heart of the corporation. 

The team of executives, headed by 
Joseph E. Antonini, currently presi- 
dent and chief operatin officer, 
which was groomed to lead the com- 
pany, have a clearly marked out path 
to follow to reach the $26 million sales 
goal while strengthening K mart’s 
core discount store operation and 
continuing the parent’s retailing di- 
versification. 


Company Goal 


Fauber enunciated the company’s 
overarching goal as “making each one 
of our retail nameplates a destination 
place. This means that any of the four 
types of stores . . . is the store to go 
to first, if you are in the market to buy 
those kinds of products.” 

The 2,204 K mart discount stores 
account for 89.5 percent of the par- 
ent’s revenue~, a slight decline from 
the 91.3 percent share in 1985. The 
discount arm will again receive a ma- 
jor share of the company’s invest- 
ment for the future, but significant 
resources will be spent on the three 
specialty store arms—Builders 
Square, Pay Less Drug Stores 
Northwest and Waldenbooks—to en- 
able each of these operations to stake 
out larger market shares. 

Besides producing the major share 
of the corporation’s volume, K mart’s 
2,086 U.S. and 118 Canadian units led 
the discount store industry in sales 
last year with $22.1 billion, up 6.3 

ercent from $20.8 billion in volume 
in 1985 from 2,062 U.S. and 118 Cana- 
dian stores. This gain was paced by 
the 5.5 percent increase in same- 
store volume last year as compared to 
a 0.4 percent drop i in 1985.

billion.

Wal-Mart Sets Hot Growth Pace; 


BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Wal- 
Mart’s story can best be told, per- 
haps, by comparing two past DSN 
headlines. “Wal-Mart Sets Its Sights 
on $8.3 Billion in 1985” read a July 
1985 headline. 

Contrast that with this headline, 
printed last month: “Walton An- 
nounces Stock Split; Sees Sales Top- 
ping $19 Billion.” Wal-Mart eventu- 
ally exceeded its 1985 prediction by 
$151 million; there’s little reason to 
suspect that it won’t reach its more 
recent projection (for fiscal 1989) 
with equal ease. 

For 1987, Wal-Mart estimates 
sales in excess of $13 billion, up 41 
percent from a record $11.9 billion in 
the previous year. The company’s 
Sales have grown an average of 37 
percent a year over the last decade, 
from a 1978 total of $678.5 million. 
Net income last year nearly matched 
that figure, at $450 million, up 37 per- 
cent from the previous year’s figure 
of $327.5 million. 

Last year, sales at Wal-Mart’s dis- 
count stores climbed 33 percent to 
$10.2 billion. With its rapidly expand- 
ing Sam’s Wholesale Club division in- 
cluded, Wal-Mart sprinted past the 
1,000-store mark in 1986, ending the 
year at 1,029 units, up from the previ- 
ous year’s 872 units. The company ex- 
pects to have in excess of 1,175 total 
units by the end of this year. 


New Wal-Mart Formats 


Included will be two new Wal-Mart 
formats: the much-heralded 200,000- 
square-foot hypermarket concept, 
which will include grocery, restau- 
rant and specialty outlets, and small- 
er 150,000-square-foot versions, to 
be called Wal-Mart Super Centers. 
The first hypermarkets will open in 
Dallas, Gace Kan., St. Louis and 
Arlington, Tex. The smaller versions 
will premiere near St. Louis, then at 
sites in Oklahoma and Missouri. 

And the impressive performance 
figures continue: Same store sales

years ago. The company operates

Target Assimilates Gemcos; 


MINNEAPOLIS — Target is 
scheduled to open the first wave of its 
50 remodeled Gemco stores this 
month as the company looks to open a 
total of 74 stores in 1987. 

The Gemco-converted locations 
and the new stores give Target a 
stronger presence in existing mar- 
kets, particularly Southern Califor- 
nia. In Los Angeles, 23 stores will be 
added, bringing the total there to 53. 
Target is also aiming at the San Fran- 
cisco Bay area, where 12 stores are 
slated to open by the end of the year. 

Target’s parent, Dayton Hudson 
Corp., acquired over 78 Gemcos from 
iad Stores for about $440 million 
in late 1986. Over 20 of the Gemco 
stores were sold off by Dayton Hud- 
son to real estate interests. The re- 
maining stores then faced extensive 
remodeling: Although the generally 
100,000-square-foot Gemco stores 
were akin in size to the typical Tar- 
gets, the interiors of the stores held 
no similarities. 

In addition to beefing up the South- 
ern California market, the Gemco- 
converted stores also give Target a 
chance to enter the San Francisco 
Bay Area and the state’s Central Val- 
ley region. The upscale retailer is also 
scheduled to open three stores in Las 
be and six in metro Detroit. 

is year Target announced it is 
also interested in entering the Pacific 
Northwest, where en to have up 
to 35 units by 1993. The first group of 
stores is slated to open in the fall of 
1988, when nine stores will open in 
Washington and another three will 
open near Portland, Ore. 


POS System Expanded 


As the company looks to grow from 
its year-end total of 246 stores to 320 
stores, its POS scanning system is 
also scheduled to be expanded. After 
a test period in 1986, Target moved 
forward with the program and antici- 
pates that 110 stores will be on the 
system by year-end. All of the Cali- 
fornia stores are scheduled to have 
the equipment this year, and Target 
expects the scanning project to be 
completed storewide by early 1989. 

Technology innovations were also 
an important aspect of Target’s new 
distribution center at Pueblo, Colo., 
opened in 1986 to service about 50 
stores in Wyoming, South Dakota, 
Montana, Arizona and Colorado. The 
distribution center represents the 
company’s fifth, as Target also has 
centers in Los Angeles, Minneapolis, 
Little Rock, Ark., and Indianapolis.

get now en an employee to the 
entrance of checkout lanes to answer 
inquiries and direct customers.

Despite Problems Zayre On Pace for $8B Sales by 1989 


FRAMINGHAM, Mass. — The 
first half 1987 has been a turbulent 
time for Zayre Corp., the discount, 
specialty and warehouse store chain 
headquartered here. 

Following a disappointing profit 
report in 1986, the company has seen 
the spin-off of its profitable specialty 
operations (T.J. Maxx, Hit or Miss, 
and Chadwick’s of Boston), the resig- 
nation of the chairman of its discount 
store division and rapid expansion of 
its reportedly unprofitable ware- 
house club division consisting of BJ's 
Wholesale Club and HomeClub. 


Reported Sales Gains 


However, the company has report- 
ed sales gains of nearly 20 percent 
through the first third of 1987, aturn- 
around of sorts for the troubled giant, 
which is the fourth largest discount 
chain in the country. 

Fiscal 1986 saw a drop in profits in 
the second quarter and third quarter, 
which was not offset by the compa- 
ny’s strong fourth quarter. Net in- 
come dipped 6 et to $89 million, 
from the 1985 figure of $94.6 million, 
although sales rose 32.6 percent on 
the year to $5.35 billion. 


Warehouse Clubs 


The warehouse club’s segment re- 
ported pretax losses of nearly $12 
million in 1986, $8 million of which 
was attributable to pre-opening ex- 
penses as both BJ’sand HomeClub 
expanded aggressively. The ware- 
house club industry as a whole has 
lost money during — growth over 
the past two years. Zayre attributes 
the ce of the losses to poor per- 
formance of three Chicago BJ’s and 
high inventory shrinkage in both of 
the companies. 

Zayre Stores, which last month 
lost its chairman when Malcolm Sher- 
man resigned, reported reduced pre- 
tax earnings of $129.9 million, down 
from $141.9 million the previous 
year. Over the past three years, 
same store sales increases have de- 


clined regularly, from a 10.4 percent 
gain in 1984 to a relatively weak 4.3 
percent in 1986. 

The company pointed to the same 
store poner Pe ennagee, reduced 
margins, and the negative impact of 
LIFO provisions as reasons for the 
chain’s disappointing 1986 perfor- 
mance. 

T.J. Maxx and Hit or Miss, Zayre’s 
specialty apparel retailers, showed 
steady if unspectacular growth last

it or Miss catalog division, Chad-

ANNUAL REPORT 


Service Merchandise Focuses 


NASHVILLE, Tenn. — This is a 
make or break year for the $2.5 bil- 
lion cataloger Service Merchandise. 

The troubled company has 
stripped down its operation to its 
core catalog business by closing down 
its Mr. HOW warehouse home center 
chain to concentrate on its 303 show- 
rooms, along with the projected 
opening of another seven stores. 

The key question is whether Ser- 
vice Merchandise’s getting back to 
its basic retailing concept—as presi- 
dent and chairman Raymond Zim- 
merman described the company’s 
costly retrenchment—will be enough 
to return the cataloger to its past glo- 
ries when it was one of the most suc- 
cessful showroom chains. 


Shutting Mr. HOW 


Shutting the Mr. HOW division at 
a net loss of $29.8 million stems a ma- 
jor source of Service Merchandise’s 
$46.9 million in red ink, but the com- 
pany still has to stop the hemorrhag- 
ing of $17.1 million in losses from its 
continuing operations. 

The company received a big boost 
inits retrenchment efforts last month 
through the negotiating of two finan- 
cial agreements. 

The first was the successful rene- 
— of its revolving bank credit 

ine, obtaining $147 million at 1.5 per- 
cent over prime, due at the end of 
March 1988. This short-term funding 
for working capital replaced $158 mil- 
lion in revolvin Sank lines of credit 
that matured Tacics the past three 
months of the year. 

The second was authorization from 
its lenders to mortgage some of the 
company’s unmortgaged properties 
to obtain up to $75 million for working 
capital. 

An executive said the company 
needed $11 million less in short-term 
bank financing because cash flow dur- 
ing the first quarter had been greater 
than expected, and the cataloger 
hadn’t needed to borrow then. 

The executive said Service Mer- 
chandise expects monies from these 
agreements along with cash flow 
from operations to provide sufficient 
resources to meet its financial re- 
quirements for the fiscal year. 

~ Qn the merchandising and opera- 

tional side, Service Merchandise’s re- 
are endeavors focus on heighten- 
ing the cataloger’s image among 
consumers as a sharp priced retailer 
of name brand hard lines, with a 
strong in-stock fe wae for the ap- 
proximately 8, sku’s featured in 
its basic book and promoted through 
its stepped-up flyer and newspaper 
ROP advertising effort. 

The company is also putting a 
greater emphasis on technology to 
improve its operations and reduce its 
costs. Among the ~~ being consid- 
ered are turning its Silent cus- 
tomer order unit into an interactive 
computerized terminal that will also 
handle credit card payment, and up- 
grading its telephone ordering sys- 
tem to make it easier for shoppers to 
phone in orders. 

These moves are expected to allow 
Service Merchandise to process a 


greater number of orders without in- . 
creasing its store-level s . The

ters staff, particularly among su

The chain’s financial difficulties 
have resulted in what Zimmerman 
calls a “reduced rate” of growth of 
seven new showrooms (compared 
with 10 showrooms in 1986 and up to 
twice that number in prior years). 
Zimmerman denied security analysts 
and trade reports that the cataloger 
planned to close showrooms. 

One Service Merchandise source 
explained that the cataloger was try- 
ing to make its showrooms more pro- 
ductive and was interested in leasin 
out excess space in larger units. “If 
someone wanted the entire store,” he 
said, “ we would consider relocating 
that showroom to a smaller store if 
we found the right site.” 

The merchandising and operations 
problems that Service Merchandise 
is trying to overcome are evident 
from its performance in 1986. 

Company sales, excluding reve- 
nues from the closed Mr. HOW arm, 
amounted to $2.5 billion, up 12.6 per- 
cent from $2.2 billion in 1985, but its 
bottom line witnessed the wrong kind 
of turnaround, going to a net loss of 
$46.9 million from a net income of 
$10.7 million. 

The reason for last year’s steep 
plunge into an unprofitable operation 
was twofold: the $29.8 million net loss 
from the Mr. HOW closing and— 
more importantly—$17.1 million in 
losses from its continuing core cata- 
log business. 

hile continuing operations re- 
corded a net loss in 1986, the ongoin 
showroom business in 1985 produce 
net earnings of $24.3 million.

volume. To counter this, the catalog- 
er engaged in heavy promotions, 
spending $93.9 million, or 3.7 percent 
of sales, on advertising, up 29.4 per- 
cent from $72.5 million, or 3.2 per- 
cent of sales, in 1985. 

The other was the two-year ad- 
verse impact from the acquisition of 
H.J. Wilson. While the 80 former

sales and helped to boost Service 
Merchandise’s volume, the acquisi- 
tion also had a host of negative im-

Ames’ Sees Brighter Future 
After ’86 Shrinkage Problem 


ROCKY HILL, Conn. — Ames 
Department Stores, the 466-unit dis- 
count and variety store chain head- 
quartered here, entered 1986 with 
expectations of another record year. 
The company had posted record sales 
and earnings ($40.4 million net on 
sales of $1.5 billion) in 1985 and was in 
the process of inco rating its re- 
cently acquired Murphy's Mart 
— through an ambitious remod- 
eling program. 

Remodeling began soon after the 
new year, and by year-end 24 dis- 
count stores (17 of them former Mur- 
phy’s Marts) had been remodeled and 
17 new stores opened. In August, for- 
mer Zayre and Fisher’s Big Wheel 
executive Peter Hollis was named 
the company’s new president, filling 
a position that had been vacant for 
nearly a year. 

At mid-year inventory, Ames ap- 
peared to be headed for a year of 
steady growth, despite declining 
sales in its higher-margin apparel de- 
partments. However, starting some- 
time shortly after mid-year, millions 
of dollars worth of merchandise was 
apparently siphoned out of the com- 
pany’s Secaucus, N.J., distribution 
center. By year-end, when the short- 
age was discovered, the total loss had 
reached $18 million to $20 million. 

Ames immediately launched an in- 
vestigation into the episode, but to 
date there have been few results. No 
one knows, for instance, if the miss- 
ing merchandise even arrived at the 
warehouse. Management has prom- 
ised full results of its investigation 
some time in early September. 

The result of the shrinkage was a 
33 percent drop in earnings to $27.1 
million, which was a bit less than the 
1984 level, on sales of $1.89 billion. 
That event has overshadowed the 
steps Hollis and chairman Herbert 
Gilman have taken to revamp the 
company’s operations.

Sam’s Poised to Become Leader of Membership Chains 


BENTONVILLE, Ark. — After 
just five years of fast-track growth, 
Sam's is poised to become the leading 
membership warehouse chain this 
year, easily passing the industry’s 
founder and premier company, the 
Price Club, in number of stores and 
likely beating it in sales, too. 


Sam’s leapfrogging the Price Club 
will be markedly aided by the acquisi- 
tion last month by its nt Wal- 


Mart Stores, of the Super Saver 
Wholesale Warehouse firm, with 17 
of the latter’s stores due to take on 
Sam’s logo once the transition period 
deal is completed at the end of July. 

Sam’s half-decade growth reflects 
Wal-Mart’s determination to broad- 
en its traditional discount store mar- 
keting to new retailing businesses, 
while also eT the top position 
in the young, but fast maturing, 
membership warehouse field. 

Since Sam’s was launched with just 
three stores in 1983, it has on the av- 
erage doubled its sales as well as size 
(in number of units and footage) in 
each of the subsequent years so that 
in 1986 it reached $1.67 billion in vol- 
ume from 49 clubs that had more than 
5 million square feet of space. 

In the previous year, Sam’s had 
$775 million in sales from 23 stores 
that contained a total of 2.4 million 
square feet. 

In the process, the membership 
warehouse chain has played a larger 
and larger role in Wal-Mart’s explo- 
sive sales growth. In 1985, Sam’s con- 
tributed 9.2 percent of its parent’s 


volume, while last year that share 
grew to 14.1 percent. Sam’s sales 
went up 116.2 percent over the 
course of the two years, while Wal- 
Mart’s volume was substantially 
less—a respective 40.9 percent. 


Sam’s sales, which range between 
$50 million and $75 million a store— 
and with a growing number of units 
reaching $100 million—are two to 
four times more than a typical Wal- 
Mart store. It’s likely that ’s will 
become the sales stallion — 
pace its parent’s revenue growth. 

The membership warehouses also 
are playing two other, equally impor- 
tant roles in the Wal-Mart marketing 
saga. Sam’s has become Wal-Mart’s 
merchandising vehicle in major met- 
ro markets—with the traditional dis- 
count stores spotted mainly in small 
towns and the suburban fringes of 
—— cities—and the striking success 
of the wholesale club division has re- 
sulted in Wal-Mart applying many as- 
pects of this operation to the parent’s 
plans to enter the hypermarket field. 

Last year, more than half of Sam’s 
new stores were spotted in large met- 
ro markets where they complement- 
ed and supported older membership 
warehouses. This move reflects 
Sam’s real estate strategy of market 
dominance and saturation that Wal- 
Mart views as the key to the ongoing 
—- of its membership ware- 

ouses. 

Sam’s learning curve contribution 
to the proposed Hypermart USA hy- 
permarket business includes the 
wholesale club’s low cost distribu- 
tion, the strong appeal of the com- 
bined selling under one roof of food 
and general merchandising, and 
shopper acceptance of bulk displays 
using warehouse-type fixtures. 

Whil e Wal-Mart is applying its 
Sam’s experience to fuel the compa- 
ny’s growth, it hasn’t reined in the 
membership warehouse’s expansion. 
This year, ’s was due to open 20 
membership warehouses, adding an-

CANTON, Mass. — Anticipating a 
faster rate of growth than it has ever

Stores is opening 12 stores to 15

1986 marked the 29th consecu-

its for Hills, with sales up 10.7 pee 
cent over 1985. Last ‘year, Hills 
showed an operating profit of $94.4 
million on $1.343 billion in sales, u 
from the $74.1 million operating prof-

New Stores in 1986

opened and comparable store sales 
increased 6 percent. The company at- 
tributed the increase to high perfor- 
mance in women’s and children’s ap- 
ate as well as electronics, toys, and 

ealth & beauty aids. Operating in-

$41.3 million, was up 27.4 percent to 
$94.4 million. 

The nonrecurring inventory

PAY LESS 


ANNUAL REPORT 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — Pay 
Less NW took advantage of parent 
K mart’s financial clout to expand its 
presence on the West Coast during 
the past year, as it aimed at becoming 
the No. 1 super drug chain within its 
marketplace. 

Just recently, at K mart’s annual 
shareholder meeting, chairman Ber- 
nard Fauber said the discount giant 
wants its Pay Less subsidiary to dou- 
ble in size by 1991, bringing the drug 
chain to nearly 500 stores. 

In 1986, Pay Less opened 39 stores 
and closed four stores, bringing its 
year-end total to 218. Plans for 1987 
call for the opening of 28 stores, and 
currently the chain has 221 units, in- 
cluding the 14-store Wonder World 
variety chain. Looking to the future, 
the company said it plans to open 40 
new stores to 50 new stores a year. 

Growth for the company in recent 
months has been centered on Pay 
Less’ longstanding niche in suburban 
and rural communities. While the 
chain acknowledged it is poised to 
meet K mart’s goals, it said the ex- 
pansion plans can be managed with- 
out leaving its marketing strategy. 
In order to avoid the high cost of ad- 
vertising, Pay Less typically stays 
out of major metropolitan markets. 

“We feel we have enough potential 
for growth in the areas where we op- 
erate now,” said Timothy McAlear, 
executive vice president, Pay Less. 

After a six-year absence, the Pay 
Less name returned to the competi- 
tive Southern California market in 
1986. In Oceanside, Calif., the chain 
opened two sites during the past 
year, and it plans on opening a third 
this fall, as the chain takes advantage 
of the area’s growth potential. Other 
stores located in the region are in 
Barstow, San Dimas, Palmdale and 
Lancaster. 

While the California market will 
continue to be an area of emphasis for 
the chain, McAlear said Pay Less will 
also be looking to do some expansion 
in Washington and Oregon. 

Since many of the new and existing 
Pay Less stores vary so greatly in 
size—from 25,000 square feet to

VENTURE ANNUAL REPORT 


Venture Improves Productivity as 


O’FALLON, Mo.:— Besides fac- 
ing stiff competition in its Midwest 
market from five major discounters, 
the major problem Venture had to 
deal with over the past year was los- 
ing three top executives to Caldor. 

After the May Department Stores 
Company took over Caldor—which 
operates on the East Coast—when it 
acquired Associated Dry Goods last 
October, it shifted Don Clarke , Ven- 
ture chairman, to Caldor chief execu- 
tive officer. Executive vice presi- 
dent, hard lines, Marc Balmuth, was 
shifted to Caldor president, and Mi- 
chael Lynch, senior vice president, 
stores, was brought into the same 
sition at Caldor. They were shifted to 
Caldor to show the chain “the Ven- 
ture way,” said Venture spokesper- 
son, Tony Wasserman. 


May is standardizing 
operating procedures 
between Venture and 
Caldor, but each chain is 
operating independently. 


“It stands to reason, it’s got to hurt 
when you lose that much experi- 
ence,” said Wasserman. Other senior 
level ers had to assume the 
burden of additional responsibilities. 
However, Venture now has largely 
recovered from the loss, he said. 

Replacing Clarke as chairman was 
Philip Otto, who previously was with 
Venture before being shifted to 
Meier & Frank, a May Department 
Store subsidiary in Portland, Ore. 

May is aeons. operatin 
procedures between Venture an 
Caldor, but each discount chain is op- 
erating independently. They share 
no services such as purchasing. 

The official May position is that no 
merger of the chains is in the offing, 
despite potential advantages that 
consolidation might bring, such as in- 
creased purchasing power and ex- 
panded markets. 

Venture faces major competition 
from chains such as Target, upon 
which Venture was patterned, Wal- 
Mart, K mart and Zayre.

states, with stores clustered around 
Chicago and St. Louis. All four new 
stores opened last year are centered 
around those two cities. A merger 
with Caldor would extend Venture’s 
market to the East Coast.

smaller cities, Venture opened last

$165, although it beats K mart’s $126

The Oklahoma opening, the first in

Another of the four new Venture

ANNUAL REPORT 


Strong Sales Prompt Zayre to Spin-Off T.J. Maxx Division 


NATICK, Mass. — T.J. 
Maxx, Zayre Corp.’s off-price 
apparel division, celebrated 
its 10th anniversary by joining 
the $1 billion club in 1986, 

osting sales estimated at 
$1.08 billion for the fiscal year 
ended Jan. 31, 1987. 

T.J. Maxx’s continued suc- 
cess through the first half of 
this year has prompted Zayre 
to spin-off the division, along 
with Hit or Miss and its Chad- 
wick’s of Boston off-price ap- 
parel catalog, in an effort to 
raise capital for expansion. 

The new company, to be 
called TJX Cos., is expected to 
have an initial offering price of 
$24 per share on the New 
York Stock Exchange. Zayre 
expects to generate about 
$192 million in capital from the 
sale of 8.5 ailien shares. 
Zayre will retain 84 percent 
ownership. 

Maurice Segall, chairman of 
Zayre Corp., will be chairman 
of the new TJX Cos. Bernard 
Cammarata, currently chair- 
man of T.J. Maxx and group 
executive of the specialty 
store division at Zayre, will be 
president and chief executive 
officer of the new company. 
Richard Lesser, president of 
T.J. Maxx, will be a senior 
vice president. 

T.J. Maxx, founded by 
Zayre in 1977, has posted im- 
proved sales and earnings fig- 
ures in each of its last five fis- 
cal years and is currently the 
second largest off-price appar- 
el chain in the country. 

Sales were up 38 percent 
last year over 1985. The chain 
also opened 35 new units last 
ey bringing to 226 the num- 

er of stores in operation by 
fiscal year-end. The chain has 
already opened five new units 
over the last five months and 
plans to open about 30 stores 
over the next six months, in- 
oa first expansion into 
the California market. 


California Expansion 


As to the difficulty suggest- 
ed by industry analysts and 
others of expanding into the 
competitive California mar- 
ket, Cammarata said, “When 
we decided to expand into the 
Midwest,everyone said it was 
going to be very difficult. 

e’ve enjoyed great success 
there. I’ve learned over the 
years not to listen to other 
people.” 

ammarata said that for 
now the California units will 
be serviced by the chain’s dis- 
tribution center in Evansville, 
Ind., but that “eventually we 
will develop distribution on 
the West Coast.” 

Cammarata said the T.J. 
Maxx concept is nothing spe- 
cial, but, he added, “It’s the 
execution of the concept that’s 
key. The way you buy, process 
through the warehouse and 
manage the store—that’s the 
difference. It’s an art, not a 
science.” 

The chain, along with Hit or 
Miss and Chadwick’s, has 
stimulated huge i i 


TJX’s net income repre- 
sented 59 percent of Zayre 
Corp. profits last year. The 
previous year, those compa- 
nies delivered 47 percent of to- 
tal income. 

For the first quarter ended 
May 2, Zayre’s earnings were 
$21 million on sales of $1.3 bil- 
lion. The three divisions that 
will comprise TJX Cos. had 
net earnings of $13.3 million 
on sales of €364.9 million, rep- 
resenting 63 percent of total 
corporation earnings while 
contributing a mere 28 per- 


cent of all Zayre sales. 

T.J. Maxx is expanding the 
number of women’s shoe de- 
ee and is also testing 
ine jewelry departments. 

Like its competitor Mar- 
shalls, T.J. Maxx specializes 
in moderate to better branded 
apparel at low prices. 

Cammarata said he consid- 
ers “anybody who’s selling off- 
price apparel” as a competi- 
tor,” but said T.J. Maxx “has 
always been after the depart- 
ment store shopper and we’ve 
never gotten away from that.”

Northwest.

with Kolhberg vis Rob-

aon through a leveraged 

uyout. Fred Meyer had tried

the retail business without its 
real estate interest, which 
was being held as a separate 
entity at the time. 


Last year’s offering, how- - 


ever, included both the retail 
and real estate interests. The

GOLD CIRCLE , ANNUAL REPORT 


Gold Circle Tops Sales 


WORTHINGTON, Ohio — 
Gold Circle Stores exceeded 
its sales and earnings goals for 
1986, according to parent Fed- 
erated Department Stores 
and chain executives, even 
though the chain fell out of 


DSN’s billion dollar club. Op- 
erating income, total assets 
and comparable store sales 
also declined during 1986. 
However, aside from a rash 
of one-time costs that hurt the 
bottom line, operating profits 


Source: DSN research 


for the year were above plan 
for the discount chain, which 
operates as a division of Fed- 
erated Department Stores, 
chairman Peter Hayes said. 

Gold Circle president Rob- 
ert Glass said, “On a day in, 
day out basis, operating profit 
was better in 1986 than in 
1985,” estimating it was about 
10 percent higher than the 
previous year. 

Residual costs associated 
with the 1985 merger with 
Richway Stores, the chain- 
wide remodeling program and 
higher than anticipated LIFO 
costs each brought down the 
bottom line, Glass said. 

The remodeling program 
has been worked into 22 loca- 
tions to date, eight of which 
were former Richway stores 


in North and South Carolina. 

Depending upon the loca- 
tion, Hayes said remodeling 
expenses can range from 
$500,000 to $700,000, not in- 
cluding the estimated 8 per- 
cent to 13 percent loss of busi- 
ness during the 90-day 
remodeling period. 

The LIFO charges affected 
all of the corporation’s divi- 
sions, according to a Federat- 
ed spokesperson, totaling $4.4 
million a 

Sales declined due to three 
factors, Hayes said, including 
the problem of bringing Rich- 
way up to the Gold Circle sales 
level. 

“There has been a learning 
curve for buyers. Gold Circle 
had been a chain that extend- 
ed from Buffalo to Cincinnati

Florida. We learned a lot last 
year, and no doubt we'll learn 
a lot this year,” he added. Gold

emphasis.

Sales volume for ladies’ wear will 
increase approximately 3.4 percent 
to $21.1 billion this year, according to

Full-line discounters will garner 
$15.8 billion in sales in 1987, a3.2 per- 
cent rise over last year. Apparel off- 
pricers will register a 4.1 percent 
gain to a volume of $5.1 billion. And 
catalogers will suffer a decrease this 
year to $200 million, a 33 percent 
plunge as a result of a general de-em- 
phasis at the catalogers on this type 
of business. 

While average department size 
will not change this year, sales per 
store will increase by $98 to $1,948, 
with sales per square foot climbing 
$10 to $195. Turns will dip to 4.5 from 
5.0, while initial markups will be 
down 1.5 percent. to 47.4 percent. 
Gross margins will increase by 1.1 
percent to 31.3 percent.

Categories within the housewares 
department underwent significant 
repositioning during 1986 as did the 
industry trade show calendar. Mer- 
chandise that up until last year had 
not permitted retailers to earn high 
margins due to their commodity na- 
ture were given new colors, moved to 
more visible locations within the de- 
partment and evolved into home de- 
cor goods. 

Ready-to-assemble furniture, 
closet/storage and clocks received 
more prominence and more promo- 
tional advertising dollars were de- 
voted to these areas than in the past 
as these categories transcended their 
basic utility value into the profitable 
world of fashion merchandise. 

The non-electrics portion of the 
projected $12.7 billion mass mer- 
chandiser housewares industry is ex- 
pected to be the only growing area in 
the department.

tensified by t the Underwriters Lab-

RTA Grows as a Category 


The basic RTA furniture selection 
went from few relatively low ticket 
television, microwave oven and home 
entertainment units in 1985 to an 
area within housewares that in some 
cases was developed as a department 
in its own right last year. Four, six or 
eight gondola runs became common- 

lace as bedroom ensembles and se- 

ected dining room pieces were added 
to the home entertainment furniture 
core. 

Discounters discovered the need 
for furniture priced under $200 and 
filled the void successfully during the 
year. Just how long it will take until 
the market is saturated and margins 
will be forced down as competition 
rises is anybody’s guess. Steady im- 
provements in the production, pack- 
aging, hardware and instructions on 
RTA merchandise have not yet been 
translated into higher costs. 

Corrugated storage boxes and gar- 
ment — dressed in pastels, whites, 
grids and florals helped take the clos- 
et department “out of the closet,” as 
one retailer put it. 

These items combined with bright 
and pastel hangers, plastic sweater 
boxes and shoe racks warranted a 
more obvious location within house- 
wares instead of hidden with mops, 
brooms, ironing boards and other 
merchandise that is difficult to keep 
well maintained. 

Many discounters learned that cus- 
tomers were not willing to pay more 
than an additional dollar or two for 
the new designs, but were more like- 
ly to shop the category due to the lure 
of colors. 

Clocks that stressed function over 
fashion dropped in popularity and 
many discounters took the boxed 
models off shelves wherever possi-

CE Sales Dampened by Fizzling VCR Market 


Nationwide DSN Report 

While the consumer elec- 
tronics industry on the whole 
is rather healthy with plenty 
of product innovation at the 
high end, discounters’ con- 
sumer electronics business 
has remained fairly flat the 
past year. Prospects for the 
future are better as the high- 
end innovation should eventu- 
ally result in renewed sales 
vigor. 

Discounters’ CE business 
was plagued by the fizzling- 
out of the VCR boom, the con- 
tinuing devaluation of the dol- 
lar against the yen, and 
intensified competition as well 
as a lack of product informa- 
tion to combat consumer con- 
fusion and create demand. 

The Electronic Industries 
Association reported overall 
industry sales for 1986 
reached $28.7 billion. EIA re- 
search projects the industry 
to pass $30 billion in volume at 
the factory level this year. By 
the end of 1988, industry 
growth is only estimated to be 
around $31 billion. 


CE Sales Total $12.6B 


Full-line discounters, cata- 
logers and specialty chains are 
expected to generate $12.6 
billion in CE sales this year, 
slightly up from last year’s 
$12.5 billion, according to 
DSN research. Full-line dis- 
counters will generate the 
same volume of $6.3 billion as 
in. 1986, specialty discounters 
will increase their CE sales to 
$5.5 billion from $5.3 billion, 
while catalogers’ CE sales are 
expected to decline to $800 
million from $900 million. 

Productivity measure- 
ments show that sales per 
store for full-line discounters 
will increase from $761,600 to 
$776,600 and sales per square 
foot will rise from $331.30 to 
$337.65. 

In contrast, areport by Kid- 
der, Peabody & Co. found that 
the average sales per store for 
public specialty CE retailers 
is $7.5 million and the average 
in sales per square foot is $921. 

Department size for full- 
line discounters will remain at 
an average of 2,300 square 
feet, while turns will rise from 
3.1 to 3.3. However, initial 
markup for full-line discount- 
ers is expected to fall from 31 
percent to 30 percent and 
gross margin will slide from 
18.9 percent to 17.2 percent. 

By comparison, gross mar- 
gin for specialty CE retailers 
averaged 29.4 percent during 
the last fiscal year, with inven- 
tory turnover averaging 4.0 
times, reported Kidder Pea- 
body & Co. 

e investment firm’s anal-

est shift in market share since 
1982 occurred between the in- 
dependents (defined as a chain 
with less than 10 stores), de- 
creasing from 53 percent to an 
estimated 40 percent this 
year, and the electronics/

The wave of the VCR revo- 
lution that many retailers 
were able to ride to generate 
profit has virtually disap- 
peared. The growth in indus-

Discount stores as well as

Full-line discounters and 
no stores will increase 
their shares of the $4.9 billion 
discount domestics market 
this year, apparently at the 
expense of catalogers, accord- 
ing to DSN research. Overall, 
sales are expected to rise 2 
— from last year’s 4.8 

illion. 

Full-liners’ sales will climb 
to $3.7 billion from $3.6 billion, 
while specialty discounters 
are expected to add $100 mil- 
lion to their total, now at an 
even $1 billion dollars. Cata- 
logers, whose involvement in 
soft lines has always been ten- 
tative at best, will see their 
sales shrink 33 percent, from 
$300 million to $200 million. 

Much of the sales growth 
ean be attributed to discount- 
ers upscaling their product 
lines and creating “home 
stores” within their outlets by 
combining domestics, furni- 
ture and housewares, or by 
moving these departments 
closer together. Most major 
chains have added luxury 
goods to attract department 
store shoppers and are nar- 
rowing their focus to pinpoint 
specific consumer segments. 

That strategy worked well 
with men’s fashion, and evi- 
dently has found acceptance in 
the growing youth market. 
Children have started making 
their wishes known to a de- 
gree never seen before in a 
wide spectrum of products, 
from clothing to wallpaper, 
and domestics is no exception. 
Sheets, pillowcases and com- 
forters in a wide variety of 
youth-oriented design 
schemes, most fueled by tele- 
vision and the toy market 
(which are rapidly becoming 
one and the same thing), have 
been actively promoted by 
discounters. Some have added 
sub-departments aimed at the 
youth market. 

Since swearing off the plain 
white sheet, discounters have 
rapidly escalated their color 
and fashion offerings. Water- 
color-look bedding was partic- 
ularly hot this year, and high- 
er-end outlets like The Home 
Front are offering hand- 
stitch-look comforters and 
spreads with vivid florals and 
geometric designs. 

The key, according to indus- 
try observers, is the percep- 
tion of quality. Most domes- 
tics shoppers are familiar with 
terminology, and are well 
aware of what thread counts 
refer to. And they are far less 
resistant to higher price 
points. 

Discounters are now almost 
head-to-head with depart- 
ment stores, and are finding 
that they have to provide 
equivalent goods to remain 
competitive. That has led to 
the introduction of brand 
names like Gloria Vanderbilt, 
Pierre Cardin and Playboy, as 
well as greater reliance — 
well-known textile mills like 
Cannon, J.P. Stevens and St. 
Marys, the latter two of which 
have increased their market 
share against Cannon’s hege- 
mony. 

Consumers have clearly 
shown that they have “out-
