Specialty 
Nationwide DSN Report 

Although the automotives after- 
market is considered a mature, flat 
market, try telling that to those who 
market ‘specialty auto parts for pick- 
ups and vans and the top auto special- 
ty chains. 

Sales figures for specialty chains— 
— their profits where available— 

gest automotives departments of 
full-line discount stores have their 
saa cut out for them. 

Out of the top 11 specialty chains, 
seven logged double digit sales 
growths for 1986. Some examples: 25 

ercent at the Pep Boys—Manny, 

oe & Jack, Philadelphia, and 35 
cent at Auto Shack, a privately held 
chain based in Memphis, Tenn. 

Moreover, the specialty truck and 
van aftermarket is predicted to grow 
by 11.2 percent a year through 1990, 
or 2% times the growth of the overall 
automotives market. 


Customized Pickups 


In many cases, the pickup has be- 
come the hot rod of the ’80s. And 
those who spawned the specialty 
market by customizing their hot rods 
in the ’60s are willing to spend hun- 
dreds, if not thousands, of dollars to 
make their pickups run better than 
and look different from the pack. In 
some circles, vans, pickups and four- 
wheel drive vehicles have now be- 
come the status vehicles of the de- 
cade. 

Accordingly, the Bradlees store 
that opened in Newark, Del., in 
March features a new specialty sec- 
tion that handles such items as pickup 
running boards and bed liner mats for 
pickups at $79.99 prices. 

The discounter share of the parts 
aftermarket is projected at $9.7 bil- 
lion for 1987, little improved from 
$9.6 billion in 1986. The full-line dis- 
counters’ share of that is expected to 
edge up to $5.5 billion from $5.4 bil- 
lion, while the share of catalogers will 
hold flat at $100 million. Sales of spe- 
cialty discounters, however, are ex- 

cted to grow to $4.1 billion from 
$3. 9 billion last year. 

Other forces at work in the after- 
market are rubbing the polish off the 
do-it-yourself market and have 
coined a new phrase, do-it-for-me. 

With the introduction of computer 
engine controls, modern cars are be- 
coming too complex for many back- 


yard mechanics. Moreover, the driv- 
ing population is aging, and the older 
the drivers get, the less inclined they 
are to spend Saturday mornings 
changing the oil in their cars. 

Another factor depressing the auto 
aftermarket is that parts are lasting 
longer. In large part because spark 

plugs are good for 25,000 miles in- 
sein of 10,000, Champion i is diversi- 
fying into such products as filters. 
Tires commonly can last for 70,000 
miles, where 25,000 once was stan- 
dard. 

Providing service and appealing to 
women—buyers of 22 percent of pick- 
up trucks—are other hallmarks of ag- 
gressive merchandising. 

However, Target and Gold Circle 
both have dropped as unprofitable 
their automotives services, which is 
keeping the Pep Boys zooming along 
in high gear. 


Service Works for Pep Boys 


New Pep Boys stores in Sacramen- 
to, Calif., for example, feature nine 
and 10 service bays. In large mea- 
sure, Pep Boys credits gains in auto- 
motives service and installation for 
the 51.3 percent increase in first 
quarter earnings to $5.9 million from 
$3.9 million in the same period of 
1986. Sales gained 15.2 percent to 
$127.3 million from $110.5 million. 

The retreat of Target and Gold Cir- 
cle from the service arena enabled 
K mart to make further gains. It fol- 
lows-a policy of catering to women 
automotives buyers and providing 
service. 

Out of some 2,200 K mart stores, 
1,500 offer automotives service, but 
K mart evaluates the profitability of 
each service center. 

Surveys over the year indicate that 
automotives buyers, especially for 
motor oil, remain loyal to their 
brands. K mart has beefed up its mix 
of branded and private label parts by 
increasing branded products by 15 
percent. In another move to capital- 
ize on the customer preference for 
branded goods, K mart is negotiat- 
ing with Delco to provide batteries 
that carry both the Delco and the 
K mart labels. 

Among brand promotions, Pres- 
tone antifreeze came in second out of 
48 brand products that consumers 
knew discount chains were promot- 
ing, and Quaker State motor oil came 


in No. 7. And motor oils continue to 
dominate brands. Out of 10 top auto- 
motive brands discounters carry, 
five were motor oils. Among the top 
five, three were oils. Quaker State 
and Pennzoil led the field, followed by 
Fram, Prestone and Havoline. 

Many discounters have found a 

way to squeeze a penny or two profit 

er quart out of motor oil, traditional- 
ly a loss-leader, by offering oil by the 
i2- -quart case as well as by the quart. 
Valvoline helped that trend along by 
offering a $3-a-case rebate, plus a $2 
bonus. 

In other oil developments, fill-top 
plastic bottles have virtually re- 
placed the oil can that required a sep- 
arate pouring spout. And few dis- 
counters are carrying more than one 
brand of the relatively new 5W-30 
motor oil that many four-cylinder 
cars require.

Nationwide DSN Report 

Last year was a relatively 
cautious year for toy buyers. 
A “back to basics” atmosphere 

ervaded the industry and 

azer Tag emerged as one of 
the hot products to drive 
fourth quarter sales. 

1987 will not be that much 
different in terms of cautious- 
ness on the buyer’s part as 
well as “back to basics” con- 
tinuing as the trend. Howev- 
er, one distinction that has re- 
tailers concerned and is 
creating a major challenge for 
them is the current absence of 
a hot product to drive this 
year’s Christmas sales. 

U.S. retail toy sales rose 
just under 5 percent to an esti- 
mated $12.5 billion in 1986 
from $12 billion in 1985, ac- 


cording to the Toy Manufac- 
turers of America, the indus- 
try’s trade association. 
William Garrity, board chair- 
man of the association, esti- 
mated 1987 toy sales to grow 
about 5 percent. 

Discount stores had the 
largest percentage of total in- 
dustry sales, accounting for 33 
percent in 1986, reported the 
NPD Group. Toy stores were 
second, generating 27 per- 
cent, while department stores 
generated 12 percent. Catalog 
showrooms garnered 6 per- 
cent of the toy market, while 
variety stores generated 4 
percent and all others consti- 
tuted the remaining 18 per- 
cent of sales.

search, full-line discounters,

Industry Change 


Another major change that 
has occurred this year in the 
industry is that it is becoming 
much more buyer/merchant- 
driven, rather than manufac- 
turer-driven, thanks to the 
greater variety of product 
available at earlier dates, al- 
lowing retailers much more 
flexibility in making their buy- 
ing plans. 

While buyers agree the 
shift in flexibility has been 
good for sales, they agree it 
can also hurt the industry. 

It seems that manufactur- 
ers have eased off on produc- 
tion and trimmed dollars 
spent on advertising, which is 
hurting the industry, said Wil- 
liam Langus, president, Toy 
& Sport Warehouse, New 
York. This year, when manu- 
facturers brought out their 
products early, they saw that 
expected orders were lagging 
and softening their TV adver- 
tising exposure, said Langus. 
And shortages may not exist 
this year because of products 
being shipped earlier with 
more choices available, which 
ean also stifle consumer de- 
mand, he said. 

“It seems that we are going 
back to the basic tey business 
from eight to nine years ago, 
when we struggled for the 
first months aad in the fourth 
"noha brought back profit,” 

angus said. 

And “back to basics” may be 
here to stay in the toy industry 
as more consumers are becom- 
ing price conscious and seeing 
better value for their money in 
basics, while retailers are see- 
ing more margin return with 
basic product.

Women DlYers Propel Discounters’ 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Price increases of 2 percent 
to 5 percent—following sever- 
al years of relative price sta- 
bility—mark the hardware re- 
tail industry, as the drive for 
the female shopping dollar 
forges ahead in a slow but 
steady pattern. 

For imported hand tools, 
the price increases range to 10 
percent or more, prompting 
some buyers to take a second 
look at domestics suppliers. 

The appeal for women shop- 
pers, couched in more attrac- 
tive packaging, easier to find 
dinnla s me | better do-it- 
yourself instructions, will con- 
tinue to get stronger. 

As the traditional shopper 
in discount stores, women are 
finding more emphasis on 
home decorating materials, 
such as inexpensive and easy- 
to-install wallpaper borders. 
But merchandisers view wom- 
en as a prime growth market 
for complex DIY projects. 


Women DIYers 


A survey by the marketing 
research division of the Na- 
tional Retail Hardware Asso- 
ciation found that women 
were involved in 45 percent of 
home improvement projects, 
primarily in tasks such as 
painting and papering. Now 
that the number of new house- 
hold formations has peaked, 
the home improvement mar- 
ket consists largely of a re- 
placement market, according 
to the NRHA. 

Consequently, a major 
growth prospect is to per- 
suade women to tackle more 
difficult DIY projects. Up- 
grading the skill levels of pro- 
jects that men undertake also 
presents a growth area, re- 
searchers conclude. 

Another marketing thrust 
the association favors is to 
capitalize better on the ten- 
dency for impulse buying. An 
association survey of hard- 
ware customers found that 
47.9 percent bought items on 
impulse, in addition to the 
items they planned to buy. Ac- 
cordingly, the association sug- 
gests that hardware retailers 
promote impulse buying with 
appropriate dump bins, end- 
caps and signage. 

ncluding paint, the dis- 
count share of hardware sales 
is projected at $6.8 billion for 
1987, compared to $6.6 billion 
in 1986. The catalogers’ share 
of hardware is expected to 
drop to $100 million from $200 
million, as major players such 
as Best and Service ieechen-

Thanks to improvement in

ple, of Black & Decker’s power

Because of technology ad-

home seeurity system. Along

cent, while Stanley scored 73 
percent. General Electric 
came in a distant third with a 
10 percent ranking. 


Revamping Hardware 


Many discounters are re- 
vamping hardware, adding 
more selection of name brands 
and a higher quality of mer- 
chandise. 

K mart, Wal-Mart, Hills, 
Caldor and Zayre have all in- 
creased their emphasis on 
brand name hardware. Target 
and Gold Circle have in- 
creased the space they allot to 
some hardware, such as locks. 

In response to home center 
competition, S.E. Nichols, 
based in New York, finally 
gave up on carrying lumber in 
its home improvement depart- 
ments and increased its em- 
phasis on hardware basics. 

In retrofitted stores, Nich- 
ols increased tools by 30 per- 
cent to 40 percent, tripled 
electrical to 236 feet from 80 
feet, and added bulk plumbin 
supplies to a mix that leane 
toward carded items. 

In another hardware devel- 
opment, K mart has drawn on 
experience with its Builders 
Square home center subsid- 
iary to develop a new proto- 
type for its Home Care Cen- 
ter. Developed in the Lawton, 
Okla. store, the prototype is 
slated to be installed in 50 of 
the 300 stores that have Home 
Care Centers. 

The major thrust of the pro- 
totype is to give K mart domi- 
nance in all key categories by 
offering shoppers choices by 
category, price, quality and 
product performance.

the Lawton store offers 36 }

most counters run 35 feet to 45 
feet long.

“Back to basics” remained 
the central theme in the flat 
sporting goods market 
through 1986 and into this 
year, as consumers turned 
away from the once-hot exer- 
cise category. “The whole in- 
dustry is waiting for some- 
thing new,” said Herman’s 
vice president George Walk- 
er, and discount buyers na- 
tionwide echoed that same 
sentiment. 

Sales industrywide were 
flat, remaining at the 1985 lev- 
el of $6.1 billion. Full-line dis- 
counters once more had the li- 
on’s share of the market, $4 
billion total. Catalogers also 
held steady at a half billion dol- 
lars, but specialty retailers 
stepped up significantly to 
$1.6 billion, a 14 percent gain 
over 1985’s $1.4 billion. 

Demographically and psy- 
chogra 
lytical buzzword, the slowing 
of the exercise equipment cat- 
egory makes sense. Ameri- 
cans are tiring of the anorexic 
look of joggers and compulsive 
exercisers, and are evidently 
looking for fun, social activi- 
ties that will get them out- 
doors and provide them with 
more natural exercise. 

Also, as the population 
ages, there is a predictable 
movement away from poten- 
tially harmful levels of exer- 
tion to forms of exercise that 
are kinder to stiffer muscles 
and more brittle connecting 
tissue.

SLR Cameras Offset Slow Sales of Disc Format 


Nationwide DSN Report ~ 

The photo/camera market 
acted its age over the past 
year; as a mature category, its 
sales are expected to be flat 
this year, according to DSN 
research. 

Industrywide, total con- 
sumer photo sales should be 
$18 billion, the same as in 1986 
and some $700 million less 
than the previous year. Of the 
$3.6 billion spent at discount 
outlets (also the same as in 
1986), $3.3 billion will be taken 
in by full-line discounters and 
the remainder by taken in by 
catalogers. 

Sales per square foot for the 
industry will rise slightly, but 
that gain will be easily offset 
by even lower margins.in what 
has traditionally been a low- 
margin category. 


Disc Cameras 


The perfect three-point bel- 
ly flop performed by the disc 
camera may have been offset 
by the very appealing SLR 
35mm cameras, which sold 
over 3.5 million units in 1986 
and should continue to sell 
well through 1987. 

Mid-price non-SLR cam- 
eras sold about 3.7 million 
units, a 30 percent gain. The 
two 35mm categories com- 
bined for $600 million in value 
at import, which accounts for 
virtually all 35mm products. 

The disc camera format evi- 
dently has failed to make an 
impact with consumers, and 
has been virtually ignored by 
the younger, more affluent 
consumers who drive the pho- 
to industry. 


Polaroid System 


Polaroid’s new instant sys- 
tem, its first in 14 years, is ex- 
pected to drive the instant 
camera category to its first 
gain in nearly a decade. Fea- 
turing automatic focus and ex- 
posure, the system has much 
the same appeal as the SLR 
35mm, and picture quality is 
roughly equivalent to one- 
hour processed 35mm film. 

Film sales have performed 
well, particularly as the one- 
hour processer becomes more 
common. 


Agfa Penetrates Market 


Fuji has challenged Kodak 
for a few crumbs of market 
share, and apparently has 
been moderately: successful, 
—-? a spokesperson for 
Agfa-Gavert, the European 
giant now trying to penetrate 
the U.S. nonprofessional mar- 
ket, said that the Japanese 
firm “spent a lot of money get- 
ting what Kodak had already 
decided to give them.” 

Agfa, well-known in profes- 
sional and technical circles in 
the United States, is followin 
a piggyback strategy—dua 
branding with discounters— 
to get name recognition. It 
hepes that customers will no- 
tice a real difference in quality 
and become repeat buyers. 
And, through word of mouth, 
Agfa hopes to build up the 
newcomer’s sales. 

The casual ene Same 
has never before had the vari- 


ety of sophisticated, idiot- 
proof eegitnent available as 
in the past two years. But 
even as unit sales rose, mar- 


gins started eroding. Most re- 
tailers cut back on sku’s to con- 
centrate on mid-priced, point- 
and-shoot mode 
become almost omnipresent in 
U.S. homes. 

Therein, of course, lies the 
rub. Even as prices fall, de- 
mand is lagging. Most con- 
sumers that want a camera 
have a camera. And the photo/ 
camera market is mainly 
aimed at replacement and up- 
grading. 

With that in mind, it’s not 
surprising that analysts are 

redicting another flat year 
or the industry. Bright spots 
appear to be instant camera 
technology and sophisticated 
accessories, which have the 
only strong margins in the 
field.

K mart Uses 
Groceries To Hype 
Holiday Traffic 


Grocery products lend them- 
selves brilliantly to seasonal pro- 
motions. Buyers and merchan- 
disers who are planning 
Thanksgiving promotions now 
Should take a look at K mart’s 
1986 Thanksgiving circular. 

Dry grocery items accounted 
for 83% of the 12 items on the cir- 
cular’s front page. 


MP ce 


Most dominant were an alumi- 
num foil, K mart’s own store 
brand, Ocean Spray cranberry 
sauce, Libby’s pumpkin pie mix, 
Stove Top stuffing mix and three 
oc of chocolate bits: 

eese’s peanut butter cups and 
Hershey's milk chocolate chips 
and semi-sweet chocolate chips. 

Also on the page were Eagle 
Snacks Honey ated Peanuts, 
K mart’s own paper towels as 
well as a variety of 20 and 30 gal. 
trash bags. 

Inside the circular, K mart did 
a spread on clip and save coupons 
which featured a number of other 
grocery products including cook- 
les, smoked oysters, egg noo- 
dles, candies, plastic tumblers, 
liquid all-purpose cleaners, laun- 
dry detergents and light bulbs. 

Managers said their sell 
throughs on the featured items 
were “excellent.” 


The Foods Shoppers Buy The Most 


Here’s a puzzler for you. The answers are milk and bread. Now 
what was the question? 

Did you say “what are the two most frequently purchased catego- 
ries in a grocery store”? 

Well if you did say that, then you get the brass ~~ because, ac- 
cording to the latest Point of Purchase Advertising Institute Food 
Store Shopper npn on Habits study, that is what shoppers do buy 
most frequently when browsing a 

In the fall of 1986, POPAI did a full scale shopper purchase habit 
study in 20 markets across the country. Their researchers recorded 
over 65,000 purchases made by a total of 4,000 food shoppers. 


The Food Categories Bought Most Frequently 
% of purchases per every 100 shoppers 

Milk 33% | Refrigerated orange juice 8% 
Packaged bread 25 Ice cream 6 
Eggs 14 Bacon 6 
Chicken 12 Potato chips 6 
Crackers 11 Concentrated orange juice 5 
Cookies 10 Hotdogs 5 
Ground beef 10 Corn chips 3 
Packaged luncheon meats 8 Snack nuts 3 
Source: POPAI 1986 Consumer Buying Habits Study 


In their preliminary analysis of that data, POPAI found that for ev- 
ery 100 shoppers interviewed during a typical shopping trip, 33 pur- 
chased milk, 25 purchased bread, and 14 bought eggs. 
Eleven out of every 100 bought crackers, 10 bought cookies, eight 
bought refrigerated orange juice and luncheon meat. 

Six bought ice cream, bacon and — chips; 5 bought concentrat- 
ed orange juice and hotdogs, and 3 bought corn chips and snack nuts. 

With the exception of chicken and ground , which were also 
mentioned as frequent purchasers, each of the categories cited are 
normally found today in most chain drug stores while the dry grocer- 
Qs cited are also found in almost every discount and mass merchan- 

ise store. 

Says Eckerd food buyer Peter Agostinio: “These categories for us 
are ‘opportunistic’ additions to our everyday mix. They help us build 
traffic and they increase the frequency or repeat visits to our stores.”

Membership Warehouse Club 
Sales Soaring 


Sales for the 228 universe of Membership Clubs jumped 82% to $8 billion in 1986. Ed- 
ible & nonedible groceries accounted for about 45% of total sales. 


W arehouse Clubs, which are 
competing with drug and dis- 
count store chains on grocery retail- 
ing, as well as on such traditional 
categories of merchandising as 
HBA, sundries, low and high ticket 
electronics, and apparel, are con- 
tinuing to show dramatic gains both 
in store counts and dollar sales. 

According to the latest survey 
done by Discount Store News, FM’s 
sister publication, sales for Mem- 
bership Warehouse Clubs hit $8.2 
billion in 1986, up an amazing 82% 
over 1985. 

The total number of units in exis- 
tence hit an estimated 228 in 1986, 
up 66% over the prior year. 

For 1987, Discount Store News is 
estimating that dollar sales for all 
Membership Clubs will hit $11.6 
million, which will represent an in- 
crease of 41% over the prior year. 

Stores will climb on estimated 
43% to 325 units, DSN is estimat- 
ing. 


Membership Clubs: The 
customer base and the mix 


Membership Warehouse Clubs 
serve a relatively unique mix in the 
retail marketplace. A hybrid that is 
half wholesale/half retail, the typi- 
cal mix of a warehouse club includes 
edible and nonedible groceries, 
health and beauty aids, apparel and 
other softwear, and a variety of hard 
line items ranging from televisions 
and stereos through tires and such 
gadgets as electronic garage door 
openers. 

The customer base is predomi- 
nately small businesses with off- 
the-street customers usually mak- 
ing up about 30% of a typical 
wholesale club’s customer mix. 


Margins average about 10% 


Sometimes, however, the custom- 
er mix can be more in the vicinity of 
50% to 50%, half small businesses 
buying on acash and carry basis and 
half individual man/woman in the 
street t consumers buying by 
the case load on low- to mid-ticket 
items and in singles on high ticket 
items like televisions. 


Many warehouse clubs carry large assortments of refrigerated and frozen foods. The mix is on 
large sizes of the highest consumption categories.

Sales will hit $20 billion by 1990 


Most Membership Club execu- 
tives and most analysts who follow 
the segment believe the total dollar 
sales will reach $20 billion by 1990. 

Some sources, such as Walter 
Teninga, President of the $185 mil- 
lion Weceloane Club chain in Sko- 
kie, Ill., think that the estimate of 


$20 billion in annual industry sales 
by 1990 is even too “conservative.” 
Fred Windsor, a retail analyst 
with Alex. Brown & Sons, Balti- 
more, says that while it is impossi- 
ble to predict how many Warehouse 
Clubs the country can ultimately 
absorb, he does wt Sta that “expan- 
sion in this segment will be swift.” 
Windsor agrees with other ana- 
lysts that the store universe will 
probably hit 600 to 700 by 1990. 
“There is room in every major city 
for a number of Membership Ware- 
house Clubs,” says Joseph Nusim, 
chairman of the Makro Self Service 
Wholesaler Club based in Cincin- 
nati. Makro, with its four stores, is 
the seventh highest volume chain in 
the segment. 
“We, as an industry,” he says, 
“have only begun scratching the 
surface.” 


What makes Membership 
Clubs work 


The secret to a Membership 
Club’s success, sources say, is the 
ability to turn a limited inventory of 
between 3,000 to 3,500 sku’s any- 
where between 12 and 20 times a 
year. 

The industry’s most successful 
chain, Price Club, boasts turns of 
between 18 and 25 a year on a mix of 
about 3,500 sku’s. 

Like Price Club which generates 
about 60% of its sales through 
wholesale customers, the more suc- 
cessful chains are concentrating on 
targeting their customers mix to 
small businesses doing a high ton- 
nage cash and carry business rather 
than to individual consumers doing 
a cherry picking “stock up” busi- 
ness. 


60% to 70% of Customers are 
small businesses 


Jeffrey H. Brotman, chairman of 
Costco, the industry’s third highest 
volume chain, says that 70% of Cost- 
co’s sales are now generated by 
wholesale purchases. 

“Maybe we’re wrong,” says Brot- 
man, “but we think we can do a bet- 
ter business by keeping out the ca- 
sual customer, and by concentrating 
on asmaller group of more loyal cus 
tomers instead.” 

“At one time, we were only gener- 
— about 40% of our sales through 
wholesaler purchases,” says John 
Geisse, chairman of the Wholesale 
Club in Indianapolis. 

“Today, our wholesale business is 
up to 69% of our sales, and we’re 
working very hard to keep increas- 
ing that share.”

Membership Clubs Push 
Groceries 


Best sellers are case lots, shrink wrapped packages, large sizes and anything con- 
sumable that offers the customer a “value” 


£ rocery product sales in whole- 
sale clubs are booming. 

Both retailers and manufacturers 
report that sales of snacks, pet 
foods, dry and packaged groceries, 
beverages and grocery household 
items are growing like “crazy” in the 
$8 billion dollar Membership Ware- 
house Club industry. 

The majority of the business is be- 
ing done, say sources, in large size 
packs or in shrink wraps that are 
generally merchandised off massive 
in-store bulk displays. 

The selection in a membership 
club is seldom extensive, but the 
displays are huge and some catego- 
ries like snacks get an average of 32 
running feet plus extensive expo- 
sure on pallets and end caps. 

Generally Membership Club 
stores will only stock grocery items 
they’ve acquired at the lowest possi- 
ble acquisition cost, and when they 
display these items, they’re at the 
lowest possible competitive price. 


Customers like to buy in huge 
quantities 


“When a customer in a Member- 
ship Club store buys a snack or a 
ocery item,” says Wrigley’s Ron 
ox, “they’re usually buying full 
box quantities. That means the sale 
is usually a high ticket and it usually 
amounts to someone buying 12 
packages at once or 20 or 24 depend- 
ing on how many items are packed to 
a case.” 
“The Membership Warehouse 
Clubs,” says Chris Abernathy, VP 
of Marketing for Borden’s, “are 
places where — are buying 
commodities. They are not taking 
that much business from the tradi- 
tional food stores, but they may be 
taking it from the mass merchandis- 
er who tries to compete with the 
food stores on price. 

“If someone is price conscious, 
there is no better place to buy a gro- 
cery item, but these stores are not 
that convenient yet, and they are 
more accessible to the small busi- 


ness person than they are to the aV- About half the customers who buy food in a warehouse club are off-the-street consumers while 
erage consumer so the bulk of their _ the rest are small business buying in case lots to replenish their own stockrooms.

Why Cleanser Sales are Growing 


According to the Charles H. Kline Company, a marketing analysis 
and research company based in Fairfield, 
ing products category will continue to show moderate, steady growth 


Kline analysts say retailers will continue to see most of the catego- 
wth coming from the soap and detergent segment of cleaners 
which currently account for about 51% of all household cleaner sales. 
According to Kline analyst Elizabeth Donovan, there are several 
wth of cleansers including the following. 
1. Major acquisitions and divestitures Boge 
Donovan  y the trend today is toward an industry consolidation 
t that the major cleanser companies are aggressively 
competing against each other for market share. 


Donovan says that manufacturers are more likely today to try to 
retain their competitive edge by extending their strongest brands 
rather than by introducing new, untested brands. 

P & G, Donovan points out, broke a long standing precedent recent- 
ly by introducing a “flurry” of extensions to Tide in 1985 and 1986. P & 
re also has new liquid detergents which use the Cheer and Bold brand 


3. Heightened consumer demand for convenience. 
Donovan says the increasing demand for convenient household 
product items will “continue to encourage product and packaging in-

EM Withdraws $8 Bid for Crazy Eddie 


HOUSTON — Entertainment Marketing withdrew its 
$8 per share bid for Crazy Eddie and said it will wage a 
proxy fight if Eddie Antar and his group do not proceed 
with their $7 per share offer. Elias Zinn, EM’s chairman, 
said he will consider making a lower bid for the chain if in- 


formation he has been requesting is obtained. Crazy Eddie 
has gr to supply EM with a list of shareholders. “We 
are S 


very interested in the ergs | but not interested 
in the $8 bid anymore,” Zinn said. EM recently increased 
its investment in Crazy Eddie and currently owns 1.7 mil- 
lion shares or 5.3 percent of the 31 million shares outstand- 
ing. The stock was selling at about $5.50 in late July. 


Buyer’s Club Enters ‘Warehouse Valley’ 


LOS ANGELES — Denver-based Buyer’s Club en- 
tered Southern California’s “warehouse valley” last 
month with a membership club in San Bernardino and 
plans a second club in Pomona later this year. Both are in 
the San Gabriel Valley, east of L.A., which contains mem- 
bership warehousers such as PACE, Price Club, Price 
Savers, Costco, HomeClub and All American SportsClub. 
Buyer’s Club was spun off last year as a separate oan gag 
from Union Hall, the two-unit discounter in Rockford, III. 


Target Opens Ist Reformatted Gemcos 


MINNEAPOLIS — Target opened its first wave of re- 
formatted Gemco stores in late July, as the discounter’s 
plans remained on schedule for the reopening of all 50 for- 
mer Gemcos by December. This group of former Gemcos 
comprised 13 of 19 stores Target opened that month. 


Wal-Mart Expands into Arizona Market 


BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Wal-Mart will e d into 
Arizona with four stores in 1988. The chain has picked sec- 
ondary cities for its market entry, with sites in Flagstaff, 
Casa Grande, Show Low and Thatcher. The Flagstaff unit 
will be 81,000 square feet; the others 66,000 square feet. 


Quick Response Session at SCAN-TECH 


PITTSBURGH — Quick Response will be the topic of a 
retail-focus session at next month’s SCAN-TECH show 
and seminar on identification technologies. The session, 
“Quick Response-The Retailer/Vendor Connection,” will 
be held Thursday, Oct. 15 from 8 a.m. to 10 a.m. at Bartle 
Hall, Kansas City. SCAN-TECH, which will feature 32 
sessions, runs Oct. 13 to 15, with seminars starting Oct. 
12. Participating in the Quick Response session will be Da- 
vid Carlson, corporate vp, K mart; R. Vincent Conant, 
chairman, Carter cwroateg Roses and Randall Nord, vp, 
Kurt Salmon Associates. They will discuss how bar codin 
can help retailers better control inventory, finance an 
production levels, as well as speed up response time with 
vendors. Information on this session and SCAN-TECH is: 
available from AIM, 1326 Freeport Rd., Pittsburgh, Pa. 
15238. Phone: (412) 963-8588. 


FOR THE RECORD. 


Best Products’ projected store count for the end of this year is 
194 units, the same as at the start of 1987, not 101 stores as re- 
ported in the top 100 chart, July 20, page 27. 

Luskin’s is based in Baltimore, Md., not Madison, Wis., as re- 
ported on the top 100 chart. It was listed correctly on page 39. 

“Shopping Line,” “ValueTelevision,” “America’s Market- 
place,” “Crazy Eddie’s World of Home Entertainment” and 
“Shopping Club” are teleshopping shows that aired and were 
eventually canceled, not planned shows that were never broad- 
cast as was implied in the Electronic Retailing column of July 20. 
“American Catalog Shoppers Network” was a planned show 
that was never broadcast.

merges its Sizes Unlimited di- 
vision into its Lerner Woman 
division. 

The new division will retain 
the Lerner Woman name but 
its headquarters will be based 
in Sizes Unlimited’s offices in 
Secaucus, N.J. Raphael Ben- 
aroya, president and chief ex- 
ecutive officer of Sizes Unlim- 
ited, will be president. 

A spokesman for Sizes Un- 
limited told DSN it was decid- 
ed that Sizes Unlimited 
“should upscale its business.”

unit chain, with stores averag-

about 3 percent nationally, 
light bulb sales growth was 
three times that figure for dis- 
counters—including member- 
ship clubs—last year. 

Light bulbs, or lamps, are a 
$2 billion industry at retail, ac- 
cording to estimates by the 
National Electrical Manufac- 
turers Association. 

Sales through discount and 
mass merchandise stores rank 


Light bulbs ‘sell like 
bananas: in bunches.’ 


—George Glidden, 
divisional merchandise 
manager, K mart 


second only to supermarket 
chains, taking approximately 
28 percent of the market. And 
that figure is growing, said the 
association. In fact, bulb sales 
through these channels are so 
good, some experts speculate 
discount stores will eventually 
“overtake” supermarkets as 
the primary retail source. 

In the meantime, competi- 
tion among all kinds of retail- 
ers for a greater share of the 
light bulb market has forced 
prices down sharply, making 
the sales climate almost fran- 
tic. This is especially notewor- 
thy since only a few years ago 
light bulbs were thought of 


merely as a standard stock 
item. 

Light bulbs “sell like ba- 
nanas: in bunches sald 


George Glidden, divisional 
merchandise manager for 
K mart, Troy, Mich. He add- 
ed that the giant discounter 
will do what is has to in order 
to “stay competitive” and as- 
sure sales. 

The light bulb category is so 
competitive that many retail- 
ers, including Caldor and 
Jamesway, refused to discuss 
the product with DSN. 

The activity and growth 
have been fueled by the indus- 
try’s three largest manufac- 
turers, GE, the undisputed in- 
dustry giant, North American 
Philips Lighting and GTE Syl- 

vania. All three have commit- 
ted themselves to product and 
program innovation, sharp 
pricing and aggressive adver- 
tising and promotional cam- 
paigns intended to build brand 
name association, drive sales 
and, hopefully, raise prices. 

In addition, the manufac- 
turers are trying tothwart the 
advances from lower priced 
imported light bulbs now en- 
croaching on the American 
marketplace, chiseling away 
market share and driving 
down bulb prices

By Richard C. Halverson 
Nationwide DSN Report 
The entry of Kodak into the 

battery market has forced all 
manufacturers to start look- 
ing over their shoulders, but 
so far the prominent film and 
camera maker has failed to 
crack the discount market in a 
major way. 

That is the major develop- 
ment in the consumer battery 
market over the past year, as 
these trends solidify: 

@ A continued push for both 
longer run and shelf life; 

& Alkaline is expected to con- 
tinue to increase its share of 
the market at the expense of 
zinc carbon general purpose 
and heavy duty batteries; 

® Given a nudge from produc- 
ers of high-drain devices that 
chew up batteries, recharge- 
able batteries are coming into 
their own, growing at a rate of 
two to three times that of the 
overall battery market; 

@ Due to a trend toward 
smaller devices, such as min- 
lature TY sets, the AAA is the 
fastest growing size; 

@® While still a high impulse 
item, batteries are becoming 
more of a shopping list item, 
with the rate of impulse buy- 
ing declining to about 80 per- 
cent from 90 percent of pur- 
chases; 

@ Marketing batteries in mul- 
tiple packs of sixes and eights 
continues to gain prominence. 


Testing Kodak Batteries 


So far, Kodak has failed to 
crack K mart and Wal-Mart, 
although K mart is testing 
Kodak batteries in its photo 
department. While Kodak has 
captured 2 percent to 3 per- 
cent of the overall retail mar- 
ket, primarily through food 
and drug outlets, its market 
share in discount department 
stores was 0.5 percent accord- 
ing toan A.C. Nielsen market 
share audit for March and 
April 1987. 

Industry giant Eveready, 
which Ralston Purina bought 
last year from Union Carbide, 
slipped to a 53 percent share of 
all types of batteries—general 
ockaage heavy duty and alka- 
ine—sold at discounters from 


59 seohaga according to the 


Nielsen audit a year earlier. 

Duracell picked up a point to 
22 percent from 21 percent, 
Nielsen showed, while Rayo- 
vac gained 4 points to 16 per- 
cent from 12 percent. 

All others, including im- 
ports such as Panasonic and 
private labels, increased to 8 
percent from almost 7 per- 
cent, Nielsen found. 

Industry estimates of annu- 
al growth in the retail battery 
market range from 6 percent 
to 8 percent, a growth rate ex- 
pected to hold through 1989. 

For 1986, the dollar value of 
the retail battery market 
came to $2.1 billion, a Rayovac 
study concluded. 

Larry Morgan, marketing 
director for Kodak, claims 
that its entry into the market 
has prompted the industry to 
increase advertising by 50 
percent and increase coupon 
efforts by 15 percent. 

Mike Plautz, Rayovac mar- 
keting director, acknowl- 
edged that Kodak “has made 
the industry more competi- 


er Life and Alkalines Charg 


tive, offering more in-store 
promotions and rebates.” He 
added, “Kodak is making ev- 
erybody a little more con- 
scious of promotions.” 

An Eveready spokesman 
said his company has in- 
creased its advertising budget 
but refused either to release 
details or to attribute the in- 
crease to new competition 
from Kodak. 

Irwin Levine, sporting 
goods buyer for S.E. Nichols, 
New York, said he has seen an 
increase in consumer rebate 
programs from Eveready, one 
of two brands Nichols carries. 
Duracell is the other. “They’re 
constantly running,” he said. 

So far, about 6 percent of 
the nation’s 7,000 to 9,000 
discount stores carry Kodak 


batteries. Chains include Hills, 
FEDCO, Caldor, Rose’s Stores, 
Fred Meyer and Meijer, Mor- 
gan said. 

In March, Kodak became 
the first manufacturer to mar- 
ket a popular size lithium bat- 
terv when it introduced its 
nine-volt unit. Kodak claims 
the battery will run twice as 
long as an alkaline battery and 
last for 10 years on the shelf, 
against two for lithium. 

At full retail, a nine-volt 
lithium retails for about $2.99, 
compared to $1.79 [at K mart, 
for example] to $1.99 for alka- 
line, Morgan said. 

Expected applications are 
for smoke detectors and ga- 
rage door openers, where long 
run and shelf lives are particu-

Longer Life and Alkalines Charge Up Discount Battery Market 


(Continued from page 55) 
larly important, Morgan said. 

A new premium flashlight 
from Black & Decker, called 
Lite Years, comes equipped 
with the Kodak lithium bat- 
tery. A one-cell battery retails 
at discount for about $9.99, 
while a two-cell light sells at 
discount for about $14.99, 
Morgan said. 

At Nichols, Levine said his 
chain is looking at the Kodak 
program. The nine-volt lithi- 
um might sell well for smoke 
detectors, he said. “People 
hate to climb up a ladder every 
year to change batteries.” To 
avoid that, they might be will- 
ing to spend $1.29 extra for a 
longer-life battery, he said. 
Nichols rejected the Black & 
Decker lithium-powered 
flashlight as too expensive. 

George Kiel, a K mart bat- 
tery buyer in sporting goods, 
said his chain considered the 
B & D lights but also rejected 
them for now because of the 
high prices. But he said 
K mart almost would have to 
carry the Kodak lithium bat- 
teries, if it took on the Lite 
Years flashlight, because, 
“customers want to replace 
with the same batteries.”’ 
Moreover, Kodak alkalines in 
the C, D, AA and AAA sizes 
could well ride into K mart on 
the back of lithium, Kiel said. 


The Future of Alkaline 


Kiel predicted that alkaline, 
which now commands a 60 per- 


cent share of the market, will | 


become the general purpose 
battery of tomorrow because 
of the drive for longer life. 
Some other type of battery, 
perhaps lithium, will take 
over the longer-life, premium 
position that alkaline now oc- 
cupies, he said. 

“Whether lithium is the an- 
swer remains to be deter- 
mined,” Kiel said. 

Eveready is introducing in 
August and September its 
version of the longer-life alka- 
line, Levine said. It will come 
in a new display card that 
claims it lasts 20 percent long- 
er. Nichols will phase in the 
new Energizer alkaline as old 
stocks become exhausted. The 
longer-life version will be 
priced the same, he said. 

Another new Everead 
program, the Gift Mate, will 
carry a 20 cents premium for a 
pair of D batteries but no ex- 
tra margin for discounters be- 
cause its cost to them will be 
higher, said the Eveready 
spokesman. In gift two-packs, 
the batteries feature on their 
jackets one of eight gift mo- 
tifs, such as white snow flakes 
on a green background for the 
Christmas season. 

Levine said Nichols won't 
pick up on the Gift Mate line 
until closer to the Christmas 
season. 

Following the lead of Rayo- 
vac, Kodak also is coming out 
with multi-packs, sixes and 
eights, Levine said. 

‘or the first time, Ever- 
eady came out this summer 
with a multi-pack program 
that offered an eight-pack of D 
cells for the usual price of six, 
and a six-pack of AA batteries 
for the usual price of four. 
Based on initial success, Ever- 
eady plans to repeat what it 


calls the Bonus Pack program 
this fall. 

In a trend that runs counter 
to the push for longer life, re- 
chargeable batteries are 
showing signs of vigor. From a 
small sales base of $150 million 
a year, rechargeables are 
growing at an annual rate that 
ranges from 15 percent to 30 
percent, depending on manu- 
facturer estimates. 

Kiel said K mart is testing 
nickel cadmium Panasonic re- 
chargeables, adding to its 
General Electric line.

pt the general public $10 


for membership privileges.

Top Chains Battle for Dominance; 
Newcomer Clubs Present Challenge 


Nationwide DSN Report 

The battle for positioning 
and market dominance within 
the sporting goods industry 
has been heating up since last 
year, and latest developments 
suggest that the battle has 
just begun. The two largest 
chains, Herman’s and Thrif- 
ty’s various sports stores, 
have been devouring smaller 
regional operators—and seem 
to be looking for more. 

At the same time, two rela- 
tive newcomers, California’s 
All-American SportsClub and 
Fort Lauderdale-based 
Sports Authority (see stories 
on this page), are high-volume 
power-retail concepts con- 
ceived with rapid growth as a 
key to success. Look for both 
to attempt to saturate their 
primary market areas, then 
go national. 

They'll face tough competi- 


tion from the major estab- 
lished forces in the market, 
Herman’s and Thrifty Corp., 
both of whom have expanded 
rapidly over the past year. 
Herman’s, the industry 
leader with $630 million in 
1986 sales, has added some 100 
stores to its total in just over a 
year, 40 by acquisition of 
Utah-based Sunset Sports. 
Thrifty, owner of Big 5 
Sports Store of California, 
purchased Michigan (MC) 
Sporting Goods, (Niles, 
Mich.) and Gart Bros. (Den- 
ver, Colo.) over the last year, 
absorbing a total of 31 stores 
and $200 million in 1986 sales. 
Each of those subsidiaries 
has expanded significantly 
since the acquistion, and each 
has in turn acquired other re- 
gional chains. MC recently 
bought three Chicago-area 
stores from Morrie Mages

Sporting Goods and an- 
nounced plans to build two 
more (of a scheduled 15 
through 1988) in the Chicago 
vulnaeie of Lombard and Or- 
land Park.

that we couldn’t make it even

the market. We had to create 
new business. 

“That’s our approach at 
SportsClub,” he continued.

man’s—we sell a whole pack- 
age. We hold clinics to teach 
people about our products, 
and we’re in the travel busi- 
ness, the camera business and 
in a lot of related areas.”

bought everything from shoes 
to clubs to umbrellas. The re- |

Antar Withdraws Crazy Eddie Bid 


EDISON, N.J. — Eddie Antar and First City Capital 
Corp. withdrew on Aug. 12 their proposal to buy Crazy 
Eddie at $7 per share. Antar and First City attributed the 
withdrawal, in part, to discussions with potential lenders. 
They said they are “prepared to work with the company 
toward a mutually acceptable transaction.” 


TEMPO TV Focuses on 45-Plus Market 


TULSA — The 45-year-old and over consumer market 
will soon have its own cable TV network. TEMPO TV, 
which was launched eight years ago as a special interest 
cable TV network, is changing its programming to focus 
on the 45-plus market. This market is expected to grow 
from 72 million people to over 105 million within the next 
15 years, representing one of the fastest growing demo- 
graphic groups in the nation. TEMPO, which currently 
reaches about 12.5 million households, had offered a num- 
ber of teleshopping shows earlier this year but found little 
interest among cable TV operators for this programming. 


Pay’n Save Acquires GO Guy Drug Stores 


SEATTLE — Pay’n Save, parent of discounter Bi- 
Mart, plans to acquire the six-store GO Guy Drug Store di- 
vision of the 65-unit Bonanza Stores variety chain. Pay’n 
Save, which operates 100 drugstores and super drug- 
stores, plans to run the acquired GO Guys as part of its 
new Pay’n Save Limited concept of smaller drugstores 
targeted for areas that can’t support its larger units. 


Zellers Adds Fifth Distribution Center 


MONTREAL — Zellers, the 210-store Canadian dis- 
count chain, is adding a fifth facility to its distribution net- 
work next month to accommodate the heavy flow of mer- 
chandise generated by its unique, one-year-old ‘Club Z’ 
incentive sales program. The Club is a repeat customer in- 
centive program that has over three million member cus- 
tomers, or roughly 40 percent of Canada’s total popula- 
tion. The membership level is already Eeasic 
management’s original expectations. The new 411,000- 
square-foot DC is the discounter’s second such facility in 

ontreal; three others are located in the Greater Toronto 
area. The discount department store division of Hudson 
Bay Co. reported a 14 percent sales increase to $1.7 million 
during 1986. Zellers Group—which includes Zellers and 
three other retail chains—reported sales of $2.3 billion for 
the year, compared with $2 billion in 1985, and operating 
profit of $92 million, up from $68 million. 


Ames Denies Buyout Rumor by Wal-Mart 


ROCKY HILL, Conn. — Ames Department Stores has 
denied the latest recurrence of a rumor that discount giant 
Wal-Mart may buy the Northeastern chain. A company 
spokesinan stated that Ames has never, as the rumor held, 
asked Wal-Mart to “take a look” at Ames. “The rumor 
started in the arbitrage community,” the spokesman said. 
He refused to speculate about motives in spreading the re- 
port, but Ames stock jumped nearly $2 on trading of over a 
million shares a day on Aug. 4 to 5 (vs. “normal” trading of 
200,000 to 400,000 shares). Chairman Herbert Gilman had 
replied to similar questions at Ames annual shareholders’ 
meeting this summer, stating that he and Wal-Mart chair- 
man Sam Walton joked about the rumor at an industry 
convention in May. “He [Walton] asked if we were plan- 
ning to buy him out,” Gilman had said. Ames has posted 
strong 1987 sales in its bid to come back from a disappoint- 
ing 1986. For the month ended Aug. 1, Ames reported an 
increase in sales of 11.8 ie over last year. Sales were 
up 14.8 percent for the 26 weeks ended on the same date, 
to $932 million. Stock prices, which reached $28.25 in the 
wake of the rumor, leveled off at $27.25 by the end of the 
week after Ames issued its denial. The stock traded at 
about $26 in the days before the rumor gained currency.

For the apparel off-pricers who 
have a well-defined strategy, have 
targeted their customer and are pro- 
—— that customer with the right 
merchandise at a value, this contin- 
ues to be a highly profitable market.

as well as such others as S&K Fam- 
ous Brands, Banker’s Note and Su- 
sie’s Deals (see story, this page), are 
experiencing strong sales and earn- 
ings growth.

to weed out the weak. Within the last 
12 months, K mart’s Designer Depot 
was shuttered (it was in last year’s 
top 10), and earlier this month The 
Limited, ee of Sizes Unlimited, 
announced it was leaving the very 
competitive off-price apparel market 
when it merges Sizes Unlimited and 
Lerner Woman (see DSN, Aug. 10,

r of other smaller off-pricers who

APPAREL. 


(Continued from page 21) 

The off-price business con- 
tinues to be dominated by 
Marshalls, a Melville Corp. di- 
vision, and T.J. Maxx, part of 
the newly created TJX Cos. 

As Bernard Cammarata, 
president and chief executive 
officer of TJX Cos., said about 
T.J. Maxx’s success over the 
last couple of years, “Our con- 
cept is nothing special. It’s the 
execution of the concept that’s 
key. The way you buy, process 
through the warehouse and 
manage the store—that’s the 
difference. It’s an art, not a 
science.” 

Spurred by T.J. Maxx’s 38 
percent jump in sales during 
fiscal 1986, parent Zayre 
Corp. earlier this year spun off 
T.J. Maxx, along with Hit or 
Miss and the cataloger Chad- 
wick’s of Boston, in order to 

enerate more revenue to fuel 

uture growth. Plans call for 
35 new stores a year for the 
next five years. 

Also, within ;the next four 
months T.J. Maxx will open its 
first 10 units in California and 
a new West Coast distribution 
center is being planned. 

T.J. Maxx continues to up- 
scale its stores, adding special 
designer departments featur- 
ing better brands. The chain is 
also expanding the number of 
women’s shoe departments 
and is testing fine jewelry. 

Marshalls, despite main- 
taining its No. 1 position with 
a 7 percent sales increase in 
fiscal 1986, didn’t meet earn- 
ings expectations, which dra- 
matizes just how difficult it is 
to remain profitable year after 
year in this business. 

Smaller apparel off-pricers 
are successfully competing 
with the billion-dollar off-pric- 
ers, aS well as the K marts, 
Wal-Marts and Targets, by 
becoming ever more special- 
ized and sophisticated. 

A chain like the 343-unit, 
Anaheim, Calif.-based 
ClothesTime, for instance, 
has successfully targeted the 
juniors market. To stay com- 
petitive they’ve started to 
track sku’s daily and have dai- 
ly shipments to their stores.

Auto Giant Transforms 


KANSAS CITY, Mo. — For the 
first time since Beneficial Finance 
bought Western Auto in 1961, details 
about the nation’s largest and oldest 
automotives chain are emerging into 
public view. 

The picture that is coming into fo- 
cus is that of an automotives veteran 
bearing a debt load that has slashed 


repositioning itself away from the 
home and auto concept that had been 
its hallmark in thousands of small, ru- 
ral towns. 

Now in public hands as a separate 
entity, Western Auto has adopted an 
automotive supermarket prototype 
that includes auto service, expanded 
the automotives side of its merchan- 


into Powerhouse Chain 


den, bicycles, major appliances and 
consumer electronies in hundreds of 
franchised stores. 

In the process, Western Auto, as 
an operator of company stores and a 
supplier to a shrinking division of 
1,744 franchised stores, is becoming 
more homogencous. 

Western Auto is continuing its 


franchised stores and weaning many 
of the remaining franchised stores 
away from a mix of automotives and 
home lines, putting them on a more 
solid diet of automotives—similar to 
that of company stores—through its 
Flag Store program. New franchised 
units are being opened with the domi- 
nant automotives format.

take place before mid-October, which

A tender for 31.5 million Southland 
shares at $77 a share expired July 30 
but was expected at presstime to be 
renewed if the Thompson family 
failed to get all the shares it seeks. 

ya Dallas, automotives manu- 
facturers’ reps are betting on a man- 
agement buyout, with the Thompson 
family still retaining a hefty—if not 
controlling interest—as the most 
likely of three scenarios to occur. The 
others are: another automotive 
chain, or chain holding company, 
might buy Chief. Or, a retail chain 
outside the auto industry might buy it. 

As for other auto chains, the Dart 
Group, which controls Trak Auto, 
and the Trump brothers from Califor- 


nia, who own Schuck’s and the former 
Lucky auto division chains, Checker 
and Kragen, are the most often 
named in rep circles as potential buy- 
ers from within the industry. 

A Dart Group executive refused to 
comment regarding Chief Auto. The 
Dart Group, controlled by Herbert 
Haft and his son, Robert, has made 
hundreds of millions of dollars in 
stock profits in the past two years 
through takeover tenders for other 
retail chains, including Supermar- 
kets General, this spring, and Safe- 
way, in 1986. 

—- for the Schuck’s, Check- 
er, Kragen auto group in Phoenix, 
Ariz., Fred Nelson confirmed that 
SCK is looking at acquiring Chief 


Auto to reach its goal of operating 
1,000 stores by 1990. SCK expects to 
hit the 500-store mark this morith and 
add 100 stores next year through in- 
ternal growth alone. 

Adding Chief’s estimated sales of 
$256 million in 1986 to SCK’s $414 
million would create the nation’s No. 
2 auto chain behind Western Auto. 

Nelson, director of corporate com- 
munications, said, “anytime an auto 
parts company comes up for sale, my 
ge company looks at it very care- 

lly. When we learned the company 
was for sale, we started looking.” 

When Grand Auto, Oakland, 
Calif., put itself on the auction block 
in March, SCK took a look, Nelson 
said. Due to the similarity in opera- 


tions, offering only parts and accesso- 
ries and no service, Chief and SCK 
would be a good mix, Nelson said. 

Another source within the SCK or- 
ganization, however, said his compa- 
ny isn’t interested in Chief. 

From outside the industry, a po- 
tential buyer is Melville Corp., par- 
ent of Marshalls. Three months ago 
Melville hired J. M. (Mickey) Robin- 
son, former chief financial officer for 
Auto Shack, Memphis, Tenn., and 
president of the Automotive Parts 
and Accessories Association. 

Robinson, director of corporate de- 
velopment, said Melville might in- 
clude an auto chain among future ac- 
quisitions, but added his firm 
“probably isn’t interested in Chief.”

Other Divisions 


Other Western Auto divi- 
sions include Tire America, a 
chain of 52 tire stores acquired 
in the same month Western 
Auto went public, January, 
1987, and Midland, an interna- 
tional importer of two-way ra- 
dios and wigs. 

Net sales and revenues in- 
creased to $759.8 million for 
the year ended Jan. 3, 1987, 
from $721 million for the year 
ended Dec. 20, 1985, the 
Western Auto annual report 
shows. On a pro forma basis, 
adjusted to include the acqui- 
sition of Tire America, total 
sales were $857.4 million in 
1987, compared to $813.1 mil- 
lion in 1986. 

On a pro forma basis, ad- 
justed for the acquisition, 
debt issued to finance the le- 
veraged buyout from Benefi- 
cial and a stock offering that 
took the company public in 
January, net earnings rose to 
$9.4 million in the fiscal year 
ended Jan. 3, 1987, from $4.8 
million in the fiscal year ended 
Dec. 20, 1985. 

On a historical basis, how- 
ever, without adjustment, 
Western Auto had earned a 
net of $21.3 million in fiscal 
1985. 

Operating profits rose 25.4 
er to $6.8 million in 1986 

rom $37.3 million in 1985. But 

interest expenses soared al- 
most four-fold to $31.7 million 
in 1986 from $8.1 million be- 
cause of the cost of debt issued 
to finance the leveraged 
buyout. 

Western Auto became a 
highly-leveraged company 
when Wesray Capital Corp., a 
New Jersey investment firm 
headed by former Treasury 
secretary William Simon, ac- 

uired it from Beneficial on 

ec. 20, 1985, (in a deal valued 
at $340 million), said Kenneth 
L. Brown, senior vp for fi- 
nance and administration. 

Because of the leverage, in- 
terest costs rose significantly, 
Brown said. 

In acquiring Western Auto, 
Wesray HPs up $17.7 million in 
cash and took on $290 million 
in debt. Prompted by soaring 


stock prices, Wesray took 
Western Auto public in Janu- 
ary 1987 after about a year of 
private ownership. 

In 1981, while still in Benefi- 
cial’s hands, Western Auto 
had developed its auto supply 
supermarket prototype, com- 
bining tires, discounted parts 
and accessories, and installa- 
tion and repair service. Some 
existing stores were closed, 
reducing store count to 197 in 
1984 from 227 in 1982. The rest 
were converted to the auto su- 

rmarket concept, the model 

or all new company stores and 
the Flag Store franchised 
units. 

On the retail, or company 
store, side, total sales rose 
21.8 percent in 1986, while 
comparable store sales gained 


10.4 percent. Western Auto 
plans to open 45 new stores in 
1987, on top of 40 opened last 
year. 

On the wholesale, or asso- 
ciate store side, Western Auto 
converted 30 franchised 
stores to the dominant auto- 
motives format and added 21 
new ones, for a total of 293 
Flag Stores. 

In 1987, it plans to convert 
50 more to the auto supermar- 
ket concept and open 30 new 
ones. No information is readi- 
ly available on any plans to 
close marginal franchised 
stores this year. 

Its Tire America division 
lans to add 15 new stores 
andling tires and ride-relat-

alignment, during this year.

ABC Cancels Home Shopping Show 


NEW YORK — The ABC-TV network last week can- 
celled Bargain Hunters, the daily 30-minute teleshopping 
ame show which it began airing in early July. Cataloger 
. Luria & Son had been sourcing merchandise for the pro- 
gram which was broadcast for only about half of its 13- 
week test. Bargain Hunter’s demise follows that of three 
other video retailing programs that had been carried on 
broadcast TV stations. The Home Sho ping Network’s 
daily half-hour Home Shopping Game tt was axed by 
CBS-TV and other stations early last month after a three- 
month airing, while ValueTelevision, which combined 
teleshopping and entertaining in a one-hour format, was 
dropped in early July by the Fox Network after a six- 
month run. Dayton Hudson Department Store Co. sus- 
pended its daily one-hour DH-Direct in June after a 13- 
week test on independent stations in 16 markets.

Macy’s Hops on Specialty Bandwagon 


NEW YORK — R.H. Macy & Co., a full-line depart- 
ment store based here, reportedly will roll out four new 
specialty store chains, beginning with a fall introduction of 
one concept. A Macy’s spokeswoman would not confirm 
this report but told DSN that Macy’s chairman and chief 
executive officer, Edward Finkelstein, will hold a press 
conference in New York by the end of September, pre- 
sumably to discuss the chain’s expansion plans. Press re- 
ports about Macy’s new specialty stores began in mid-Au- 
gust when Women’s Wear Daily ran a story about the 
retailer’s plans to open specialty stores based on an inter- 
view with Finkelstein. The story in the Aug. 11 issue re- 
ported that pilot stores are “expected to open” in North- 
ern California and possibly New J ersey, and would include 
Junior, misses’ and young men’s merchandise. 


Dart Group Is Interested in Chief Auto 


NEW YORK — Another discount automotives chain 
has emerged as a potential buyer of Chief Auto, Dallas. 
The Dart Group, owners of Trak Auto, Landover, Md., in- 
tends to make an offer to buy the 475-store chain from 
Southland Corp. soon as it receives a sales prospectus 
Chief is preparing. Trak operates about 222 stores. South. | 
land announced that it intends to sell Chief and other as- 
sets to help pay for a $4 billion leveraged buyout. Previ- 
ously, Checker Schuck’s Kra en, Phoenix, Ariz., said it 
was interested in Chief to help it reach its goal of 1,000 
stores. It now operates about 500. Industry sources said 
Michael Manor, division manager of Chief, is attempting 
to line up financing for a management buyout of the chain.

ers Distributing (US.). He was head of Weiboldt Stores.

By Peter Hisey 


NITRO, W. Va. — Former 
Service Merchandise presi- 


dent John Isaac has been 
named president of Heck’s, 


the 95-store discount chain 


headquartered here. Isaac, 
42, replaces Theodore Kazle- 
man, who resigned in July. 
Heck’s chairman Russell 
Isaacs, who announced the ap- 


pointment of Isaac (no rela- 


tion), said, “His extensive re- 
tailing background will be 
instrumental 
Heck’s affect the recovery it 
has been working so diligently 
to achieve.” 

The company has been Op- 
erating under Chapter 11 
since March. 

“Obviously, our first priori- 
ty is developing a plan of reor- 
ganization acceptable to all 
parties (in the Chapter 11 pro- 
ceedings),” Isaac told DSN. 
“But we also have to be sure 
that it works. 

“I think the company has 
been making good progress in 


redefining its basic core group 
of stores and in re-evaluating 


its future direction,” he add- 
ed. “I’m very optimistic about 
our prospects.” 


Grand Auto Off Block 


OAKLAND, Calif. 
Grand Auto has taken itself off 
the auction block and appoint- 
ed a new president to ride the 
112-store chain out of its earn- 
ings slump. 

Thomas F. Herman, for- 
merly a senior executive of the 
Lucky Auto division, which 
operated Checker and Kragen 
stores, has been named chief 
executive officer and presi- 
dent, Grand Auto announced. 

In addition, Grand told 
Shearson Lehman Brothers to 
stop looking for a buyer for the 
chain. 

Back in March, Grand had 
retained the investment bank- 
ing firm to seek a buyer, but 
no offers were received that 
the board found acceptable. 

In other news, sales re- 
mained flat for the second 
quarter ended July 27, 1987, 
while earnings declined. Sales 
totaled $43.7 million for the 
second period, compared to 
$43 million the previous year. 

After-tax income plunged 
to $105,000 for the quarter 
from $409,000 a year earlier.

The DISC award, established by DSN in 1979, recog- 
nizes the outstanding community service efforts of dis- 
Last year’s award recipient was Fra-

U.S. Shoe Sells Six Front Row Stores 


CINCINNATI — U.S. 
Shoe announced it has sold all 
six of its Houston, Tex., Front 
Row off-price family apparel 
stores to Edmond Wulfe, 
founder of a commercial real 
estate, brokerage and consult- 
ing firm in that city. 

The stores will continue to 
be operated as Front Row 
with Edmond’s brother, Emil 
Wulfe, as president and chief 
executive officer. 

The six stores represent $20 
million in annual sales, accord- 
ing to U.S. Shoe. Six other 
Front Row stores in Atlanta, 
Chicago and Indianapolis— 
representing $30 million in an- 
nual sales—will continue to be 
run by U.S. Shoe. 

“Houston has a depressed 


economy, and we felt an inde- 
pendent could run it more effi- 
ciently than we could from 
Cincinnati,” said Edward 
Klee, vice president of fi- 
nance. 

Additional Front Row units 
might be constructed in the 
Atlanta and Chicago markets 
in the future, according to 
chairman Philip Barach. 

In addition to the Front 
Row sale, the company also 
recently sold three entire divi- 
sions: the 218-unit J. Riggings 
men’s wear division; The 
Home Front, a 26-store linens 
and domestics chain; and the 
men’s shoe manufacturing and 
wholesale division. 

The company plans to open 
two T.H. Mandy off-price 


stores before year-end. de- 
7 flat sales, bringing the 
chain to 19 stores. 

Another 100 specialty ap- 
parel units are planned by Jan- 
uary 1988 among Casual Cor- 
ner, August Max and Petite 
Sophisticate. 

U.S. Shoe also announced it 
will soon begin manufacturing 
performance athletic and 
walking shoes called “Easy 
Spirit.” Barach estimates the 
new division will generate as 
much as $25 million in sales 
within a three-year period. 

Corporate sales were up . 
12% for the second quarter to 
$511 million. Net earnings 
rose to $5 million from a loss of 
$5 million during the period 
last year.

By Arthur Markowitz 


iscount stores burst on the 
American retail scene ina big 
way in the ’60s. 

The discount concept, however, 
can be traced back a half century ear- 
lier to innovative merchants with 
small apparel stores in New York 
City. The industry itself started to 
take shape in the late 1940s and early 
1950s, as a number of companies pio- 
neered this new retailing format. 

In 1912, Samuel Klein opened 
S. Klein on Union Square in down- 
town Manhattan, geared to volume 
selling and rapid turnover of apparel 
at low prices. A dozen years later, 
Joe Weinstein started Mays in down- 
town Brooklyn, while in 1928, George 
Farkas launched Alexander’s in the 
Bronx. Weinstein and Farkas added 
the idea of buying samples, overruns 
and closeouts of fashion apparel to 
Klein’s low-margin, high-volume 
merchandising concept. 

The discount concept in the 1930s 
saw Mary Chase open Chase Cloth- 
ing in 1933 as a piperack apparel dis- 
counter, while Steve and Philip Mas- 
ters applied the idea to hard goods in 
1937 when they unveiled Masters, of- 
fering radios, a hot depression item, 
at discount prices. Within a decade, 
discounting as a merchandising idea 
began to take on the rudiments of to- 
day’s discount store industry. 

In the late 1940s, shuttered New 
England factories and mills were con- 
verted into discount stores by such

Retailing Leadership: 
A Quarter-Century History of the Discount Industry 


merchants as Ollie Cohen and Mur- 
ray Candib of King’s and Lester Pal- 
estine of Arlans. Meanwhile, in a for- 
mer New Jersey diner, Herbert and 
Sidney Hubschman launched Two 
Guys as an appliance discounter. 

New York City, which was the 
birthplace of the discount concept al- 
most a half century earlier, saw Eu- 
gene Ferkauf start Korvettes in a loft 
as a semi-membership store, first 
selling brown and white goods and 
then a broad mix of hard lines. 

National newsweeklies made Fer- 
kauf and Korvettes a cover story sub- 
ject, turning the discount concept 
practiced by a scattering of retailers 
into a national phenomenon. 


Discounting Picks Up Speed in ’50s 


The industry’s growth picked up 
speed in the 1950s; the list of chains 
launched then reads like a founders’ 
Who’s Who of discounting. Innova- 
tive merchants started Caldor, Brad- 
lees, Hills, Heck’s, Goldmans and 
Leonard’s; Gibson was launched as a 
franchise operation; Fed-Mart, 
Fedco and GEM began as member- 
ship stores; and the booming discount 
field attracted other retailers. 

Zayre, Shoppers Fair, Zody’s and 
Barker’s were founded by apparel 
specialty chains; Big K and Masons 
by variety store operators; Valu- 
Mart by a credit jewelry company; 
Fred Meyer, Grand Way, J.M. Fields 
by supermarket firms; and Inter- 
state Stores (Topps and White Front) 
by a department store operator. 


While this was going on in full pub- 
lic view, another discount format— 
catalog showrooms—was starting to 
take shape in the 1950s, quietly and 
often in stores that weren’t open to 
the public, but only to card holders. 

The seeds of the catalog showroom 
industry go back to at least the late 
1800s, when wholesalers, and a few 
‘retailers,’ used catalogs to sell to 
their customers. Merchandise could 
be ordered by mail from the retailers, 
including firms that eventually grew 
into today’s Sears Roebuck and 
Montgomery Ward. 

While most catalog companies in 
the 1930s, 1940s and early 1950s were 
wholesalers and jobbers, a few sold 
goods to the general public, but only 
on a closed-door basis. This began to 
change in the late 1950s as the whole- 
salers and jobbers and the handful of 
small local retailers like jewelry 
stores that used makeshift catalogs 
started to sell to the general public. 

Buying groups and enterprising in- 
dividuals started to put together 
more professional catalogs, using col- 
ored illustrations and original art. 

Many small retailers and former 
wholesalers began using the books 
and displaying samples. These in- 
cluded post exchange suppliers (EIll- 
man’s), book distributors (Best Prod- 
ucts), tobacco jobbers (Paysaver), 
jewelers (Edison Jewelers), candy 
distributors (Fred Gattas), silver- 
ware suppliers (L. Luria & Son), 
hardware jobbers (Anchor Distribu- 
tors), grocers (Brendle’s), and do- 


mestics stores (Sam Solomon). 

Some still sold on a closed-door ba- 
sis, but others opened their ‘stores’ to 
the public. These new catalog show- 
rooms became members of a new 
type of organization, a group that 
used a catalog put together by one 
company, the catalog coordinator. 

The stage was now set for the evo- 
lution of the discount concept into 
two retailing formats: 

One was the explosive growth of 
full-line discount stores that rapidly 
made these merchants the nation’s 
leading retailers of general merchan- 
dise. This path was paved in the 
1960s by the launching of a host of 
chains like K mart, Wal-Mart, Tar- 
get, Venture, Clover and Gold Cir- 
cle, that today are the backbone of 
the discount field. 

The other was the more measured 
growth of catalog showrooms as spe- 
cialty discounters that merchandised 
mainly jewelry and hard goods. The 
late 1950s saw this industry coalesce 
into about a dozen groups, including 
today’s surviving coordinators, Paul 
Schultz Catalogs, Merchandisers As- 
sociation Inec., Jeweleor Merchandis- 
ing, American Merchandising and 
Associated Charter. The dozens 
more retailers that opened their 
doors to the public in the late 1950s 
and early 1960s include the about four 
dozen chains that currently comprise 
the showroom industry, companies 
like Service Merchandise, Best, 
Luria, Dahlkampers, Brendle’s, 
Fred Gattas and W. Bell.

1962 to 1966: 


Korvettes Is Sales Leader; Today’ s Big Three Chains Born 


count industry of today, then 
1962 was a premier year. 
quarter century ago, K mart, 
Wal Mart and Target opened their 
first stores, setting the stage for 
their eventual development into the 
nation’s three leading discounters. 

In the process of becoming the in- 
dustry’s stellar chains, K mart con- 
verted a stagnant S.S. Kresge vari- 
ety company into the country’s 
second-largest general merchandise 
retailer, Wal-Mart made a small Ar- 
kansas variety chain into a national 
merchant, and Target made discount 
retailing the highest-volume opera- 
tion for the Dayton Hudson conven- 
tional department store firm. 

The trio entered a strapping indus- 
try of full-line chains that already hed 
just under 1,500 stores and that had 
recorded $4.25 billion in sales the 
year before, DSN reported in its very 
first issue. 

The industry at the start of the 
1960s, for the most part, was com- 
posed of chains that aren’t around to- 
day. DSN’s listing of these discount- 
ers was led by Korvettes, the volume 
leader with over $200 million in sales 
(and 15 stores); Interstate (24 units); 
GEM (15); Spartans (22); and Two 
Guys (16). Other early discount pow- 
erhouses that aren’t around today 
were J.M. Fields, Masters, Arlans, 
Atlantic Mills, Clark’s, Shopper’s 
Fair, Fed-Mart, Bargain City, Max- 
am’s, Floyd Bennett, King’s and 
Towers Marts, along with smaller op- 
erations like Globe, Jefferson, Mam- 
moth Mart, Community Discount 
Center and Grand-Way. 


Today’s Leaders Date Back to 62 


But there are a handful of current 
chains that go back a quarter of a cen- 
tury: Zayre (a power even then with 
$100 million in sales from 27 stores), 
Bradlees, Caldor, Fred Meyer, Ann 
& Hope, Meijer, FE edco, Hills, James- 
way, TSS-Seedman’s and Nichols. 
For the most part these were small 
chains, focusing on a regional opera- 
tion, intent on learning the new dis- 
count form of retailing and perfecting 
their business before expanding. 

Other companies, attracted by the 
industry’s fast-track growth, tested 
the discount waters in 1962 by 
launching chains. Variety store oper- 
ator F.W. Woolworth started 
Wooleo, while Neisner Bros. un- 
veiled Big N. and Allied Department 
Store began Almart. Down the road, 
these three chains also wouldn’t 

rove as successful as the K mart, 
al-Mart and Target trio. 

While the industry was attracting 
enterprising new companies, along 
with established retailers, conven- 
tional department stores, for the 
most part, looked askance at the dis- 
count concept and the upstart chains. 
The head of the National Retail Mer- 
che ints Association, the department 
store industry’s trade group, called 


[ f the 1960s gave birth to the dis- 


Two Guys, the fifth largest discount chain 25 years ago, was launched in the ’40s 


by Sidney and Herbert Hubschman—Two Guys from Harrison, N.J. 


discounters “sinners” in 1962 and said 
discounters and discounting wouldn’t 
be discussed in public. 

The situation quickly changed due 
to the impact discounters were hav- 
ing on retailing. The NRMA began 
sponsoring seminars on discounting 
to enable members to learn about this 
new retailing concept and be better 
equipped to compete with discount- 
ers and even launch their own dis- 
count store chains. 

Within two decades, department- 
store-bred discounters like Target, 
Venture, Clover and Gold Circle 
would be among the industry’s most 
successful chains. Discounters, 
meanwhile, became the major retail- 
ers of basic hard lines, while depart- 
ment stores focused their merchan- 
dising on apparel, particularly 
designer labels, and lifestyle catego- 
ries like home furnishings. 

While discount stores were becom- 
ing a major merchandising force in 
the early 1960s in full view of other 
retailers and the public, the other in- 
novative discounting format—cata- 
log showrooms—was unobtrusively 
taking shape behind closed doors and 
in low-rent industrial areas. Many 
companies traced their roots back to 
at least the 1950s, if not earlier, when

they were mainly skewed to whole- 
saling and jobbing, selling to busi- 
nesses and to those consumers who 
had a shopping card. 

Now in the early 1960s, the cata- 
logers were sharpening their opera- 
tions and opening their doors to the 
general public, putting together full- 
color catalogs and unveiling larger 
display areas. 

The catalog industry was all but ig- 
nored by other retailers because of 
the limited number of showrooms and 
the specialized focus of its merchan- 
dising: jewelry and hard goods. 

The boom full-line discount store 
industry, however, was closely moni- 
tored and avidly shopped by tradi- 
tional retailers and the public. The 
result: The industry’s growth and de- 
velopment in 1962 set the pattern for 
what followed during the next few 
years. 

In the early 1960s, the prime con- 
cerns of discounters included the so- 
called Fair Trade laws and Sunday 
Blue Laws. Discounters, supported 
by consumer groups and even the 
Federal Trade Commission and the 
National Better Business Bureau, 
won some battles against Fair Trade 
and a growing number of non-apparel 
manufacturers began selling direct to 
chains. 

Sunday Blue Laws, however, 
wouldn’t be overcome until the late 
1970s and early 1980s, with scattered 
localities even today still banning the 
sale of selected items on Sunday. 

The acquisition trend, which would 
result in the consolidation and con- 
traction of the discount industry 
within two decades, showed a low 

rofile in 1962 as Diana Stores, a 

eased apparel operator, bought the 
Great Eastern and Gulf-Mart chains, 
while Jewel, a supermarket opera- 
tor, moved into the discount general 
merchandise arena by acquiring 
Turn-Style. The pace picked up dur- 


ing the next few years as larger com- 
panies like lessee Unishops bought 
scattered small operations like Clar- 
kins, while closed-door operators 
GEM and Parkview combined. 

The big blockbuster deal, howev- 
er, came midway through the 1960s: 
Spartan Department Stores merged 
with Atlantic Thrift Centers early in 
1966 to create the second largest 
chain in units (after K mart) and the 
combined Spartan Industries then 
acquired Korvettes, creating a $1 oe 
lion-plus retailer that top 
K mart, which was just under ek 
million in volume. 

The industry’s explosive growth 
was already evident in the early 
1960s. 

In 1962, when DSN first began 
tracking the industry’s performance, 
the 2,025 stores generated $6 billion 
in sales. Soon after, in 1966, the num- 
ber of units had grown to 2,684 
stores, an impressive 32.5 percent in- 
crease. This percentage, however, 
paled before the explosive volume 
jump of 91.8 percent to $11.51 billion. 

In 1966, two familiar names, 
K mart and Zayre, were the leading 
chains in units, with 162 and 83 
stores, respectively. There were 
only eight Targets then and about the 
same number of Wal-Marts. The oth- 
er leading discounters in stores mid- 
way through the 1960s were Arlans, 
71 units; Interstate, 66; Woolco, 52; 
King’s, 41; and Two Guys and Park- 
view-GEM, each with 33. 


Chains Trading Up Merchandise 


The growth in stores alone didn’t 
account for the big jump in sales. A 
major factor was the attempt by 
many chains to trade up their mer- 
chandising to broaden their customer 
base by attracting higher-income 
consumers. Key to this effort was 
making their stores more appealing 
and easier to shop through the use of 
the newest fixtures that highlighted 
the better quality lines becoming 
available to discounters. 

The industry’s sales clout, along 
with the upgraded image of many 
chains, resulted by 1965 in increasing 
numbers of shopping center develop- 
ers rolling out se welcome mat for 
discounters. While strip centers con- 
tinued to be the industry’s core loca- 
tion, discounters were becoming 
more successful in their drive to be 
included in new malls so they could 
benefit from the higher traffic. 

Many discount stores started life in 
the early 1960s as partly or wholly 
leased operations. Even predomi- 
nately company-operated chains like 
K mart included leased sections. As 
discounters became more mature in 
their merchandising, two trends be- 
came evident by 1966: Lessees start- 
ed to merge to form one company to 
run a chain, while companies began 
taking over leased sections through 
either acquiring the lessee or adding 
buyers for these departments.
