1967 to 1971: 


Industry Matures; Chains Go Public to F 


he discount industry grew u 
in the five years between 1967 
and 1971. 

Let’s measure the ways: 

@ New entries. A dozen traditional 
department store companies and va- 
riety store chains boosted the ranks 
of the industry by launching full-line 
discount stores, while other retailers 
tested the catalog waters by starting 
up showrooms. 

@ Acquisition/mergers. Almost as 
many full-line discounters and cata- 
logers were involved in either merg- 
er or acquisition deals, reflecting 
each a of discounter’s efforts to 
strengthen its operation through the 
quick and low-cost takeover route. 

@ Going public. Wall Street’s fasci- 
nation with both types of discounters 
saw a handful of privately held chains 
turn to the stock market to fuel their 
expansion—and also deliver a hand- 
some return to the original investors. 
@ Bullish investor interest in dis- 
counters. Stock analysts highly rated 
a number of full-line discounters, cit- 
ing these chains’ ability to get finan- 
cial backing and expand. 

@ Changing of the guard. A new gen- 
eration of executives moved into the 
top corporate offices of the full-line 
chains as the industry began to reap 
the benefits of raising discount-ori- 
ented management. The small cata- 
logers, meanwhile, remained in the 
hands of the founding fathers. 

e@ A trade association for full-line dis- 
counters was born in 1968, the Mass 
Merchandising Research Founda- 
tion, which changed its name to the 
National Mass Retailing Institute a 
year later. 

But the good times didn’t go on for- 
ever: A recession, tight money and 
high interest rates descended over 
the nation in 1970 and 1971, taking its 
toll among discounters and catalog- 
ers, including sending some chains 
into the bankruptcy courts. 

The industry's maturity was sym- 
bolized in 1967 with the announce- 
ment by Federated Department 
Stores that it planned to launch a dis- 
count chain. The new Gold Circle, an 


upscale full-liner similar to Target, 
opened its first store in Ohio in 1968, 
the same year that two other tradi- 


a 


Caldor founder Carl Bennett (center) attends an opening in the '60s.(DSN photo) 


tional retailers disclosed plans to join 
the parade. Rich’s opened two Rich- 
way stores in 1968 in Atlanta, while 
the May Co.’s Venture debuted two 
units in St. Louis two years later. 
May’s announcement came when 
Target, up to then only located in the 
Twin Cities, expanded by opening a 
store in St. Louis and targeted Hous- 
ton as a new market for 1969. 

The next year, 1970, saw a host of 
new full-line discounters besides 
Venture and Richway. Strawbridge 
& Clothier in Philadelphia started 
Clover, while three variety store 
chains launched discounters: J.J. 
Newberry unveiled Lee’s in South 
Carolina, Danners opened 3D in Indi- 
ana and G.C. Murphy launched Mur- 
phy’s Mart in Pennsylvania. Duck- 
wall, another variety store operator, 
launched ALCO with three units in 
1971. 

While the discounters started by 
the four conventional department 
stores, along with ALCO, were suc- 
cessful, Lee’s was eventually shut- 
tered; G.C. Murphy was taken over 
by discounter Ames in 1985; and 3D, 
ail that was left of Danner’s, was ac- 
quired early in 1987 by Maxway. 

While catalog showrooms still 
were a “secret” business during this 
period, the industry showed similar 
growth. Paul Schultz, who had been 
active in the showroom fieid, started 
coordinator Paul Schultz Catalogs in 
1967, encouraged by Harold Roiten- 
berg who in 1960 had founded what 
later became the premier group, Cre- 
ative Merchandising. When all but 
one Creative Merchandising member 
left that coordinator in 1983, they 
joined Paul Schultz Catalogs as the 

remier Merchandising & Marketing 
division. 

Two showrooms operators made 
key moves in 1967. Brendle’s—now 
one of the top five catalogers— 
opened a showroom in Winston-Sa- 


lem, N.C. This second Brendle’s unit 
marked the grocery company’s con- 
version into a showroom operator, as 
the unit was open to the public and 
the duo fa in management 
searching out a coordinator for its 
book, joining MAI the next year. 
Save-Rite, meanwhile, was spun off 
into a separate showroom division in 
1967 by its parent, Daniels Tobacco. 

As new companies entered full-line 
discounting, older chains went on an 
acquisition and merger binge as big 
companies gobbled up smaller opera- 
tors. In 1967 alone, Zayre bought 
Shopper’s World; Two Guys obtained 
Unimart and Food Giant; Gray Drug 
bought Bargain City/Rink’s; and 
Gamble-Skogmo took Buckeye 
Marts. The next few years saw 
King’s add Miracle Mart; Gaylords 
grab Giant Tiger; Daylin take over 
Wonder World; and Cook’s acquire 
Clark’s. 

While these takeovers were hailed 
as positive steps when they occurred, 
in reality they hid a core defect in the 
discount business—the weak man- 
agement and operation of many of the 
chains involved in the marriages. The 
larger discounter that resulted from 
a takeover operated more stores and 
recorded higher sales, but the wed- 
ding rarely added management ex- 
pertise or better operational con- 
trols. Of these eight acquiring chains, 
only Zayre continues to this day, with 
the last remaining Cook’s likely to be 
phased out this year. 

The recession in the early 1970s re- 
sulted in the first concrete signs of 
the underlying weakness lurking in 
many chains showing up at three 
leading operators. Interstate, which 
rode two horses, Topps and White 
Front, and was a player in the take- 
over game, saw profits plunge and 
then turn to red ink. It sharply scaled 
down its discount growth in 1971, 
putting its muscle behind its toy spe- 


uel Expansion 


cialty store operation which eventu- 
ally became Toys “R” Us and the sur- 
viving firm when Interstate filed 
Chapter 11 in 1974. 

Arlans, another giant, also spurted 
red ink and, in 1971, management of 
the chain was taken over by the much 
smaller Family Bargain Center, 
which then proceeded to close stores 
and cut expenses. But it wasn’t 
enough, and Arlans also filed bank- 
ruptcy three years later. 

orvettes, which symbolized tie 
industry, started a profit slide after 
its merger with Spartan Industry. 
Its latest owner, Arlen Realty and 
Development Corp., separated its 
retailing arm into the Korvettes and 
Atlantic divisons and tried a host of 
moves—all to no avail. The slide con- 
tinued and Korvettes’ last owner, a 
French company, phased out the 
chain at the end of the decade. 


Wall Street Gets Interested 


The goods times of the late 1960s 
that preceded the subsequent reces- 
sion generated extensive Wall Street 
interest in all forms of discounting— 
and encouraged a number of compa- 
nies to go public. Dayton’s, the con- 
ventional department store chain, 
made the move in 1967 and said the 
funds would be used to bolster its 
Target arm. Joining in the trend 
were Alexander’s in 1968 and Wal- 
Mart in 1970. 

That year, 1970, can be fingered as 
the time catalog showrooms burst on 
the mass retailing and Wall Street in- 
vestment scenes. It goes back to Best 
Products, which went public in 1970, 
and Barron’s wrote a highly compli- 
mentary piece on the showroom in- 
dustry. Going public the following 
year were Service Merchandise and 
Creative Merchandising, which took 
the name Modern Merchandising to 
better reflect its joint coordinator 
and showroom chain business. 

The human side of the discount in- 
dustry’s growing up during the late 
1960s can be seen in the executive 
changes. In 1968, for example, Eu- 
gene Ferkauf, who founded and sym- 
bolized Korvettes, left as the new 
Spartan Industries owners put its 
own team in place. Two years later, 
Harry Cunningham, who launched 
K mart, irreversibly changing an old 
line variety store chain, S'S Kresge, 
into a discounter, turned over the 
chairman and chief executive office 
post to president Robert Dewar. May 
Co., meanwhile, tapped John Geisse, 
an architect of Target, to head its 
new Venture chain. 

Finally, another sign of the indus- 
try’s growing up during the 1967 to 
1971 period: Dun & Bradstreet in 
1969 said full-line discounter’s $18.4 
billion volume accounted for 5.8 per- 
cent of the nation’s total retail sales. 
In that same year, K mart and Gib- 
son became the first discount “billion- 
aires” with sales of $1.25 billion and 
$1.1 billion, respectively.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, September 14, 1987 


1972 to 1976: 


For Discounters, It Was Best of Times, Worst of Times 


he discount industry was on a 

roller coaster ride in the early 

'70s, as some full-liners 
reached new sales highs while others 
fell by the wayside. 

As the 1970 to 1971 recession abat- 
ed, full-line discounters seemed to be 
in position to attain new sales and 
earnings peaks. Chains added stores 
at a record pace while expanding 
their merchandising into such new 
growth categories as do-it-yourself 
and leisure living. 

But a mini-recession hit the nation 
in the mid-’70s, intensifying the fail- 
ure of weak discounters and even 
reaching out into the conventional re- 
tailing field by striking down W.T. 
Grant. Discounters, particularly 
K mart, catalog showrooms and the 
emerging specialty discounters 

uickly gobbled up many of the closed 
Grant units available after 1976. 

The now grown-up, full-line dis- 
count industry hadn’t escaped the 
first economic slide in the early ’70s 
unscathed and during the next few 
years underwent a shakeout, as weak 
operators were acquired or folded. 

Catalogers had started to become a 
significant retail segment by the mid- 
70s, and when the mini-recession hit, 
some smaller and weaker showroom 
operators failed or were acquired by 
larger catalogers. 

The recession had taught discount- 
ers two vital lessons. 

One was that chains, having satu- 
rated most major metro markets, 
now had to turn to medium and small- 
er communities for expansion. These 
markets, however, required scaled- 
down stores and chains began paring 
their prototypes. 

A 1972 DSN survey found that only 
30 percent of new discounter stores 
opened that year were in the top 50 
markets, down from 38 percent the 
year before. This situation, in part, 
reflected the fact that chains like 
Jamesway and Wal-Mart, whose ex- 
pansion was starting to make an im- 
pact, operated in smaller markets 
with stores ranging between 35,000 
square feet and 50,000 square feet. 

Concurrently, major chains that 
typically ran units in the 70,000- 
square-foot to 100,000-square-foot 
range, like K mart, Zayre, Target,

Sol Price (left), ousted after FedMarts acquisition by a German retailer, went

Two Guys, Giant and Mammoth 
Mart, unveiled scaled back stores for 
smaller markets. 

The trend to smaller stores was 
clear by 1976, when units in the 
40,000-square-foot to 50,000-square- 
foot range accounted for 35 percent of 
the new stores, more than any other 
size. This development was aided by 
K mart’s unveiling of 125 Group Nine 
(40,000-square-foot) stores. 

The other lesson was that the more 
competitive retail scene meant dis- 
counters, in order to survive, would 
have to market the latest merchan- 
dise and sharpen their operations, in- 
cluding using the latest technology. 

Discounters in 1972 were starting 
to test hand-held tag readers that 
manufacturers were beginning to of- 
fer as auxiliary equipment to the elec- 
tronic registers that were becoming 
the standard point-of-sale terminals. 
However, chains were holding back 
on making major commitments to the 
rapidly changing technology while 
they awaited development of stan- 
dardized systems. 

The contending marking methods 
were the existing supermarket in- 
dustry-developed UPC bar code and 
a system using human-read digits be- 
ing developed by conventional de- 
partment stores, some discounters 
and general merchandise manufac- 
turers working through the National 
Retail Merchants Association and 
the National Bureau of Standards. 

When the NMRA/NAB system, 
called OCR-A, reached fruition by 
the mid-’70s, it received scant atten- 
tion from discounters. Most were al- 
ready selling UPC-marked basic 
items and consumables, but 10 years 
would pass until discounters, led by 
chains like K mart, Wal-Mart and 
Gold Circle, would begin point-of- 
sale scanning of UPC. The National 
Mass Retailing Institute, the indus- 
try’s trade group, in 1986 adopted 
UPC as the preferred technology. 

Discounters began using technol- 
ogy to solve other operational prob- 
lems in the early ’70s. Keying in sku 


(DSN photo) 


numbers became common, and 
chains like Woolco, Zayre, and J.M. 
Fields began using courier services 
for overnight delivery to headquar- 
ters of stores’ register tapes. By the 
mid-’70s, many discounters were get- 
ting overnight sales reports from 
their stores. 

In more sophisticated moves, Kor- 
vettes, Zayre, Woolco, Fedco and 
J.M. Fields, as early as 1972, used 
stand-alone terminals to verify credit 
cards. Among catalogers, Service 
Merchandise in 1976 began using 
computerized order terminals with a 
cathode ray tube (TV screen). The 
unit showed clerks the stock situation 
of each item, and suggested alternate 
goods for out-of-stock merechandise. 

On the marketing front, discount- 
ers phased in do-it-yourself depart- 
ments to counter the advent of home 
centers as a new, fast growing full- 
price specialty retailer. Merchandis- 
ing of such leisure living sections as 
consumer electronics and sporting 
goods also was beefed up in response 
to changing lifestyles. 

The two recessions in the ’70s sav 
over a dozen discounters fail, includ- 
ing leading operators like Arlans, 
Mammoth Mart, Interstate (Topps 
and White Front), Parkview-GEM 
and Unishops. Meanwhile, Mangles 
closed its Shoppers Fair discount arm 
and Zodys filed Chapter 11 in 1975 
and then emerged a year later. 

All told, about 500 discount stores 
were shut, but about 1,000 units, in- 
cluding recycled stores, were opened 
by the surviving chains. These dis- 
counters included K mart, Zayre, 
Target, Bradlees and Wal- Mart, 
along with chains like Two Guys, 
Woolco, Korvettes, Gemco, J.M. 
Fields and Gibson, that would later 
fail or be phased out. Other retailers 
recycled about 100 units. 

While discounters were concerned 
about the shakeout in 1975, the indus- 
try, unknowingly, would be forever 
changed by a simple deal made then. 

That year Hugo Mann, a German 
retailer, bought FedMart, with the 


goal of turning it into a hypermarket, 
the hot European discount retail for- 
mat. It never happened and FedMart 
finally folded in 1982. 

But shortly after Mann bought 

FedMart, the discounter’s long-time 

resident, Sol Price, was ousted. 

rice went on to launch a discount 
store that would borrow some hyper- 
market merchandising techniques 
like warehouse fixtures. In 1976, he 
launched the Price Club—and be- 
came the father of the membership 
warehouse industry. 

The discount industry’s shakeout 
in the early ’70s didn’t seemed to slow 
the start up of new discounters. In 
1972, variety store operator Wacker 
opened five discount stores, apparel 
retailer Robert Hall launched Robert 
Hall Village, and three food retailers, 
Harvest Markets’ Big H, Harris- 
Teeter’s The General Store and Cen- 
teno started superstores that com- 
bined food and general merchandise. 
The following year Rayless, another 
apparel retailer, opened R-Way. 


Market for Specialty Discounters 


Paradoxically, the shakeout 
among full-liners during the early 
70s made the seemingly stable show- 
room industry a more attractive re- 
tailing field. It also opened market 
niches for a new kind of discounter— 
specialty discounters that focused on 
a specific product category. 

The catalog industry’s trade 
gros , the National Association of 

ta og Showroom Merchandisers 
was launched early in 1972, a year 
flooded with new showroom chains. 

Almost all the showroom indus- 
try’s current major chains were born 
prior to the ’70s. However, Consum- 

s Distributing (U.S.) only goes 
back to 1972, when May Department 
Stores, parent of discounter Ven- 
ture, and a successful Canadian cat- 
aloger, Consumers Distributing, 
launched the U.S. chain as a joint 
venture. May three years later 
bought out CD (Canada)’s interest, 
only to sell CD (U.S.) to the Canadian 
cataloger in 1978. 

Like catalogers, many specialty 
discounters started in the late ’60s as 
small one- and two-store operations. 
By the ’70s, the specialists were 
starting to carve out growing market 
shares. 

In the auto accesories area, for ex- 
ample, the top 10 chains in 1976 ac- 
counted for about $1 billion in sales, 
led by Western Auto with over $700 
million. The top consumer electronics 
retailers accounted for éver $500 mil- 
lion, with Lafayette, which was later 
acquired by Circuit City, the leader 
with almost $90 million in volume. 
The 10 leaders in the toys and the 
sporting goods area also accounted 
for about $500 million in each seg- 
ment, with Toys “R” Us, at just un- 
der $2.00 met heading the former, 
and Herman’s, at about $100 million, 
topping the latter.

1977 to 1981: 


Discounting 


n the late ’70s, discounting en- 


tered its Golden Age. Full-line 
discounters were on a roll during 
this five-year period, gaining over 
350 new stores per year. Individual 
chains sighs agrnscone their marketing 
through such moves as merchandis- 
ing Levi’s and designer jeans, gour- 
met cookware and name brand home 
sound systems. 

They became the nation’s domi- 
nant retailer of hard lines and were 
capturing a growing share of the ap- 
parel business. 

But dark clouds could be seen 
through the golden rays. While there 
were a half dozen $1 billion-plus dis- 
counters, a large part of the seg- 
ment’s growth in the late ’70s was due 
to the acquisition of weaker chains. 

That period also saw the demise of 
a number of pioneering chains, in- 
cluding Korvettes, a venerated name 
that goes back to the late ’40s and the 
industry’s origins. It was phased out 
at the end of 1980, finally done in by 
its last owner, a French conglomer- 
ate that didn’t know American retail- 
ing. Korvettes, however, had ‘died’ 
a before as it went through the 

ands of anumber of companies, each 
of which had a different—often incon- 
sistant—merchandising and market- 
~—— for the chain. 
he catalog segment in the late ’70s 
saw many of the founding chains 
grow and expand by opening new 
showrooms, culminating in Best 
Products becoming that industry’s 
first $1 billion company in 1981. 

But the industry wasn’t a retailing 
utopia. Many new companies tried 
their hand at running a showroom 
during this period, but in the end al- 
most all failed. The same fate awaited 
a number of undisciplined catalogers 
that couldn’t stand up to the inten- 
sively competitive environment. 

Specialty discounters, on the 
whole, fared better during this peri- 
od. These retailers positioned them- 
selves between high priced conven- 
tional department stores and full-line 
discounters. By focusing on growth 
categories like toys, consumer elec- 
tronics and off-price —-. the spe- 
cialty discounters filled an over- 
looked marketing niche that allowed 
them to expand. 

The late ’70s saw one discount for- 
mat blaze into the retailing skies: 
membership warehouses. Once Price 
Club’s success became evident, en- 
trepreneurial merchants cloned the 
concept and the membership ware- 
house industry entered a stage of 
rapid growth that carried into the lat- 
er 80s. 

One event played a crucial role in 
full-liners entering the Golden Age of 
the late ’70s. That was W.T. Grant’s 
bankruptcy in 1975 and the chain’s 
subsequent closing. This made avail- 
able to discounters a host of stores as 
well as former Grant customers 
whose demographics made them nat- 
ural discount store sheppers.

No other chain symbolized the in- 
dustry as did K mart, which was until 
1977 just the logo on discount stores 
run by 8.8. Kresge, a variety store 
chain. For almost a decade, K mart 
was Kresge’s dominant retailing 
business and that year it finally 
changed its corporate name to 
K mart Corp. 

As the late ’70s progressed, 
K mart passed the $10 billion sales 
mark in 1978, when its volume 
reached $11.2 billion. The list of bil- 
lion-dollar discounters by that time 
also included Woolco, $2.6 billion; 
Gibson, $1.4 billion; and Zayre, $1.2 
billion. In a few short years, four oth- 
er chains joined the list: Wal-Mart, 
Target, Gemco and T.G. & Y., while 
Hills, Bradlees, Caldor, Fred Meyer 
and Meijer’s were knocking on the 
door by 1981. 

The industry’s two-pronged 
growth in the late ’70s saw chains fill 
in their core markets at the same 
time they extended tentacles into ad- 
jacent areas. 

K mart and Woolco continued 
their national expansion while Zayre 
probed into Chicago and the Mid- 
west. Regional chains, meanwhile, 
reached into adjoining markets: Tar- 
get eyed a Sunbelt thrust from its up- 
per Midwest base, Wal-Mart main- 
tained its torrid expansion into the 
Southeast and upper Midwest from 
its South Central base and Bradlees 
moved south from the Northeast. 

Store expansion alone didn’t make 
the late ’70s a Golden Age. In that 
time the successful discounters un- 
derwent some key changes. They up- 
graded their merchandising to keep 
pace with the greater expectations of 
their shoppers and _— efficien- 
cy by incorporating the latest retail- 
ing technology. 

The caeanibinn changes cen- 
tered on first expanding the apparel 
departments and then adding fashion 
goods and branded lines like Levi's 
and designer jeans to develop a fash- 


(DSN photo) 


ion and value image. This set the 
stage for the next step, merchandis- 
ing the latest fashion private label ap- 
parel. That move got underway in the 
early ’80s and saw K mart, for exam- 
ple, first offer an exclusive Jonathan 
Logan line, to be followed by a vari- 
ety of ladies’ and men’s brands in sub- 
sequent years. 

Target, Caldor, Prangeway, Brad- 
lees, Hills and Venture, among oth- 
ers, either were developing or had 
begun to sell private label apparel by 
1981. 

Zayre’s approach was to have the 
entire store make a fashion state- 
ment and in 1977 it began using its 
Waltham, Mass., store as a laborato- 
ry for merchandising ideas and dis- 
play techniques that were then fed 
into its other units. Zayre that year 
also recognized the potential of the 
emerging off-price apparel specialty 
field by Sandee T.J. Maxx, which 
eventually grew into a $1 billion chain 
in 1986. T.J. Maxx, along with 
Zayre’s other specialty apparel busi- 
nesses—Hit or Miss and Chadwick’s 
of Boston—this year was spun off 
into a separate publicly held compa- 
ny, TJX Cos. 

*’ne groundwork for the computer- 
ized discount store of the future was 
laid in the late 70s through such mile- 
stone moves as Target in 1978 install-

gram that forecast the sales of 
individual items and recommended 
replenishment orders. 

hat year K mart began testing its 
K mart Information Network that

sales by broad categories and trans-

Later on, K mart tied KIN intoa new 
computerized store replenishment 
system. In that program, clerks used 
hand-held equipment to read UPC 
bar code-marked shelf labels and 
then entered the reorder quantity.

DISCOUNT STORE NEWS, September 14, 1987

iversification has been the 
hallmark of the discount in- 
dustry in the ’80s. 

The industry’s divergence into dif- 
ferent discount segments was driven 
by a number of separate but interre- 
lated developments: 

@ The nation’s growth in population 
and wealth resulted in a marked in- 
crease in the number of middle and 
upper income consumers. This 
spurred major lifestyle changes as 
consumers’ buying habits switched 
from basics to fashion apparel and 
home goods, as well as the new prod- 
ucts spawned by the technological 
revolution in electronics. 

@ Conventional department stores, 
targeting the expanding upscale cus- 
tomer market, relinquished the sell- 
ing of hard goods to discounters and, 
instead, focused their merchandisin 
on fashion goods in the apparel an 
home products areas. 

@ The contraction among full-line 
discounters and catalog showrooms, 
triggered by the recession in the late 
’70s, continued without !etup, often 
striking down chains that go back to 
the early days of each discounting 
segment. 

e Aided by the fallout among full-lin- 
ers and catalogers, specialty dis- 
counters captured a growing share of 
the mass retailing market. These cat- 
egory-targeted merchants carved 
out bigger market shares by the tra- 
ditional retailer routes of either ex- 
panding their operation or acquiring 
smaller chains. 

@ Technology sparked the develop- 
ment and growth of non-store retail- 
ers, including the launching of new 
electronic discounters who use cable 
TV, computers and/or kiosks to di- 
rectly market goods to consumers. 

While the roots of the discount in- 
dustry’s contraction and divergence 
go back to the late ’70s, the full impact 
became evident by 1982 and peaked 
in 1986. 

The industry’s fluctuation saw the 
full-line segment contract into a core 
of about 50 major discounters by 
1987, about one-third the number at 
the start of the decade. It also wit- 
nessed large jumps in the sales of the 
surviving discounters along with ma- 
jor shifts in the lineup of the indus- 
try’s leaders as they acquired weaker 
competitors. 

In 1982, K mart, Wal-Mart and 
Target were the leaders with sales of 
$16.5 billion, $2.5 billion and $2.1 bil- 
lion, respectively. The trio remained 
the powerhouse discounters right 
through the ’80s, with sales last year 
of $22° 1 billion, $10. 2 billion and $4.4 
billion, respectively. 

Sales, however, are only one indi- 
cation of the leadership position 
staked out by these three discount- 
ers. Other signs include their exten- 
sive use of the latest retailing tech- 
nology like point-of-sale scanning of 
UPC-marked merchandise and satel- 
lite communication networks, along

Diversifi ication, Technology Drive Discounting in the ’80s 


with thrusts into new retailing ven- 
tures like Wal-Mart’s yen of 
Sam’s membership warehouses in 
1983 and K mart’s 1984 acquisition of 
the Builders Square home centers. 


Offering the Latest Fashions 


Just as important, the sheer size of 
these chains has enabled them to pick 
off top retail sites and make manufac- 
turers highly responsive to their 
marketing demands. Not to be over- 
looked is the fact that the trio has also 
traded up their merchandise to keep 
pace with the changing lifestyles of 
their customers, including offering 
the latest fashions in apparel and 
home furnishings. 

Where once the list of leading dis- 
counters was almost exclusively full- 
liners, now the top 100 chains include 
the Price Club and eight other mem- 
bership warehouses, Service Mer- 
chandise and four other catalog show- 
rooms, Consolidated Stores and 
another closeouter, and 44 specialty 
discounters. Leading the specialty 
segment are Toys “R” Us in the toy 
field, Marshalls in apparel, Circuic 
City in consumer electronics, West- 
ern Auto in auto accessories and Her- 
man’s in sporting goods. 


Shrinkage in Industry 


Missing from the 1986 lineup of top 
full-liners were such 1982 powers as 
Woolco, Gemeo and T.G. & Y., the 
next three sales leaders, along with 
eight long established chains: Jeffer- 
son/Ward, Zodys, Howard Bros., 
Murphy’s Mart, King’s, Grand Cen- 
tral, Gaylords and Magic Mart. 

The shrinkage among full-line dis- 
counters hit its peak in 1982, when 
Wooleo, FedMart, Twin Fair and 
May’s Family Center closed, while 
J.W. May’s, Maloney’s, Zodys, 
King’s and Howard Bros. filed Chap- 
ter 11, with the latter three eventual- 
ly folding. These failures dumped 
close to 300 stores on a giutted mar- 
ket, so that units went to a variety of 
retailers and other users. Target was 
a big gainer, taking over 33 Fed- 
Marts, including 28 in Southern Cali- 
fornia to mark its entry into that mar- 
ket area. 

Operational troubles also became 
evident that year at other major dis- 
counters like Cook United, Gemco/ 
Memco and T.G. & Y. The demise of 
these discounters, however, was 
spread out over a number of years 
and actually helped boost the growth 
of surviving discounters, which took 
over stores, and in some cases, trou- 
bled chains, as a fast, low cost way to 
expand. 

In 1982, for example, Memco’s was 
shuttered and its stores, all in the 
Baltimore/Washington area, were 
taken over by Bradlees; within four 
years troubled Gemco on the West 
Coast would be closed by its super- 
market parent, Lucky Stores, as that 
company sharply scaled back its o 
erations to fight off an suivioudls 


takeover. Lucky also sold off its other 
non-food operations: Checker Auto 
specialty stores, White Front conve- 
nience discount stores and Hancock 
Fabrics. 

Target took over 50 Gemcos, open- 
ing about two dozen in Southern Cali- 
fornia to become the dominant dis- 
counter in that area. Another dozen 
are to open in Northern California 
later this year to mark Target’s entry 
into that market. 

Ames, meanwhile, acquired bank- 
rupt King’s and its 42 stores in 1983 
and three years later bought Mur- 
phy’s Mart, another discounter fac- 
ing an unfriendly takeover. The lat- 
ter move almost doubled Ames’ sales 
to $1.5 billion in 1986, along with put- 
ting the discounter into t the variety 
store business with over 100 G.C. 
Murphy units that it has retained. 

Two billion dollar-plus T.G. & Y. 
was phased out in 1986 as a discount- 
er when the company was acquired 
by the McCrory variety store con- 
glomerate. Maloney was acquired in 
1985 by Heck’s shortly befo re that 
discounter ran into problems, even- 
tually filing Chapter 11 early in 1987. 
Cook, meanwhile, went into Chapter 
11 for the second time early this year. 


Deals Among Catalogers 


On the cataloger side, a similar sto- 
ry was being played out. The block- 
buster deal in 1982 was Best Prod- 
ucts, the leading cataloger, acquiring 
Modern Merchandising, the No. 3 
company which ran six different 
chains along with Creative Merchan- 
dising, the leading coordinator. 
Best’s move came shortly after it 
took over troubled cataloger Basco. 

Not to be outdone that year, Ser- 
vice Merchandise, the second largest 
showroom operator, acquired two 
Kessler showrooms, along with Sam 
Solomon, a top 10 chain which had 
technically just come out of Chapter 
11. Service pulled off a blockbuster 
deal in 1985 when it took over H.J. 
Wilson, the No. 3 cataloger. 

Sutton Place, started by the now 
defunct discounter Two Guys, closed 
in 1982. Two years later, Towers, the 
last cataloger founded by a discount- 
er, was sold to Service Merchandise, 
paving the way for the showroom’s 
parent Gaylords to be acquired six 
months later by discounter Zayre. 

Best’s 1982 acquisition of Modern 
Merchandising eventually resulted in 
a major catalog industry realign- 
ment. To concentrate on its core 
showroom business, Best sold Cre- 
ative Merchandising the following 
year to conglomerate Carlson Cos., 
parent of cataloger Ardans. Carl- 
son’s commitment to the showroom 
industry, however, was questioned 
by all the Creative Merchandising 
members, except Ardans, and these 
14 catalogers then left the gr group, 
joining Paul Schultz Catalogs. Carl- 
son, which had been scaling down Ar- 
dans during the early ’80s, finally 


threw in the towel in 1986 and shut 
the remaining units. 

The showroom industry’s contrac- 
tion in the ’80s saw such weak major 
catalogers like Century House and 
Broadman’s just this year fold while 
over 50 mom-and-pop operations and 
small chains either closed or convert- 
ed to jewelry stores. This trend also 
affected the coordinator end of the 
business, forcing the closing of small- 
er groups like Federated Merchan- 
dising and driving larger coordina- 
tors to merge: Charter Catalog and 
George Associates forming Associat- 
ed Charter, for example, while the 
larger chains within Mutual Mer- 
chandising joined MAI. 


Specialty Discounters Boom 


While the full-line and showroom 
segments of the discount industry 
were undergoing these extensive 
changes, the specialty discount por- 
tion was booming. The reason: These 
specialists offered consumers a 
broader selection in a focused catego- 
ry than did full-line discounters or 
catalogers, with the merchandise 
competitively priced. 

The dozens of companies that com- 
~ the specialty discounter field 

ave varied histories, with some 
even extending back to the discount 
industry’s early days when they were 
leased department operators like 
Wards, the predecessor of Circuit 
City, or Toys “R” Us, which was ac- 
quired by discounter Interstate 
Stores and survived that company’s 
bankruptcy. 


Membership Warehouses Grow 


span discounters came of age 
in the early ’80s and by 1982 there 
were a dozen and a half chains with 
$100 million-plus in sales. That year 
also witnessed the five-year-old 
Price Club going public and trigger- 
ing what subsequently became the 
explosive growth of the membership 
warehouse industry. 

By 1986, there were 47 specialty 
discounters with $100 million-plus in 
sales, including four—Toys “R” Us, 
Marshalls, TH Maxx and Circuit 
City—in the $1 billion club. 

Similar explosive growth marked 
the membership warehouse field 
since the Price Club went public, to 
be quickly joined during the next two 
years by another dozen companies, 
including three started by discount- 
ers—Wal-Mart’s Sam’s, Zayre’s BJ’s 
Wholesale Club and Buyers Club by 
Union Hall, and one, Price Savers, 
owned by the Kroger supermarket 
company. 

These stores tailor a mix of about 
4,000 sku’s to commodity goods, 
along with products geared to other 
businesses, which are the club’s 
“hago customers. But the mix also 

as great appeal to consumers who 
can join if they are members of specif- 
ic groups like public employees.

Diversification, Technology Drive Discounting in the ’80s 


(Continued from page 47) 

Price Club’s $100 million business 
in 1982 in four years quickly grew to 
an $11 billion membership warehouse 
industry, with Price Club, at $2.6 bil- 
lion and Sam’s, at $1.7 billion, the 
leaders, and another half dozen with 
volumes ranging from $747 million 
down to $157 million. Besides Price 
Club, Costeo, PACE, the Wholesale 
Club and the Warehouse Club have 
gone public within the past two 
years, while Super Savers was in the 
process of doing so earlier this year 
before being acquired by Wal-Mart. 


Warehouses Lead to Hypermarkets 


Consumers interest in shopping in 
membership warehouses has af- 
firmed the idea of some retailers that 
a similar mass display format com- 
mon in EKurope—hypermarkets— 
could be successful on the American 
retail scene. Discounters Fred Mey- 
er, Meijer and Lloyds already use 
common checkouts for food and gen- 
eral merchandise in the same manner 
as do hypermarkets. 

America saw its first true hyper- 
market when Biggs was launched in 
1984 in Cincinnati by a group of com- 

anies that included Euromarche, a 
| leading French hypermarket chain, 
and Super Value Stores, the super- 
' market parent of discounter ShopKo. 
: Growth pains resulted in Biggs re- 
maining static with one unit since 
then, but it’s due to open additional 
units starting in 1988. 

By then, Biggs should have plenty 
of company, as at least two other hy- 
permarkets are due to be opened. 
Carrefour, the founder of the concept 
and leading hypermarket operator, 

lans to open its first American store 
ater this year in the Philadelphia 
area to lead off a projected chain in 
the Northeast. 

Discounter Wal-Mart, meanwhile, 
has formed Hypermart USA, in a 


joint venture with supermarketer 
Cullum Cos., and plans to open its 
first unit later this year. On its own, 
Wal-Mart plans to open Wal-Mart 
Super Centers which will follow the 
core hypermarket formula of a com- 
bined food and general merchandise 
unit. The discounter will use these 
stores as its growth vehicle in major 
metro markets, retaining the tradi- 
tion Wal-Mart format for suburban 
and rural areas. 

The most radieal retailing diversi- 
fication has been the development 
and growth of electronic marketers 
during the past two years. While cat- 
aloger Consumers Distributing, for 
example, was part of a computer in- 
formation and marketing test in Can- 
ada in 1982, electronic retailing also 
started to make a impact during the 
past two years. 


Teleshopping is Key Format 


The key format is teleshopping— 
buying goods at home from programs 
aired on cable TV channels and 


broadcast TV stations. This type of - 


retailing has been probed for a num- 
ber of years, but the first successful 
operator was Home Shopping Net- 
work, which started out as a local St. 
Petersburg cable show in 1982, went 
national in 1985, and became a public 
company a year later. HSN this year 
branched out into broadcast TV by 
buying about a dozen stations as ca- 
ble TV operators began to pick up 
teleshopping shows from other com- 
panies. 

HSN’s success has attracted a host 
of marketing clones, with four main 
competitors. Cable Value Network 
was started in 1986 as a joint venture 
between closeouters C.O.M.B. and 
Tele-Communication Inc., the larg- 
est cable TV operator, and was sub- 
sequently joined by 17 other cable 
companies. CVN grew to dominate 
C.O.M.B. and the closeouter this

Traditional retailers have put their 
hands into electronic retailing, par- 
ticularly video merchandising. 

A K mart division, the Ultra Buy- 
ing Network, this year began supply- 
ing all the goods except for consumer 
electronics to the Consumer Dis-

launched last year by Entertaining 
Marketing, a CE and computer close- 
outer.

of its merchandise to QVC, another 
teleshopper started last year, while 
cataloger L. Luria is sourcing goods 
for Bargain Hunter, a combined tele- 
shopping and game show for broad-

Dayton Hudson, meanwhile, ran a 
13-week test merchandising goods 
from its department store arm and 
then called off the show on broadeast 
TV stations when the results failed to 
meet its expectations. 

J.C. Penney is the retailer most

tailing. It is financing Shop TV, 


which is due to start airing next 
month, along with handling fulfill- 
ment and distribution for the show. 
The conventional department store 
also = to launch an interactive ca- 
ble shopping service called Telaction, 
this fall. Consumers will be able to 
use their phone to first access a host 
of retailers and service suppliers, in- 
cluding Penney, Marshall Field, 
Nash Finch supermarkets and Ame:- 
ican Express, and then order goods. 
A competing interactive service is 
due to be launched next year by Gen- 
eral Telephone and Electronics, 
whose partner at one time was Pen- 
ney. Penney later joined up with a 
Canadian firm, Cableshare, to devel- 
op the Telaction technology. 

Next year will also see the startup 
of Trintex, an interactive computer 
shopping and information service 
that isa joint venture between IBM 
and Sears. Trintex employs a text 
and graphics technology called tele- 
tex, which had been used by failed 
pioneering computer shopping and 
information services like Viewtron 
and Gateway, along with more tar- 
geted computer services like Compu- 
Serve whose menu includes the Elec- 
tronic Mall as its retailing offering.

MEN’S WEAR 


Increased Floor Space Needed for Men’s Wear, Chains Report 


Nationwide DSN Report 

A more sophisticated and 
individualistic attitude of to- 
day’s male consumer toward 
casual dressing has dramati- 
cally impacted men’s wear de- 
partments at full-line discount 
and off-price apparel stores. 

From increased open-to- 
buys for younger, fashionable 
and relaxed sportswear cate- 
gories to the way fashion prod- 
ucts are being merchandised 
at store level, young men’s 
and men’s wear executives are 
reacting in increasing num- 
bers to the new lifestyle atti- 
tudes of their male customer. 

A confidential poll conduct- 
ed exclusively for Discount 
Store News by Jerard Less 
Inc., a New York-based retail 
apparel consultant, revealed 
that 67 percent of all respon- 
dents rated as “very impor- 
tant” or “important” such cus- 
tomer attitudes defined as “a 

relaxed, casual attitude 
towards dress” that expresses 
“his [the customer’s] individ- 
uality,” along with the atti- 
tude that “no single style ap- 
proach determines the way he 
dresses.” 

The er of vice presidents, 
genera! merchandise manag- 
ers, divisiona: nerchandise 
managers and buyers of men’s 
wear at 27 discounters and off- 
pricers, representing close to 
4,500 individual units across 
the country, also found that an 
overwhelming majority of 
these executives felt an in- 
crease in square footage was 
necessary as well as overdue. 
They said that they could easi- 
Py maximize any increase in 

oor space in their respective 
departments. 

A majority of the merchan- 
disers surveyed said that 
these new attitudes of a grow- 
ing customer base are having 
an influence on sales at their 
stores. Hence, they are buy- 
ing with that in mind. As one 
executive put it, “The defini- 
tion of men’s is no longer cate- 
gorized by age or gender. [It’s 
an] open market.’ 

The nationwide survey also 
uncovered a strong negative 
reaction to the Men’s Apparel 
Guild in California (MAGIC) 
show’s move to Las Vegas in 
fall 1989. As many as 85 per- 
cent of the respondents said 
they were against the move, 
citing two major reasons: 


There are considerably fewer 
retail stores to view in Las Ve- 
gas, and Las Vegas is not con- 
ducive to a business environ- 
ment, which will make the trip 
more expensive. 

However, when asked 
whether they were planning 
to attend MAGIC in Las Ve- 
gas two years from now, 76 
percent said they would. That 
compares to the 82 percent 
who said they will be at this 
month’s show. The 6 percent 
who said they plan to forgo 
MAGIC in Las Vegas are buy- 
ers from the larger chains (50 
or more units), which indi- 
cates that MAGIC isn’t as im- 
portant for them as it is for the 
smaller chains (under 50 
units). 

Overall, the survey showed 
that many discount store and 
off-price men’s wear merchan- 
disers feel they have to be as 
tuned-in to their more trend- 
conscious customers as their 
department store counter- 
parts. 

Specifically, 68 percent of 
the respondents said that 
spring and fall 1988 open-to- 
buy will increase for catego- 
ries of relaxed, casual sports- 
wear. When asked what 
percentage of their total mix 
in men’s and/or young men’s 
departments is “fashion” mer- 
chandise, the responses aver- 
aged out to 41 percent, with 
smaller chain buyers report- 
ing a predictably higher 45 

ercent, while larger chain 

uyers identified 37 percent of 
their men’s apparel mix as 
“fashion” ertiandins. 

There is even a greater dis- 
crepancy between smaller 
chains and larger chains when 
it comes to breaking out a sep- 
arate young men's depart- 
ment from men’s—10 retailers 
from the smaller chain group 
vs. just five from the larger 
chain group separate young 
men’s from men’s, the survey 
found. 

When it comes to the com- 
etition, K mart—with 11 ac- 
nowledgments—was cited 

most when merchandisers 
were asked who they view as 
their primary competition in 
the men’s wear market. 

The No. 2 men’s wear com- 
petitor, with six mentions, 
was Wal-Mart. The balance of 
responses was equally distrib- 
uted among Target, Bradlees,

Dart Bids for — 


Dart Bids for Dayton-Hudson 


WASHINGTON — The Dart Group, owners of dis- 
counters Crown Books and Trak Auto, have made a sec- 
ond attempt to acquire Dayton Hudson Corporation, own- 
er of Target Stores. Though rebuffed in a previous 
attempt in June, Dart Group on Sept. 17 made a tender, 
which Dart values at $65 a share, or about $6 billion, for 90 
percent of Dayton Hudson stock. Dart already owns about 
5 percent. So far Dayton Hudson hasn’t indicated how it 
will respond to the latest takeover attempt. But in June it 
went to great lengths to avoid a takeover, including get- 
ting the Minnesota legislature to pass a tough anti-take- 
over law. The Dart Group is controlled by the Haft ngmer d 
in Washington and has become known as a corporate raid- 
er for its stabs over the past two years at: The May Compa- 
ny, owner of Venture and now Caldor, Beatrice, Safeway 
and Supermarkets General. Although the attempts failed, 
the Dart Group made hundreds of millions of dollars in 
vrofits by selling stock it bought in the target concerns. 


K mart Opens More Banking Centers 


TROY, Mich. — K mart has opened leased banking cen- 
ters in seven stores in the greater Washington, D.C., mar- 
ket and plans to shortly add these financial service sec- 
tions to units in Kentucky and Pennsylvania. The in-store 
banks are operated by First Nationwide Bank and are 
among the 150-plus financial service centers that FNB and 
affiliates of the First Nationwide Network plan to open in 
K marts this year. Since the program was started three 
years ago, the discounter and the banking company have 
opened financial service centers in 145 K marts in eight 
states: California, Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, 
Missouri, New York and Ohio, besides the seven in Mary- 
land and Virgina. 


Proposal Could Increase Welfare Costs 


NEW YORK — Major retailers could experience wel- 
fare cost increases of 100 percent or more if a Senate pro- 
posal establishing a minimum level of health benefits for 
all employees passes, a survey by Towers Perrin Forster 
& Crosby indicates. Specifically, the percentage of retail 
organizations with abn ne plans that do not meet selected 
provisions of the Kennedy proposal for mandated medical 
coverage are listed below: 
®@ 82 percent do not meet the requirement to provide med- 
ical coverage for a!l employees and dependents including 
part-time employees working as few as 17.5 hours; 

@ 82 percent do not provide coverage for the treatment of 
pre-existing conditions; 

@ 82 percent do not begin coverage within at least 30 days 
of employment; 

e 73 percent do not cover well baby care; 

e 73 percent do not provide free coverage for “lowest 
paid” employees; 

@ 91 percent do not meet the requirement that contribu- 
tions for dependent coverage not exceed 20 percent of pre- 
mium; 

@ 45 percent do not meet the requirement that individual 
coverage not exceed 20 percent of premium. 

If such legislation is enacted, 35 percent of total survey 
participants said they would stop hiring part-time employ- 
ees completely or reduce part-time hours to fewer than 
17.5 hours a week.

Firm Launches ‘Smart’ Card Test 


AUCKLAND, New Zealand 
— An electronic credit/debit 
card has been launched in New 
Zealand. 

The so-called “smart” card 
contains a computer chip that 
stores a wide range of financial 
and personal information 
about the cardholder, includ- 
ing past purchases. The infor- 
mation enables the card to be 
used as either a traditional 
credit card or debit card, as 
well as for such purposes as 
storing the cardholder’s per- 
sonal medical history, serving 
aS a security pass to access 
bu‘ldings and a mass transit 
payment system. 

ilot efforts have been un- 
derway since the early ’80s to 
launch smart cards in the 
U.S., France and Canada, but 
with limited success. The New 


Zealand effort is the first time 
a smart card has been intro- 
duced on a national seale. 

Called the “Asset” card, the 
smart card is licensed by Mas- 
terCard International, with 
New Zealand merchant bank- 
ers Fay, Richwhite the local 
backers. Asset is the first card 
to use the ISO (International 
Standards Organization) chip 
standard which has received 
MasterCard’s backing. 

Shoppers can use the smart 
card as anormal credit card or 
as a debit card to directly 
charge a purchase to their 
checking account. The latter 
method provides almost in- 
stant payment to the retailer. 
Customers determine the 
payment method at the point- 
of-sale when they make a pur- 
chase. 


Fay, Richwhite has been 
studying electronic banking 
systems for three years. It de- 
cided to introduce Asset be- 
cause of the payment options 
and other benefits it offers to 
cardholders and retailers, said 
Michael Fay, chairman of 
Fay, Richwhite. 

Russell E. Hogg, Master- 
Card International’s chief ex- 
ecutive, added: “We believe 
the introduction of smart 
cards will provide major new 
marketing opportunities for 
banks and retailers. It also 
will lead to a significant reduc- 
tion in credit card fraud be- 
cause the information in the 
chip can’t be stolen in the way 
data can be skimmed from 
standard credit cards. Ang 
the smart card is almost im- 
possible to duplicate.”

brand. Metamucil already 
dominates the laxative PMA, 
placing eight sku’s in the top 
15 including the No. 1 spot 
with a bonus 17.5-ounce size of 
the regular powder.

reformulation of its sugar-free 
put-ups which boast superior 
flavor and consistency. The 
Metamucil brand will also be 
touted for its high-fiber con- 
tent. Fiber efficacy in reduc- 
ing blood serum cholesterol 
levels and an apparent corre- 
lation between a high-fiber 
diet and a reduction in colon 
cancer are presently receiving 
wide publicity in the media. 
Antacids are experiencing 
moderate increases with ex- 
tra-strength formulations 
demonstrating the strongest 


growth. Maalox 12-ounce led 
the Boston PMA followed by 
Mylanta 12-ounce. Extra

II, came in at No. 3 while Maa- 
lox’s Extra Strength Plus 
brand ranked No. 4. Pepto 
Bismol, soon to test an extra- 
strength formulation, took 
Nos. 5 and 6.

sics category is more what did 
not happen than what did.

most notably McNeil’s Medi-

Wholesale Club Opens 4th in Cleveland 


INDIANAPOLIS — The Wholesale Club will cap its 
four-store expansion program for 1987 by opening a mem- 
bership warehouse later this month in Elyria/Lorain as its 
fourth in the Greater Cleveland market. That unit was the 
chain’s 15th and was preceded by stores in Ft. Wayne and 
South Bend, Ind., its third and fourth in the Hoosier 
State, and in the Inver Grove Heights area of St. Paul as 
its fourth in the Greater Minneapolis/St. Paul market. 


Allbright to Speak at PLMA Breakfast 


NEW YORK — New Dayton Hudson president and for- 
mer Target chairman Bruce Allbright will be the featured 
ane! at the Private Label Manufacturers Association’s 

alute to Excellence Award Breakfast. The breakfast will 
be held during the PLMA’s 1987 Store Brands Supershow, 
Nov. 15 to 18 at the O’Hare Expo Center, Chicago. Retail- 
ers and manufacturers ean obtain registration information 
from the PLMA, Suite 1500, 41 East 42nd St., New York 
10017. Phone: (212) 972-3131. 


New Club Targets Medical, Dental Biz 


SAN DIEGO — Another new firm has announced plans 
‘to jump on the membership warehouse club bandwagon 
with a specialty concept aimed at the medical and dental 
professions. MedClub will open its first warehouse, slated 
to be between 50,000 and 80,000 square feet in size, here 
next year. The club will sell front and back office supplies 
for medical- and dental-related businesses as well as drug- 
store-type products for consumers. Although the compa- 
ny is fashioning itself after membershi clubs—and will 
set up some type of membership rules—MedClub said the 
interiors will represent an upgraded appearance due to 
the nature of the products being sold. The first store is ex- 
pected to open in early 1988. Additional site pps will 
rest on the success of the initial warehouse. The company 
said long range plans call for the opening of additional loca- 
tions throughout the West Coast, Arizona and Colorado. 


Ames Donates Vitamin A to Third World 


ROCKY HILL, Conn. — Ames Department Stores, 
the 330-store discount chain headquartered here, has do- 
nated a half-million vitamin A capsules through the 
C.A.R.E. organization to various Third World countries, 
including India, Bangladesh and Pakistan. i ce | to 
Ames, vitamin A deficiency leads to blindness from glau- 
coma in 500,000 Third World children each year, as well as 
measles and other illnesses. The 50,000-unit megadose 
capsules are being made for Ames by Tishcon Corp. in con- 


junction with pharmaceutical giant Hoffman-LaRoche.

39% Say Brands Are Up 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Discount chains continued 
to sell more national name 
brand merchandise this year 
in all areas of their stores. 

The trend toward greater 
national brand assortments, 
documented by DSN five 
years ago in its first Top 
Brands Survey, showed only 
marginal sign of slackening as 
39 percent of discount store 
managers surveyed this year 
reported their stores are car- 
rying more brands than they 
did a year ago. 


Competition Increases 


About half of the managers 
surveyed said they are selling 
about the same number of 
name brand items this year. 
After name brand gains of 61 
percent in 1983, 54 percent in 
1984, 48 percent in 1985 and 
another 48 percent in 1986, 
this year’s results are perhaps 
a portent of increased compe- 
tition among national suppli- 
ers for space on discounters’ 
shelves. 

For the second year in a 
row, housewares and health & 
beauty aids were the catego- 
ries exhibiting the strongest 
brand name growth. Other 
fast-growing brand name cat- 
egories this year were house- 
hold chemicals, sporting 
goods and men’s and ladies’ 
apparel. 

Twenty-four percent of the 
discount store managers sur- 
veyed cited housewares as a 
category in which the number 
of national brands being car- 
ried has increased since last 
year. Among upscale dis- 
counters like Target, house- 
wares brand growth was more 
dramatic. Almost four out of 
every 10 upscale store manag- 
ers cited housewares as an ex- 
ample of increased brand pen- 
etration. 

Health & beauty aids was 
mentioned by 21 percent of the 
managers surveyed. Again, 
upscalers helped spur brand 
name growth in this category 
as nearly one-quarter of up- 
scale store managers men- 
tioned H& BA as adepartment 
that has added more national 
brands. 

Household chemicals, un- 
ranked last year, jumped onto 
the top 10 ranking in 1987 as 

(Continued on page 65)

Store Managers 
Attribute Success 


To Effective Ads 


Nationwide DSN Report 
Viscount store managers 


| most often attribute the suc- 


cess of their best performing 
brands to advertising. It is not 
so much the product as the ef- 
fectiveness of its advertising 
that is seen by store managers 
as creating’ winners. 

Those observations are 
culled from a special supple- 
ment to DSN’s 1987 Top 
Brands Survey that asked 
store managers to present the 
reasons behind the success of 
their top brands. They also 
help explain why brands re- 
garded in their judgment as 
top performers are not neces- 
sarily the brands with the 
highest sales volume. It ap 
pears that an effective adver- 
tising program, especially one 
that reaches store managers, 
can create a belief in the field 
that a brand is a top seller. 

Product performance and 
product variety were other 
reasons cited most often by 
store managers as contribut- 
ing to the success of their top 
performing brands. Signifi- 
cantly, wea J a product’s price 
point is regarded as very im- 
portant, price promotion is 
downplayed as an attribute of 
a winning brand. According to 
managers, top performing 
brands are more likely ones 
that have a good price point 
than products that are fre- 
quently on sale. However, up- 
scale discounters placed more 
emphasis on price promotion 
than did their counterparts at 
conventional discount chains. 

Of course, the importance of 
various attributes to the win- 
ning sales formula varies from 
product to product. For exam- 
ple, good pes are most often 
credited for spurring the suc- 
cesS of consumer electronics 
and soft goods brands. A wide 
variety of products in a line is 
seen as an important element 
in the success of toys and chil- 
dren’s clothing brands. Good 
displays can make the differ- 
ent in women’s apparel. And, 
store location is most often 
critical to the success of candy, 
food and snack brands. 

The chart above lists some 
of the most frequently men- 
tioned attributes that contrib- 
ute to top brands’ success.

Gitano Closes Gap on Lee in Ladies’ Brands 


Nationwide DSN Report 

A number of name brands broke 
the stranglehold of fashion jeans that 
formerly dominated DSN’s list of 
best performing brands in ladies’ ap- 
parel. 

In past surveys, the top 10 per- 
forming brands in the ladies’ apparel 
department, according to discount 
store managers, consisted of nine 
fashion jeans labels plus Playtex. 

This year, nationally branded 
jeans and their concurrent line exten- 
sions account for just one-half the top 
10 names on the 1987 Top Brands 
Survey, with the other half a mixture 
of private label and popular names in 
undergarments. 

The most popular brand names in 
the ladies’ apparel department con- 
tinue to be Lee and Gitano, according 
to responses from discount store 
managers. 

Interestingly, K mart’s Jaclyn 
Smith and Hunter’s Glen labels made 
the top 10 in ladies’ apparel, ranking 
5th and 10th, respectively. Although 
these brands are exclusively made 
for and sold by K mart, they raced by 
such popular brands as Jordache and 
Calvin Klein, which fell to 11th and 
12th place, and Gloria Vanderbilt and 
Sasson, which did not make the list 
this year.

year, Lee held a convincing lead over 
Gitano.

well by retailers operating small 
stores (under 60,000 square feet),

stores (over 100,000 square feet).

NEW YORK —The first of at least 
three specialty chains R.H. Macy’s 
will be opening is called Aeropostale, 
a casual sportswear/weekend wear 
store with an “Indiana Jones”/Ba- 
nana Republic-like merchandising 
environment. Three pilot units, 
ranging fron 3,500 square feet to 
4,500 square feet, will open within 
two weeks of each other, starti 
early next month, in Jersey City 
Short Hills, N.J., and in the Fleasan- 
ton suburb of 
name ee which is a Macy’s

years, is based on the French airmail 
service in Europe, North Africa and 

The second specialty chain, which 


is still under development, will be 
called Charter Club (also the name of 
another Macy’s private label line), 
this one featuring career-oriented, 
higher-priced sportswear in misses’ 
and petite sizes. The first Charter 
Club unit, which is expected to open 
next spring, could be in the New 
York metropolitan area. The third 
specialty chain will be developed 
around a private label intimate ap- 
arel line called Fantasies by Morgan 
ylor, though the exact name of the 
chain has yet to be determined. 
As many as eight new units among 
the three chains could be added next 
ear, said Edward §. Finkelstein, 
acy’s chairman, adding that the re- 
tailer estimates a $500 million-plus 
sales gross from the specialty store 


venture by 1992. Richard Crystal, a 
senior vice president at Macy’s New 
York, has been named president of 
the specialty store division.

NEWARK, Calif. — Ross Sicres, 
Inc., the off-pricer based here, re- 
bounded in the second quarter to the 
profitable side of the ledger. In the 
quarter, earnings were $4.7 million, 
or 17 cents a share, up from a loss of 
$515,000 a year ago. Sales increased 
18.5 percent to $131 million from 
$110.5 million. In the six months end- 
ed Aug. 1, earnings were $556,000, 
compared to the year-ago period’s 
loss of $6.8 million, Sales for the six 
months increased 16.5 nt to 
$257.1 million from $220.6 million.

Nationwide DSN Report 

While all other housewares vendor 
rankings were scrambled this year, 
the two dominant manufacturers, 
Rubbermaid and Corning, main- 
tained: their leading positions on 
DSN’s 1987 Top Brands Survey. 

The significantly different top 10 
vendor roster can be attributed to 
several reasons. Acquisitions among 
top vendors was one factor that al- 
tered rankings. An apparent shift in 
consumer preference for relatively 
new product lmes over established 
brands was another element that re- 
sulted in the new order.

brands tied for third place. Together 
with ninth-ranked Wearever Proc-

the top 10 roster.

fifth place and Visions—previously 
not on the chart—earned its way to 
sixth place, partially contributing to 
the drop in the ranking of Pyrex to 
10th from seventh last year. The ex- 
plosive growth of Visions indicates 
just how far truiy new products can 
gain recognition in housewares with-

the category.

this survey.

among those surveyed. The very sale

“SEE YOU AT 
THE SHOW!!!" 


It’s that time of 
year again— 
when everyone 
in the Housewares Industry 
starts preparing for The Show. 
There's only one. NHMA’s 
Housewares Show, of course. 
Actually, NHMA manufac- 
turer members call it their “Cus- 
tomers’ Show’’—because of the 
way it has been designed for 
1988. Every inch of the more 
than 730,000 square feet of 
product displays has been rede- 
signed and 
newly deco- 
rated to show- 
case each of 
NHMA'ss six 
major display 
categories. This enables buyers 
to more easily locate and make 
contact with manufacturers. No 


longer will any category be 
divided between buildings. And 
no longer will buyers have to 
spend valuable time covering 
parts of three buildings, because 
we ve consolidated into two. 

We're also releasing floor 
plans and a roster of all exhibi- 
tors and their booth locations, 
extra early this year. This means 
more than 14,000 buyers will be 
able to plan their movements, 
appointments and business long 
before their arrival in Chicago. 

And, we're providing spe- 
cific buyer lounges throughout 
McCormick Place so buyers 
from each class of trade will have 
their own rendezvous points 
to meet or find their peers. 

You see, 
NHMA wants to 
make certain 
the time and 
energy House- 
wares buyers 
commit to attending this 
world-class event are the most 
rewarding and gratifying they 
spend on business anywhere 
in the world. 

So, now s the time to 
double-check your travel and 
hotel plans. NHMA’s “‘Cus- 
tomers’ Show” opens Sunday, 
January 10 through Wednesday, 
January 13. 

See you at “The Show!!!”

performance. 


The best performing region

When asked why a particu- 
lar brand was among their 
best performing, the most of- 
ten mentioned reason cited by 
Target, Zayre and Wal-Mart 
store managers was “good, 
low prices.” While K mart 
store managers named “good 
quality product” most often as 
a reason, “good, low prices” 
closely followed. 

This se the way the 
industry has been since its 
very beginning. Consumer 
electronics is a very price-ori- 
ented market. While CE 
chains are most often thought 
of as the most price competi- 
tive retailers in the consumer 
electronics business constant- 
ly guaranteeing “the lowest 
prices around,” results indi- 
cate that full-line conventional 
and upscale discounters are 
not far behind. 

Target, Zayre and Wal- 
Mart store managers named 
good — products as the 
second most important reason 
why they selected the brands 
they did as top brands. 

Of the store managers who 
cited General Electric as a top 
brand, most stated the reason 
for that selection was the com- 
pany’s heavy advertising. The 
majority of store managers 
who cited Emerson and Sh 
as top brands all felt good, low 
prices was the reason behind 
those brands’ success. Store 
managers cited good quality 
products most often as a rea- 
son for Panasonic’s rating as a 
best performing brand.

Kodak, No. 1 in every cate- 
gory a year ago, was No. 1 
again in DSN’s 1987 Top 
Brands Survey, although its 
margin was slimmer in some 
areas than a year ago. 

Overall, however, Kodak 
had nearly double the men- 
tions of Polaroid, its closest 
competitor, nearly three 
times the total number of men- 
tions as a best performin 
brand than No. 3 Canon an 
nearly 10 times the support of 
Fuji in the No. 5 spot. 


Top Five Brands Unchanged 


Most of what changes there 
were in the rankings of photo 
and camera department 
brands were in the lower half 
of the top 10. The top five 
brands remained unchanged. 

Keystone, the only new en- 
try in the Top 10, knocked 
Eveready off the list and took 
over Vivitar’s No. 9 spot. Vi- 
vitar slipped to No. 10. 

Nikon, Pentax and 3M/ 
Scotch shuffled their posi- 
tions. 

At K mart, Kodak was a big 
winner, with more than nine 
out of 10 managers inter- 
viewed mentioning the Roch- 
ester, N.Y.-based giant. 

However, Polaroid racked 
up its highest rating at 

mart, and Fuji nearly tri- 
pled its overall rating over a 
year ago. 

The highest rating received 
by Kodak was from Wal-Mart 
with 94 percent. Polaroid also 
drew its strongest response 
with seven of 10 Wal-Mart 
managers mentioning the 
brand. Canon and Minolta, 
both with relatively stron 
showings at K mart, fell off 
dramatically in mentions at 
Wal-Mart. 

Fuji, dropped by Wal-Mart 
during its Buy American blitz, 
rated barely a mention. How- 
ever, 3M/Scotch placed a 
strong third, marti offset- 
ting its omission by K mart. 

odak received the fewest 
mentions from Zayre, al- 
though the brand still finished 
a comfortable first. Polaroid 
also had a tough time on its 
home turf, rating only one- 
half of Zayre’s mentions. Min- 
olta and Vivitar, on the other 
hand, both made strong show- 
ings, rating third and fourth 


overall at Zayre. 

The two top brands overall 
did not receive as many men- 
tions from upscale discount- 


ers. Polaroid fell to the third 


Kodak was the 
overwhelming winner 
in the store managers 
survey, but several 
managers indicated 
that Fuji was making 
inroads in the film 
market due to the 
clarity of the finished 
product and slightly 
lower prices. 


ranking while Canon finished 
second. Minolta was stronger 
among upscale discounters 
than conventional discount- 
ers, as was Nikon, both aided 
by support from Target. 

Regionally, Kodak was 
weakest in the Northeast but 
still garnered mentions from 
eight of 10 store managers 
there. Canon performed well 
above its national average in 
the Northeast, with about 
one-third of respondents cit- 
ing the brand. Fuji received 
little mention from Northeast- 
ern discounters. 

The West was also a bit soft 
on Kodak, saving its laurels 
for Minolta, Fuji and Pentax, 
all of which performed well 
above their national averages. 
Vivitar and 3M/Scotch were 
not mentioned by any West- 
ern discounters.

Store Size Consistency 


Managers of large, medium 
and small stores were fairly 
consistent in their brand name 
ratings. Kodak received al- 
most even ratings across the 
spectrum, although the man- 
agers of larger stores were a 
bit less enthusiastic than 
those in the other sizes. Canon 
did very well in large and me- 
dium-size stores, but smaller 
stores gave it a one in five rat- 
ing. Minolta also underper- 
formed in smaller (under 
60,000 square feet) outlets. 

Fuji was clearly more fa- 
vored by medium size (under 
100,000 square feet) store 
managers, while managers of 
larger stores gave it a low rat- 
ing. Nikon garnered strong 
support from the medium size 
segment, but was virtually ig- 
nored by small stores. 

Although there were few 
surprises in this year’s sur- 
vey, the surge in sales this 
29 indicates that there may 

e a few next year. By then, 
the results should be in on new 
products like disposable cam- 
eras and the rising sales of re- 
cent innovations like dual lens 
“automatic” cameras will have 
created an even greater im- 
pact on the market. 

More important, perhaps, 
will be the success (or lack 
thereof) of the challenge to 
Kodak’s dominance mounted 
by brands like Konica, Fuji 
and Agfa, and Kodak’s re- 
sponse with new products to 
meet the competition.

New Safety Features 


The impact of the new UL 
(Underwriters Laboratories) 
uideline governing safety 
eatures on hand-held hair dri- 
ers,which went into effect Oct. 
1, could also result in a dra- 
matically different top 10 list- 
ing next year, depending on 
whether price, styling or ease 
of use was negatively changed 
by the new standard. 

The UL ordered all hand- 
held hair driers to have a safe- 
ty mechanism which would 
make it safe to submerge the 
unit in water while plugged 
into an electric socket, when 
not in the “on” position. 

Despite the sale of General 
Electric’s small appliance 
business to Black & Decker 
over a year ago, the GE name 
continues to have top of mind 
awareness among the ranks of 
discount store managers sur- 
veyed. GE’s percentage rank- 
ing did, however, fall in the 
four regions charted and at 
the K mart, Wal-Mart, Zayre 
and Target stores. 

Black & Decker, ranked 
sixth in 1986, rose to the No. 5 
rank this year.

K mart’s decision to eliminate 
appliances that offer rebates 
could already have trickled 
down to store level and im- 
pacted the way managers 
think of particular brands. 
K mart managers’ mention of 
all of the top five brands ex- 
cept the Black & Decker name 
fell between 1986 and 1987. 
Vidal Sassoon remained es- 
sentially unchanged. 

Black & Racker is one of the 
few manufacturers which has

ing rebates.

number of store mana bed

brands is also true at this

Some of the shifting prefer- 
ences among retailers, re- 
gions and outlet type could be 
linked to the large number of 
household cleaners and chemi- 
cals on the market today. 

When store managers were 
asked what their top perform- 
ing brands were, they named a 
total of 45 different products. 
Additionally, they identified 
some manufacturers as brand 
names and their answers also 
included private label prod- 
ucts and “other” mentions. 

According to the managers 
polled, specific household 
cleaners and chemicals are 
successful because they are 
heavily advertised and carry 
substantial national brand 
name recognition. Price is a 
third consideration and com- 
pany reputation and rebates 
are considered almost negligi- 
ble for sales and popularity.

Nationwide DSN Report 

Motor oils increased their domi- 
nance of the top 10 brands in the auto- 
motive departments of discount 
stores, accounting for six of the top 
spots in this year’s Top Brands Sur- 
vey, compared to five in last year’s 
report. 

ncluding products associated with 
oils, such as Fram oil filters and STP 
oil treatment, oil and oil-related 
brands accounted for eight of 10 top 
brands that store managers cited in 
the 1987 DSN survey. 

The ranking of the top five: Quaker 
State, again the leader, Pennzoil, 
Fram, Havoline and Valvoline. 

Rankings of first, second and third 
remain unchanged from last year’s 
survey. But Havoline moved up a 
notch to fourth from fifth and Valvo- 
line rose two places to fifth from sev- 
enth. Their gains came as the ex- 
pense of Prestone, which slipped to 
sixth from fourth. 

Largely because of a mild winter, 
antifreeze sales for the entire indus- 
try slumped 18 percent last year. 

Rounding out the top 10 were: 
STP, No. 7; Castrol, No. 8; Turtle 
Wax, No. 9; and AC-Delco, No. 10. 

The growing importance of oil and 
oil-related products among the top 10 
brands appear to reflect the increas- 
ing complexity of cars that often lim- 
its the do-it-yourself options for 
many motorists to changing their oil 
and polishing their cars. Other indi- 
cators of that trend: Turtle Wax rose 
to No. 9 in the top 10 this year from 
No. 31 last year, while Champion 


Turtle Wax crept into ninth place from No. 11 in 1986, reflecting increased activ- 
ity in waxes and chemicals as the do-it-yourself movement peaks. (DSN photo)

sification, however, would have come 
too late to be reflected in the 1987 
brands survey, conducted in June.

State was fairly uniform by region:

In the Northeast, Quaker State’s 
standing improved to more than six 
out of 10.

For the third consecutive 
year, Fisher-Price and Mattel 
were mentioned most often by 
discount store managers as 
top performing brand names 
in their toy departments, ac- 
cording to DSN’s 1987 Top 
Brands Survey. 

More than half of all dis- 
counters polled said that Fish- 
er-Price was among their top 
brands, while a little less than 
half named Mattel as among 
their best performing toy 
brands. 

Contributing to the 
strength of Fisher-Price as a 
top brand was an increase of 
support this year by upscale 
discounters. Nearly eight out 
of 10 upscale store managers 
named Fisher-Price as among 
their top brands, up from 
about two-thirds last year. 
Fully three-quarters of store 
managers at Target named 
Fisher-Price as among their 
top brands, up from about half 
a year ago. 

Mattel showed slightly low- 
er percentages of mentions by 
store managers across the 
board this year from last year, 
but it was still able to hold its 
No. 2 position with four out of 
10 store managers naming 
Mattel among their top per- 
forming toy brands. 

Coleco also remained in its 
same fourth position. Two out 
of 10 store managers named 
Coleco among their best per- 
forming brands. Coleco ap- 
_ to garner less support 
rom Zayre and K mart man- 
os polled this year than in 
the past. 

Playskool, ranked again as 
the third most often men- 
tioned brand, received more 
mentions than Mattel among 
upscale discounters, with four 
out of 10 upscale store manag- 
ers naming Playskool as 
among their best performing 
brands. Store managers at 
K mart and Target also men- 
tioned Playskool more often 
this year than last, while men- 
tions of the brand by Wal- 
Mart and Zayre managers de- 
creased this year.

u e discounters for both 
Playskool and Fisher-Price 
supports an industry trend

. Discount retail sales have increased 22% over the last five years. 
. The big GM chains, through acquisitions and mergers, are getting even bigger. 


. Membership warehouse clubs—an almost negligible segment up until recently—increased their 
sales 264% to $4 billion last year. 


. Leased department operators are fading away in favor of company-run units.

COSMETICS/TOP BRANDS 


Cosmetics Success Attributed to Pricin 


Nationwide DSN Report 

Top ranked cosmetic brands 
underwent a shift in chain and 
regional dominance, accord- 
ing to DSN’s 1987 Top Brands 
Survey. 

Low price, wide brand as- 
sortment and national distri- 
bution were among the prima- 
ry factors determining which 
brands store managers at 
chains like K mart, Wal-Mart, 
Zayre and Target selected as 
their top cosmetics depart- 
ment performers. 

According to the store man- 
agers polled, last year’s four 
brand leaders—Maybelline, 
Revlon, Cover Girl and Max 
Factor—were again identified 
as the top performing brands 
in the cosmetics category. 

Despite the fact that last 
year’s top four brands main- 
tamed their respective rank- 
ings overall, there was a 
change in the best performing 
brands by type of di scounter. 

For example, managers at 
—- discounters such as 

arget Stores mentioned the 
top four brands more often 
than they did last year. 

In comparison, K mart, 
Wal-Mart, Zayre and other 
conventional full-line discount 
department stores cited the 
top four brands less frequent- 
ly than the previous year. 

The higher incidence of

received slightly more men- 
tions by all discounters over 
last year’s study.

Ames to Add Security to Fight Theft 


(Continued from page 1) 
burgh, a central warehouse in 
New Jersey and in company 
trucks en route from that 
warehouse to stores. 

A company spokesman re- 
vealed that security seals on 
delivery trucks were some- 
times slit and at other times 
replaced entirely at highway 
stopovers, whereupon items 
were removed from packing 
containers. The containers 
were then checked in at re- 
ceiving docks without a piece- 
by-piece inventory. 

In his address to analysts, 
Hollis said that a comprehen- 
sive anti-shrink program has 
already been implemented at 
Ames, which will “bring 
shrink down from 2.5 percent 
at cost in the first half of the 
fiscal year [which is already 
down from 2.7 percent in the 
second half of the last year] to 
2 percent at cost for the second 
half of this year.” 

In forecasting further re- 
sults, he said, “Our midterm 
goal is to reduce shrink to no 
more than 1.8 percent for the 
first half of next year.” He 
added that the company’s 
anti-shrink program would 
“put us in the forefront of in- 
ventory shrink control, and 
that will increase our profits.” 

Some of the steps Ames has 
taken include engaging Coo- 
pers & Lybrand audit and con- 
sulting divisions to perform a 
detailed audit of every ac- 
counting procedure, system 
and report related to inven- 
tory; hiring security special- 
ists Royal-Schutt Internation- 


al; retaining loss prevention 
experts Jack L. Hayes Inc.; 
and conducting its own in- 
depth reviews of distribution 
and trucking systems, physi- 
cal plant locations and person- 
nel integrity testing systems. 

The company is also addin 
somewhere between 500 an 
1,000 security employees who 
will work in a variety of func- 
tions at a number of locations. 

Public accountants Arthur 
Andersen have been contract- 
ed to conduct “a comprehen- 
sive review of all the manual 
and automated systems at our 
distribution centers and ware- 
houses,” Hollis said. 

To date, no arrests have 
been made and a company 
spokesman cautioned that evi- 
dence so far had failed to un- 
cover any widespread conspir- 
acy to systematically loot the 
company’s inventory. Rather, 
the spokesman said, evidence 
so far indicates that the com- 
pany’s accounting system, 
particularly that employed by 
the former Murphy Marts, 
was vulnerable in several ar- 
eas to pilferage by employees 
and service companies. 

Ames has already tightened 
its inventory receiving sys- 
tem, replaced security seals 
with new ones more difficult to 
circumvent by simply remov- 
ing the door at the hinge or re- 
placing the whole mechanism, 
and added nearly undetect- 
able anti-theft strips to mer- 
chandise in “several” stores 
(see story, page 3).
