How Pet Care Performs 


With drug and discount stores expanding facings and ads for pet care, sales are up 

10% and better in most chains 

Ais strive to expand their 
convenience appeal to local 

shoppers, more space and more fea- 

ture activity is being focused on the 

pet food category. 

Buyers for both drug and dis- 
count stores say they are continuing 
to advertise the best selling brands 
of pet food heavily to lure value con- 
scious shoppers into their stores. 

At the same time, most discount 
store chains are expanding their pet 
food departments to include a wide 
variety of pet accessories including 
many items and brands previously 
only available before in pet supply 
stores (see accompanying story). 

Drug chains, for the most part, 
are continuing to rely on Hartz and 
Sargeant for most of their everyday 
pet accessories, but some drug 
chains like Osco, Walgreen’s, 
Revco, etc., are also starting to fea- 
ture offbeat types of pet accessories 
like pet transporters or automatic 
food and water dishes in their ads. 

When pet food buyers and store 
managers talk about pet care, how- 
ever, they still tend to stress the 
traffic building potential of the 
brand name food items like Purina, 
Carnation, Alpo, Gaines Burgers, 9 
Lives, ete. 

Most drug and discount store pet 
food buyers say that the core of their 
pet food departments is still the 
food section, and in most chains, 
foods for dogs, cats, birds and small 
animals usually accounts for be- 
tween 50% and 80% of both space al- 
locations and sales. Bicis Gy May Garland

There were 52 million pet cats in the nation in 1986, according to the Pet Foods Insti- 
tute. Owners were out buying everything from food through cedar chip beds. 


specializes in the sale of birds and 
small animals, and that chain, Perry 
Drug, leases rather than runs its 
live pet departments. 

Buyers for drug chains say they 
tailor their ads and their plano- 
grams to the “convenience minded 
shopper whu appreciates a value.” 
The strategy is to buy the brand 
name foods on deal and then to ad- 
vertise them at a super low price to 
undercut the food stores which have 
the largest share of pet food sales. 

The discount store buyers try to 
be even more competitive on foods 
than the drug chains. However be- 


16 


cause their stores have more space 
for pet care items, their ads also fea- 
ture the 25- and 50-lb. bags of dry 
dog food as well as the best selling 
brands of 10-lb. kitty litters. 

One Wal-Mart manager says that 
pet foods give his chain an opportu- 
nity to “build a low price image” 
while simultaneously enhancing 
profits. 

“We never promote pet foods at 
cost,” he says. “Instead we try to 
buy our advertised specials from 
deal to deal, and although that strat- 
egy lets us be super competitive on 
price, it also lets us make a healthy 


profit on the category.” 

According to some sources, Wal- 
Mart usually makes at least a 10% 
margin on its featured pet foods, 
and can make as much as 25% on its 
private label dog food, Ol’Roy. 

Primarily because of the in- 
creased emphasis on promoting and 
expanding pet care sections, drug 
and discount stores are getting 
more growth from the pet care cate- 
gory than the food stores, which 
currently do about 91% of total pet 
food sales in the country. 

According to F'M estimates based 
on research done by Malcolm Knapp 
Inc., in New York, sales of dog and 
cat foods in discount stores in- 
creased 10% last year to approxi- 
mately $95 million. 

To date, Malcolm Knapp is esti- 
mating that pet food sales in dis- - 
count stores will go up another 8% 
this year to $103 million. 

In drug stores, Knapp estimates 
that pet food sales increased about 
11% in 1986 to $56 million, and 
should grow another 11% in 1987 to 
$62 million. 

In contrast, SAMI estimates indi- 
cate that food stores only increased 
their pet food volume by about 3% in 
1986 to $5.25 billion, and food stores 
are expected to generate about the 
same growth in 1987. 

The most dramatic growth in pet 
food sales last year came from the 
high volume wholesale clubs that 
are starting to proliferate across the 
nation. 

Malcolm Knapp is estimating that 
pet food sales in the $8 billion whole- 
sale club industry increased about 
90% in 1986 to $154 million. 

In 1987, when this fast growth in- 
dustry is projected to do close to $12 
billion a year in sales, Knapp is esti- 
mating that pet food sales will in- 
crease another 55% to $239 million. 

The everyday pet food depart- 
ment in wholesale clubs is already 
averaging over 80 to 90 ft. Canned 
foods are usually sold in case lots off 
pallet displays while 25- and 50-lb. 
bags of dried food are also merchan- 
dised off pallets or ends. 

In suburban and rural markets, 
discount chains like Wal-Mart and 
K mart are also featuring 25- and 
50-lb. bags of the leading brand dog 
foods as well as large size cat foods 
and kitty litters. 

Buyers say that when they adver- 
tise a well-known brand like Carna- 
tion or Purina at a competitive 
price, they can usually sell through 
their ordered quantities in “less 
than two weeks.”

Regional preferences make Mexican beer “hot” 


oi 


he drug and discount store buyers who are managing the alcoholic 
beverage category report tremendous success in 1986 and 1987 
with several regional beers. 

In: the northeast, buyers say their sales of Molson Golden and 
Moosehead, both Canadian imports have been soaring. In the west 
and southwest, buyers say that the Corona Mexican beer is the hot- 
test thing to come down the pike since the Jalapeno pepper. 

Liquor buyers for drug and discount chains with stores in the west 
say that Corona beer sales are “escalating.” 

In some Texas markets, buyers say that regional sales of Corona 
have increased “more than 300%,” and that Corona is starting to out- 
sell Heineken, the country’s number one imported beer. 

“Corona is a Mexican beer which is why it sells so well in states like 
Texas and Louisiana,” says one buyer. “In the northeast, Molson and 
Moosehead, which are Canadian beers do especially well. 

“People today are traveling more,” said one buyer, “and they’re also 

oing to more ethnic restaurants, Mexican, Chinese, Japanese, etc. 
Phey're being exposed to different types of imported beers in these 
surroundings, and then they discover they like them, and they seek 
them out in retail stores. 

“There’s also more of a status appeal in the imported beers. People 
who want to make an impression will order a Heineken or a Moose- 
head rather than a Budweiser or an Old Milwaukee.”

Merchandising liquor means promoting

Drug and discount chains are expanding facings and ads for coolers, light and im- 
ported beers, and fruit flavored liqueurs 


discount chains that carry beer 
has been to expand facings and 
feature promotions for the fast 
growing imports and lighter beers. 

Liquor buyers for drug and dis- 
count chains say their best sellers in 
beer this year are the Mexican beers 
like Corona, Dos Equis, Tecate, and 
Carta Blanea; the Canadian beers, 
especially Moosehead and Molson; 
the West German beers, Becks and 
St. Pauli Girl; and category leader, 
Heineken, from the Netherlands. 

In domestic beers, the country’s 
best seller was still Budweiser, 
which had a 25.8% share of the en- 
tire domestic beer market in 1986. 
Budweiser, even though it competes 
in the premium category of domes- 
tic beers which was flat in 1986, 
gained another 0.7 share points last 
year. 

Miller Lite in 1986 continued to 
hold onto the No. 2 share spot 
among domestic beer, according to 
IMPACT, which also reports that 
Miller Lite had a one tenth ofa point 
share gain in 1986. 

In the wine category, most drug 
and discount store retailers re- 
sponded to the growth in cooler 
sales by eliminating facings on their 
wine wall for table, dessert and 
sparkling wines, and turning it over 
to the top four and five brands in the 
cooler category. 

More chains are also now promot- 
ing the coolers instead of liters or 
the popular California and Italian 
jug wines. 

Most buyers say that coolers have 
caught on with Americans because 
they are lower in alcohol which ap- 
peals to consumers who want to 
moderate their drinking. They are 
blended with fruit drinks to attract 
the health conscious consumer, and 
they are portable and easy to serve, 
as well as sweeter than traditional 
wines. 

The success of the wine coolers 
has also led to the emergence of sev- 
eral other new segments that buy- 
ers report are selling well. These 
are the fruit flavored wines like the 
natural peach and raspberry wines 
from Riunite; the rootbeer and ap-

“Peach flavored wines like Riun- 
ite appeal directly to the same con- 
sumer who supports the wine cooler 
category,” says Stan Bevis who 
buys alcohol and other beverages 
for the 145 unit K & B chain in New 
Orleans.

ment is profiled in this issue, says 
that Riunite Peach sales have been 
“excellent” in K & B stores this 
year. 

Along with coolers, one of the few 
bright spots in a tough category. 

In different parts of the country, 
other retailers also say they are 
building more floor displays and us- 
ing more endcaps for the sweeter 
and fruitier drinks. 

More chains are also expanding 
their merchandise mix to include 
strong selling regional favorites like 
Mexican beers in the south and 
western parts of the country and 
Canadian beers in the Ncitheast. 

Many others aie continuing to 
cross merchandise party goods, 
snack foods and assorted bar acces- 
sories in their liquor departments to 
encourage incremental sales. 

A few, like K & B, Longs’, etc., 
are dressing up their wine depart- 
ments with artifacts like trellises 
and vines.

more ad and floor space to the best 
selling brands within the more tra- 
ditional categories.

chain, “I’ll promote the most popu- 
lar brand like Absolut and Stolich- 
naya. 

“If I’m promoting tequilla, it’ll be 
Jose Cuervo or maybe Sauza.” 

At K & B, Bevis says he’ll use a 
best selling brand like Jack Daniels 
to make consumers aware that K & 
B has the top brands at the best 
prices. 

“When a category is flat, the best 
thing you can do,” says one buyer, 
“is identify the top sellers, and pro- 
mote the hell out of them.”
